papers.abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
authors: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
bullets: Addresses the tight coupling between utterance timing and audiovisual diarization in video captioning.
Uses a two-stage approach: synthetic-caption training on 225K clips, followed by reinforcement learning from 2.9K human-corrected clips.
Generates transcripts, utterance timestamps, speaker grouping, and visual descriptions for each utterance.
On DiaDemBench, achieves strong diarization and substantially better timestamp accuracy than Gemini 4 Argon (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME).
Maintains performance on multilingual and minute-long videos and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with similar-looking speakers. Each track shows one model’s predicted utterances over time, colored by the ground-truth speaker that its description depicts, with wrong speakers outlined in dark red.

Figure 11. A one-word turn right before another speaker (Mandarin). The young man answers with a single syllable lasting 0.3s (first frame), and the man in the gray suit continues immediately (second frame). DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E keep the short turn as a separate line with the correct speaker. Gemini 4 Argon and DiaDem merge it into the next speaker’s line, so turn A is lost. Gemini’s timestamps also miss every boundary (TIME 0), and DiaDem predicts none. This example shows that accurate timestamps and diarization are tightly coupled, as a model without precise turn boundaries tends to absorb a short turn into a longer neighboring one.

Figure 2. Overview of DiaCap. A speech recognizer Ψ transcribes the audio, and an audiovisual LLM Θ takes the transcript T together with the video and audio to predict the timestamps and speaker of every utterance. DiaCap-E2E predicts Y directly without a recognizer.

Figure 7. Failure case: off-screen speaker merged with the on-screen one. In a handheld phone video, a girl (A) asks her mother where she is going, and the mother (B) answers from off-screen. DiaCap describes a single speaker, gives the mother’s reply (“I’ll go wherever I want”) to the girl, and drops the mother’s cut-off last words. Since only the girl is ever on screen, the model does not infer that a second person is speaking.

Figure 9. Off-screen speakers in a multi-shot scene. The first and last turns are spoken while the camera shows someone else. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and describe these speakers as off-screen voices. Gemini 4 Argon gives the woman’s “Uh, Nal-what?” to the man in the blue lab coat and truncates it. DiaDem describes both men only as “man in a lab coat”, so the second man’s two turns go to the first man.

Figure 8. One speaker who goes off-screen. In this typical shot/reverse-shot conversation, a single woman speaks both lines. During the second line, the camera cuts to the listener and the speaker is off-screen. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute both lines to the same speaker. Gemini 4 Argon gives the second line to the visible listener (short reddish-brown hair). DiaDem’s description (“woman with shoulder-length brown hair”) is too generic to identify the speaker, so neither of its lines is credited.

Figure 10. A speaker seen only from behind. The last line is spoken by the man with his back to the camera. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute it to him. Gemini 4 Argon gives it to the man in the gray suit and DiaDem to the man with the mustache, the two people whose faces are visible.

Figure 12. A short interjection from a third speaker. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and place every boundary within the collar. Gemini 4 Argon merges the woman’s two turns into one line, so when scoring Gemini, we merge consecutive groundtruth utterances from the same speaker, which leaves three ground-truth turns. Gemini’s timestamps miss most boundaries (TIME 33). DiaDem describes the speaker of the final interjection only as “man’s voice”, which depicts none of the people in the scene.

Figure 13. Four speakers in one room. DiaCap, DiaCap-E2E, and Gemini 4 Argon attribute all five turns correctly. DiaDem gets three of the five turns wrong. It gives “Are you serious?” (C) and “Me too.” (D) to the young woman, and gives her own “I’m okay with that.” to a young man. Gemini’s timestamps drift by about 0.7s on the last three turns (TIME 40), whereas both DiaCap variants place every boundary within the collar (TIME 100).

Figure 3. Training data curation and annotation. (1) Audio, audiovisual, and visual experts tag each clip. We remove clips with unrelated or out-of-sync audio, deduplicate and resample the rest to balance language, speaker count, and visual scenes, and add no-speech clips with empty targets. (2) An audiovisual LLM annotates who says what, and a speech aligner timestamps each utterance. (3) Human annotators correct hard clips mined from the SFT corpus, plus fewer single-speaker clips, to form the RL corpus.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video question answering enables blind and low-vision (BLV) users to query their immediate surroundings through natural language. However, existing benchmarks and models primarily optimize for semantic agreement with reference answers, reducing visual assistance to a purely factual matching task. In real-world scenarios, a factually correct response remains practically unhelpful if it lacks the spatial orientation, actionable detail, or conciseness required by the immediate task of the user. Drawing upon real BLV egocentric videos and authentic user queries from EgoBlind, we construct the PA-EgoQA, a preference-aligned dataset that reconstructs reference answers according to empirical BLV communication criteria. Based on this dataset, we introduce Preference-Aligned Visual Egocentric Learning (PAVE), a unified learning and inference framework that couples structured answer-policy fine-tuning with deterministic question-conditioned routing to adapt response formulation directly to the surface form of the query at inference time. We further align the model via Filter-GRPO, which pairs a hierarchical correctness-quality reward with contrast-based candidate-group filtering to extract learning signals from both factual accuracy contrasts and fine-grained quality variations among correct answers. Extensive experiments across three vision-language backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in factual accuracy alongside substantial gains in assistive response quality. These results establish a concrete paradigm for translating human-centered response requirements into egocentric supervision, generation policies, and post-training objectives. Code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/PAVE.
authors: Nan Li, Shaofeng Liang, Shiyun Zhao, Keni Shi, Zhencheng Huang, Bowen Tian, Jiemin Wu, Wenshuo Chen, Kaishen Yuan, Runwei Guan, Yutao Yue
bullets: Addresses the gap between factual answer matching and practically useful visual assistance for BLV users.
Introduces PA-EgoQA, a preference-aligned dataset built from EgoBlind videos and authentic user queries.
Combines structured answer-policy fine-tuning with question-conditioned routing to adapt response formulation at inference time.
Uses Filter-GRPO to learn from correctness contrasts and quality differences among correct answers.
Experiments across three vision-language backbones show improved factual accuracy and assistive response quality.

papers.abstract: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/
authors: Juntao Jiang, Wenqi Zhong, Guangyu Guo, Dexia Chen, Yilong Hu, Yunhao Bai, Zhenyu Yi, Jianwei Xu, Tony C. W. Mok, Muxuan Gao, Ling Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang, Zhongwei Qiu
bullets: Addresses inaccurate, poorly calibrated decisions caused by autoregressive decoding and reliance on irrelevant anatomy in 3D medical multimodal models.
Uses anatomy-guided visual compression: query-selected organ features attend to 2D slice details within predicted anatomical bounds.
Predicts candidate probabilities in a single forward pass, avoiding autoregressive decoding.
Introduces Counterfactual-Calibrated Training to link confidence changes to the presence or removal of relevant and irrelevant organ evidence.
Evaluated on the CT-Verdict benchmark across binary, multiple-choice, and ordinal tasks, with reported gains in accuracy, calibration, and robustness to distribution shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Framework of the proposedRadev. (a) The Organ-Grounded Visual Encoder uses organ masks and learned mask queries to extract 3D organ tokens. Question-selected organ tokens attend to 2D slice features within their anatomical bounds. The language backbone and candidate scoring head predict an answer distribution in a single forward pass. (b) Training proceeds through projector–evidence alignment, verdict fine-tuning, and Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT). (c) CCT constructs factual, target-ablated, control-ablated, and evidence-blind views by intervening on visual features. The first three views receive task supervision, while the evidence-blind view receives a confidence-margin penalty.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/
authors: Hanzhao Xi, Zhonghao Li, Suxuan Liu, Shanghan Zhou, Zesheng Chen, Qiufeng Wang, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets VLM errors in exact Part IDs, unsupported parts, and inconsistent cross-step assignments.

PlanRefine audits assignments against available inventory and removes the lowest-confidence conflicts while flagging uncertainty for review.
On the IAW dataset, CAPER achieved 83.33% finite-inventory consistency with zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences.
It reduced inventory-overuse pairs from 9 to 0 and excess units from 51 to 0.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language model on its own failures is a direct way to repair it, but accuracy on held-out failures, the obvious measure of success, misleads. Many mined failures are not model errors: a human audit of 100 failures of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on questions generated from COCO and GQA found label errors in 37. And mined failures share wording regularities: question-only classifiers get both answers right on 73.2% of held-out failure pairs. We study both traps with verified failure-driven repair (VFR): typed minimal-pair failure mining, verification by three LLM judges that answer without seeing the stored labels, answer-first corrective targets, and LoRA fine-tuning with replay. VFR repairs 82.8% of held-out failures (base model: 10.0%), and on independently labeled, unconditioned pairs it raises overall accuracy from 87.4% to 92.4% through spatial relations, whose accuracy rises from 66.7% to 96.8% even where the wording points to the wrong answer. Yet on negation, of which it repairs 88.9% of held-out failures, its accuracy on unconditioned pairs falls from 88.7% to 79.7%: it breaks negations about absent objects, rare in its training set. Without verification, accuracy on unconditioned pairs falls to 80.8%, below the base model's 87.4%, through a negation shortcut our development benchmarks miss; without failure selection, it stays at 92.0% (one seed) while repair falls to 73.4%. Training also lowers two-image relation accuracy (74.3% to 49.6%; replay data alone: 48.4%); multi-image replay partly and unevenly reverses this. Paraphrasing the spatial questions keeps most of the gain (87.3% vs. the base model's 62.0%), though rewording lowers spatial repair on held-out failures from 92.9% to 76.8%. On What'sUp's independent photos of objects under others, caption choice stays perfect while accuracy on our yes/no pairs falls from 84.5% to 26.4%.
bullets: A human audit found 37% of 100 mined Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct failures had incorrect labels, while question wording alone often predicted answers.
The proposed VFR method uses typed minimal-pair mining, LLM verification, answer-first targets, and LoRA fine-tuning with replay.
VFR raised held-out-failure repair from 10.0% to 82.8% and overall accuracy on independent pairs from 87.4% to 92.4%, especially for spatial relations.
Verification prevented a negation shortcut: removing it reduced independent-pair accuracy to 80.8%; VFR nevertheless hurt negation and two-image relation performance.
Gains were sensitive to wording and distribution: performance dropped on rephrased spatial questions and independent What'sUp photos, where accuracy fell to 26.4%.

papers.title: When Repair Accuracy Misleads: Training a VLM on Its Own Failures
papers.tldr: Verified failure-driven fine-tuning substantially improves some VLM weaknesses, but held-out failure accuracy can hide label noise, wording shortcuts, and serious out-of-distribution regressions.

papers.abstract: Reliable driving VLMs must do more than answer correctly or localize relevant scene actors: they must determine whether the available visual evidence is sufficient to support an answer. Existing evaluations largely treat grounding and answerability as separate measurements, making it difficult to distinguish well-supported predictions from those localized to relevant but insufficient evidence. We introduce DriveAnswer, a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families, that operationalizes this distinction using matched strong- and weak-evidence configurations. Each pair preserves the underlying scene fact and semantic answer while changing whether the observations support answering, making abstention the appropriate response under weak evidence. On the six-family evaluation, the strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both answer-abstain behavior and complete grounding. With controlled adaptation, Gemma-4-12B reaches 63.29% on this joint capability, nearly tripling its zero-shot performance. Qwen3-VL-8B exhibits the same broad improvement in evidence-sensitive answering and grounding. These results show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities that should be evaluated jointly.
authors: Nhat Ha Nguyen, Sudipta Chowdhury, Lokesh Das
bullets: Introduces 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families with matched strong- and weak-evidence scene configurations.
Tests answer correctness, abstention under weak evidence, and complete grounding jointly rather than separately.
The strongest zero-shot baseline achieves 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy but only 21.55% joint answer-abstain and grounding performance.
Controlled adaptation substantially improves evidence-sensitive answering and grounding, with Gemma-4-12B reaching 63.29% joint capability.
Findings show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities.

papers.tldr: DriveAnswer benchmarks whether driving vision-language models can distinguish sufficient visual evidence for answering from insufficient evidence requiring abstention.

papers.abstract: Metacognition includes knowing one's own strengths and weaknesses across kinds of tasks, not only judging whether a single answer is correct. We test whether vision-language models (VLMs) know in advance which kinds of visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them, across a wide range of open and proprietary models. Because some tasks are hard for every model, we separate what a model knows about this shared difficulty from what it knows about itself. We find that VLMs know little in advance about their visual weaknesses. They misjudge their overall accuracy and do not even know which kinds of tasks are hard for every model, and most misjudge how degraded images affect them. We further train VLMs to predict their own accuracy, which teaches them their own level of accuracy on kinds unseen in training but not which kinds are hard for them. However, information about these weaknesses appears once a model starts solving. On a few unlabeled questions of a kind, the probability a model assigns to its own answers follows weaknesses particular to the model, across kinds of tasks and image conditions. VLMs thus hold information about their own weaknesses that their stated predictions do not yet reflect. By separating what is particular to a model from what holds for every model, our evaluation offers a test for methods that aim to teach VLMs their own weaknesses, and the answer probability offers them a signal to start from.
bullets: Evaluates metacognition across visual task types and image conditions in open and proprietary VLMs.
Separates model-specific weaknesses from difficulties shared by all models.
Finds VLMs misjudge both their overall accuracy and the effects of degraded images.
Training models to predict accuracy transfers across unseen task kinds but does not reveal which kinds are personally difficult.
After solving a few unlabeled examples, answer probabilities reflect model-specific weaknesses and provide a signal for improving self-awareness.

papers.title: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? Probing Capability-Level Metacognition
papers.tldr: Vision-language models generally fail to anticipate their own visual weaknesses, but their answer probabilities reveal these weaknesses after seeing a few examples.

papers.abstract: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. Specifically, we first present shared-space projection, activation reconstruction and encoding (SPARE), which represents original visual, adapted visual, and textual features through shared soft-gated sparse encoding, with branch-specific reconstruction to preserve their respective information. Second, we devise bridge--text embedding and activation matching (BEAM), a bidirectional cross-modal alignment module that aligns adapted visual and textual features at both the sample and neuron levels, establishing fine-grained cross-modal correspondence. Finally, we introduce prompt-conditioned residual integration of vision and adapted features (PRIVA), a prompt-guided residual fusion module that models vision--language interactions through gating and attention and integrates complementary information from original and adapted representations through residual fusion. Extensive experiments show that SAVERA achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering while reducing object hallucination.
authors: Jiajun Shen, Chuancheng Shi, Jiayi Lyu, Yanpeng Sun, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses cross-modal alignment while preserving visual information before and after language adaptation.
Uses SPARE for shared soft-gated sparse representations with branch-specific reconstruction.
Uses BEAM to align adapted visual and textual features at sample and neuron levels.
Uses PRIVA for prompt-conditioned gating, attention, and residual fusion of original and adapted visual features.
Reports competitive image-captioning and visual-question-answering performance with reduced object hallucination.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.
authors: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Multimodal compression and cross-modal agreement can unintentionally amplify salient, consistently supported signals.
This creates a vulnerability in ranking decisions that content manipulation can exploit.
C3H is an inference-time attack that aligns a target item’s multimodal content with implicit recommendation criteria.
Unlike noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, it manipulates content without changing model training.
Experiments show increased target-item exposure while preserving overall recommendation utility.

(2) Stealthy Editing (Stage II) amplifies fh, fs via text shaping and a low-distortion image transform, gated against the stealthiness set B.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.

papers.abstract: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.
authors: Chuancheng Shi, Shangze Li, Wenhua Wu, Zifeng Cheng, Pengyang Shao, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua

Across 15 MLLMs, MRS and KSS expose instability missed by accuracy; an MRS-inspired regularizer improves generalization of edited knowledge.

papers.abstract: Specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint acquire complementary capabilities, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) can consolidate them into a single model. However, we find that existing consolidation methods, from weight merging to MOPD, fall short when specialists diverge substantially from the shared checkpoint, whereas prior studies mostly examine specialists that remain close to it. We present a unified recipe for multimodal MOPD that consolidates such specialists back into the single student they branched from. The recipe specifies initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities for consolidation, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists. In an industrial setting with six specialists, the student closely approaches each specialist in its own domain and surpasses the perception specialist. It recovers 97.0% of their average gain, compared with 79.8% for IM-MOPD. In the fully open five-domain setting with Qwen3-4B, our method recovers 95.7% of the specialists' average gain after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, compared with 94.1% for IM-MOPD. We further analyze the full pipeline through mechanism ablations and training dynamics, providing practical guidance for diagnosing incomplete consolidation. Code will be released.

With six industrial specialists, the student closely matches each domain specialist and surpasses the perception specialist.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.
authors: Yi Zou, Zhuang Yan, Yudong Zhang, Xu Wang, Yang Wang
bullets: Models can preserve over half their full-image accuracy even when local evidence is masked, revealing shortcut reliance.
STAR creates counterfactual image worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but different answer-relevant facts.
A teacher compares real and mean-color crops to identify visual corrections, while spatial-attention divergence guides token-level target reconstruction.
STAR improves Qwen3.5 by up to 8.04 percentage points across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD’s final accuracy 4.7× faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.
authors: Haozhan Shen, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Tiancheng Zhao, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Addresses costly, narrow, and target-presupposing QA supervision in multimodal on-policy distillation.
Uses fixed, image-agnostic caption prompts covering descriptions, parts, colors, counts, text, and layout.
Distills a model’s crop-view outputs into a full-image student using varied prompts across region rollouts.
Requires only images and region boxes—no questions, answers, or larger teacher model annotations.
Outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks when trained on the same images and regions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Caption Handoff. (a) Given a boxed full image, the student generates a general caption whose first sentence typically identifies the target object. (b) Standard distillation retains the box cues during training and supervises the entire caption, causing the student’s perception to rely on oracle boxes. (c) The proposed caption handoff removes the box cues from both the student’s image and prompt, while keeping the teacher’s cropped view unchanged. The first sentence serves purely as a textual anchor (masked from the loss), and only the remaining detailed description is supervised on the clean full image.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on questions with false premises. Each question presupposes an absent target: (a) a scooter rather than a bicycle, (b) a dog figurine rather than a real dog, and (c) a bowl of strawberries rather than oranges. QA-trained baselines (Vision-OPD, S2VOPD, and VAD) blindly follow the question’s premise and hallucinate the queried object, whereas CaptionOPD faithfully identifies what is actually present and rejects the false premise. All models are based on Qwen3.5-9B. More examples are shown in Appendix E.

Figure 1: Comparison of prompt construction and rollout allocation between previous fine-grained OPD and CaptionOPD. (a) Previous fine-grained OPD relies on a large VLM to synthesize a tailored question qi for every image–region pair and spends all K rollouts answering that same question qi, tying training to costly QA curation while supervising only a single queried detail per region. (b) Our CaptionOPD eliminates per-region QA generation by reusing a fixed, image-agnostic pool of caption templates (detailed in Section 3.1) across all images, assigning diverse prompts across the K rollouts to supervise multiple visual aspects of each region.

papers.abstract: Visual decision-making demands accurate judgments and timely responses. Yet for multiple questions sharing the same visual input, autoregressive multimodal large language models generate answers token by token, accumulating sequential decoding costs as question count grows and delaying completion of the decision set. Their predictions can also vary with question order. We introduce ViDM, which transforms multi-question visual inference into parallel decisions in a single forward pass, improving both accuracy and inference efficiency. ViDM organizes shared visual context, multiple questions, and question-specific decision slots into one sequence, reusing the native language-model head to produce all answer distributions simultaneously. A Decision-Query Mask aligns each decision query's direct attention with shared context and its corresponding question, while case-balanced multi-order training strengthens robustness to question reordering. Across nine benchmarks spanning image, multi-image, and video tasks, ViDM improves Qwen3.5-4B's average accuracy from 73.49% to 77.55% while achieving 8.4x the baseline's average end-to-end throughput. On GQA, where each evaluated image has 11.4 questions on average, the end-to-end speedup reaches 20.3x. ViDM also improves mean and worst-order accuracy while reducing order-induced variation across multiple benchmarks, with further validation on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and InternVL3.5-4B.

bullets: Addresses sequential decoding costs and sensitivity to question ordering in multi-question visual inference.

Case-balanced multi-order training improves robustness to reordered questions and reduces order-induced variation.
Across nine benchmarks, ViDM raises average accuracy and achieves substantial throughput gains, including up to 20.3× speedup on GQA.

A shared decision head reuses native LM-head rows to map decision states to K answer distributions in parallel, without autoregressive answer decoding. (Right) During training, the same question set is presented in M distinct orders, with predictions aligned to their question-specific labels. papers.abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

Introduces IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark for evaluating robustness to diverse annotation conditions.

The models achieve F1 scores of 0.81 and 0.83 on IntentBench, outperforming the cited commercial and open-source baselines.

papers.abstract: Diagnosing with X-rays often requires reasoning about the 3D locations of abnormalities and their spatial relationships to surrounding anatomical structures, yet such reasoning remains challenging due to the loss of spatial information in 2D projections. To address this challenge, we propose Dreaming in CT (DiCT), a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that leverages a CT vision-language model (VLM) to guide an X-ray VLM. Through this CT-guided transfer, the student acquires CT-informed 3D reasoning capabilities, enabling it to reason directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference time. The framework begins with instruct the dreamer, which equips the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning capabilities and establishes a structured interface that distinguishes X-ray observations from CT imagination. Building on this structure, visualize the dream introduces CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD), where the CT teacher selectively guides the X-ray student's reasoning trajectories to transfer 3D anatomical knowledge. Finally, manifest the dream adapts the acquired reasoning capabilities from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. Experiments across two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA demonstrate DiCT's effectiveness across radiological reasoning tasks, achieving a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77$\times$ lower inference computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongYep/DiCT.
authors: Zhenghao Lu, Xiaotian Zhang, Songtao Jiang, Yiqun Lin, Siming Fu, Hualiang Wang, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Addresses the loss of 3D spatial information in X-ray projections, which complicates reasoning about abnormalities and anatomy.
Uses a three-stage CT-to-X-ray transfer process: initial CT-oriented reasoning, CT-guided on-policy distillation, and adaptation from synthetic DRRs to clinical X-rays.
Separates observed X-ray evidence from imagined CT information to structure the student’s reasoning.
Evaluated with two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA across radiological reasoning tasks.
On 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification, improves 1.66 percentage points over a CT-reconstruction baseline with 12.77× lower inference computation.

papers.abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.

papers.abstract: Reference-guided photographic color grading helps users realize their aesthetic intent by selectively drawing on the color and tonal characteristics of a reference photograph. Doing so requires understanding which characteristics users wish to adopt and translating these preferences into controllable edits. However, image-only reference methods align overall appearance without instruction-grounded selection, while pixel-space generative editors typically produce flattened images without editable parameters, limiting subsequent refinement. To address these challenges, we introduce JarvisAura, a multimodal aesthetic agent that formulates photographic color grading as structured decision-making in an editable parameter space. JarvisAura offers three key advantages: (1) an aesthetic agent paradigm that integrates visual attribute perception, strategy-level reasoning, and parameterized execution for interpretable and controllable photographic color grading; (2) a unified reasoning-to-execution pipeline that connects aesthetic planning with backend rendering and editable parameter refinement; and (3) a three-stage training strategy comprising Parameter-Grounded Continual Pre-Training for parameter-appearance grounding, Reference-Grounded Supervised Fine-Tuning for reference-guided reasoning and parameter decisions, and Reference-Aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization for rendered-outcome refinement with multidimensional rewards and dynamic data derivation. On Ref-Bench, JarvisAura achieves the best scores among methods with results across reported automatic metrics and a 74% human-rated task-success rate, exceeding GPT-Image-2.5 by 9 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual reasoning that requires global structure, spatial relationships, and high-level semantics. We propose Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation (VC-OPD), which extends teacher-side privileged information beyond local image regions to question-conditioned visual cues. Advanced MLLMs generate cues capturing key visual details, structural relationships, and semantic evidence needed to answer each question. A multi-stage quality filtering process selects reliable cues, which are provided only to the teacher during training. This enables informative token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, helping the student learn to identify and reason over critical evidence directly from the original image. No additional information is required at inference time. Since advanced MLLMs are used only for visual cue generation, VC-OPD is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary black-box models. Experiments on STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements across model scales over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines. Notably, a 4B model trained with VC-OPD outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters, demonstrating effective capability transfer through question-conditioned visual cues.
authors: Qinxuan Wang, Zheyu Zhang, Yijing Yang, Han Shu, Chuang Wang, Peipei Yang, Shuo Tang, Jie Hu, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Addresses the limits of cropped or zoomed image regions for reasoning involving global structure, spatial relations, and semantics.
Uses advanced MLLMs to generate question-specific cues containing relevant visual details, relationships, and evidence.
Applies multi-stage quality filtering before providing cues exclusively to the teacher for token-level on-policy supervision.
Works with open-weight and proprietary black-box models because advanced MLLMs are used only during cue generation.
Improves performance across STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks; a 4B model surpasses many larger baselines, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are advancing in physical reasoning, but whether they can understand external physical drivers from internal observations remains an open question. Existing benchmarks have not specifically targeted this setting. To this end, we introduce CaveBench, a benchmark for abductive physical reasoning from internal observations. Models receive apparatus descriptions and internal images while the external controls remain hidden, and must infer the operations responsible for the observed responses. CaveBench spans 20 apparatus scenes in five physical domains and contains 10,200 simulated episodes, split into 9,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 200 test episodes. Questions span one to six events and require the complete control set at every event, testing whether an explanation accounts for the entire process. Synchronized observations and control records provide the inputs and reference answers. Evaluating 27 VLM configurations yields six-event exact-match accuracies of 68.0% for the strongest closed-source model and 12.5% for the strongest open-weight model. Seven adaptation baselines show that single-event gains need not improve complete sequences. Error analysis identifies failures in visual identification, physical inference, evidence integration, and action composition, specifying where current models struggle to connect internal phenomena with their external causes.

papers.abstract: Achieving both interpretable and high-performance inference is a key challenge in deep learning. While Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide inherent interpretability, they are constrained by task-specific training and rely on isolated visual concepts that fail to capture higher-order visual semantic relationships. Conversely, Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate zero-shot capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, standard CoT lacks a strict causal dependency between the generated rationale and the final output, compromising faithfulness. To bridge this gap, we propose Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs), a novel training-free framework that transforms any off-the-shelf LVLMs into inherently interpretable models in a plug-and-play manner. RBMs consist of two stages: (i) Structured Rationale Generation (SRG), which explicitly models semantic interactions between visual concepts as subject-predicate-object triplets, and (ii) Rationale-Grounded Decoding (RGD), which enforces a strict causal dependency between the rationales and the final output. RGD aggregates rationale-conditional next-token distributions via an importance-weighted product-of-experts strategy, strictly excluding the image inputs from the decoding context. Extensive zero-shot evaluations across diverse benchmarks and LVLM backbones demonstrate that RBMs achieve superior interpretability while improving task performance over CBM baselines, entirely without task-specific fine-tuning.
bullets: Addresses the limited relationships captured by Concept Bottleneck Models and the weak causal faithfulness of standard Chain-of-Thought reasoning.
Uses Structured Rationale Generation to represent visual semantics as subject–predicate–object triplets.
Applies Rationale-Grounded Decoding to make final predictions depend strictly on generated rationales, excluding direct image input during decoding.
Works as a training-free, plug-and-play framework for off-the-shelf Large Vision Language Models.
Zero-shot evaluations across diverse benchmarks and backbones report improved interpretability and task performance over CBM baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Proposed Method. Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs) consisting of (i) Structured Rationale Generation (SRG) and (ii) Rationale-Grounded Decoding (RGD). (i) SRG produces rationales for the final output by a set of semantic relation triplets of visual concepts in an input image. Each rationale is defined by a semantic relational triplet (subject, predicate, object) and an importance score. This structured rationale representation enables rich interpretability of high-level visual semantic relationships between concepts beyond the independent visual concept rationales often used in CBMs. (ii) Given rationales from an input image and a query, RGD constructs a composite next-token distribution by ensembling conditional distributions for each semantic relation triplet via importance-weighted product-of-experts. By decoding output tokens with this composite distribution, RBMs ensure the interpretability of the final outputs.

Figure 1. Overview. We propose an interpretable model, Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs), based on large vision language models (LVLMs) in a plug-and-play manner. Previous Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) offer limited interpretability through their isolated concepts and are often limited in their applicability to the fixed task during training. In contrast, our RBMs can provide informative rationales, formed by visual semantic relation triplets with selfverbalized importance scores, and can be flexibly applied to various tasks that backbone LVLMs can solve without additional training.

papers.abstract: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
authors: Xiangwei Wang, Jianyuan Lin, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge
bullets: Standard ES/ARS for VLMs can overfit patch-grid artifacts and catastrophically forget general or OOD capabilities.
It extracts a contrastive visual basis from paired cross-grid views to focus perturbations on shared spatial signals.
A soft subspace prior anchors shallow visual-fusion layers while allowing deeper reasoning layers to adapt.
Paired-view scoring filters view-fragile perturbations during top-k ARS selection.

On Qwen3-VL-8B, it reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO and maintains OOD performance, achieving 75.41% average single-view micro accuracy across seven benchmarks versus 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO.

papers.abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.
authors: Yicheng Huang, Feng Ke, Linhan Chen, Ziyi Jiang, Xiu Yin Zhang
bullets: Addresses static text-like tokenization and backbone damage from direct contrastive alignment of continuous radar streams.
Uses a frozen physical world model with Batch-VICReg temporal prediction and a stop-gradient alignment head with false-negative masking.
On a 4,541-window, tri-domain suite, R→T R@10 increases from 5.95% to 15.01% and MedRank improves from 107.0 to 60.0.
Preserves physical readouts for blackout tilt, cluttered UAV altitude, behind-wall range, virtual-RIS invariance, and fall detection.
Across five LLM families, improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in all 10 runs, with blackout-tilt gains varying by model family.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ
authors: Minchan Kang, Kyeonghye Park, Seoyoung Cho, Junhee Lee, Daeshik Kim, Yucheol Cho
bullets: PTQ degradation is traced to outliers that dominate shared quantization ranges, causing many typical values to collapse to zero.
The work shifts attention from increasingly complex calibration strategies to the underlying quantization representation.
RRQ combines local Hadamard transforms, group quantization, and group-aware execution.
Across 8 multimodal tasks, RRQ improves performance over prior baselines while reducing inference time and memory use.
At W4A4, it retains over 96% of full-precision performance for 8B models and over 99% for a 32B model; baselines retain less than 8%.

papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of latent generative models (LGMs) makes generated image source attribution essential for copyright auditing and data governance, yet practical attribution should remain reliable under common post-processing and platform-induced processing. Existing reconstruction-based attribution methods summarize an image's reconstruction response to a single global scalar, such as the reconstruction error or the ratio of two consecutive errors. These summaries discard channel-frequency structure, allowing image content and post-processing variation to obscure source evidence and making attribution after spreading difficult. We instead uncover a more stable source-discriminative cue under post-processing: the frequency-resolved evolution of residual energy across repeated applications of the same reconstruction operator. Motivated by this insight, we characterize a phenomenon we term Spectral Contraction and use it to build SpCon, a source-attribution framework that accesses only the target model's VAE. SpCon obtains adjacent residuals through two deterministic reconstructions, builds a spectral-contraction representation from their frequency-resolved relative energy change, and aggregates Student-t response densities for each source-condition pair over a finite set of fitted reference components. The same representation supports three settings according to non-belonging reference availability: none (Target-Only, TO; belonging references only), external out-of-domain sources (External-Reference, ER), or known in-domain competitors (Known-Reference, KR). Across seven LGMs, TO, ER, and KR attain average AUROC/AP of 0.8786/0.6344, 0.9404/0.7886, and 0.9652/0.8626 over the 35 conditions, all outperforming the strongest baseline (0.8154/0.5277), and achieve 0.8581/0.5507, 0.9369/0.7549, and 0.9734/0.8773 on the three social platforms.
authors: Chao Wang, Zijin Yang, Yaofei Wang, Yuang Qi, Weiming Zhang, Kejiang Chen
bullets: Existing methods reduce reconstruction behavior to a single scalar, losing frequency-specific source evidence.
SpCon uses two deterministic VAE reconstructions to measure frequency-resolved relative changes in residual energy, termed Spectral Contraction.
The framework supports target-only, external-reference, and known-reference attribution settings.
Across seven latent generative models and 35 conditions, all settings outperform the strongest baseline; performance remains strong on three social platforms.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this issue, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which shows that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.
authors: Jianhong Pang, Ziyi Ye, Qiuxia Hou, Yanhao Zhang, Zuxuan Wu
bullets: RL can increase capability while making errors harder for humans to recognize.
ITHV contains 2,728 visually grounded instances distinguishing obvious from elusive hallucinations.
DAPO-V combines verifiability-aware rewards with adaptive dual control under a risk budget.
Across three MLLM base models, it improves elusive-hallucination accuracy by 5.78–9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO.
A blinded human study found DAPO-V hallucinations easier to detect than those from the base model.

papers.abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.
authors: Yuncheng Zhang, Songtao Jiang, Yitian Tang, Zijie Meng, Zihan Xu, Xuxiang Ren, Jian Wu, Hualiang Wang, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and incompatibility of deploying independently developed specialist medical VLMs.

Introduces HuluOPDCorpus (914k prompts) and HuluOPDBench (47k test items), with evaluation on 132k items across five imaging specialties.
Models using 10% and 2% of the specialists’ combined parameters retain 94% and 89% of their question-answering performance, respectively.

papers.abstract: Comparing two entities in an image, multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) often answer wrongly. We find that the answer bias enters not when the model sees, but when it decides with the image in view: the model's own descriptions of the two entities often already hold the right answer. We therefore propose D$^3$ (Describe, Don't Decide): the model describes each entity alone, decides from these descriptions without the image, and merges this decision with its direct answer. Without any training, D$^3$ improves all 79 model-benchmark pairs across ten benchmarks and eight 7-9B MLLMs. On held-out GQA comparison questions, the mean accuracy of these models rises from 72.4% to 83.2% (up to +21.5% per model), higher than that of Qwen2.5-VL-32B answering directly (82.8%). Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/describe-dont-decide.
bullets: MLLMs often identify the correct comparison evidence in their descriptions but make errors when deciding with the image visible.
D³ has the model describe each entity independently, compare the descriptions without the image, and combine that decision with its direct answer.
The training-free method improves all 79 model–benchmark pairs tested across ten benchmarks and eight 7–9B MLLMs.
On held-out GQA comparison questions, mean accuracy increases from 72.4% to 83.2%, with gains up to 21.5% per model.
The approach is evaluated for image-based comparison questions; the abstract does not establish broader task coverage beyond these settings.

Given the image and the original question, the MLLM answers wrongly; pimg (orange) is its probability for each option. Right: the three steps of D3; in the first two, the MLLM takes the box on its left and returns the one on its right. papers.selection_reason: Presents a training-free inference strategy to correct answer bias in multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Describe, Don't Decide: Correcting Answer Bias in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: D³ reduces answer bias in multimodal LLMs by making them describe image entities separately before deciding between them.

papers.abstract: Even when multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer incorrectly, their internal cues often point to the relevant region. A widely used remedy re-presents the cue-selected region as an enlarged crop to supply finer detail. However, we find that much of its gain requires no new detail: it largely survives when the crop comes from the already-seen low-resolution input, and partly even when the region's cached tokens are merely copied. Part of re-presentation's gain thus comes from drawing attention to evidence the model already holds. We propose InCue, a test-time framework that makes better use of this evidence without additional visual input. InCue treats visual attention and predictive-entropy gradients as Internal Cues, couples them into a spatial target, and optimizes only an offset on the existing visual tokens to steer attention toward it. Under matched visual-token budgets, InCue achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming recent test-time methods and improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V$^*$ and 23.4% on its hard samples. Its gains carry over to eight general benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/InCue.
authors: Shuwei Wu, Siyue Yu, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: Re-presenting cropped regions helps partly by highlighting evidence the model has already seen, not only by supplying finer detail.
InCue combines visual-attention and predictive-entropy gradients to identify a spatial target.
It optimizes an offset over existing visual tokens, avoiding additional visual input while preserving matched token budgets.
The method reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V* and 23.4% on hard samples, with gains across eight general benchmarks.
Scope: InCue is a test-time framework and relies on internal cues available from the MLLM.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of InCue. The MLLM stays frozen, and the only free variable is an additive offset ∆U on the cached visual tokens U0. SCC couples the read-out attention cue A with the sensitivity cue S, obtained by backpropagating the predictive entropy H(p), into the joint response J . RCR amplifies J inside the best-scoring window W ⋆ to form the spatial target T . Test-time optimization then updates ∆U to increase the overlap between the current attention A(k) and T (k). The cues and the target are refreshed at every step k, and the answer is read out after K steps (Output): here it changes from (C) pink to the correct (D) black.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a test-time optimization framework that steers MLLM visual tokens using internal cues, fitting both test-time learning and multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: InCue: Making Better Use of What Multimodal LLMs Already See at Test Time
papers.tldr: InCue improves MLLM test-time reasoning by steering attention toward internally identified evidence already present in the input, without adding visual information.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.
authors: Ruixiao Shi, Fu Feng, Yucheng Xie, Jing Wang, Xin Geng
bullets: GUI grounding benefits from additional views, but effective inspection must balance fine detail with contextual meaning.
SPARK uses exploration probes to identify relevant context and target details, then verification probes to test emerging localization hypotheses.
Spatial attention guides where to look, probe responses determine crop extent, and observation history promotes complementary views.
Uncertainty-weighted voting combines observations into final predictions.
On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves single-view accuracy by 13.9–25.2 percentage points across three VLM backbones and also gains on four additional benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SPARK. (a) Probe-guided adaptive focusing translates contextual and local-detail attention into view placement and context-dependent crop extent. (b) SPARK uses the focusing mechanism in (a) to construct local views guided by exploration and hypothesis-conditioned verification probes. The resulting localization predictions are passed to the aggregation module. (c) Uncertaintyweighted voting accumulates entropy-based prediction weights within spatial clusters and returns the medoid of the highest-scoring cluster as the final location.

papers.title: Your VLM Knows What to Inspect: Semantic Probe-Guided Adaptive Focusing for GUI Grounding
papers.tldr: SPARK uses a frozen VLM’s semantic guidance to adaptively inspect GUI regions, substantially improving grounding accuracy without training.

papers.abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.
authors: Saraswathy Amjith, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, Yoon Kim
bullets: A topic or animal preference can be distilled between vision-language models via number sequences.
The transferred animal preference affects image generation and representations, but color and style preferences do not.
A constant component of the student’s parameter change explains much of the shift toward the transferred trait.
The effect depends on how concepts are distributed across prompt tokens: whole-prompt traits transfer more readily than single-token attributes.
The proposed weight lens detects subliminal traits in nearly every trained student, including traits absent from generated images.
