papers.tldr: Subliminal learning can transfer preferences across text, vision, and image generation through seemingly meaningless training data.

papers.abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.
authors: Xinhe Wu, Yicheng Ye, Yadong Jin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering machine-readable measurements embedded in compound scientific figures.
Combines figure localization, panel decomposition, OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided MLLM reconstruction.
Adds batch processing, caching, and structured logging for high-throughput repository-scale extraction.
Applied to 605 toxicology/pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle articles, producing 468 and 242 tabular outputs, respectively.
Links reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata for downstream AI4Science applications.

papers.abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably plan and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.
authors: Aadi Palnitkar, Dmytro Kurdydyk, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: Fixed zoom procedures can constrain frontier VLMs that are capable of planning and tool use.
RVLM-X uses a code REPL containing the full-resolution image, enabling recursive self-selection of regions and context.
The same harness operates across photographs, charts, and maps without task-specific changes.
It outperforms a single full-image call on all seven public benchmarks and achieves the highest pooled accuracy.
On the introduced MapGenBench, RVLM-X reaches 71.4% accuracy versus 55.5% for the strongest baseline.

papers.title: RVLM-X: Towards a Universal VLM Harness
papers.tldr: RVLM-X lets a VLM recursively choose and inspect high-resolution image regions, improving visual search across diverse tasks and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.
authors: Tongxiao Hu, Yikai Zhao, Qiyan Zhao, Xiaosong Yuan, Xuhang Chen, Pengzhou Cheng, Xiaofeng Zhang
bullets: High-confidence token commitments are often insensitive to image evidence, limiting confidence-based decoding.
Degenerate and hallucinated outputs show increased entropy in deep-layer attention organization.
CD-APC adjusts candidate scores using visual evidence within a base-supported pool.
Dual gating and an inverse-window mechanism adapt commitment decisions to acceptability and decoding difficulty.
The method consistently improves results across two backbones and five benchmarks.

papers.title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: CD-APC is a training-free decoding method that uses visual evidence to reduce image-insensitive commitments and improve multimodal diffusion language model outputs.

papers.abstract: Cognitive neuroscience learned that an activation map is not a map of necessity. Regions that light up during a task are not always needed for it, and only lesions reveal which ones are. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) vision-language models come with an activation map for free, since the router records which experts respond to image and text tokens, and recent work reads modality-specialized experts off this map. We bring the lesion. In Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, Kimi-VL-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3 to 12% of the experts are vision-exclusive: image tokens route to them at up to five times the uniform rate and text tokens almost never. In Qwen3-VL they receive a quarter of all image-token routing, and lesioning all of them costs less than one percentage point on average over eight perception benchmarks and free-form OCR, no more than lesioning a random set of the same size. In Kimi-VL and Gemma-4 the lesion also costs no more than a random set. Scoped lesions, which remove an expert set only at image positions or only at text positions, then show where the models do depend on their experts. In Qwen3-VL, silencing every expert at every image position costs 3 points, against 45 at text positions, where the dependence sits in dual-use experts that text-only tasks need as well. Across models the image-side dependence is 2 to 3 points in Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL and 26 in Gemma-4. Reading text in images is the one ability that needs image-position experts in every model. The exclusive experts receive informative patches, produce outputs of ordinary size, and stay inert under sensory deprivation: text-only training recruits them only when load balancing forces it. In Kimi-VL the balancing bias itself manufactures most of them. Load balancing draws the modality map in the part of the computation the models depend on least. Expert selection, pruning and skipping should follow the lesion, not the map.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Kexin Geng, Wei Qiu
bullets: Across Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL and Gemma-4, 3–12% of experts are vision-exclusive and can receive substantial image-token routing.
Removing vision-exclusive experts usually performs no worse than removing an equally sized random expert set.
Scoped lesions reveal stronger dependence on text-position experts than image-position experts in Qwen3-VL, while image-side dependence varies substantially across models.
Reading text in images is the only capability consistently requiring image-position experts across all three models.
Exclusive experts process informative patches but remain inactive under text-only inputs; load balancing may create many of them, especially in Kimi-VL.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes expert specialization and dependence in mixture-of-experts vision-language models.
papers.title: Lit Up but Not Needed: Scoped Lesions Show Where Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts Depend on Their Experts
papers.tldr: Lesion experiments show that MoE routing maps overstate the importance of modality-specialized experts, so pruning should follow causal dependence rather than activation frequency.

papers.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
authors: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume
bullets: Provides four matched real/fake audio-video combinations per source clip, enabling direct measurement of modality reliance.
Covers face swaps, whole-frame video diffusion, and voice conversion across four tasks: authenticity, manipulation type, identity verification, and explanation.
Evaluates multimodal LLMs, trained detectors, and LoRA-fine-tuned MLLMs.
MLLMs perform poorly on four-way authenticity and detect video-only fakes much more reliably than voice-only fakes; trained detectors perform strongly in-distribution.
Held-out-generator testing shows reduced detector performance, while LoRA improves explanation scores; generalization and explanation remain open challenges.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for audio-video deepfake detection with a recognition objective and systematic evaluation of multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
papers.tldr: MOZAIC is a paired audio-video deepfake benchmark that disentangles whether models detect fake visuals, fake audio, or both, revealing strong performance gaps and weak generalization and explanation.

papers.abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? In this work, we first verify that MLLMs contain stable reusable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting normal generation. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{Lo}ok \textbf{Ba}ck in the \textbf{L}atent \textbf{S}pace (\textbf{Lobals}), a training-free decoding method that identifies the contiguous layer window with the strongest visual-token attention and re-forwards through it, allowing the model to revisit visual evidence in latent space. We demonstrate that this latent-space revisit strategy can improve MLLMs' performance across diverse multimodal settings, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks.
bullets: MLLMs contain stable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting generation.
LoBaLS identifies a contiguous layer window receiving the strongest attention from visual tokens.
The method re-forwards this window to let the model revisit visual evidence in latent space.
It improves performance across general vision-language, visual hallucination, and vision-centric tasks.
The approach is training-free and operates at test time.

papers.abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making text-pretrained decoders effectively interpret continuous audio representations without degrading text performance.
Introduces C-Gate, an interface that represents audio as continuous convex combinations of the decoder’s frozen text embeddings.
Achieves a VoiceBench aggregate score of 75.36 and 62.50% accuracy on MMAU Test-mini.
Outperforms compared interfaces on aggregate spoken-language performance, especially on spoken knowledge and reasoning.
Shows trade-offs: stronger baselines perform better on some audio-understanding and transcription tasks.

papers.title: ConvexLLM: Scaling Convex-Hull Speech Interfaces to General-Purpose Audio Intelligence
papers.tldr: ConvexLLM uses convex combinations of frozen text embeddings to connect audio to language decoders, improving spoken-language reasoning while preserving text capabilities.

papers.abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.
authors: JB Kim, Byungwoo Jeon, Kyungmin Lee, Hyeonmo Kang, Cheonbok Park, Shinyoung Joo, Jinwoo Shin, Jeonghoon Kim
bullets: Problem: Visual understanding and generation use heterogeneous representations, making them difficult to integrate in one model.
Method: Abstraction Fusion builds shared visual tokens from hierarchical frozen-encoder features.
Method: Block-wise MoT adds a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model at block boundaries.
Result: Shared representations improve generative learning while preserving pretrained understanding and maintaining comparable reconstruction fidelity.
Implication: Pretrained vision-language representations can serve as an effective foundation for visual generation.

papers.abstract: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. We introduce Second-Look Prompting (SLP), a training-free method that repeats the image-question pair in the input. In the repeated copy, every visual and textual token can attend to the complete input, yielding a unified multimodal encoding of the pair. Moreover, the added visual tokens contribute computation beyond re-exposing the image: even a blank image in their place can improve reasoning. Across 12 benchmarks, SLP improves the overall average score of every evaluated model, spanning nine open-source models (3B-72B) and three proprietary frontier models, with gains reaching 5.6 points for Gemini 3 Flash on MATH-Vision. Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms: the question guides where the second image attends, and the added visual tokens act as a prefill scratchpad whose hidden states retain answer-relevant information from the image and question. These findings highlight input presentation as a simple yet effective way to improve VLM performance.
authors: Yicheng Zhang, Xun Zhang, Jingyuan Ma, Tianyu Yu, Yuan Yao
bullets: Addresses causal-attention limitations, where the first modality is encoded without seeing the rest of the input.
Uses a training-free repeated image-question input to create a unified multimodal encoding.
Added visual tokens also serve as a computation scratchpad; even blank replacements can help reasoning.
Improves average performance for all evaluated models across 12 benchmarks, including gains up to 5.6 points on Gemini 3 Flash for MATH-Vision.
Analysis identifies question-guided visual attention and answer-relevant hidden-state retention as complementary mechanisms.

papers.abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

Evaluated on 28 e-commerce benchmarks across eight business scenarios and 64 public general-purpose benchmarks.
The largest model outperforms substantially larger open-source models on e-commerce tasks; all models outperform similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterparts on general-purpose evaluations.
Deployed across hundreds of WeChat use cases, serving billion-scale requests per day, with weights and code publicly released.

papers.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.
authors: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu
bullets: Existing CD evaluations can be confounded by candidate filtering, generation trajectories, and response biases.
CONCOR uses controlled comparisons between ground-truth and hallucinated candidates.
Its Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM) measures correction direction, composition, and reliability.
Different CD methods trade off consistent grounding against stronger but more error-prone corrections.
Contrast strength can help or hurt methods depending on their correction behavior, motivating direct evaluation of contrastive corrections.

papers.abstract: In video temporal grounding, a correct interval can come from finding the event, answering blind or fitting one annotation style, and Recall at IoU scores them alike. We measure evidence dependence, how much the answer rests on the event's frames. Our fixed-answer audit edits either the frames inside the annotated interval or, as a placebo, as many frames elsewhere in the same video, and compares the two drops in the annotated answer's likelihood. Supervised fine-tuning and three public checkpoints trained with IoU-reward reinforcement learning raise the accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 9 to 20 points, partly by answering blind and by fitting one annotation. Yet their answers rest on the event no more than the base model's, and the same holds for IoU-reward training on our data at the audit's frame rate. This comparison is a difference of the model's own likelihoods, so we can train on it. A placebo contrast and a bound on the placebo drop rule out learning to react to any edit. With them, evidence dependence rises in all five base models we train, and the weight on clean supervision controls how much. Added to IoU-reward training, the objective raises evidence dependence while keeping the accuracy gain. Masking the event's frames makes the trained models decline or miss the event more often than their base; masking as many other frames does not. The dependence moves to another event when the query names it, and holds on a second dataset and under patch scrambling, an edit never used in training.
authors: Zijie Jin, Shuai Zhao, Haoran Tao, Chaomin Huang, Liwen Luo
bullets: Introduces an evidence-dependence audit comparing likelihood drops after editing frames inside the annotated interval versus an equal number of frames elsewhere.
Finds that supervised fine-tuning and IoU-reward reinforcement learning improve accuracy but do not increase reliance on event frames.
Uses a placebo contrast and a bound on placebo effects to train models against generic edit sensitivity.
Evidence-dependence training increases reliance on relevant frames across five base models, while preserving IoU-reward accuracy gains.
The effect transfers to other queried events, a second dataset, and patch scrambling not seen during training.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates evidence dependence in video temporal grounding using Qwen2.5-VL. This provides a methodological advance for Multimodal Large Language Models in grounding tasks.
papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Evidence: Measuring and Training Evidence Dependence in Video Temporal Grounding
papers.tldr: Accuracy alone can hide blind or annotation-fitting behavior, so the paper measures and trains models to rely on the event evidence in video temporal grounding.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a fundamental task in multimedia understanding, where state-of-the-art methods have achieved prominent success relying on the assumption of complete, well-aligned multimodal inputs. However, real-world unconstrained scenarios often suffer from unpredictable modality degradation and information loss, leading to catastrophic performance collapse of existing MER models that heavily depend on facial cues as the core inference anchor. However, few systematic works evaluate model robustness under diverse, fine-grained incomplete settings, as prior works are limited to coarse-grained full-modality removal and neglect interpretable analysis of emotional reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formally define the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task, which benchmarks model generalization and robustness under multi-grained modality and emotional information loss. We further construct MIME, a dedicated IMER benchmark with 2,000 video segments covering realistic fine-grained facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and extreme full-modality loss, surpassing the limited coarse-grained settings of prior works. We also propose the Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis paradigm with tailored metrics to dissect the fine-grained emotional cue perception and reasoning process of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Extensive experiments on seven mainstream MLLMs reveal that body language and scene context act as critical compensatory mechanisms under facial degradation, while a pronounced gap exists between models' basic visual perception ability and high-level cognitive reasoning. Our work provides a focused evaluation platform and actionable insights for advancing robust multimodal emotion recognition. Our dataset and code are public at https://yuxinokk.github.io/MIME.
authors: Yuxin Jia, Xing Lan, Wensong Wang, Jian Xue, Feiliang Ren, Ke Lu
bullets: Introduces the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task for evaluating robustness under varied emotional and modality degradation.
Provides MIME, a benchmark of 2,000 video segments spanning facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and complete modality loss.
Proposes Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis and tailored metrics to examine emotional-cue perception and reasoning in MLLMs.
Experiments with seven mainstream MLLMs show that body language and scene context can compensate for degraded facial information.
Finds a gap between basic visual perception and higher-level emotional reasoning; dataset and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently become a central paradigm for advancing Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), as demonstrated by systems such as OpenAI's o3 and the R1 series. Despite significant progress in LLMs, how to leverage RFT to unify visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic tool use into one coherent training paradigm remains an open challenge. In this work, we present Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++), a unified framework that extends RFT to both visual perception tasks and multimodal agentic workflows, enabling LVLMs to reason with images, act upon images, and evaluate their own outputs using verifiable reward. With Visual-RFT++, open-source LVLMs not only show significant gains on diverse visual perception tasks, but also acquire agentic abilities such as web searching for real-time information and code-based image manipulation (e.g., cropping, rotation, and analysis). Across visual perception tasks, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, reasoning grounding, and open-vocabulary detection, Visual-RFT++ delivers strong gains over SFT, including a +24.3 percentage points improvement in one-shot fine-grained classification and +21.0 percentage points on COCO's 4-shot setting and +15.4 percentage points on LVIS with around several hundred samples. To evaluate agentic behaviors, we introduce the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) with MAT-Search and MAT-Coding. Visual-RFT++ surpasses its baseline by +18.6 F1 / +13.0 EM percentage points on MAT-Coding and +10.3 F1 / +8.7 EM percentage points on MAT-Search. It also shows gains of 29.3 F1 and 25.9 EM percentage points on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2Wiki and HotpotQA, demonstrating strong cross-modal generalization. Visual-RFT++ introduces a data-efficient and reward-driven framework that strengthens both visual reasoning and agentic adaptability.
authors: Ziyu Liu, Zeyi Sun, Xiaoyi Dong, Yuhang Cao, Haodong Duan, Dahua Lin, Jiaqi Wang, Yuhang Zang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic workflows in LVLMs.
Enables models to reason about and manipulate images, search the web, and evaluate outputs through reward signals.
Improves diverse visual tasks over supervised fine-tuning, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, and grounding.
Introduces the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) for evaluating search and code-based image manipulation.
Reports gains on MAT tasks and multi-hop QA, indicating cross-modal generalization with relatively few training samples.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate, understand, and predict human motion, but mainly from RGB cameras. Depth, LiDAR, mmWave, and WiFi complement RGB under poor lighting, through occlusions, and in privacy-sensitive applications, but existing multisensory models cover only some of these sensing tasks. Covering all of them from any sensor subset is challenging, since the tokens of heterogeneous sensors are semantically inconsistent and spatially misaligned, paired multisensory data are scarce, and the tasks need different temporal granularities. We present OmniSenMo, a multisensory language model that takes the human skeleton as a common reference for all sensors. Its skeleton-grounded motion representation turns each sensor into joint tokens, one per body joint, so that any sensor subset is fused joint by joint and expressed in the motion vocabulary that the language model learned from motion capture and text. We pretrain it on all five sensors generated by our multisensory simulator, and Multi-Granularity Observation gives each task the frames it needs. On a cross-action split of MM-Fi, the same model with all five sensors outperforms the models compared on each task, including LEO-Fuse in pose estimation (84.1 vs. 89.0 mm MPJPE) and HoloLLM in unseen-action recognition (69.2% vs. 42.8%). Even without RGB, it outperforms both methods that use RGB, and in a cross-dataset validation on XRF55, it recognizes unseen actions far better than HoloLLM.
authors: Cheng Guo, Qiming Cao, Pu Perry Wang, Pu Wang, Hongfei Xue
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous, spatially misaligned sensors, scarce paired data, and task-specific temporal requirements.
Represents each sensor as joint-level tokens using the human skeleton as a common reference for fusion.
Pretrains on simulated multisensory data and uses Multi-Granularity Observation to match task-specific frame needs.
On MM-Fi, achieves 84.1 mm MPJPE for pose estimation versus 89.0 for LEO-Fuse, and 69.2% unseen-action recognition versus 42.8% for HoloLLM.
Maintains strong recognition without RGB and generalizes to unseen actions on XRF55; evaluation focuses on the reported datasets and simulated pretraining setup.

papers.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Defines a task combining speech understanding, object retrieval, speaker localization, and delivery.
Provides a dataset with three query types, eight subtypes, and varied object-selection and delivery requirements.
Integrates motion-aware spatial audio into an audio-visual large language model to track spatial cues during movement.
Uses multitask instruction tuning for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding.
Reports baseline results in seen and unseen environments; code is planned for public release.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our baseline framework. Details of the Motion-Aware Spatial (MAS) Audio Encoder are shown in the left panel. The original audio encoder preserves speech understanding, while the parallel MAS Audio Encoder extracts binaural spatial cues and updates them according to the agent’s motion. A lightweight projector maps these features into the language model’s token space, where they are combined with speech, visual, and textual tokens to predict executable skills. The action executor interacts with the environment and returns execution feedback for closed-loop decision making.

Figure 1. Overview of Audio-Visual Rearrangement. Given a spoken request, an agent must (1) search for and pick up a suitable object and (2) navigate to the requesting speaker and hand it over. papers.abstract: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.
authors: Dankai Liao, YuFeng Wu, Ziyue Wang, Guanxi Liu, Tianyi Zhang, Zeyu Liu, Linghan Cai, Yueming Jin
bullets: The work addresses the gap between pathology AI and pathologists’ trajectory-based, multi-region, multi-magnification diagnostic workflow.
Five pathologists’ viewing trajectories across 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images and ten organs support PathStreamBench, covering response timing, morphology, session-level findings, and diagnosis.
PathStream jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis, using a diagnosis-attention loss to focus on relevant accumulated visual and textual evidence.
It outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines; its trajectory WSI Relevance score is 77.87 versus 62.76 for the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline.
Without additional training, the model generalizes to educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

papers.abstract: Can a language model learn more from the same information simply by encountering it in different forms? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing Multimodal View Training (MVT), a simple training approach that presents identical information through text, speech, and images, without requiring new facts or supervision. Starting from a text sample, MVT generates corresponding audio and rendered-text image views, and trains a multimodal language model to produce the same target output across all three views. To further bring these benefits to text-only large language models (LLMs), we train lightweight connector modules to pretrained audio and vision encoders, allowing the LLM to learn from multimodal inputs while retaining its text-only architecture at inference. Across question answering, machine unlearning, and knowledge editing, adaptive MVT improves QA recall by +15.2 percentage points, forget quality by +40.7 points, and editing generality by +25.2 points over text-only training. Combining MVT with standard augmentation further improves QA and editing generality. Our theoretical analysis illustrates how training across modalities can shift weight updates toward shared factual content and reduce their reliance on features specific to each view.
authors: Devang Kulshreshtha, Priyanka Kaswan, Minh Pham, Chinmay Hegde, Niv Cohen
bullets: Uses identical content in text, audio, and rendered-text image views, training the model to produce the same output from each.
Connects pretrained audio and vision encoders to text-only LLMs through lightweight modules, preserving text-only inference.
Improves question-answering recall, machine unlearning, and knowledge-editing generality over text-only training.
Combining MVT with standard augmentation further benefits QA and editing generality.
Theory suggests multimodal training emphasizes shared factual content over view-specific features.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models can extract structured fields from scanned financial documents, yet they provide no indication of when a field might be wrong. We derive per-field confidence estimates from the token log-probabilities the model already produces, via a token-to-span alignment procedure that maps logprobs onto each extracted value within the structured JSON output. Evaluated on two benchmarks (CORD v2 receipts, Kleister NDA legal contracts) with three VLM families, the minimum token probability per field achieves Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) 0.74-0.91 for error detection, far exceeding verbalized confidence (0.53-0.56). The uncertain fields form a natural training curriculum: fine-tuning via Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves accuracy from 78.5% to 87.5% on CORD (67 examples) and from 70.7% to 75.1% on multi-page NDA contracts (259 examples), while substantially improving error detection on Kleister NDA (AUROC 0.70 to 0.85, Area Under the Accuracy-Rejection Curve (AUARC) 0.78 to 0.92). The loop requires no annotation beyond the training-split ground truth, demonstrating that confidence-guided curriculum selection transfers to complex multi-page documents when combined with native multi-image training. A frontier model (Claude Sonnet 4) used as a pseudo-label judge achieves ~92% reward agreement with ground truth on both benchmarks, suggesting this loop can operate without human annotation.
bullets: Addresses the lack of trustworthy uncertainty estimates when VLMs extract structured fields from scanned financial documents.
Aligns token log-probabilities with extracted JSON spans; the minimum token probability per field is a strong error signal.
Across CORD v2 and Kleister NDA with three VLM families, token confidence reaches AUROC 0.74–0.91, outperforming verbalized confidence.
Using uncertain fields as a GRPO training curriculum improves extraction accuracy and, on Kleister NDA, error-detection AUROC from 0.70 to 0.85.
A frontier model can serve as a pseudo-label judge with about 92% reward agreement, suggesting reduced reliance on human annotation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.
authors: Xu Yuan, Pangjing Wu, Wenqi Fan, Qing Li
bullets: Addresses fragmented encoding pathways that limit shared supervision across heterogeneous inputs.
Uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert all inputs into a common visual substrate for a vision-language model.
Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding creates compact retrieval representations while preserving global and fine-grained information.
Interventional Rendering Learning promotes sensitivity to content changes and robustness to rendering variations.
Outperforms prior same-scale models on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, including a 1.7-point MMEB Overall Precision@1 gain over MetaEmbed and stronger out-of-domain performance.

papers.abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.
authors: Chen Li, Xiaoling Hu, Chao Chen
bullets: Binary correctness labels miss differences between occasional errors, frequent failures, isolated successes, and consistently correct behavior.
The method combines an individual response’s correctness with query-level empirical success rates from repeated generations.
An independent confidence estimator uses the query and full response, trained with LoRA adapters and a confidence head via mean squared error.
Repeated generations are needed only to construct supervision; inference evaluates each response in a single pass.
The paper proves ordering and mean-preservation properties and derives a selective-risk bound, then evaluates calibration and selective prediction in language and vision-language models.

papers.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
authors: Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jinxi He, Xiyuan Yang, Pan Wang, Han Liu, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful evidence in a single pass under bounded frame storage and unknown future questions.
Groups recurring failures by cause and searches papers, model cards, and code for adaptable methods or pretrained perception models.
Can jointly add perceptual capabilities and revise how their evidence is stored and retrieved.
Selects accuracy-improving revisions on validation streams, then optimizes for faster revisions within a quality tolerance.
Across three benchmarks, it achieves the best accuracy within frozen-backbone comparisons; on OVO-Bench, it reaches 75.1% accuracy with 0.30-second average response time using Qwen3-VL-8B.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces MORSE, a framework for optimizing the memory harness of a frozen video-language model (Qwen3-VL-8B). It addresses the problem of selecting evidence to retain in a streaming video system, which aligns with both Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Efficient AI (token eviction/pruning). papers.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
papers.tldr: MORSE improves streaming video memory by using recurring failures to search for and integrate external research, achieving strong accuracy and efficient querying with frozen video-language backbones.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation enables the recognition of arbitrary categories through natural language descriptions and has recently been extended from natural images to remote sensing. However, existing approaches primarily focus on three-channel optical imagery or limited-band multispectral data, while pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to directly exploit the rich spectral information of hyperspectral imagery (HSI) without additional adaptation. More importantly, different land-cover categories rely on distinct spectral cues, which may be weakened by uniform fusion. To address these challenges, we propose SpectralRoute, a training-free framework for open-vocabulary hyperspectral segmentation. Specifically, we construct complementary spectral views from HSI and enrich category descriptions with external spectral knowledge, enabling frozen vision-language models to extract diverse spectral-semantic responses. We then introduce a class-adaptive spectral routing mechanism that selectively amplifies discriminative spectral responses for each category, overcoming the limitations of uniform fusion. Furthermore, physical spectral priors are incorporated to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories. Experiments on three hyperspectral benchmarks demonstrate that SpectralRoute consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods without additional training.
authors: Qingmei Li, Xiaoya Fan, Juepeng Zheng, Jianxi Huang, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of applying vision-language models to hyperspectral imagery with rich, category-dependent spectral information.
Constructs complementary spectral views and enriches text descriptions with external spectral knowledge.
Uses class-adaptive spectral routing to amplify discriminative spectral responses instead of uniformly fusing them.
Incorporates physical spectral priors to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories.
Outperforms existing methods across three hyperspectral benchmarks without additional training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SpectralRoute. The framework starts with knowledge-enhanced text representation and multiview spectral construction, followed by vision-language feature extraction using frozen CLIP to compute cross-modal similarities. Spatial pooling and softmax transform the similarities into routing weights. Class-adaptive spectral routing inputs both the routing weights and visual features to perform weighted summation and amplification. Physics-guided refinement integrates spectral prototypes, semantic gating, and initial scores to generate the final prediction.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of segmentation maps on the Pavia University dataset. Previous methods suffer from severe category confusion and fragmented boundaries, whereas SpectralRoute achieves sharper boundaries and finer category separation.

Figure 4. Parameter sensitivity analysis of temperature τ and scaling factor γ. While simpler scenes favor smaller values, highly complex scenes rely more on strong spectral amplification. Our method adaptively scales with scene complexity and maintains robust performance.

Figure 1. Motivation of SpectralRoute. The task requires pixelwise prediction from HSIs and open vocabularies. However, RGBpretrained VLMs miss continuous spectra, causing visual ambiguity among certain categories. In contrast, hyperspectral signatures provide distinct physical evidence. SpectralRoute exploits this through multi-view routing, semantic enrichment, and physical priors to achieve fine-grained separation. in hyperspectral classification and semantic segmentation, existing methods predominantly operate under a closed-set assumption [35], where models are trained to recognize a predefined set of categories using annotated samples. Such dependence limits their flexibility in handling previously unseen categories [9, 18] and adapting to diverse Earth observation scenarios [28]. In practical applications, land cover categories may vary across regions, sensors, and requirements, making repeated data annotation and model retraining impractical [49]. Therefore, enabling flexible, textdriven recognition of land cover categories without additional training represents an important direction for hyperspectral image interpretation [15, 41].

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR) requires finding the video and time interval that match a text query in a corpus of videos. We present RELAY, a training-free framework for VCMR that shares memory across queries. RELAY processes a batch of queries in three stages: search with a query bank, ranking with video notes, and localization with video prompt caching. In the search stage, an embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank penalizes videos that score highly for many other queries in the batch. In the ranking stage, a vision-language model (VLM) writes notes on each candidate video's scenes, people, objects, and actions once. Then, a large language model (LLM) reranks the candidates from these notes. In the localization stage, a VLM predicts the time interval of the moment in the top-ranked video. When multiple queries select the same video, prompt caching lets the VLM reuse its frames. On the three VERIFIED benchmarks, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 without training. Without any labeled moment, its predicted intervals are shorter than the annotated ones. In VCMR, it achieves similar performance to VideoSearch-R1 on one benchmark and trails it at IoU 0.5 on the other two. Human annotators also mark shorter moments than the original annotations of the benchmarks. A single margin, calibrated on a few labeled queries, widens the predicted interval to the annotation convention of the benchmarks. With it, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in VCMR at IoU 0.5.
authors: Chenwei Xu, Shang Wu, Zhenyu Pan, Jianshu Zhang, Pranav Maneriker, Lie Lu, Fan Du, Manling Li, Han Liu
bullets: Processes query batches through search, candidate ranking, and temporal localization.
Uses a query bank to reduce cross-query confusion and video notes for LLM-based reranking.
Caches video prompts and frames when multiple queries target the same video.
Outperforms trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 on three VERIFIED benchmarks.
Predicted intervals are initially shorter than annotations; a single calibrated margin improves VCMR at IoU 0.5.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of RELAY. The top row follows one query of a batch through the three stages. The bottom row is the memory that the queries of the batch share. 1⃝ Search: the embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank subtracts a bias from each score. The bias is larger for a video that matches more queries. 2⃝ Ranking: a VLM writes notes on each candidate video once. An LLM orders the candidates from their notes. Reciprocal rank fusion merges this order with the embedding-based ranking. 3⃝ Localization: the VLM predicts the start and end of the moment in the top-ranked video. papers.title: Towards Agentic Video Corpus Moment Retrieval

papers.abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.
bullets: The benchmark evaluates transcription fidelity beyond CER, including invented errors, edit-markup precision/recall, and line structure on 1,000 Brazilian Portuguese essays.
Fine-tuning LightOnOCR-3-1B on 647 pages produced 2.06% CER, improving on the best open baseline’s 5.6% CER.
The model recovers 67% of insertions, 77% of illegible deletions, and preserves line structure on 97% of pages.
It still changes 60% of likely misspellings, and unseen words remain a challenge on another corpus.
The 4-bit model runs on ordinary CPUs at about one minute per page; released resources include the model, benchmark code, and review data.

papers.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (-3.8% average and -14.3% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours - versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches - with a +17.1% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
authors: Qie Sima, Wei Xue, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets performance saturation caused by naively mixing heterogeneous robot, task, and environment data.
Uses a 15M-parameter proxy and frozen reference model to learn domain sampling weights via proxy-reference DRO.
Transfers learned weights without retuning to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters.
On 9,500 real-world Open-X Embodiment episodes, improves average success from 68.4% to 76.2% over uniform mixing and matches Re-Mix within evaluation noise.
Reference removal causes over-pessimistic weighting, while entropy regularization prevents weight collapse; optimization costs 11 GPU-hours and is backbone-independent.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The ProMix Framework Architecture. The pipeline consists of two stages: (Stage 1) a proxy-reference optimization loop that learns optimal domain weights p∗ by minimizing the worst-case excess loss of a 15M trainable proxy against a frozen reference model; (Stage 2) single-pass training of the final VLA model using the transferred weights p∗. The entire mixture search costs 11 GPU-hours,whereas a full-scale Re-Mix search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B.

Fig. 2: Evolution of the domain weights during the proxy search. Each panel traces the seven domain weights pi from uniform initialization (top to bottom: full method, without the reference model, without entropy regularization); the shaded band marks the final 10k-step window averaged into p∗.

Fig. 3: Summary of the main empirical effects. (a) Mixture-search cost: a full-scale search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B, whereas the ProMix search is fixed at 11 GPU-hours regardless of backbone. (b) Per-domain improvement over uniform mixing at the 50M scale. (c) Transfer of the 15M-learned mixture to final models at three scales without re-tuning (95% CIs over 5 seeds).

papers.title: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO

papers.abstract: Accurate chest X-ray radiology report generation (RRG) requires recognizing clinically relevant abnormalities and accurately describing them. Although Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves the clinical accuracy of generated reports, our analyses suggest limited improvements in visual representations for abnormality recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a selective regional visual distillation framework that enhances visual representations of challenging abnormalities while preserving existing visual capabilities. Specifically, we train a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on challenging anatomical regions to acquire complementary visual knowledge. Rather than transferring all teacher features, we verify their utility through regional feature replacement and select only those that improve the original student's performance. We further introduce a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) to distill these verified features while minimizing interference with the student's existing visual representations. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray demonstrate improved clinical report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition across different multimodal large language model backbones, while largely preserving performance on non-target findings.
authors: Rui Zuo, Qinyue Tong, Ziqian Lu, Zheming Lu
bullets: Targets the limited visual-representation gains of language-focused GRPO for radiology report generation.
Trains a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on difficult anatomical regions.
Uses regional feature replacement to identify only teacher features that benefit the student.
Applies a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter to distill selected features while reducing interference.
Improves report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, while largely preserving non-target findings.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed selective regional visual distillation framework. Region-Aware Teacher Training: A region-aware teacher is trained with region-specific questions and anatomical annotations to enhance visual representations of disease-associated regions in challenging cases. Regional Feature Utility Verification: Teacher features are substituted into the corresponding student regions, and the resulting changes in the student’s correct-answer scores are used to identify beneficial regional features for distillation. Selective Regional Distillation with SGRA: A Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) learns from the selected teacher features through regional feature distillation, while a feature preservation loss constrains changes to non-target regions.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of visual attribution before and after regional distillation. Representative error-correction cases from MedGemma 1 4B (top) and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (bottom), showing changes in generated reports and visual attribution to the corresponding abnormality regions. Attribution maps are computed using gradient × activation. papers.abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.
authors: Lang Lin, Tianyu Chen, Yi Gu, Yang Zhao, Xinran Song, Xinyang Liu, Jianpeng Cheng, Mingyuan Zhou
bullets: Evaluates 33 open models—12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs—on 51,060 questions across 94 image, video, and audio tasks plus 102 closed-loop games.
On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM on images and is nearly tied on video and audio.
Decision-focused post-training mainly improves probability calibration; on video, System-1 models generally achieve lower Brier scores than their MLLM counterparts.
Extended MLLM reasoning provides only slight accuracy gains and often worsens Brier scores.
In closed-loop games, System-1 models achieve markedly higher progression and tolerate up to 1.1-second decision latency without measurable loss in real-time play.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark comparing System-1 models and MLLMs on multimodal decisions, including video and closed-loop game environments, relevant to MLLM evaluation and video understanding.
papers.title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
papers.tldr: S1Arena-MM benchmarks System-1 models and MLLMs on multimodal decisions, finding System-1 models highly competitive on static tasks and substantially better in latency-sensitive game loops.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.
authors: Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang, Gang Zhou
bullets: Different sampling pipelines can make teacher reasoning depend on evidence unavailable to the student, creating a Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap.
The framework first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior, then optimizes its execution across multiple observations.
Execution-Aware Reference Regularization preserves the prior when executable and permits adaptive changes when observations differ.
Across multiple backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks, the approach outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, including on held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our acquisition-to-execution framework. Stage I uses SFT on student observations to distill black-box teacher trajectories with correct answers into a reasoning prior. Stage II computes GRPO losses separately for multiple temporal observations of the same video and aggregates them to update a shared student policy. Reference regularization uses a larger KL weight when the frozen Stage-I model answers correctly under the current observation and a smaller weight otherwise.
Figure 1: Motivation and framework for observation-conditioned distillation for Video-LLMs.

Figure 4: Main comparison across two student reasoning regimes and six video reasoning benchmarks. We compare SFT, GRPO, LUFFY, T-GRPO, and our method on Qwen3-VL-4BThinking and InternVL3.5-4B. Each point shows the score change from the pretrained baseline, where positive values indicate improvement. Shaded regions denote the best method for each backbone. Our method achieves the largest gain in 11 of 12 backbone-benchmark settings.

(b) Changing only the temporal sampling phase, while keeping the frame rate fixed, still causes substantial outcome flips across models.

papers.abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.
authors: Kiana Taktehrani, Maryam Hosseini, Amir Keynia, Aram Montazami, Arash Mohammadi
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining time-series and language foundation models for lead- and scale-dependent ECG signals.
Uses a lead-aware interface to a frozen time-series foundation model while retaining MedTsLLM’s reprogramming pathway.
Fuses temporal and language-aligned representations with adaptive residual integration, branch-specific supervision, and cross-branch alignment.
Reports 71.10% accuracy/62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL and 89.73% accuracy/65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing.
Outperforms MedTsLLM on both datasets; the approach is focused on ECG classification and preserves lead-specific temporal structure.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-foundation framework fusing a time-series foundation model with a language model (MedTsLLM) for ECG classification, addressing modality mismatch through lead-aware fusion.
papers.title: LAF-ECG: Multi-Resolution Lead-Aware Fusion of Time-Series and Language Foundation Models for ECG Classification
papers.tldr: LAF-ECG improves ECG classification by fusing lead-aware, multi-resolution temporal features with language-aligned representations from frozen foundation models.

papers.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.
authors: Annette Rios, Lukas Fischer, Sarah Ebling
bullets: Professional audio describers evaluated movie AD scripts from two AI pipelines against human-authored descriptions.
Evaluation covered description quality and errors in content, character references, fluency, and coherence.
GPT-4o performed better than the Qwen-based systems, but both produced more errors and received lower quality ratings than human work.
The most critical issues were incorrect or inconsistent character references and content errors or hallucinations.
The study focuses on Italian- and German-language movie descriptions and does not establish human-level quality.
