papers.selection_reason: Presents a method for internalizing agentic tool use into a single-pass CoT for multimodal medical visual diagnosis.
papers.title: Med-Agentic: Distilling Agentic Medical Reasoning with Internalized Meta-Capabilities
papers.tldr: Med-Agentic internalizes modular medical reasoning capabilities into a single-pass, capability-tagged chain of thought, improving diagnostic accuracy across diverse imaging settings.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity. We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.
bullets: Introduces StateBind-200: 200 real images with refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces.
Physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a +15.30-point source-image-balanced gain.
Calibration and extra reasoning do not close the remaining gap; localization can succeed while value-lattice binding fails, especially for two-endpoint ruler spans.
Proposes Factorial StateBind, a training-free verifier that independently checks target and lattice evidence before deterministic resolution.
Its high-precision mode achieves 91.67% candidate precision on 36/128 held-out images, covering 28.12% of images and 9.68% of ordered cells.

papers.selection_reason: Exposes symbol-to-state binding gaps in visual measurement with geometry-aware evaluation and a verifier; directly fits spatial intelligence and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: StateBind: Exposing the Symbol-to-State Binding Gap in Visual Measurement
papers.tldr: StateBind shows that reliable visual measurement depends on binding numerical candidates to image-specific physical states, and that explicit physicalization plus evidence verification substantially improves accuracy.

papers.abstract: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.
authors: Zihan Deng, Xinpei Lin, Du Tiantian, Lequan Yu
bullets: Evaluates order-level quotes from six phone views plus a diagnostic screen, rather than isolated defects or attributes.
Uses Score100 from 0–100 within matched protocols: images only or images with detector sidecar; a declared upper bound is not ranked as a peer.
Introduces field-only LoRA, which adapts attention projections to predict staff fields while leaving the defect list empty.
On image-only T1, the 3B model improves from 26.6 to 33.3 at 0.928 coverage; the remaining gap to human performance is large.
Scope: results are reported on a 335-order, iPhone-heavy cut, and model answering coverage affects comparisons.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks and adapts multimodal LLMs for order-level visual inspection; directly relevant to multimodal large language model evaluation and fine-tuning.
papers.title: PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection
papers.tldr: PhoneQC benchmarks multimodal LLMs on complete smartphone trade-in forms and finds that field-focused adaptation improves open-model scoring, but human appraisal remains substantially ahead.

papers.abstract: Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. These results suggest that hybrid VLMs reason better by answering first and thinking once than by thinking longer.
authors: Tianyi Tan, Wentao Wang, Xiaohan Li, Zining Ren, Siyuan Li, Xutao Mao, Rui Qian, Luoxi Zhang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Hybrid VLMs can loop or exhaust their thinking budget, making extended reasoning worse than direct answering.
YOTO uses probe-weighted voting among direct answers and invokes one thought only when answers remain unsettled.
A failure head monitors the thought and returns to direct answers when failure is predicted.
With frozen model weights and two linear probes, YOTO gains up to 5.9 accuracy points over the strongest early-exit baseline at a matched 20k-token budget.
On MathVision, it raises Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, with gains transferring across additional benchmarks and a second model family.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The failure head at work on two MathVision problems with Qwen3.5-2B. Dots are the head’s score at each check of the thought. Top: the thought falls into a loop; the score sinks below θ at the fourth check, YOTO stops the thought there, and four more direct answers settle the problem, while the released thinking mode returns no answer. Bottom: the direct answers disagree, two wrong ones with high probe scores; the head keeps the thought, which finishes and decides the vote.

Figure 3. Dynamic routing across Qwen3.5 scales on MathVision (% of 3,040 problems): released thinking (left), YOTO return stage (middle) and YOTO outcome (right). Under one threshold, YOTO shifts from hand-over at 0.8B to Stage-1 settling at 4B. Ribbons connect the same problem groups across columns; widths are normalised by the full benchmark. A wrong or unfinished released thought can still lead to a correct YOTO decision through direct support, rather than determining the final answer.

papers.selection_reason: Improves hybrid VLM reasoning by answering first and thinking once with failure-based early stopping; fits multimodal LLMs and inference efficiency.
papers.title: You Only Think Once: Rescuing Hybrid Vision-Language Models Lost in Thought
papers.tldr: YOTO improves hybrid VLM visual reasoning by answering directly first, attempting at most one thought, and abandoning failed thoughts rather than forcing their answers.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.
authors: Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, Caiyan Qin, Yang Du, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets failures on motion attributes such as speeding up or slowing down, which models may otherwise solve using static visual cues.
Constructs order-necessary supervision through time-reversal pairs, matched spatial extent, and uniform interval coverage.
Uses six procedural motion primitives, low-rank adaptation, answer-level training, and self-distillation replay on real videos.
Training on 4,000 synthetic clips improves mean accuracy across four motion benchmarks by 7.6, 4.9, and 5.1 points for three video LLMs.
Shuffled-frame training yields less than one point of change, supporting the importance of order-dependent supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ORDO. (a) The curriculum consists of six motion primitives, shown with generator frames and the construction that makes each label order-dependent. (b) The answer loss on curriculum clips trains low-rank adapters of the language model, and a replay loss on real videos keeps the option distribution close to that of the frozen base model.

The three base models and their shuffled-frame controls answer “constant speed”, and ORDO answers correctly on all three backbones. Bottom: change in the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Fine-grained motion understanding in video LLMs via order-necessary supervision; directly fits video understanding and multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: ORDO: Fine-Grained Motion Understanding in Video LLMs via Order-Dependent Supervision
papers.tldr: ORDO improves video LLMs’ fine-grained motion understanding by training them on examples where motion labels can only be inferred from frame order.

papers.abstract: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.

papers.abstract: Nautical charts encode safety-critical maritime information through standardized symbols, attributes, text, and heterogeneous geometries. Interpreting these charts and assessing the navigational significance of successive chart updates requires recognizing nautical features, determining their spatial relationships, and applying navigational knowledge. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising approach to nautical-chart interpretation, yet systematic evaluation of their fine-grained nautical feature recognition, chart-based spatial reasoning, and application of navigational knowledge to assessing chart changes remains limited. We introduce ENC-QA, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 77,312 questions derived from 6,612 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs). The benchmark evaluates four complementary capabilities: ENC Perception, Spatial Reasoning, Joint Perception and Spatial Reasoning, and Application. Of these, 8,227 questions form a progressive subset that decomposes selected chart-change cases into linked questions progressing from change detection to criticality assessment, enabling case-level analysis of how models use perceptual and spatial evidence to determine the navigational significance of chart changes. Evaluations of 10 open-weight VLMs reveal substantial limitations in fine-grained nautical feature recognition and feature-grounded spatial reasoning. Controlled evidence interventions show that relevant perceptual and spatial information improves change-criticality accuracy. Our findings establish ENC-QA as a diagnostic resource for nautical-chart understanding and safety-critical navigational decisions. We will release the benchmark and evaluation code upon publication.

papers.abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

The most consistent models were not necessarily the most factual.

papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.

papers.abstract: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

Curriculum-based reward scheduling reduces reward interference, stabilizes training, and limits proxy over-optimization.

papers.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.
authors: Xu Yuan, Liangbo Ning, Yujuan Ding, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan
bullets: Targets the loss of local multimodal evidence and high overhead in text-centric and earlier Vision-RAG systems.

Represents each page with local region vectors plus a global vector, trained using multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning.
Uses late-interaction matching to estimate region relevance, then rearranges selected regions into a compact visual context.
Across five benchmarks, it improves retrieval and generation over corresponding baselines while reducing visual tokens and computation.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.
authors: Ahmed Aly, Darya Taratynova, Lotfi Abdelkrim Mecharbat, Roman A. Sandler, Joseph Z. Sokol, Joshua Penn, Klaus H. Maier-Hein, Numan Saeed, Mohammad Yaqub
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between full-study reports and view-specific visual evidence, which can cause spurious associations.

Uses multilevel alignment of cardiac structures, videos and studies with report text, guided by a visibility matrix.
Achieves mean AUROC 0.890 for classification and mean quadratic weighted kappa 0.530 for severity grading across 10 unseen external datasets.
Supports detection, severity grading, measurement estimation and cardiac-structure segmentation across 62 clinical findings.

Shading shows how much the curves vary between tasks: at each value of 1 − specificity, the middle 80% of tasks have a sensitivity inside the band. c, Scores computed from text prompts, by reported grade, on MIMIC-IV-Echo, with Spearman’s rank correlation [26] between score and grade. d, Expected grade by reported grade with QWK [27], and AUROC for moderate or greater and for severe valve regurgitation, in the private test set. e, Segmentation contours on CAMUS [28] images: expert (white, dashed) and EchoAlign (navy).

papers.abstract: PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.
authors: Awais Naeem, Zhongling Xu, George Huang, Amy Coffey, Nkechi Okonkwo, Mario Saab-Chalhoub, John Lee Sang, Dina Kokh, Muhammad Zulfiqar, Ankita Shukla, Hairong Wang, Chandra Krishnan, Ying Ding
bullets: Includes 157 cases, 229 original images, and 6,870 augmented images spanning organ, pathology, anatomy, and magnification metadata.
Provides open-ended, five-option multiple-choice, and yes/no questions, with paired correct and incorrect answers for many open-ended items.
Uses ratings from five additional pathologists and two vision-language-model judges to assess item quality.
Offers balanced metadata-based manifests for subgroup evaluation and paired answers for constructing preference examples.
Six models were evaluated zero-shot across all three question formats, without reported comparative performance in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PathOPEN construction and evaluation. Two clinical pathologists collected 157 cases and authored open-ended, multiple-choice (MCQ) and yes/no questions. The example shows one original image, its MCQ with the correct answer and one of four distractors, and four augmentations of the same image. The listed transformations are examples from the augmentation pool. Applying 30 augmentations per available original image yielded 6,870 derived images from 229 originals. Derived images inherit their source questions, answers and metadata. The PathOPEN dataset includes these records and four balanced manifests that select existing augmentations separately for each metadata field. Selections can overlap. Original records and comparator datasets enter the relevant evaluations. Benchmark 4 uses a separate evaluation set of 174 augmented images (Section 2.6.3). Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model (VLM) judges score items using rubrics. Six answering models respond zero-shot across the three question formats. Table 1 gives the dataset and rater scope for each rubric benchmark.

Figure 2: Composition of the PathOPEN metadata. a, b, Case counts by organ system and categorization. c, Counts of the 229 available original images by magnification. d, The fourteen most frequent regional anatomy classes shown in the plot, with 110 cases across the remaining 97 classes. e, Question–answer composition by item type. f, Magnification co-occurrence within cases: diagonal cells count cases with only that magnification, and off-diagonal cells count cases with both magnifications. g, Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients for all four metadata fields, including every class; the diagonal represents equal class proportions. h, Case counts for the 13 most frequent organ systems and 8 most frequent categories. The displayed cells contain 134 of 157 cases, and 41 of the 104 combinations are observed. Grey marks combinations with zero cases. Panel g uses case-level weighting for magnification (Supplementary Note 2). Axis labels use abbreviated display forms where needed; Supplementary Table S7 maps them to the full stored values.

Figure 7: Zero-shot answering across datasets, formats and metadata strata. a–c, Per-model MCQ accuracy, close-ended accuracy and open-ended BERTScore F1. Dashed lines mark dataset-specific MCQ chance levels (2–16 options) and the 50% close-ended chance level. BERTScore F1 is rescaled so that zero denotes similarity no greater than unrelated text; filtered PathVQA falls below zero for two of six models. d, Model ranks within each format (1 = best). Table 8 gives the Spearman rank correlations. e, Kruskal–Wallis H for performance by magnification, for each model and format; 2 of 18 tests reach uncorrected P < 0.05. f–k, Performance by magnification (left) and organ system (right) for MCQ (f, g), close-ended (h, i) and open-ended questions (j, k). Item counts are printed per bin, with counts below n = 30 in red. The comparator records used here lack this metadata. a and b show bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; c shows point estimates. Open-ended results in d, e, j and k use token F1 (Section 2.7.2). Section 4.4 gives the rank and magnification tests and their interpretation. Table 7 reports pooled comparisons.

Figure 5: Wrong-answer difficulty tiers, judge agreement and distractor attraction. a, Pathologist-assigned tiers for native open-ended answers and multiple-choice question (MCQ) distractors. Both Benchmark 2 criteria are pooled. The denominators are 668 native and 1,773 MCQ score pairs with a tier from both the pathologist and Qwen. b, Confusion matrices for Error Proximity and Deductive Plausibility alone, with 1,248 InternVL and 1,221 Qwen score pairs across both answer types. Rows give the pathologist tier and columns the judge tier. Below the diagonal, the judge assigned a harder tier. c, Distractor attraction, measured as the percentage of offered distractors selected within each tier. Five of six models select near-miss distractors more often than far-miss distractors. Item-level accuracy, annotated in the panel, follows the expected direction for only 2 of 6 models. Benchmark 2 scores of 2, 1 and 0 define near-miss, moderate-miss and far-miss tiers; −1 has no tier. Section 4.2 and Table 6 give counts, agreement coefficients, full-pool results and the limits of the three-bin significance test.

Figure 3: Selection and text characteristics of the PathVQA comparator. a, Filtering stages. Images with more than 10 detected nuclei were retained as a proxy for H&E content. We then require at least five words for both the question and answer in open-ended pairs and for the question alone in close-ended pairs. The final subset has 612 open-ended and 3,005 close-ended pairs after applying the length filter. The length filter excludes 86% of open-ended pairs that passed image selection. b, Openended question and answer length distributions for raw PathVQA (dotted lines) and the image-filtered set (solid lines). c, Percentages of open-ended questions, open-ended answers and close-ended questions in three word-count bands (< 5, 5–9 and ≥ 10 words). H&E denotes the image-filtered set. Panels b and c compare the first two stages in a, before the length filter. Section 2.4 gives the filtering procedure and counts.

Figure 4: Ratings of pathology question–answer pairs. a, Word-count distributions for questions, correct answers and wrong answers; violins show the distributions and lines mark medians. Four asterisks denote P < 10−4 in two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests. Filtered PathVQA provides no matched openended wrong answers. b, Percentage of pathologist ratings scored −1 (unable to evaluate) per criterion. The PathOPEN denominators are 231 for each Benchmark 1 criterion and 230 for Benchmark 3. c, d, Rank-biserial effects against filtered PathVQA for Benchmarks 1 and 3, respectively. In c, the first native PathOPEN open-ended slot contributes 231 human ratings per criterion, against 624 reasoning and 622 grounding ratings for PathVQA. Each judge scored 229 versus 612 items. The historical PathVQA totals come from the Benchmark 1 score columns. These include 12 reasoning and 10 grounding scores recorded on close-ended rows (Section 2.6.2). In d, the human comparison uses 230 versus 50 items and each judge comparison uses 229 versus 50. e, Exact agreement, quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ and Gwet’s AC1 between the Qwen judge and the pathologist who rated each item. f, Effects against Quilt-VQA, with 229 versus 724 open-ended items and 229 versus 257 yes/no items per judge. g, Mean scores across disjoint pathologist pools: dots mark means, bars their ranges and adjacent values the spreads; n.s. denotes Kruskal–Wallis P ≥ 0.05. Effects have bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (2,000 resamples), with negative values indicating higher PathOPEN scores; the dashed line marks zero. Encoded −1 values remain in these summaries. Section 4.1 gives the denominators for pathologists and each judge.

Figure 6: Judge assessment of MCQ options and full-context answering. a, b, Mean Benchmark 5 scores by criterion and dataset for correct options (5a) and distractors (5b). Circles denote InternVL and diamonds Qwen; connectors show their score differences, colours identify datasets and whiskers show bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. The judges reverse their dataset ordering on both distractor criteria, so their results are shown separately. c, Standalone Completeness score distributions for InternVL. d, Zero-shot multiple-choice question (MCQ) accuracy with the image and all options present; dashed lines indicate dataset-specific chance levels for option counts from 2 to 16. e, f, Judge–judge quadratic-weighted κ for 5a and 5b, with separate scales. Benchmark 5 has no pathologist baseline: these coefficients measure agreement between the two judges. Short criterion labels in the panels refer to the full rubrics in Supplementary Tables S5 and S6. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 report the option assessments and full-context answering results, respectively.

Figure 8: Ratings of augmented images and class balance after selecting subsets. a, Benchmark 4 ratings from five pathologists and two judges. Dots show the percentage receiving the maximum score; grey bars show the remaining percentage, broken down by score at right. b, Visual Grounding ratings on augmented images (Benchmark 4) and originals (Benchmark 1), using unpaired pools and differently worded criteria. c, Largest-to-smallest class ratios before and after field-specific retention, on a logarithmic scale. d, Ranked class counts before retention (dashed) and after retention (solid), including the flat tail of retained rare classes. e, f, Gini coefficients and normalised Shannon entropy. Uniform 30× augmentation has the same class proportions as the originals and is omitted from these panels. g, h, Gini coefficients and selected image counts across the retention-cap sweep (Section 2.3.2). Colours identify metadata fields. The four manifests each select existing augmentation files for one field and may overlap. Section 4.5 gives the balance results; Table 9 reports augmented-image ratings and agreement.

Table 1: Evaluation design. Each row identifies the object receiving a rubric score. MCQ-derived correct and wrong answers are rated under Benchmarks 1 and 2 as open-ended records; Benchmark 5 separately assesses the options in their MCQ role. The full rubrics are in Supplementary Tables S1–S6.

Table 2: PathOPEN record counts for collected slots and available files. Each question applies to every image in its case. The collected counts include the image slots for cases 9 and 79, which retain their text and metadata. The available counts include only records linked to files. Augmented counts are 30 times the available original-image counts. MCQ denotes multiple-choice question. Pooled correct and wrong counts combine native open-ended answers with individual MCQ options. Section 3 describes the units and relationships.

Table 7: Pooled zero-shot performance across datasets. Means pool six answering models, treating each (model, item) pair as one observation in the Items column. Percentile bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) use 2,000 resamples of those observations. Multiple-choice question (MCQ) and close-ended accuracies are percentages; above-chance accuracy is a percentage-point difference from each dataset’s chance level. Open-ended scores are token F1 multiplied by 100, using the full reference set. Rank-biserial correlations are positive when the first named dataset tends to rank higher. For above-chance MCQ scores the tests compare the ranks of individual model–item scores after subtracting each item’s guessing baseline. The order of these ranks can differ from the order of the dataset means. Mann–Whitney U tests are Holm-corrected within format. The bootstrap treats repeated items and within-case observations as independent, so intervals may understate uncertainty from those dependencies (Sections 2.7.3 and 4.4).

Table 6: Judge and pathologist assignments of wrong-answer difficulty tiers. The upper and middle blocks use Error Proximity and Deductive Plausibility, with 1,248 InternVL and 1,221 Qwen score pairs. Both near-miss ratios use the pathologists’ frequency in the InternVL-matched pool as their denominator. The middle block gives each judge’s distribution conditional on the pathologist tier. The lower block summarises quadratic-weighted κ across both criteria and six answer slots per judge. By authoring route, OE-native denotes native open-ended wrong answers, and MCQ-derived denotes multiple-choice question distractors. Near, Moderate and Far abbreviate near-miss, moderate-miss and far-miss. Scores of −1 carry no tier. Section 4.2 describes the evaluation pools and agreement.

Table 9: Pathologist ratings and judge–pathologist agreement on augmented images. The upper block gives each pathologist’s mean score, maximum-score percentage and unscorable percentage under Benchmark 4; P1–P5 identify the five pathologists. Spread is the range of their means, and P is the Kruskal–Wallis test across their disjoint pools. These summaries retain encoded −1 values. The lower block gives exact agreement, quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and Gwet’s AC1 on shared judge–pathologist items. The three statistics describe agreement under the concentrated score distributions (Section 4.5).

Table 4: Unscorable-item rates across pathologist pools. Entries give the percentage of items scored −1 (unable to evaluate) by each pathologist (P1–P5). Range is the largest minus the smallest percentage, in percentage points; n−1 is the pooled count of unscorable ratings. B1 and B3 denote Benchmarks 1 and 3; their full criterion names are given in Supplementary Tables S1 and S3. The disjoint item pools combine rater and item-composition differences; −1 does not identify a single cause (Section 4.1).

Table 3: Answer ratings and unscorable items in PathOPEN and filtered PathVQA. Scores use {−1, 0, 1, 2}; −1 denotes inability to evaluate. Means, effects and per-pathologist summaries include −1 alongside scores for items that could be rated. Means and effects pool the five pathologists; maximumscore and unscorable percentages average their percentages. Effects are rank-biserial correlations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with negative values indicating higher PathOPEN scores. Rater spread is the range of pathologist means across disjoint pools. B1 and B3 denote Benchmarks 1 and 3. The shortened criterion labels refer to Knowledge Interpretation and Deduction and Visual Grounding (B1), and Visual Grounding/Reasoning (B3), as defined in Supplementary Tables S1 and S3. Historical PathVQA Benchmark 1 counts include entries recorded on close-ended rows (Section 2.6.2). Section 4.1 gives denominators and tests.

Table 5: Mean scores across pathologist pools. P1–P5 identify the five pathologists, each rating a disjoint item pool; n is the pooled rating count per criterion. Means and Kruskal–Wallis tests retain encoded −1 values (Section 2.7.3). Spread is the range of the five means; the test compares their score distributions, with n.s. denoting P ≥ 0.05. B1 and B3 denote Benchmarks 1 and 3, whose full criterion names appear in Supplementary Tables S1 and S3. These separate pools do not support per-item inter-rater coefficients (Section 4.1).

Table 8: Model rank correlations across question formats. Spearman correlations compare the six models’ mean performance on PathOPEN for each pair of formats. MCQ denotes multiple-choice question. None of the three observed correlations reaches P < 0.05; six-model estimates leave uncertainty about the relationship between rankings. Section 4.4 also reports the MCQ–open-ended correlation after averaging across datasets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (ORBIT), an algorithmic intervention that mitigates this collapse at inference time. ORBIT estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations, targeting the cross-lingual degradation induced by low-resource evidence. Experiments across 81 configurations reveal that ORBIT substantially recovers both accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings, exposes calibration offset norms as a diagnostic proxy, and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines.
authors: Huy Trieu, Duy-Minh Nguyen-Tran, Thanh-Dat Nguyen, Huy Tien Nguyen, Tung Le
bullets: Addresses the disproportionate cross-lingual accuracy collapse of small vision-language models on low-resource evidence.
Estimates offset vectors from parallel claim–evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations.
Evaluated across 81 configurations, ORBIT substantially improves low-resource accuracy and F1-score.
Calibration offset norms provide a diagnostic proxy for cross-lingual degradation.
Outperforms translation-based and other activation-steering baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ORBIT. (i) One-time calibration aggregates per-sample claim and evidence shifts from parallel instances into per-language steering vectors vc and ve. (ii) Inference-time steering adds these vectors to hidden states at layer l, realigning the claim span Sc and evidence span Se toward the anchor space without parameter updates.

papers.title: ORBIT: Offset-based Activation Steering for Cross-lingual Multimodal Fact Verification
papers.tldr: ORBIT uses bilingual, span-specific activation offsets at inference time to improve small vision-language models’ multimodal fact verification in low-resource languages.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.
authors: Jiakang Huang, Xueyan Zhang, Renyi Cai, Jingcheng Niu, Jiaru Li, Yining Wang, Josh Zhang, Jiahe Jiang, Jinman Zhao, Gerald Penn, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
bullets: Existing merging rules lose accuracy unevenly across tasks, with recoverable information remaining in each task’s residual.
HR-Merge weights residuals by each task’s validation headroom, re-merges them with the base operator, and adds the result back at a validation-selected strength.
It is a wrapper around any model-merging method and falls back to the base merge when refinement does not help.
On six LLaMA-3 8B NLI adapters, it improved TIES normalized accuracy from 93.29 to 94.29, mainly helping the weakest task.
Across CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improved or preserved accuracy and achieved the best model in every reported setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The HR-Merge pipeline. HR-Merge wraps a base merging method, re-merging headroom-weighted residuals and adding them back at a fail-closed strength.

(c) Gain under headroom weighting: one point per task, validation headroom gt against test gain, pooled over nine cells and colored by backbone.

The dagger and shading mark the main configuration. Zero-shot and Individual are our evaluations.

Table 14: Imbalance of per-task test normalized accuracy before and after HR-Merge. The bottom quartile averages the worst ⌈T/4⌉ tasks of each model. Bold marks an improvement. None of these statistics enters the strength selection, which maximizes the mean.
Table 9: Absolute per-task accuracy of DC-Merge and HR-Merge on the 20-task suite, sorted by the ViT-B/16 gain.

The last column gives the p-value without SVHN. †Here c > b.

Each entry is the mean over three subsamples, with the smallest in parentheses; the 100% column is the deployed run, which uses no subsample.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free model merging method (HR-Merge) that weights residuals by validation headroom to recover lost accuracy, applicable to both LLMs and vision models.
papers.title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
papers.tldr: HR-Merge improves training-free model merging by using validation headroom to selectively re-merge task residuals, recovering accuracy lost by the base merge.

papers.abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.
authors: Zhiqiang Yuan, Qiwei Yan, Liwei Yang, Jinzhe Liu, Yang Liu, Zhongyan Hou, Liyan Xu, Peixiang Luo, Jiapei Zhang, Ying Deng, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Targets on-device deployment, where separate specialized models duplicate capacity under tight memory and compute budgets.
Introduces MGVB to allocate a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained visual information.
Uses ULKD for soft teacher guidance and SEMO for loss/exposure regulation and memory-constrained optimization.
Improves joint representation-generation performance, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74 across five evaluation groups.
Achieves slightly higher balanced performance than the strongest separate-model stack with 61.9% less resident weight memory and 2.64× higher HCD.
papers.selection_reason: Unified on-device multimodal LLM with visual token budgeting and multitask optimization; directly fits multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
papers.tldr: WePM unifies vision-language representation, generation, and decision capabilities in one memory-efficient pocket model by reconciling visual-scale and multitask training conflicts.

papers.abstract: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.
authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Jiajun Zha, Hanqing Wang, Zhenhao Zhang, Huihao Jing, Shing-Chi Cheung, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang
bullets: Auditing five public benchmarks reveals image-only label predictability; same-image prompt probes achieve 0.9645 AUROC without seeing images.
A controlled evaluation crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, preventing any single-modality rule from exceeding 0.500 group-ranking accuracy.
Linear probes on intermediate states reach 0.958 for Qwen3-VL-8B and 0.930 for SmolVLM2-2.2B, indicating scene-intent conjunctions are decodable.
Concatenated image and text representations recover most of the signal, so decodability alone does not prove a fusion mechanism.
Probe-based screening is cheap but generalizes poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks.

Image-first causal masking makes the final prompt token the earliest state that sees both modalities, and controlled modality ablations expose which modality each evaluation suite rewards. Panel a plots measured Qwen3-VL-8B attention weights over token blocks [v1, . . . ,v4,r1, . . . ,r3,e]: visualto-text attention v → r,e is identically 0.0, while the final prompt token e attends across visual and textual keys. Panel b confirms bit-exact visual invariance max |∆hI|= 0.0 under matched-length prompt swaps in image-first prefill versus 155.7 in a prompt-first control. Panels c and d show fixed-probe prompt interventions shifting scores by 0.26–1.86 SD and flipping 6.3%–32.2% of predictions on public benchmarks alongside 65.7%–93.4% on same-image intent pairs. Panel e contrasts retrained modality ablations: on same-image pairs the blind text probe matches the joint probe, whereas on symmetric four-way scene-action groups the joint probe far exceeds the 50.0% unimodal ceiling.

Figure 1. Safety benchmarks can be solved from one modality, and a symmetric control is needed to test joint scene-intent information. Panel a, top: on identical MOSSBench photographs paired with benign and harmful prompts, a probe that sees a blind gray canvas reaches 0.9645 to 0.9846 AUROC, so the text alone decides the label. Panel a, bottom: our four-way MSSBench control crosses a safe and a hazardous scene with an observation and an action request, so that risk requires both modalities; an intermediate joint probe ranks the unsafe case first in 0.958 of groups, against a 50.0% bound for any single-modality rule. Panel b, a secondary result: on Qwen3-VL-8B a cached probe costs 0.234 ms per request at batch size 1, against 95.82 ms for an independent safety pass, and in a separate end-to-end run it adds 0.36% to the 68.0 ms prefill.

Figure 3. Cross-benchmark transfer fails through ranking collapse, which threshold recalibration cannot repair. In panels a and b, applying a source-calibrated 5%-FPR threshold across VSCBench and MSSBench over L1–L4 inflates hollow-circle FPR up to 79.5% on MSSBench→VSCBench. Recalibrating at the 95th percentile of labeled benign target scores with fixed probe weights places all 16 solid-circle points at 4.2%–5.1% FPR, shown with 95% Wilson intervals; because the same benign rows set and evaluate the threshold, this FPR is in-sample by construction. In panel c, transferred AUROC drops to 0.48–0.67, well below the 0.80–0.98 target ceiling. In panel d, percentile-calibrated recall at 5% FPR reaches 6.4%–14.4% TPR, and oracle-threshold recall shown as diamonds reaches 6.9%–14.8% TPR, far below the 34.4%–88.9% target ceiling bars.

Figure 4. Image-disjoint splits remove shared-image leakage, and cached probing anchors the lowlatency deployment frontier. Realized test TPR in panel a and realized test FPR in panel b show 95% Wilson intervals under a 5% calibration FPR target on image-disjoint splits: cached probes lead on both SmolVLM2 suites, within-benchmark safety passes lead on both Qwen3-VL suites, and the hollow circle marks the inflated 88.0% recall produced by request-grouped leakage on Qwen3-VL with MSSBench. Panel c plots the four Qwen3-VL-8B screening routes from Table 4 against batch-1 marginal latency, spanning 0.234 ms for cached probing to 95.82 ms for an independent safety pass.

papers.title: Unimodal Shortcuts and Joint Scene-Intent Dependence in Vision-Language Safety Representations
papers.tldr: Situational safety benchmarks can be solved through unimodal shortcuts, so high accuracy does not establish that vision-language models jointly represent scene and user intent.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.
authors: Guangcheng Song, Weichuan Wang, Linqi Song
bullets: Evaluates open-source VLMs on binary visual mathematical questions using a paired benchmark.
Compares visual inputs with Chain-of-Thought prompting and textual descriptions that replace or supplement images.
Finds that explicit reasoning particularly improves paired consistency accuracy.
Textual descriptions do not consistently help and can reduce performance.
Suggests description-based intermediate representations need better design.

papers.abstract: Initial public offering (IPO) filings describe what a company does and what it intends to become. Yet whether individual forward-looking claims are subsequently realized is difficult to assess. We introduce Vision Follow-Through (VFT), a benchmark and agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment. \vftclaims{} contains 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 IPO filings, while \vftverify{} adds verifiability tiers, follow-through outcomes, and cited later evidence for 1,000 claims. Across language models, classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings. Extraction coverage also varies sharply by category, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered far less often than Market Opportunity claims. Follow-through assessment poses a separate challenge: model judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than exhibiting a single consistent bias. These results show that reliable assessment of corporate follow-through requires both finding the relevant claims and grounding subsequent judgments in later evidence.
authors: Vidhyakshaya Kannan, Shiv Banafar, Michael Galarnyk, Sagnik Nandi, Soumeya Kannan, Shauray Arora, Abanoub Abdelmalak, Sudheer Chava

Language models classify annotated claims more reliably than they extract claims from complete filings.
Extraction varies by claim type, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered less often than Market Opportunity claims.
Follow-through judgments differ from human assessments in varied ways, underscoring the need for evidence grounding.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGLE employs a fine-grained dataset to screen visually-grounded attention heads, followed by entity-aware grounding to extract target-specific regions. It then integrates hierarchical evidence construction and question-guided routing to select optimal view combinations, feeding them into the frozen MLLM to enhance fine-grained visual understanding. Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B demonstrate that EAGLE consistently improves performance across both backbones and achieves SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K compared with existing methods using the same backbone.
bullets: Addresses unreliable attention-head grounding and weak connections between local details and global scene context.
Screens visually grounded attention heads using a fine-grained dataset, then extracts entity-specific regions.
Builds hierarchical evidence and uses question-guided routing to select complementary image views.
Improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B across evaluations, achieving reported SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K with matched backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1. EAGLE overview. (a) Offline voting builds a 128-head pool; the dynamic ranker selects Top-K heads per entity word, with K = 16 chosen on the validation set. (b) Question-guided word weights combine their heatmaps into an entity-phrase grounding map. (c) Two localization rounds construct intermediate and detail images from original pixels. Question-guided routing selects the final views for the frozen MLLM.

Figure 2. Head selection and entity grounding on the soda-can example. (a) Attention maps for “soda” from all 28 heads of the displayed HiDe layer and EAGLE’s selected Top-16 heads. (b) HiDe’s token-wise crops lead to “silver”, whereas EAGLE combines “soda” and “can”, refines the region, and answers “green”.

Figure 4. View-combination examples. O, I, and D denote the original, intermediate, and detail views. Only I + D correctly identifies the blue backpack in (a); O + I + D recovers the car–lion relation in (b); and O + I preserves the context needed for the hall–bus relation in (c). Green marks the correct prediction for each case.

Table 2. Component ablations with Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Accuracy (%). Attr, Spatial, and Avg denote attribute, spatial, and overall accuracy. O, I, and D denote the original, intermediate, and detail images. Fixed-view variants disable routing. Bold marks the best result in each column.

papers.title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
papers.tldr: EAGLE improves fine-grained high-resolution image understanding by grounding target entities and routing hierarchical visual evidence into frozen MLLMs.

papers.abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. Starting from a 4-bit Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint, we apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to the vision, language, attention, and MLP modules and train with instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 examples. We compare this model with an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline, a zero-shot Qwen3-VL configuration, and additional internally evaluated alternatives. On the 1,198 valid CROHME test examples, the CROHME-only model obtains 524 exact matches (43.74%) and a corpus BLEU-4 score of 77.67, compared with 4.92% and 43.26 for the task-specific ViT baseline. An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment issue rather than an automatic benefit from more data. The principal contribution is therefore an evidence-backed, resource-efficient formulation of HMER as multimodal structural generation, together with a controlled data-composition ablation and an analysis of the remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct structure.
authors: Manh Tuan Ha, Xuan Bao Viet Tran, Vo Minh Dat Nguyen, Minh Nhat Vo, Quoc Trung Nguyen, Van Bay Nguyen
bullets: HMER must recover both symbol identities and two-dimensional mathematical structure, not just locally plausible tokens.
The approach fine-tunes Qwen3-VL-4B with rank-16 LoRA across vision, language, attention, and MLP modules using instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 data.
On 1,198 valid test examples, the model achieves 43.74% exact match and 77.67 corpus BLEU-4, versus 4.92% and 43.26 for an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline.
Adding 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples reduces exact match to 42.32%, indicating a domain-alignment problem rather than an automatic benefit from more data.
The study highlights a remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct mathematical structure.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we analyze multi-layer visual representations in large vision-language models (LVLMs) and examine the effectiveness of layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection. Representative LVLMs connect visual encoder features to a language model through a projector. In this design, deep visual encoder features carry high-level semantics and alignment with text representations, whereas shallow and intermediate layers retain information relevant to vision-centric tasks, such as local appearance and fine-grained shape. It is therefore important to choose layer representations and fusion methods according to the nature of the downstream task. Focusing on anomaly detection, we compare layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion across multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers, and examine from several perspectives how multi-layer visual representations affect downstream performance. By analyzing the resulting performance differences, we further discuss the contribution of each layer representation to anomaly detection and provide empirical insights into representation selection for vision-centric tasks.
authors: Satoshi Hashimoto, Hitoshi Nishimura, Mori Kurokawa
bullets: Deep layers provide semantic, text-aligned features, while shallow and intermediate layers preserve local appearance and fine-grained shape information.
The study compares individual layer features with multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection.
Experiments cover multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers.
Layer contributions are analyzed to provide guidance for selecting representations in vision-centric tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that visual tools can improve multimodal reasoning. However, the effects of tools vary substantially across samples, and benchmark accuracy alone does not reveal whether tool interactions are beneficial or redundant. We present $R^2$, a framework that recognizes and reduces redundant visual tool use in vision-language models. We first introduce a sample-level Category Analysis of Tool Utility (CAT), which categorizes samples according to whether a model can benefit from tools. This analysis reveals that benchmark scores may obscure a model's tool-use ability. Across seven benchmarks, samples benefiting from tools account for at most 12.44% of each benchmark, while the majority gain little from tool interaction or are even harmed by it. To assess individual calls, we propose the Visual Feedback Dependency (VFD) metric, which compares the likelihood of the same subsequent reasoning under actual and alternative visual feedback without an external evaluator or trajectory regeneration. Redundancy-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO) combines this dependency signal with a category-conditioned base call cost to assign relative efficiency advantages among correct trajectories, supplementing outcome-based supervision. Across the seven benchmarks, RA-GRPO reduces the mean number of tool calls by 12.39% relative to Vanilla GRPO at comparable benchmark accuracy. Evaluated by tool-utility category, RA-GRPO improves category macro-average accuracy over Vanilla GRPO by 3.35 percentage points.
authors: Yilin Zhao, Jinyu Wang, Wenming Yang
bullets: CAT classifies samples by whether visual tools help, revealing that tool-benefiting samples comprise at most 12.44% of each of seven benchmarks.
VFD measures whether a tool call affects subsequent reasoning by comparing actual versus alternative visual feedback, without external evaluation or trajectory regeneration.
RA-GRPO uses VFD and category-conditioned call costs to reward efficient, nonredundant tool use alongside outcome correctness.
RA-GRPO reduces mean tool calls by 12.39% at comparable accuracy and raises category macro-average accuracy by 3.35 percentage points over Vanilla GRPO.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of R2 for recognizing and reducing redundant visual tool use. CAT compares rollouts with and without tool access to characterize sample-level tool utility and guide training-data selection. VFD measures the dependence of the same subsequent reasoning on actual versus alternative visual feedback. RA-GRPO combines VFD-based redundancy costs with a base call cost for Tool-Independent samples to assign relative efficiency advantages among correct trajectories, supplementing outcome supervision.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.
authors: Jie Gui, Hang Tu, Wen Sha, Xiuquan Du
bullets: Addresses text-mask conflicts caused by repetitive clinical language and vision-dominated cross-attention, especially for multi-site or multi-lesion descriptions.
Uses Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning with soft text-similarity labels to reduce false negatives during pretraining.
Introduces Bidirectional Complementary Attention so visual and textual modalities each guide their own interaction pathway.
Adds KAN-based Attention Gating to strengthen multimodal feature representations without updating the language encoder.
Reports improved text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.
authors: Haoyang Xu, Christian Iha, Colbren Fujimoto, Yingfei Dong, Rui Ning, Liuwan Zhu
bullets: Addresses location leakage from ordinary images even when GPS metadata is removed.
Uses a multimodal proxy to identify location-relevant cues, grounds high-impact regions, and applies localized semantic edits.
Reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models on street-level image datasets.
Preserves perceptual quality more closely to original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines.
Open challenges include deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and evaluation against adaptive attackers.

papers.abstract: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. Visual information gain (VIG) is the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one. It splits exactly into global information, carried by image statistics, and layout information, which shuffling the patches within the image destroys. We apply it to decoders with 158M to 1.04B parameters that read pixel patches through a linear embedding, evaluated every billion tokens up to 40B, and to 19 public checkpoints. In our decoders the image lowers the loss by 3% to 46%, depending on the image type. Global information is present after the first billion tokens. Layout information starts near zero, grows slowly with training and does not grow with model size on five of six image types, and a larger batch reaches the same loss with less of it. With a frozen SigLIP 2 encoder in front of the same decoder the loss is lower only when the arrangement of the image is intact. On shuffled images the losses with and without the encoder agree to within 0.04 nats on five of six image types, so the net advantage of the encoder in the loss is layout information, above all the ability to read text in images. Public encoder-free models at production scale (Gemma 4 12B, NEO, Mono-InternVL) do acquire layout information. On the same documents they have 0.53 to 0.76 nats of it, against 0.65 to 0.82 for recent encoder-based models and 0.04 to 0.07 for our decoders, and their released training stages show it rising. These results agree with the reported parity of the two families when both are trained from scratch and place the reported advantage of a pretrained encoder in layout information.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Wei Qiu
bullets: Visual information gain (VIG) measures how much an image reduces loss versus a uniform replacement and separates global statistics from spatial layout.
In 158M–1.04B encoder-free decoders, global information appears early, while layout information grows slowly and is largely insensitive to model size.
A frozen SigLIP 2 encoder helps only when image arrangement is preserved; on shuffled images, its loss is nearly identical to the encoder-free setup.
Production-scale encoder-free models acquire substantial layout information, approaching recent encoder-based models on documents.
The findings support parity between model families trained from scratch and attribute pretrained-encoder benefits primarily to layout information.
