papers.title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
papers.tldr: Visual encoders mainly improve multimodal pretraining by providing layout-sensitive information—especially text-reading ability—rather than simply lowering text loss.

papers.abstract: Zooming into a region often turns a wrong answer from a vision-language model (VLM) into a right one, and a growing literature takes this as evidence that the model lacked the pixels. But a zoom changes several things at once. It removes the surrounding context, re-tokenizes, at a higher density, pixels the model has already seen, and, if the first pass was downsampled, exposes detail the model never received. We separate these factors for each failure. Holding the first pass fixed, we vary only the second look and assign every failure to the cheapest one that fixes it: reusing cached tokens, isolating the region, re-tokenizing the seen pixels, or acquiring new ones. The study covers 2,753 zoom-rescued failures of Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3 on V*, ZoomBench and TextVQA, at first-pass budgets from 17x fewer pixels than the source to native resolution. First, most rescued failures did not lack the pixels: upsampling the pixels the model had already seen fixes 47-73% of them even at 17x downsampling, against 1-3% for a random region. Second, the first-pass budget decides how often new pixels are needed: depending on the benchmark, new pixels are required for 23-50% of the rescues at 17x and for 12-23% at 4x. The missing-pixel reading and the accounts that dispute it thus hold at different budgets. Third, the useful magnification is large and differs between objects and text: seen pixels fix more failures up to 6-12x their first-pass size per side on objects and saturate by 4x on text, and even native pixels gain from being rendered beyond native resolution. Allowing any magnification, 68-94% of the failures at 17x need no new pixels. These models more often need a better rendering of evidence they already have than new pixels, which motivates re-tokenizing a region before acquiring it.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Kexin Geng, Wei Qiu
bullets: The study decomposes zoom benefits into cached-token reuse, region isolation, re-tokenization of seen pixels, and acquisition of new pixels.
Across 2,753 zoom-rescued failures in three VLMs and three benchmarks, upsampling previously seen pixels fixed 47–73% of failures, versus 1–3% for random regions, even under heavy downsampling.
New pixels were needed for 23–50% of rescues at 17× downsampling and 12–23% at 4×, showing that the initial pixel budget changes the interpretation of zoom success.
Useful magnification differs by content: seen pixels help up to 6–12× per side for objects and saturate around 4× for text; even native pixels can benefit from further enlargement.
With unrestricted magnification, 68–94% of failures at 17× downsampling required no new pixels, motivating re-tokenization before acquiring additional image content.

papers.title: What Does a Zoom Actually Add? Decomposing Fine-Grained Perception Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Zooming often fixes VLM errors by rendering already-seen pixels better—not by revealing new visual information—and the balance depends on the initial image resolution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for embodied perception and reasoning, yet their physical understanding is largely evaluated on questions answerable from images. Many properties critical to manipulation, such as an opaque bottle's fill level or an object's compliance, may only be revealed through touch. We introduce TouchBench, an egocentric vision-language-tactile benchmark that distinguishes visually answerable questions (Tier A) from those involving properties hidden from the camera (Tier B). It pairs head-mounted video with synchronized 137-channel whole-hand tactile sensing, comprising 900 clips from five participants across 11 tasks, with 900 absolute and 4,102 relative questions. Four state-of-the-art VLMs average 66.4% accuracy on Tier A relative questions but only 49.8% on Tier B, near chance (50%). To bridge this gap, we propose Tactile-as-Prompt (TaP), which presents 34 interpretable tactile statistics as text, enabling VLMs to reason with touch without a learned tactile encoder. TaP raises zero-shot Tier B relative accuracy to 62.9% and reaches 73.1% after leave-one-user-out fine-tuning, outperforming video alone (67.4%) and a learned tactile-token encoder (67.3%). The gains extend to unseen objects and users. On a separate 20-hour in-the-wild corpus, tactile text improves fine-tuned contact-question accuracy from 67.1% to 75.5%. These results highlight the limits of vision-only physical reasoning and establish language as an effective interface for tactile perception.
authors: Ziyao Zeng, Ziyi Kou, Chuan Qin, Mia Huang, Roger Boldu, Zhiwen Fan, Daniel Rakita, Eric Whitmire, Li Guan
bullets: Introduces an egocentric vision-language-tactile benchmark separating visually answerable questions from camera-hidden physical properties.
Combines head-mounted video with synchronized 137-channel whole-hand tactile sensing across 900 clips, 11 tasks, and five participants.
Four VLMs achieve 66.4% on visually answerable relative questions but only 49.8% on touch-dependent questions, near chance.
Tactile-as-Prompt (TaP) represents 34 tactile statistics as text, raising Tier B zero-shot accuracy to 62.9% and leave-one-user-out accuracy to 73.1%.
Tactile text also improves contact-question accuracy on a separate in-the-wild corpus from 67.1% to 75.5%.

figures.caption: Figure 3. The Tactile-as-Prompt interface can turn the input whole-hand touch into a prompt for VLM inference. The glove stream is summarized by 34 interpretable statistics in four groups (ϕ) and serialized as text into the prompt (σ). For illustration, each card and prompt shows a few of its group’s statistics with their values for this clip. The video frames, this line, and the question form a prompt for VLM inference. papers.abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).
authors: Yixuan Duan, Kexin Geng, Hanwen Xu, Wei Qiu
bullets: Addresses two gaps: H&E-only pathology models lack mIF-derived cell phenotypes, and final-answer rewards do not verify intermediate reasoning.

A process reward checks each stated quantity against cell-level mIF ground truth during R1-style reinforcement learning.
Across four colorectal cancer TIME tasks, HERMES achieves 84.5% average accuracy, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline at 74.7%.
Maintains strong performance without retraining on CODEX images and on head and neck cancer, though its scope is evaluated on field-level tasks and specific cohorts.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of knowledge transfer when visual token compression creates mismatched teacher and student token counts.
Reconstructs teacher visual states after the final LLM layer and before an important intermediate layer.
Uses response-level supervision at the intermediate layer instead of direct token-wise KL or MSE matching.
Adds an attention-readout loss to align contextual information integration during response prediction.
Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show improved performance for token-compressed students while retaining inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Multi-step visual reasoning suffers when early visual misinterpretations persist as incorrect premises in subsequent reasoning. We argue that how visual evidence is represented during reasoning matters as much as how much of it is gathered. Rather than appending observations and inferences to an ever-growing dialogue, we introduce a Visual Board-centered harness that separates visual observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning within a structured, capacity-bounded, and revisable workspace. This separation makes each premise explicit and auditable, so that conflicts between what is seen and what is derived become detectable even by a text-only critic and can trigger targeted reinspection of the original image. Without task-specific training, our harness consistently outperforms standalone models across 4B, 8B, Qwen3-VL-Flash, and 32B configurations on Euclid30K, SolidGeo, and ChartQA bar charts, with gains of up to 11.68, 18.42, and 24.82 percentage points, respectively. Under identical tools, critic, and interaction limits, the structured Board outperforms shared free-form notes by 6.67 to 13.00 points and no-Board retries by 7.35 to 18.80 points while using 7.9\% to 38.2\% fewer tokens. Supervised fine-tuning on harness trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with positive transfer to chart reasoning.
bullets: Addresses error propagation from treating uncertain visual interpretations as established premises.
Separates observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning in a capacity-bounded, auditable workspace.
Enables text-only critics to detect conflicts and trigger targeted reinspection of the original image.
Without task-specific training, outperforms standalone models and free-form or no-Board alternatives across geometry and chart tasks.
Supervised fine-tuning on Board trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with transfer to chart reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the Visual Board-centered harness. (c) Supervised fine-tuning of a Qwen3-VL-4B Solver on geometry harness trajectories helps critic-free tool use far more than direct answering.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.
bullets: Introduces a multimodal Jacobian lens that maps vision and language states into the decoder vocabulary’s shared semantic space.
Uses token sets and internal concept interventions to measure concept accessibility, selective access, and causal effects.
Finds that accessed concepts participate in downstream computation and reasoning through counterfactual tests.
Proposes two J-space metrics for tracking cross-modal concept alignment, which develop before reliable selective access.
Observes similar accessibility, query-dependent selectivity, and intervention patterns across VLM families and sizes, despite differing internal organisation.

papers.abstract: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.

papers.abstract: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.

papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
bullets: Evaluates five LLMs editing convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks.

ERT rehearses the direct closed-form weight edits performed by LLMs and achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.
authors: Yuqi Tang, Yang Shi, Yuran Wang, Tengfei Liu, Rundong Wang, Zongyang Qiu, Qixun Wang, Zhuoran Zhang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yifan Xu, Yiyan Ji, Shujie Li, Shixuan Liu, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Chengwei Qin

Built from 50,000 examples across eight egocentric video sources and evaluated on five benchmarks.

Reports leading performance among evaluated open-source models, with additional gains over specified proprietary baselines on PhysCapBench and Minerva-Ego; ablations support the reward design and coarse-to-fine annotation.

papers.abstract: Agentic visual reasoning improves vision-language models by selectively enlarging evidence without adding new scene content, but the benefit depends on whether fine structure remains accessible and whether local observations stay grounded in the full scene. We identify three recurring bottlenecks: high-frequency detail can be attenuated during visual-token formation; spatially distributed evidence can remain encoded yet difficult for the language model to retrieve; and isolated crops can weaken whole-detail correspondence through scale and positional mismatch. ResVision addresses these limitations with two complementary components. Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) estimates image complexity and selects an adaptive global sampling scale, avoiding unnecessary enlargement on simple inputs while allocating more visual tokens to detail-rich images. Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) returns each inspected crop together with the complete working view, preserving local detail and global context across tool turns. We evaluate Direct and Agentic variants on four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks spanning six visual-reasoning families. Complete ResVision (Agentic Base plus SMR plus CPI) is best for every model, improving by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base. These results show that adaptive visual sampling and context-preserving inspection address distinct, complementary constraints in multimodal reasoning.
authors: Guojian Zhan, Jiahao Xu, Yahui Liu, Yao Hu, Chuan Mu
bullets: Targets three bottlenecks: lost high-frequency detail, difficult retrieval of distributed evidence, and weakened crop-to-scene correspondence.
Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) selects a global sampling scale based on image complexity, avoiding unnecessary enlargement while allocating more tokens to detailed images.
Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) pairs each inspected crop with the complete working view to retain local detail and global grounding.
Evaluated across four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks covering six visual-reasoning families.
The full Agentic system improved over Direct Base and Agentic Base for every model, with gains of 3.36–4.94 and 1.87–2.94 points, respectively.

papers.abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png
authors: Maximilian Seeth, Chengzhi Martin Hu, Marie Kempkes, Paul R\"ottger, Leo Schwinn
bullets: Textual skills are easy to transfer but cannot be continuously optimized; model finetuning is optimizable but model-specific.
The method uses gradient descent to optimize skill-like images through a frozen VLM’s vision encoder.
A single image can be jointly optimized for an ensemble of VLMs, enabling transfer across those models.
Across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks, Skill.png outperformed frontier-LLM-optimized textual skills in 9 of 16 settings.
Combining optimized image and text skills further improves agent performance; image skills use 64–256 tokens versus roughly 900–2,000 text tokens.

papers.abstract: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.
authors: Yu Zhao, Jiaxin Zhang, Rohit Saxena, Fazl Barez, Pasquale Minervini, Yiwen Guo
bullets: TwI models often invoke zooming but ignore the returned visual evidence, especially when questions are answerable without tools.
The method dynamically selects questions where zoomed evidence remains necessary and useful as the model improves.
A synthesis pipeline creates fine-detail questions about localized small objects, while an adaptiveness reward discourages unnecessary tool use.
The approach improves visual search performance by 11.6% on V*, 7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and 9.4% on HR-Bench 8K, and outperforms compared TwI baselines on multimodal hallucination benchmarks.
Results indicate that faithfulness and accuracy can improve together without directly supervising the reasoning process.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework with three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills the explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.
authors: Wei Dai, Jinkun Liu, Jiayi Chen, Han Liu, Wenbo Ding, Shaolun Huang
bullets: Addresses failures in tool-contract following, limited access to frontier teacher internals, and imitation degradation under rollout distribution shift.
Synthesizes and filters teacher trajectories, distills explanation-and-code targets into a trainable 9B VLM, then optimizes student rollouts with runtime-error-penalized rewards.
Uses the same primitive-free Python tool throughout, exposing only visual observations and seven-dimensional end-effector control.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks, held-out success improves from 0/100 for the base model to 14/100 after SFT and 84/100 after RL; median calls per episode fall from 36 to 11.
Finds and mitigates a self-reinforcing runtime-error failure mode through failure monitoring and sampling-side curation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The EmbodyAgent full-pipeline post-training framework; the photographs are LIBERO Spatial frames. Center: the three-stage pipeline. Stage 1 (black-box data synthesis) queries Astra Medium on training-split initial states without accessing teacher weights and filters successful think-then-code episodes into 1,475 targets; Stage 2 (multimodal SFT) distills these targets into an open-weight 9B VLM; Stage 3 (online RL) optimizes the student’s own rollouts via group-relative outcome credit. The purple dashed line indicates the black-box Astra Medium teacher’s collection acceptance rate (32%, validated episodes over valid attempts, averaged over tasks); under RL, student rollout success rises from 8.4% to 87.7%, surpassing the teacher’s collection rate. The shaded band marks rounds 21–33, where runtime-error episodes dominated failures. papers.abstract: Images under non-uniform coupled degradations require diverse restoration capabilities for different degraded regions. Existing methods employ globally uniform operations, potentially overlooking regional differences and causing incomplete restoration or even damage to image content. Moreover, a degraded region may require successive restoration actions, and earlier actions may alter residual degradation characteristics or introduce artifacts, potentially hindering subsequent restoration. To address these challenges, we propose RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework that trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) through two-stage preference learning to generate a region-specific restoration action at each iteration. Specifically, we first train the VLM to select an action suited to the current region through step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using preferences derived from immediate restoration feedback to supervise only the differing component in each action pair. To account for the effects of current actions on subsequent restoration, we then apply trajectory-level DPO, using preferences derived from complete trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing action in each trajectory pair. Furthermore, as conventional image-pair datasets do not directly provide preferences over regional restoration decisions, we construct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs for two-stage VLM training. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and single degradations. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of two-stage preference learning in improving restoration quality.
authors: Weiyu Zhou, Jiacong Tang, Tao Hu, Axi Niu, Jinqiu Sun, Peng Wu, Wei Dong, Qingsen Yan
bullets: Targets mixed or coupled degradations where globally uniform restoration can miss regional needs or damage content.
Uses step-level DPO to choose actions based on immediate regional restoration feedback.
Uses trajectory-level DPO to account for how earlier actions affect later restoration and artifacts.
Introduces a regional preference dataset with 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs.
Experiments across multiple datasets show strong performance on mixed and single degradations; ablations support both preference-learning stages.

papers.title: RegionAgent: Two-Stage Preference Optimization for Regional Image Restoration
papers.tldr: RegionAgent trains a vision-language model with two-stage preference optimization to select iterative, region-specific restoration actions for images with non-uniform degradations.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a \emph{Pixel Diffusion Head} tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight \emph{HiGate} pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.
authors: Jiahao Hu, Jingdong Du, Yichen Zhang, Yi Song, Zhenyu Zhang, Jiaxin Niu, Ruihang Li, Xiangzhao Hao, Yiqian Zhang, Yong Huang, Zefeng Zhang, Zheyuan Gu, Shuohuan Wang
bullets: Targets the fragmented architectures commonly used for multimodal understanding and generation.
Reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both tasks, with specialization confined to the output side.
Introduces a Pixel Diffusion Head for direct pixel-space generation and a HiGate pathway to restore fine spatial details lost by semantic visual representations.
Maintains a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while achieving competitive image generation and editing performance.
Experiments indicate that one shared dense backbone can support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation.

papers.abstract: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.
authors: Jongbhin Woo, Jaewook Jeong, Joon Son Chung
bullets: The identified attention heads shift with the queried sound and follow it as it moves, while disrupting them often harms timestamp accuracy.
Intervals read directly from these heads recover events missed by the model’s original timestamps and outperform its answer.
Head-guided decoding preserves the model’s sound-presence decision and rescores candidate timestamps using attention-derived priors.
Heads selected on development data transfer to new recordings and free-text queries, improving timestamps across three audio LLMs.
On post-training recordings, mIoU increases from 0.07–0.36 to 0.48–0.56.

papers.title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
papers.tldr: Audio LLMs may detect when a sound occurs but fail to verbalize its timing; using a few sound-tracking attention heads enables training-free timestamp correction.

papers.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.
authors: Yutong Guan, Meixing Shi, Haoran Sun, Bing Sun, Yuxiang Cai, Yankai Jiang
bullets: Builds a hierarchical, time-indexed memory that aligns diverse evidence along a unified video timeline.
Uses temporal cues from retrieved evidence to constrain and guide subsequent memory access.
Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces EvoMem, a memory agent for long-video reasoning that uses self-evolving retrieval skills guided by RL, addressing procedural errors in long-context video understanding.
papers.title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
papers.tldr: EvoMem improves long-video question answering by using time-aware memory retrieval and self-evolving skills to maintain coherent evidence chains.

papers.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
authors: Linjia Kang, Binhan Jiang, Juan Yang, Zhiqin Song, Xiangsen Wu, Qionglin Ren, Jiang Liu, Zhongjiang He, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses limited guidance for intermediate decisions and the cost of repeated planning in tool-augmented VLMs.
Uses policy learning and experience evolution, including RSPO for process-aware training and WDL for weakness-targeted demonstrations.
At inference, LAWR reuses suitable workflows for a fast path, while a ReAct-based path handles novel tasks.
Label-free feedback from execution, workflow adoption, and cost savings updates workflow memory.
Across three benchmarks, reports up to 8.0% relative improvement and up to 52.1% lower token consumption.

(C) Inference with Experience Evolution: The agent follows a fast path by reusing suitable parameterized workflows or a slow ReAct-based path for adaptive reasoning. papers.abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.
authors: Qiming Huang, Hanze Dong, Jipeng Zhang, Mike Zheng Shou, Xinxing Xu, Furu Wei
bullets: Introduces Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four medical image types with answer-relevant masks and multiple renderings.
Shows that different presentations of the same mask can substantially alter model behavior.
Finds that masks can reveal missed diagnostic evidence but also induce incorrect associations, even when the mask is correct.
Introduces TUNE, which manages evidence acquisition, presentation, and answer updates.
TUNE improves mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points for a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone across three public medical VQA benchmarks, and by 9.1 points over direct tool use across seven benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spurious correlations can give image predictors high in-distribution accuracy but poor generalization under distribution shift. We introduce $\textbf{Rank2Replace}$, which transfers knowledge of task-relevant evidence from pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) to small predictors through training-time augmentation for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance and guides rank-dependent replacement with same-rank slot embeddings from another image. This augmentation retains the original image's label, encouraging reliance on preserved task evidence as incidental cues change, and supports combination with existing OOD methods. Across four datasets and six splits under shared frozen slot embeddings, the default cross-entropy configuration reaches macro-averaged average-group and worst-group accuracies of $80.43\%$ and $65.28\%$ without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning. Slot corruption improves both macro-averaged metrics for all fourteen OOD training methods. Combining it with slot ranking and IRM reaches $81.96\%$ and $72.68\%$. Controlled ablations support the ranking and replacement design, with gains across five ranking VLMs and six extractor--predictor combinations. Permutation-invariant predictors further improve both macro-averaged metrics over their unaugmented counterparts while using VLM guidance only during training for efficient inference.
authors: Bo-Han Feng, Keng-Te Liao, Shou-De Lin
bullets: A VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance, then replaces slots with same-rank slots from another image.
The method preserves the source label while changing incidental visual cues, encouraging predictors to use task-relevant evidence.
It works without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning and can combine with existing OOD methods.
Across four datasets and six splits, the default setup achieves 80.43% macro average-group and 65.28% macro worst-group accuracy; combining ranking with IRM reaches 81.96% and 72.68%.
Benefits are observed across 14 OOD methods, five ranking VLMs, and six extractor–predictor combinations; VLM guidance is needed only during training.

papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
bullets: The study separates CHAIR improvements into reduced verbosity versus genuine hallucination reduction by matching object recall with truncated base-model captions.
A frozen, 11-feature probe trained on 500 annotated images reproduces at least two thirds of beyond-brevity gains for most evaluated methods, with RLAIF-V as the main exception.
At matched recall, the base model plus probe generally outperforms truncation across LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, COCO, and AMBER evaluations.
Probe- or CLIP-based preference labels recover substantial portions of ground-truth-labelled DPO gains, while outperforming random labels; CLIP labels perform better on COCO.
Human checks support the probe’s deletions, but also identify insufficient precision in the CHAIR evaluator as a limitation.

papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.tldr: Much of anti-hallucination training’s apparent benefit comes from shorter captions and can be replicated by a cheap post-hoc probe, though some methods and backbones retain gains beyond brevity.

papers.abstract: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.
authors: Yingshuo Wang, Weixiang Zhao, Guancheng Li, Jiahe Guo, Yu Zhang, Yanyan Zhao
bullets: Rationale hallucination includes unsupported visual facts and incorrect safety interpretations of grounded content.
Hallucination remains common across generation methods, vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, even with higher classification accuracy or model scale.
Fine-grained attributes and relations are especially problematic; visual tools are often underused or lack sufficient spatial focus.
Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning (TCG-RL) rewards tool use only when it improves grounding over a tool-free reference.
The findings support evaluating safety guards for both prediction accuracy and verifiable rationale grounding.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies and mitigates rationale hallucination in multimodal safety guards, relevant to vision-language foundation model reliability and grounding.
papers.title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.
authors: Youngwoo Shin, Jongsuk Kim, Junmo Kim
bullets: SFT can make VideoLLMs rely on textual regularities instead of video evidence, even when in-distribution accuracy improves.
VETO intervenes in the fine-tuning update rather than defining or filtering shortcut-related data.
It identifies the subspace occupied by text-only inputs and projects updates onto its orthogonal complement.
Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves in-distribution SFT gains and improves performance on six shifted-distribution benchmarks.
The method is designed to ground answers in the full video-text input, though its scope is evaluated on the reported models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
authors: Yajie Qi, Wei Wei, Lin Li, Lijun Zhang, Jianye Hao
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards, long horizons, and inconsistent goals from prompt-only language-model guidance.
Introduces CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset built from Craftax-Classic interaction trajectories.
Uses offline KLTDPO fine-tuning to align the VLM with goal preferences, followed by online goal-guided RL.
The method collects diamonds earlier and achieves the highest score and reward in experiments.
It attains the highest success rates on most achievements; results are scoped to Craftax-Classic.

papers.abstract: DeepStack-style vision-language models feed visual tokens to the language model at its input, and again at deeper layers. We call these the main entry and the later entries. What do the later entries add when the model already has the image? We give the entries versions that differ in one object's color and see which one the answer follows. On photographs, the original DeepStack follows the later entries, while Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follow the main entry. Does weakening the main entry give the later features more influence? On synthetic images, we keep this conflict and reduce color saturation at the main entry only. The unchanged later features gain a stronger effect on the relative scores of the two colors, in all four models, including Granite Vision. This holds even under mild desaturation, when accuracy without the conflict stays at 100%. To test whether later features can also correct errors, we degrade both entries and restore only the later ones. The same blur costs both Qwen models 50 percentage points of accuracy on stripe orientation. The 32B model recovers 48 points and the 8B model only 8. Accuracy with one clean entry predicted which entry each model can lose, and five of six tested predictions held on new GQA attribute questions. With the other entry zeroed, Qwen3-VL-8B loses only 0.3 points on its main entry alone, and DeepStack at most 3.45 points on either entry alone. In split inference on these questions, DeepStack can then send only its main-entry features at higher precision. This takes 49% fewer bytes than all entries at a shared precision, at similar accuracy.
authors: Yucheng Du, Yi Nian, Ruixue Lian, Yue Zhao, Xiyang Hu
bullets: The study compares conflicting object-color information placed in the main input entry versus later-layer entries.
On photographs, DeepStack follows later entries, whereas Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follows the main entry.
Reducing saturation only at the main entry increases the influence of unchanged later features across four models, even when normal accuracy remains 100%.
When both entries are blurred and only later features are restored, Qwen3-VL-32B recovers 48 of 50 accuracy points, while the 8B model recovers 8.
Entry-specific influence predictions generalize to most tested GQA attribute questions, enabling DeepStack split inference with 49% fewer bytes at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.
authors: Jiatong Ma, Yuchen Liu, Longteng Guo, Yichen Yuan, Yuze Wu, Dongze Hao, Ru Zhen, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu, Jing Liu
bullets: Models must use visual evidence both before and after knowledge retrieval, including identifying clues, retrieving images, and localizing or verifying matched knowledge.
The benchmark distinguishes internal versus external images and provides traceable textual and visual evidence in a controlled multimodal knowledge base.
Twenty-one MLLMs are evaluated across no-knowledge, provided-evidence, knowledge-base retrieval, and open-web search settings.
Results show that vision-centric reasoning remains difficult, with fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition as the main bottleneck.
Agentic retrieval suggests benefits from multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration.

papers.abstract: An age prompt can change how a vision-language model (VLM) rates the emotion evoked by an image. Does the change predict how people of different ages rate that same image? We evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and estimate image-specific age differences from ratings by 822 participants. Without an age cue, models closely track average human valence (median Pearson $r=0.891$). Under an older-adult prompt, 16 of 17 models assign lower valence on average than under a young-adult prompt. Yet after adjusting for image pleasantness, correlations between model and human age effects range from $-0.030$ to $0.093$, against an estimated ceiling of $0.595$. The discrepancy is clearest on 54 sensitive images rated as pleasant. Across models, the older prompt reduces valence by $0.845$ points on average, while older participants rate these images $0.443$ points higher than younger participants. Providing human ratings from other images improves agreement on the direction of age differences, although image-specific fidelity remains modest on 600 held-out images ($r_{\mathrm{part}}=0.105$). These results show why evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models need human comparisons at the level of individual stimuli. Project page available at https://shahriyar-zaman.github.io/age-conditioned-emotion-reasoning/
authors: Shahriyar Zaman Ridoy, Azmine Toushik Wasi, Lin Gu, Ruogu Fang
bullets: Evaluates 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images with young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts, comparing them with ratings from 822 participants.
Without age cues, models closely match average human valence, but age-conditioned effects show near-zero agreement with human age effects.
Older-adult prompts lower model valence for 16 of 17 models, whereas older participants often rate sensitive pleasant images more positively than younger participants.
Human ratings from other images improve prediction of the direction of age differences, though image-specific agreement remains modest.
Findings emphasize evaluating demographic personalization against human judgments for individual stimuli, not only aggregate behavior.

papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.
authors: Zihan Xiao (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Boshen Xu (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Pei Fu (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jianzhong Ju (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Zhenbo Luo (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jian Luan (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Qin Jin (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China)
bullets: Video MLLMs face major memory and latency costs from large numbers of visual tokens.
Existing compression methods are difficult to compare fairly because evaluations use different setups, tasks, and models.
VidToC provides a controlled framework spanning representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time-encoding strategies.
Experiments across three video-understanding tasks show that compression behavior depends on the task, compression placement, time encoding, and backbone.
The study offers empirical guidance for selecting compression strategies, including across hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures.

papers.abstract: In multimodal multi-turn dialogue, dialogue history plays a dual role: reliable responses provide useful context for subsequent turns, whereas hallucinated responses can propagate errors across turns. Existing training-free methods globally adjust the effect of dialogue history on generation, making it difficult to suppress misleading information without weakening useful context. To address this trade-off, we introduce Support-Guided Triadic Decoding (SGTD), a training-free framework that selectively controls the influence of unreliable history and fuses complementary predictions during decoding. Specifically, Historical Answer Support Estimation measures the visual support of historical responses against type-matched alternatives and identifies low-support content that may mislead later generation. Support-Targeted Attention Intervention then weakens the influence of this content while preserving the surrounding dialogue, producing a support-refined prediction. Triadic Decoding combines this prediction with the full-history prediction and answer-free visual evidence, while the Support-Adaptive Plausibility Constraint filters implausible tokens using visual agreement and historical support. Experiments on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench across representative LVLMs show that SGTD consistently achieves the highest accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving the benefits of factual context.
authors: Yiheng Li, Wenhao Wang, Xingyi Li, Zhilin Tang, Zichang Tan, Zhen Lei, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets error propagation from hallucinated responses in multi-turn multimodal dialogue.
Uses historical answer support estimation to identify responses with weak visual grounding.
Applies targeted attention intervention to suppress misleading history while retaining useful context.
Fuses full-history, support-refined, and answer-free visual predictions with plausibility filtering.
Evaluated across representative LVLMs on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench, achieving the highest reported accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving factual-context benefits.

papers.title: Support-Guided Triadic Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Dialogue with LVLMs

papers.abstract: Despite strong multimodal capabilities, large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate when linguistic priors outweigh visual evidence or when predictions are grounded in irrelevant or misleading image regions. Training-free contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by contrasting the original prediction with an auxiliary one that exposes linguistic priors. Yet existing methods focus on altering the auxiliary input or computation and do not ensure that either branch uses query-relevant visual evidence during decoding. We propose Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding (VEGD), a training-free framework that identifies query-relevant visual evidence and guides its use throughout contrastive decoding. VEGD locates this evidence by aggregating localization heads with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure, then selectively weakens it in the auxiliary image. During generation, VEGD directs visual-carrier heads in both branches toward the same evidence location, strengthening access to intact evidence in the main branch while anchoring the auxiliary branch to its weakened counterpart. An adaptive distribution fusion strategy then combines or contrasts their predictions according to distribution divergence. Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that VEGD consistently reduces hallucinations.
authors: Yiheng Li, Wenhao Wang, Xingyi Li, Mingda Jia, Zichang Tan, Yinhang Tang, Zhen Lei, Yang Yang
bullets: Addresses hallucinations caused by linguistic priors and irrelevant or misleading image regions.
Uses localization heads to identify query-relevant evidence with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure.
Selectively weakens the identified evidence in the auxiliary image and guides visual-carrier heads in both decoding branches to the same location.
Adaptively fuses or contrasts branch predictions based on their distribution divergence.
Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks show consistent hallucination reduction.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding. (a) Visual Evidence-Guided Auxiliary Branch Construction identifies queryrelevant visual evidence with selected localization heads and uses it to construct the auxiliary image. (b) Dual-Branch Evidence Anchoring guides visual-carrier heads in both branches toward the same evidence during decoding, followed by adaptive fusion of their predictions.

Figure 1. Comparison of visual evidence utilization between our method and existing decoding methods. (a) Standard decoding is distracted by irrelevant visual content. (b) Existing contrastive decoding exposes language priors through the auxiliary branch, but the main branch may still rely on irrelevant or misleading visual evidence. papers.abstract: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.
bullets: Combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech synthesis in a self-contained checkpoint.

Reports 74.22% on MMMU, 82.26% strict IFEval accuracy, and 89.40% on MATH-500.
Achieves 390 ms speech first-chunk latency and 594.41 output tokens/s for a concurrent 128-answer batch on NVIDIA GB10.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

TuringPAI-Drive stays within 1.2% of a full-token baseline on evaluated ADE/FDE metrics and runs at 12 Hz on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Dooman Arefan, Shandong Wu
bullets: Addresses the risk that visual-token compression removes contextual information needed to interpret subtle mammographic lesions.
Uses a bilateral-guided token selector to prioritize lesions and their local and contralateral-breast context within a shared token budget.
Applies a bilateral reward to encourage diagnostic reasoning that benefits from preserved cross-image evidence.
Experiments on datasets built from CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo report better evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets.
Inference benchmarking shows reduced prefill latency.
