papers.abstract: Recent multimodal safety alignment heavily relies on a text-centric paradigm, assuming risks are explicit in language or globally prominent in images. However, real-world hazards are often visually subtle or peripheral, causing existing models to fail due to their reliance on coarse, global visual representations. In this work, we study fine-grained visual safety alignment and introduce a challenging 1,200-sample benchmark across four domains, where hazards necessitate localized inspection. To address this, we propose Fine-Grained RLAIF (FGR), a reinforcement learning framework that casts image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy. FGR employs a decomposed reward design to jointly align three core safety behaviors: (i) where to look via a visual evidence reward, (ii) when to act via a tool-formatting constraint, and (iii) how to reason via visually grounded safety explanations. FGR achieves accuracy ranging from 86.71% to 93.00%, consistently outperforming strong multimodal and agent-based baselines.
authors: Chunxue Xu, Yiwei Wang, Yujun Cai, Songze Li
bullets: Introduces a 1,200-sample benchmark spanning four domains, focused on hazards requiring localized visual inspection.
Frames image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy through reinforcement learning.
Uses decomposed rewards to guide where to look, when to use the tool, and how to produce visually grounded safety explanations.
Reports accuracy of 86.71%–93.00%, outperforming the evaluated multimodal and agent-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.
authors: Yikang Qiao, Jianye Zeng, Duan Huang, Ziying Song
bullets: Introduces a training-free framework separating permutation, retention, precision, and statistical replacement effects.
On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations changed TinyLLaVA accuracy by only −0.17 points on average, despite altering 4.69% of predictions.
Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements reduced accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points, respectively.
Additional experiments show that transformation effects depend on original feature values and evaluation setting.
Provides empirical guidance for evaluating visual-token transformations and designing multimodal interfaces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.
bullets: Across 15,170 held-out trials, stated payoffs shifted reports in both image and text conditions.
Exact compliance with a three-unit reporting incentive was lower from images than text for three of four small open VLMs; one model showed no reliable gap.
Adding the true value as text to image prompts eliminated the image–text gap across models.
Writing the visual reading before the final report sometimes removed the gap, but effects varied by model and prompt wording.
Visual input did not reliably increase truthfulness: several models still shaded reports even when told the client wanted the truth.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of incentive-driven misreporting in vision-language models; fits MLLM behavior and evaluation.
papers.title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
papers.tldr: Visual input makes incentive-driven misreporting less consistently compliant than text-based reporting, with the effect depending on explicit value reading, prompt wording, and output order.

papers.abstract: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.
authors: Tianyi Zhao, Qihao Xu, Jiawen Xi, Duanni Meng, Bo Zhao, Maoxun Yuan, Xingxing Wei, Bo Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of turning complementary RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) information into effective, task-specific decisions.

Applies hierarchical relation-guided rewards to align modality evidence, relation-state prediction, and final outputs.
Improves RGB-T grounding and robustness to sensor degradation over Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving general RGB-T reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Automatic evaluation of artistic style transfer remains an open problem: existing metrics score an image pair in isolation, without seeing an example of the intended style transformation, and correlate poorly with human judgment. We introduce StyleJudge, a compact vision-language evaluator conditioned on a small set of reference source-to-stylized pairs before scoring a query pair, mirroring how a human rater calibrates to a style before judging a candidate. On a human-annotated benchmark of 878 rated pairs across 12 artistic styles (728 from 10 training/validation styles, 150 from 2 unseen styles), our efficient 0.8B-parameter StyleJudge reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.291 (Spearman 0.325) with human ratings on seen styles and 0.381 on unseen ones. On seen styles, it achieves the highest positive correlation among tested metrics: Gram-matrix style loss and CLIP similarity correlate weakly ($r=0.041$, $r=0.168$), while LPIPS (scored higher when closer to the source) correlates negatively ($r=-0.404$). We achieve this by distilling evaluation knowledge from a 72B-parameter vision-language teacher used only during training, which reaches $r=0.327$, confirming that most of its human alignment survives compact distillation. For training, we build a dataset of source-to-stylized pairs across the 12 styles via LoRA-adapted diffusion, densified with graded intermediate examples from a high-resolution image-morphing pipeline so the evaluator recognizes partial and complete stylization. On two held-out validation styles, StyleJudge reaches 28.2% exact-match agreement with its teacher's structured scores versus 1.1% for the untuned base model, with 67.8% shorter reasoning traces, and scores a pair in 39 s (median) using 2.5 GB of GPU memory on one NVIDIA T4. We release the human-rating benchmark, annotation guideline, SDXL-adapted FreeMorph code, and model weights.
authors: Lokesh, Pramukto Mandal, Somanshu Juneja, Jashnoor Singh, Amit Kumar, Pranav Adlinge, Richa Thakur, Kunal Swami, Aditya Nigam

papers.abstract: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.
authors: Jinyu Li, Zhiming Zhang, Hao Fang, Hongyao Yu, Bin Chen, Albert Ma, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Addresses response-level reinforcement learning, which can penalize correct content alongside hallucinated claims.
Uses on-policy self-guidance with direct and reciprocal token weighting based on grounding support.
Applies guidance only when overall and hallucination-specific advantages agree.
Employs a reference-calibrated reward to improve factuality without encouraging information omission.
Outperforms evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR while retaining multimodal capabilities.

papers.abstract: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153$\times$7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.
authors: La Jiang, Lingfeng Chen, Jiaqi Zhu, Fengrong Guo, Jiehua Zhang, Panhe Hu, Li Liu, Zhen Liu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 405 large SAR images averaging 7153×7153 pixels.

papers.abstract: Recent pre-trained vision-language models often encounter a Multi-Domain Task-Incremental Learning (MTIL) scenario in practice, where a set of classes of multi-modal tasks arrive incrementally. Due to privacy concerns and memory constraints, MTIL with pre-trained models encounters forgetting of knowledge from old tasks, degradation of zero-shot transfer capability, and underfitting of new-task knowledge. To overcome these challenges, previous MTIL methods attempt to learn a discriminative cross-task identification (CTI) module and an effective new-task adaptation (NTA) module. However, current CTI modules suffer from severe task confusion between seen and unseen tasks, and NTA modules cannot adaptively balance the performance and parameter cost while incorporating task-specific knowledge. To alleviate the above dilemmas, we propose an effective and efficient TSP-DLoRA method for MTIL, which consists of Task Subspace Projection (TSP) and Dynamic Low Rank Adapter (DLoRA) modules. Specifically, our TSP module includes a task identifier classifier based on task-specific subspaces and a feature projection strategy that can determine the identifier associated with samples from both seen and unseen tasks. Our DLoRA improves the knowledge adaptation from new tasks by dynamically assigning Low Rank Adapter (LoRA) across transformer layers based on the task distributions. Experimental evaluations across 11 datasets, using three performance metrics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/FerdinandZJU/TSP-DLoRA.
authors: Hao Fu, Qian Feng, Hanbin Zhao, Jiahua Dong, Xu Tan, Lina Wei, Chao Zhang, Hui Qian
bullets: Addresses forgetting of old-task knowledge, reduced zero-shot transfer, and underfitting of new tasks under privacy and memory constraints.
Uses Task Subspace Projection to identify seen and unseen tasks through task-specific subspaces and feature projection.
Uses Dynamic LoRA to allocate low-rank adapters across transformer layers according to task distributions.
Evaluated on 11 datasets with three metrics, showing the method’s effectiveness.
The abstract does not report specific numerical results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The training process of the DLoRA module in our method. The DLoRA module integrates LoRA into the first Lt transformer layers of both the image and text encoders. The gating mechanism before the LoRA modules in the image encoder determines whether to activate the LoRA based on the feature F ′ v(x) derived from the original CLIP. Only the LoRA and the gating mechanisms are trained, while the remaining parts are kept frozen.

Figure 1: (a) Comparison with existing methods. Unlike ZSCL, our method eliminates the need for additional storage and improves parameter efficiency. Compared to MoE-Adapter, our approach incurs significantly lower computational overhead with fewer trainable parameters. In contrast to DIKI, ours not only achieves higher accuracy but also precisely distinguishes whether samples belong to previously seen tasks (Precise Task ID). (b) Mechanism comparison. Existing training-free CTI applies the same NTA operation to both seen and unseen tasks, restricted by a weight “W ”. Conversely, our TSP module explicitly identifies the boundary between tasks, directing unseen samples to the original CLIP while processing seen samples with DLoRA. (c) Performance trade-off. Our method achieves a superior trade-off between average accuracy (both seen and unseen tasks) and parameter efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 3: The workflow of the TSP module of our method in training and inference processes. During training phase, for image dataset of every task, the TSP module decomposes the image features via SVD and selects top r singular vectors from the right singular vector matrix to be the corresponding task subspace. During inference phase, for every test sample, the TSP module computes the cosine similarity between the raw feature extracted from original CLIP and the subspaces associated with each seen task. The result is compared against a threshold, denoted as “thres.”. The sample is classified using the corresponding DLoRA module if the cosine similarity exceeds the “thres.”. Otherwise, the original CLIP model is utilized to classify the sample.

Figure 6: Visualization of six task-specific distributions generated by the TSP module. We randomly selected 1,000 samples from each dataset. The majority of samples are correctly classified, as shown by their corresponding colors. A small number of samples are misclassified as unseen tasks, while an even smaller number are incorrectly assigned to other seen tasks. Overall, the TSP module achieves an accuracy exceeding 90% for each task.

Figure 4: The distribution of similarity scores for the TSP module across different tasks. The red line denotes a threshold set at 0.96. The majority of samples exhibit similarity scores above this threshold. The dense distribution of similarity scores also indicates the TSP module’s capability to effectively capture and extract critical information from each task.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
authors: Yuhao Wang, Yucheng Zhao, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Hongcheng Liu, Qichao Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Wang
bullets: Introduces 380 deep-research-style tasks spanning four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels.

Evaluation of 18 representative models shows persistent limitations in long-horizon workspace execution; the best average score is 65.93.
Analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring failure modes.
Proposes OmniFocus, combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Yanjun Fu, Quanzeng You, Jiadong Guo, Yujie Lu, Sai Charitha Akula, Haiping Wu, Miao Liu, Sanghamitra Dutta, Lu Yuan
bullets: Identifies SFT data quality—not increasingly complex RL—as a key bottleneck for combining logical reasoning with visual tool use.
Introduces a fully automated data engine that creates challenging, visually grounded questions and human-like, structured Zoom-in tool traces.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B on LogT data was evaluated across seven benchmark test sets.
Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieved stronger results than prior SFT+RL methods using 3.1× less data and over 120× fewer GPU hours.
Adding simple RL to LogT-SFT further surpassed complex prior RL methods by 9.59 points, with improved tool-use accuracy, efficiency, and reasoning consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 3 A detailed overview of LogT SFT data synthesis engine. Part 1 (top; Section 3.1) synthesizes visual search QA pairs using the full image (I0) along with rich visual contexts (IC and IF , top left) related to randomly selected target objects. After generating candidate QAs, we apply a simple heuristic filter and use a VLM-as-a-Judge to ensure quality. Part 2 (bottom; Section 3.2) generates reasoning traces for the selected QA. For easy questions, we directly generate traces without tool calls (omitted here). For other questions, we first create logic chains (LM and LE) based on two human-like strategies. A logic chain selector then chooses the more appropriate one, which is subsequently used to guide the synthesis of multi-turn reasoning traces with tool use.
Figure 7 System prompt for the QA generator. The remaining rules and in-context examples are omitted for brevity.

Figure 8 System prompt for the reasoning trace generator. Each logic-chain entry of the form ⟨short noun phrase⟩(k) specifies a target object or region and its source image Ik. Here, I0 is the original image, and Ik for k ≥ 1 is the crop returned by the k-th Zoom-in call. The reasoning trace generator locates the specified target in Ik, predicts its bounding box, and invokes Zoom-in on that image using the predicted box. For example, “Backpack (2)” corresponds to “Backpack (I2)” in Figure 3 and instructs the generator to zoom in on the backpack within the person crop returned by the second tool call. The remaining rules and in-context examples are omitted for brevity.

Figure 6 Tool call efficiency. We report the average number of tool calls per question across the seven test sets. Despite achieving better performance compared to prior SOTA, LogT-SFT model uses 2.7× fewer tool calls, and LogT-RL uses 2.3× fewer.

Figure 9 An example of an exhaustive search logic chain and its corresponding tool-use reasoning trace. To locate the pink sign held by a person in the crowd, the logic chain begins by instructing the trace generator (see Section 3.2) to identify the crowd, then systematically search it from left to right. Since the trace generator successfully detects the target sign and the person in the crop returned by the third Zoom-in call, it stops scanning the rest of the crowd and instead zooms in on the identified region to extract the final answer.

Figure 2 Result highlights. By applying SFT to a Qwen2.5VL-7B model using 5.4k to 7.1k of our synthesized data, LogT-SFT surpasses the best-performing Mini-o3-RL on average across seven test sets, while using up to 3.1× less data and >120× fewer GPU hours. With a simple RL setup without any tool-specific design, LogT-RL further outperforms baselines by 9.59.

Figure 1 Main idea. We generate reasoning traces based on human-like strategies including (i) direct answering for simple questions, (ii) multi-hop reasoning by focusing on different regions, and (iii) exhaustive search for more difficult cases. For easy questions where the base model’s average@8 is 1, we synthesize direct answering traces without Zoom-in. Otherwise, we first generate logic chains that specify key tool-use steps and then use them to guide the VLM in synthesizing tool-use reasoning traces.

Figure 4 Training dynamics after applying our simple RL procedure to the baselines and LogT-SFT. During RL, our model’s validation accuracy steadily improves, whereas other SFT baselines perform on par with, or worse than zero-RL. LogT greatly improves the RL performance ceiling.

Figure 5 Tool call accuracy. We report tool call accuracy on V* for the base model and all post-trained models. The base model is prompted to use Zoom-in in a zeroshot setting. Our LogT-SFT and LogT-RL models achieve the highest Zoom-in accuracy.
Figure 13 Instructions for Human Evaluation.
Figure 12 Qualitative case study of SFT data synthesized by Pixel Reasoner, Chain-of-Focus, Mini-o3 and LogT.

Figure 15 Qualitative case study comparingmodel responses to a V* question between baseline models and LogT-RL. We show the generated reasoning traces, including Zoom-in calls, for both baseline models and LogT-RL. While Qwen2.5-VL7B-RL, Pixel Reasoner-RL, and Chain-of-Focus-RL produce the correct final answer, their responses contain hallucinations or self-contradictions. The remaining baselines make erroneous Zoom-in calls and ultimately produce incorrect answers. In contrast, LogT-RL follows a coherent and consistent reasoning chain: it first identifies the front cabin of the truck, then locates the tissue box, and finally answers the question correctly without hallucinations.
Figure 10 Normalized distribution of Zoom-in call counts in theSFTdatasetgeneratedbyLogT. The number of tool calls per trace in the dataset ranges from 0 (direct answering without tool use) to 6.

Figure 11 Ratio of easy questions. We compute the ratio of questions in existing and our SFT datasets for which Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves an average@8 = 1 without needing tools (easy questions). Our dataset synthesized by LogT contains only 24%, significantly lower than existing datasets.
Figure 14 Per-annotator breakdown of human evaluation. All three annotators preferred responses generated by LogT-RL over those from Mini-o3-RL.

Table 6 Ablation on models used for data synthesis. We replace the models used by LogT in Section 3 with much smaller variants and re-synthesize 4k SFT samples. After SFT, the average performance across V*, VisualProbe, and HR-Bench remains nearly unchanged, indicating that our method is robust to the choice of synthesis models.

Table 8 Performance on V*-Rotated. We construct V*-Rotated by rotating images in V* by angles randomly sampled from 30◦ to 330◦. LogT-RL uses a rotation tool at inference time that was not seen during training, improving over the base model by 21.99 points.
Table 7 Error rates across different stages. We randomly sampled 100 samples from each stage and manually evaluated their error rates.
Table 4 Ablation on question difficulty. Training the VLM on the harder half of our SFT dataset leads to significantly improved performance on challenging tasks like those in VisualProbe-Hard.

Table 5 Ablation on logic chain-driven reasoning trace synthesis. Incorporating logical chains into the data generation process of LogT improves overall SFT performance and yields substantial additional gains after subsequent RL.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for autonomous driving through question-answering benchmarks, yet high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily reflect visually grounded reasoning. We present a diagnostic evaluation framework that systematically probes whether VLMs base safety-critical driving decisions on visual evidence or instead rely on language priors, answer biases, and dataset regularities. Our benchmark comprises two task categories, Adverse Weather and Junctions \& Intersections, with a nuScenes spatial reasoning extension, and evaluates open-source (general, driving, and spatial-reasoning) VLMs along four diagnostic protocols: image versus no-image evaluation, counterfactual weather sensitivity, linguistic robustness under paraphrasing and negation, and spatial reasoning. All ground-truth labels are derived programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM annotations, enabling reproducible evaluation without manual labeling. Across all models, we find that competitive overall accuracy conceals systematic failure modes, including strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance performance on negated questions despite high paraphrase consistency, and confident driving decisions even without visual input. These results demonstrate that current open-source VLMs remain insufficiently grounded for safety-critical autonomous driving and underscore the need for diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy.
authors: Shankar Gangisetty, Muskan Singh, C V Jawahar
bullets: Tests VLM reliance on visual evidence versus language priors and dataset regularities.
Covers adverse weather, junctions/intersections, and nuScenes-based spatial reasoning.
Uses four protocols: image removal, counterfactual weather changes, paraphrase/negation robustness, and spatial reasoning.
Finds affirmation bias, poor counterfactual sensitivity, near-chance negation performance, and confident answers without images.
Concludes that current open-source VLMs are not sufficiently grounded for autonomous driving decisions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed diagnostic driving evaluation framework.

Fig. 1: Motivation for diagnostic evaluation of driving VLMs. Existing driving benchmarks may report high accuracy even when VLMs are not visually grounded. Our framework probes three complementary failure modes: (top) counterfactual scene sensitivity under controlled weather changes, (bottom left) reliance on language priors through image versus no-image evaluation, and (bottom right) robustness to linguistic variations via paraphrases and negation. Together, these diagnostics expose failure modes that are hidden by aggregate benchmark accuracy.

Fig. 3: Qualitative analysis of the Adverse Weather task. Semantic question types: best- and worst-performing models on matched image-question pairs across perception, action, hazard, and adversarial questions. Counterfactual SCS: PaliGemma-3B adapts its prediction across clear, fog, rain, and snow, whereas Moondream-2B remains weather-invariant. Linguistic variation: InternVL3-8B is consistent across the original question and paraphrases but fails under negation. Zoom in for details; additional details are provided in the Supplementary.

Fig. 4: Qualitative analysis of the Junctions & Intersections task. Semantic question types: best- and worst-performing models on matched nuScenes examples spanning spatial reasoning, prediction, and planning. Linguistic variation: responses to the original question, paraphrases, and the negated variant illustrate differing robustness to semantic reformulation, with InternVL3-8B partially recovering under paraphrasing and negation while Moondream-2B remains inconsistent. Zoom in for details; additional details are provided in the Supplementary.

Fig. 5: Targeted qualitative analysis of reasoning failures. Representative failure cases from each diagnostic protocols showing that VLMs often generate plausible driving decisions from language priors rather than visual evidence. Examples illustrate hallucination, safety-prior reasoning, negation blindness, paraphrase inconsistency, counterfactual scene insensitivity, spatial reasoning failure, and no-image guessversus-refusal behavior. Each panel reports the question, ground truth, prediction, and generated rationale. Zoom in for details.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yuhu990424/RAVEN-Bench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/TerraSenseAnalytics/RAVEN-Bench.
authors: Yu Hu, Jianyang Gu, Yue Cao, Hao Liu, Kangnan Wang, Jozsef Hamari, Zheng Liu, Mohsen Zardadi
bullets: Introduces a benchmark for challenging low-altitude aerial video QA, where targets are small, transient, viewpoint-dependent, and modality-specific.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.
authors: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of screenshot-and-action learning, which discards tutorials’ audio-visual information.
Uses a watch–act–rewatch paradigm to combine external demonstrations with reflection on agent behavior.
Introduces video-SALMONN-VEX, an audio-visual computer-use agent, and AGGO to optimize video-derived guidance for action prediction.

Reports a 22% relative OSWorld success increase over the Qwen3.5 backbone; generated guidance also improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision-language reasoning requires a control decision that conventional grounding methods leave implicit: which input is entitled to determine the answer? Auxiliary text may be a defeasible claim about an image, a binding task instruction, or compatible context. Correcting every image-text conflict toward the image therefore repairs false claims but overwrites valid task rules. We formalize this setting as mixed-authority vision-language reasoning and introduce AITHER, an Authority-Informed Text-Image Hierarchy for Evidence Routing. Its final policy, the Semantic-Frame Router, is a training-free black-box control layer that (i) compiles explicit task directives, (ii) recovers standardized spatial frames from metadata-scrubbed pixels, (iii) resolves the semantic polarity of remaining notes, and (iv) routes among frozen observable candidates with fail-closed semantics. This ordered decomposition converts authority arbitration from an unconstrained prompt preference into a reproducible inference program. Across 1,620 MATRIX predictions, AITHER reaches 95.1% accuracy, exceeding the strongest task-and-frame baseline by 9.1 points with a 95% record-cluster interval of 6.8-11.5 points and no harmed records. It further reaches 100.0% on 1,800 controlled FRAME predictions and 93.3% on GQA-MATRIX. The results show that explicit authority routing can simultaneously improve false-claim correction, preserve task-defined answers, and eliminate clean-context overcorrection.

papers.abstract: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.
bullets: Represents long videos as timestamped segments and initially processes a sparsely sampled version.
The model selects segments for 4× denser decoding while removing unselected segments from context.
Reuses surviving KV caches by applying one shared M-RoPE positional offset across temporal, height, and width dimensions.
Content-hashed caching also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for retained segments.
Preliminary tests show lower prefill and rebuild latency with usually unchanged answers; self-selection does not improve accuracy when the target was missing from the sparse sample.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.
bullets: CompHall is not purely visual: some part-whole questions can be answered from text alone, and compositional accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe.
The original loss mostly scored image-placeholder tokens and harmed both LLaVA models; a corrected loss improved CV-Bench spatial accuracy across all three model families.
Control experiments indicate that gains require spatial training questions, while some LLaVA-NeXT improvement transfers to relation words seen only as incorrect options.
On CompHall, improvement was significant only for LLaVA-NeXT; gains were small on true/false statements and did not generalize consistently.
Fine-tuning also increased LLaVA-1.5’s tendency to answer “true” and raised its yes-bias on POPE.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the effects of hard-negative fine-tuning on Multimodal Large Language Models, providing controlled evidence on compositional reasoning and hallucination.
papers.title: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
papers.tldr: Hard-negative fine-tuning can improve spatial reasoning, but its benefits are narrow, model-dependent, and sensitive to the training loss and evaluation design.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for image super-resolution can recover scene content while producing distracting artifacts or unbalanced colors. We study whether a large language model (LLM) can improve perceptual quality by editing a small subset of existing U-Net weights without a clean reference image. The proposed framework provides the editor with architecture code, selected weights, activation summaries, and sampling previews. It permits up to 1,020 candidate trials while limiting accepted changes to three layers and fewer than 0.1\% of model parameters. The evaluation protocol uses ResShift, SinSR, and SUPIR and compares GPT-6 Astra with a specified Qwen3-VL model under matched access. Feedback metrics guide editing, while separate quality metrics and blinded human comparisons evaluate the final weights. We also report an executed color calibration experiment using real photographs and two small residual networks. This experiment demonstrates correction of a fixed color shift and reveals that an improving feedback score can accompany worse performance on unseen scenes. A separate lightweight super-resolution experiment isolates modest changes in luminance detail while preserving color. The findings motivate restricted updates and independent evaluation of perceptual weight editing.
bullets: Targets distracting artifacts and color imbalance without requiring clean reference images.
The editor uses architecture code, selected weights, activation summaries, and sampling previews to propose up to 1,020 trials.
Accepted updates affect only three layers and fewer than 0.1% of model parameters.
Evaluation covers ResShift, SinSR, and SUPIR, with separate feedback, quality, and blinded human assessments.
Auxiliary experiments show fixed color-shift correction and modest luminance-detail changes, while exposing limitations in feedback-based evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a large language model to edit diffusion model weights for super-resolution, demonstrating a novel application of LLMs in model editing and perceptual quality control.
papers.title: Perceptual Weight Space Programming for Diffusion Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: An LLM can improve diffusion super-resolution perceptual quality by making highly restricted edits to a few U-Net weights, but feedback scores may not generalize to unseen images.

papers.abstract: Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs) extend large language models to heterogeneous modalities, demonstrating strong potential across a wide range of open-ended tasks. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been widely adopted to improve reasoning performance in LMRMs; however, existing approaches overlook the critical role of visual perception uncertainty in guiding reasoning processes. We term this limitation Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where the misalignment between visual perception uncertainty and reasoning depth leads to over-allocation of deep reasoning under uncertain visual grounding, resulting in unnecessarily long reasoning trajectories and degraded performance. To address this issue, we propose ThinkWise, a perception-aware RLVR framework that jointly models task difficulty and visual perception state to regulate reasoning depth. Specifically, we introduce an instance-adaptive visual perception modeling mechanism that enables context-aware calibration of perception uncertainty, leading to more accurate perception estimation. We further design a structured reward formulation that jointly considers perception, correctness, and task difficulty. In particular, an answer reward provides supervision for correctness, a perception- and difficulty-conditioned length reward adaptively regulates reasoning depth, and a perception reward encourages trajectories with stronger visual grounding. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkWise consistently improves the trade-off between accuracy and reasoning efficiency across both 3B and 7B models. These results highlight the importance of perception-aware reasoning and establish a principled framework for advancing LMRMs.
authors: Wenkang Zhou, Chen Yang, Jiaheng Peng, Xitong Li, Hongzhi Yin, Yunke Zhang, Lu Yu, Peng-Fei Zhang, Xuhui Ren, Shijie Zhang
bullets: Addresses Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where uncertain visual grounding can trigger unnecessarily deep reasoning and hurt performance.
Uses instance-adaptive visual perception modeling to calibrate perception uncertainty in context.
Combines correctness, perception, and difficulty in a structured RLVR reward, including adaptive length regulation and visual-grounding supervision.
Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and 3B/7B models show improved accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.
Scope: focuses on perception-aware control of reasoning depth in large multimodal reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering systems can produce confident responses that are weakly supported by their input images. Contrastive decoding can reduce this dependence on language priors, but a fixed correction may also overturn a correct answer, while selective answering can conceal errors by reducing coverage. We develop evidence-calibrated selective decoding, a framework that separates three decisions: whether local visual evidence supports a candidate, how strongly to correct the original distribution, and whether the resulting answer should be released under a verification budget. Evidence Verification across Crops (EVC) measures visual support and disagreement; Adaptive Contrast Correction (ACC) applies a bounded modification within the backbone's plausible candidate set; Budgeted Selective Answering (BSA) calibrates an answer-admission threshold on held-out images. We provide a complete mathematical specification, bounded-perturbation analysis, and an evaluation protocol that distinguishes forced answering from selective risk. Our quantitative analysis re-examines published baselines on POPE instantiated over MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, together with four MME subtasks. These public measurements reveal variation across backbones, tasks, and correction settings that motivates adaptive control. The proposed framework has not yet undergone model-level evaluation; its effectiveness remains a falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established empirical result.
authors: Shiyu Gu, Luis Miguel Santana, Rafael Enrique Cruz
bullets: Targets confident VQA answers that are weakly supported by the image.
Uses Evidence Verification across Crops to measure visual support and disagreement.

Uses a held-out-image verification budget to set answer-admission thresholds.

papers.abstract: Clinical adoption of ophthalmic Artificial Intelligence remains limited by low interpretability and a lack of finely annotated multimodal data. Most existing datasets provide only coarse disease labels without the granular pathological findings required for differential diagnosis. We present LogicEye$^{Agent}$, a dual-pool inference and verification agent that emulates clinical reasoning by jointly verifying positive inclusion signs and negative exclusion criteria. Using LogicEye$^{Agent}$, we curate LogicEye$^{Data}$, a large-scale multimodal dataset of 804,461 fundus and OCT images paired with structured pathological reports spanning 38 diseases and 29 subtypes, with quality assured through joint verification by multimodal large language models and clinical experts. Building on this dataset, we further develop LogicEye$^{Bench}$, which incorporates a category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation. Grounding coarse labels into verified visual findings effectively curtails diagnostic hallucinations and establishes a solid foundation for interpretable vision-language modeling in ophthalmology. The code is available at:https://github.com/Eden35/LogicEye-Agent-Driven-Multimodal-Dataset-for-Interpretable-Ophthalmic-Diagnosis.

Provides 804,461 fundus and OCT images with structured pathological reports covering 38 diseases and 29 subtypes.
Builds a benchmark with category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation.
Grounding disease labels in verified visual findings is intended to reduce diagnostic hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models can support both visual understanding and generation, yet generative training does not necessarily improve understanding. We argue that this limitation may arise from a mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the perceptual representation used for understanding. Conventional generation objectives primarily optimize synthesis-oriented spaces such as discrete visual codes or generative latents. We therefore introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates generation as progressive prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations. The model constructs a multi-scale representation hierarchy from coarse to fine, while pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward. Controlled comparisons show that the representation-prediction objective accounts for most of the understanding improvement, while a data-matched control leaves the group means nearly unchanged. UMM-JEPA reaches a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71, against 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, and the text mean also rises. Compared with discrete-code and latent-flow generation objectives, perceptual representation prediction yields stronger and more consistent transfer to understanding. Linear probes and visual-evidence interventions further reveal richer object and spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific information. These results suggest that generation can benefit understanding when it directly supervises the perceptual representations that understanding consumes.

papers.abstract: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.
authors: Ha Pham Thien Dinh, Ming Liu, Jiesi Guo, Matteo Vergani, Kewen Liao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that pretrained LoRA adapters usually require the same model backbone.
Retrieves a relevant adapter from a modality-aware library and transfers it using a learned linear bridge between feature spaces.
Transfers Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL across ten text tasks and reuses Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs on five multimodal tasks.
Outperforms randomly initialized LoRA on most evaluated tasks.
Scope: evaluated on selected text and multimodal continual-learning tasks and backbones.

The latter group is initially empty and can be used from task 2 onward, if selected; no reported run selected from it. Multimodal LoRAs already work with Qwen2.5-VL. papers.abstract: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.
authors: Ningxin Pan, Guochen Yan, Jialong Wu, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Tool access improves aggregate VQA accuracy but can cause correct no-tool answers to become incorrect.
Tool-enabled reasoning trajectories are substantially shorter, indicating greater reliance on external outputs and less intrinsic visual reasoning.
ReVision adds optional, tool-free intrinsic reconsideration alongside search and code execution.
The model decides when to reconsider, avoiding fixed reflection stages and paired rollouts.
It improves over standard tool use across all six benchmarks by 1.28–7.51% and uses a comparable number of reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled more natural interaction with visual and spoken information, creating new opportunities for intelligent audio-visual question answering (AVQA) and hallucination detection systems. AVQA extends traditional visual question answering by requiring models to jointly understand an input image and a spoken question to generate accurate, context-aware responses. Despite recent advances, AVQA and hallucination detection tasks remain challenging for modern standard Arabic (MSA) due to the limited availability of multimodal datasets and the need to reason across Arabic speech and text modalities alongside visual inputs. In this paper, we present an MLLM-based framework for AVQA that takes an image and a spoken question as input and generates answers. In addition, we utilized this framework to detect hallucination in text-image pairs. The proposed approach is evaluated on the ImageEval 2026 Task (Ayn-VQA) benchmark, which focuses on culturally grounded Arabic AVQA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively understands spoken queries, grounds their responses in the visual content, and produces accurate answers. The results underscore the capacity and limitations of different LLM architectures for both English and MSA and under various conditions.
bullets: Targets AVQA by jointly interpreting an image and a spoken question to generate context-aware answers.
Extends the framework to detect hallucinations in text–image pairs.

papers.abstract: Narrative video understanding requires more than recognizing visible events: models must extract evidence from dialogue, bind it to speakers, and use it to infer narrative meaning. Existing video benchmarks evaluate aspects of this problem, including video question answering, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, but rarely test whether these abilities form a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips. We introduce \textbf{CineMME}, a human-verified benchmark designed to diagnose dialogue-grounded plot understanding, supported by approximately $1,600$ expert person-hours of annotation. CineMME contains $975$ curated short narrative video clips and two linked tracks: \textit{CineMME-Grounding}, with $13,554$ timestamped speech segments and $33,083$ speaker face boxes for temporal dialogue localization, transcription, and active-speaker grounding; and \textit{CineMME-Reasoning}, with $1,600$ multiple-choice and $316$ open-ended questions spanning perception, audio, narrative, social, and scene-presentation understanding. Our main evaluation compares $20$ MLLMs on reasoning and $9$ omni-modal models on grounding. The results reveal a pronounced who-what-when decoupling: Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue in time ($68.34\%$ tIoU) and transcribes it with a WER of $28.99\%$, yet achieves only $7.74\%$ vIoU for active-speaker grounding while achieving $67.66\%$ MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Modality ablations further show that vision is not uniformly beneficial: it improves performance on perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning. CineMME provides a compact diagnostic testbed for evaluating how multimodal video models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence, and narrative meaning.
bullets: Targets a missing evaluation link: coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chains within the same narrative clips.
Includes 975 human-verified clips with grounding and reasoning tracks covering speech localization, transcription, active-speaker grounding, and narrative questions.
Evaluates 20 multimodal LLMs for reasoning and 9 omni-modal models for grounding.
Finds strong time localization and transcription but weak active-speaker grounding, revealing a who–what–when gap.
Vision helps perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding and generation. However, generating interleaved image--text content remains challenging, as it requires tightly integrated multimodal understanding and generation capabilities. Although existing MLLMs provide promising solutions, most rely on additional training with augmented data, which is computationally expensive and remains limited in preserving visual subjects, temporal consistency, and physical plausibility. In this work, we propose self-correction optimization (SCO), an effective training-free method for consistent interleaved generation. SCO treats the classifier-free guidance update as a reference and performs minimal self-correction under two complementary constraints, including new-event and state-preserving constraints. Specifically, the new-event constraint promotes temporal consistency across image--text sequences, while the state-preserving constraint maintains the coherence of visual subjects throughout subsequent generation steps. Experiments on challenging interleaved multimodal generation benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements in temporal coherence and visual-subject preservation. Furthermore, SCO can be extended to video generation and improves the modeling of physically grounded processes, including robot manipulation and long-horizon handcrafting.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generating coherent image–text sequences without costly additional training.
Uses classifier-free guidance as a reference and applies minimal self-correction.
Combines new-event constraints for temporal consistency with state-preserving constraints for subject coherence.
Improves temporal coherence and visual-subject preservation on challenging interleaved-generation benchmarks.
Also extends to video generation and physically grounded processes such as robot manipulation and long-horizon handcrafting.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce a metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, a simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to $3.58\times$, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.
authors: Sicheng Feng, Zigeng Chen, Song Wang, Gongfan Fang, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Visual dependence strongly affects draft-token acceptance: acceptance drops from 46% in the lowest-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest.
The framework adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly.
For long-video inputs, sparse attention reduces redundant computation and improves drafting quality.
Across multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless speedups of up to 3.58×, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.
authors: Tao Hu, Ling-Xiang Zhang, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and linear parameter growth in task-specific MoE expansion.

Factorizes remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact private cores.
Uses frozen historical retrieval keys and orthogonally regularized new keys to stabilize routing.
Dynamically routes inputs across shared and private pools without requiring task labels at inference; experiments report superior performance with substantially lower parameter overhead.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual realism, aesthetic quality, and instruction following. However, real-world prompts often go beyond explicit visual descriptions and require implicit facts, structured knowledge, and domain-specific commonsense. Existing evaluations mainly focus on explicit prompt-to-image semantic alignment or specific knowledge subdomains, lacking unified evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I models. We introduce KnowVis for dual-view evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I generation. Built on a hierarchical knowledge taxonomy with case-level annotations, KnowVis combines two complementary benchmark views with a structured MLLM-based VQA judge protocol. The Skill-Tree Benchmark supports fine-grained atomic knowledge evaluation, while the Generalized Benchmark examines open-ended knowledge composition and expression. The protocol uses Required VQAs to assess atomic knowledge correctness in the Skill-Tree Benchmark, and combines Required, Optional, and dynamically discovered knowledge expressions with human-judge collaborative evaluation in the Generalized Benchmark. We validate the protocol's reliability on the Skill-Tree validation split, enabling scalable evaluation and diagnostic error attribution. Experiments show that KnowVis reveals notable gaps in world-knowledge grounding across existing T2I models and provides structured diagnostic signals for knowledge-intensive image generation.
authors: Yonghang Yu, Ruoyu Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Lin Qi, Yawei Zhou, Changqian Yu

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal performance, yet they remain prone to object hallucination---generating answers that are linguistically fluent but visually ungrounded. This issue is especially severe in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment causes models to rely more on language priors than on image evidence. Existing remedies either require costly multilingual annotations or external translation/reward models, or intervene at inference time in ways that can distort the output language. We propose VEPO(Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization), a training-time method that transfers reliable visual grounding from English to other languages without external models. VEPO first localizes key visual evidence using English queries via mid-layer cross-modal attention, then constructs preference pairs that share the same correct answer but differ in evidence sufficiency (full image vs.\ key-region masked image). Direct preference optimization on these pairs encourages low-resource inputs to prefer answers supported by complete visual evidence. Experiments on multilingual POPE and MME with Chinese, French, and Hindi show consistent hallucination reduction and perception gains, with the largest improvements on the lowest-resource language. Analyses further confirm that VEPO sharpens question-relevant attention and that evidence-guided masking outperforms random masking.
authors: Chengpeng Fu, Xiaocheng Feng, Wenshuai Huo, Yichong Huang, Baohang Li, Duyu Tang, Ting Liu

papers.abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.
authors: Saisuchith Mahajan, Aditey Nandan, Rohit Singh, Nishanth Shetty, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula
bullets: Existing Jacobian-diagonal methods confuse memorization with smooth or predictable regions and require a null prompt or earlier checkpoint.
JaRS uses Jacobian row sums to distinguish memorization from local averaging without a reference map.
JaRS+ combines JaRS localization with an image-level detection score computed at an early denoising step.
Evaluated on multiple conditional and unconditional diffusion models, JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.

papers.abstract: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarification and enumeration behaviors, but also elicits them on unambiguous cases. AmbiSteer addresses this using a linear classifier to predict input ambiguity and condition the steering direction accordingly, increasing the proportion of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. Our work sets the ground for lightweight approaches to reduce model overconfidence in uncertain multimodal settings.
authors: Monica Riedler, Samuele Antonelli, Barbara Plank, Raffaella Bernardi

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.

papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
