papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.
authors: Haolin Yang, Wenshan Wu, Jin Jiang, Yu Cheng, Yan Xia, Ting Song, Yangyu Huang, Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, Hangbo Bao, Yuzhe Zhang, Wen-Da Wei, Tengchao Lv, Li Dong, Lei Cui, Furu Wei
bullets: Existing agentic coding systems couple visual reasoning to an agent’s built-in perception, limiting performance and excluding text-only agents.
Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) treats general-purpose multimodal LLMs as external utilities rather than relying solely on intrinsic vision.
VHarness implements VaaT through five atomic actions in a unified framework.
Across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D tasks, VHarness improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for text-only and multimodal agents.
The approach provides a modular, flexible foundation for visual reasoning in agentic coding systems.

papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.
authors: Xintong Wang, Haihan Nan, Ruidong Li
bullets: Introduces a real-world benchmark of 1,762 text–time-series pairs from Weather, Wikipedia traffic, and Finance, labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified.
Evaluates ten pretrained models zero-shot on text selection, combination, error diagnosis, and forecast revision control.
Aligned, directly predictive text generally performs best; conflicting text often worsens forecasts relative to using no text.
Combining forecast-oriented text with related-condition text improves MASE for six models and directional accuracy for seven.
A training-free rule limiting oversized revisions improves both metrics for four models, with gains reported in the abstract.

papers.title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
papers.tldr: ACU-Bench diagnoses how multimodal forecasting models handle text that aligns with, conflicts with, or omits trends in sensor histories, showing that selective text combination and revision control can improve forecasts.

papers.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of assistants that respond only after user prompts.
Introduces Model-Initiated Conversation, Stream-Aware Tool Calling, and Interactive Visual Grounding.
Adds Long-Horizon Interaction Memory for continuity across extended video streams.
Uses a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and three-stage training scheme to integrate these behaviors.
Reports leading performance among open-source streaming models on public benchmarks and releases model weights and inference code.

papers.abstract: Federated vision-language models (FedVLMs) represent one of the emerging frontiers of machine learning, aiming to integrate federated learning within the fine-tuning pipelines of vision-language models (VLMs). In this work, we introduce BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance the personalization and generalization capabilities of FedVLMs. BLEND proposes a selective VLM parameter fine-tuning and aggregation strategy that consists of (i) global vision and text adapters shared across clients, and (ii) a personalized vision projection adapter tailored to each client. BLEND further introduces a novel loss function that blends the outputs of the global and personalized adapters to achieve personalization, while simultaneously promoting generalization through a principled anchor design implemented via the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to effectively balance personalization and generalization across diverse system settings. (Code is available at: https://github.com/payamsiabd/BLEND.git)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving both client personalization and cross-client generalization in FedVLMs.
Fine-tunes and aggregates global vision and text adapters shared across clients.
Uses a personalized vision projection adapter for each client.
Blends global and personalized adapter outputs, with zero-shot VLM projection heads providing generalization anchors.
Experiments show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse system settings.

papers.abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
authors: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li, Mike Lewis, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Luke Zettlemoyer, Lucas Beyer, Mengye Ren, Jakob Verbeek, Saining Xie, Hu Xu
bullets: The study disentangles visual pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement under controlled compute and data.
A vision encoder trained jointly from scratch performs on par with a pretrained encoder, making a separate visual-pretraining stage unnecessary.
Removing dedicated vision capacity harms visual understanding, even when the backbone is enlarged by an equivalent parameter count.
Vision-only modules integrated into early backbone layers perform comparably to pre-fusion encoders and may reduce time to first token.
Findings persist across backbone sizes, free encoder-pretraining assumptions, and pretrained language-model initialization.

papers.abstract: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.
authors: Kerui Gu, Xing Fu, Shuoyang Sun, Cheng Peng, Jingru Duan, Huayu Gu, Zhenyu Chen, Jiaxin Huang, Cheng Wen, Rui Zhen, Kairui Chen, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang

Introduces the Actor as a dedicated, streaming embodied-output module that reuses native Thinker and Talker representations with modest latency overhead.
Directly conditions multimodal generation on omni-modal inputs to reduce information loss from staged designs.
Evaluation across seven benchmarks reports strong multimodal understanding and high-quality, natural, coordinated motion generation for embodied responses.

papers.abstract: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Minh Son Hoang, Hyeontaek Hwang, Jaesung Lee, Hyojin Choi, Tran Tuan Phong, Seon Kwon Kim, Saad Wazir, Daeyoung Kim

papers.abstract: Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective for building multimodal representations. We show that alignment as a \emph{sole} objective is lossy wherever modalities are informationally asymmetric---where neither can express what the other carries. Visual question answering is an obvious case: a question is a selective relational operator probing a dense visual field whose fine-grained features no query recovers, so what alignment preserves is not what the task requires. We prove an \textbf{Alignment Redundancy Bound}: alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant information atom $\Red(Z; X_1, X_2)$, annihilating private modality-specific structure $\Unq(Z; X_m)$ and cross-modal synergy $\Syn(Z; X_1, X_2)$. We introduce \textbf{Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA)}, which factorizes latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers. The shared core retains most of the structure alignment targets; the private fibers recover what alignment discards, via contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence. Under information asymmetry, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surviving only on binary queries. D-JEPA averts this collapse, substantially improving downstream accuracy over both alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and restoring a positive multimodal synergy gap in place of the baseline's inverted gap. Information-theoretic audits confirm that D-JEPA recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and causal fiber-swap interventions demonstrate that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.
bullets: Alignment alone preserves redundant cross-modal information but can discard private and synergistic information under modality asymmetry.
The method decomposes each latent into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers.
Contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence train the private fibers to recover discarded structure.
On compositional reasoning benchmarks, D-JEPA avoids alignment-only semantic collapse and improves downstream accuracy over alignment-only and reconstruction baselines.
Information audits and fiber-swap interventions indicate that recovered information is substantial and causally localized in the private fibers.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning can teach vision-language models (VLMs) to decline harmful image-text requests, but how safe the result becomes is set indirectly, through reward weights found by trial runs. Stating safety as budgets on the rate of harmful assistance and the rate of over-refusal, enforced by Lagrange multipliers inside GRPO with an off-the-shelf scorer as the cost, is the natural fix, and it fails twice. The multiplier compares the scorer's mean with the budget, and scorers built for ranking get the mean wrong: a fixed-point analysis shows that the mean bias, not the budget, then decides whether the multiplier settles, saturates or switches off. And standard GRPO standardizes the penalized reward within each group, which cancels the multiplier before it reaches the gradient. Two-channel constrained GRPO repairs both: the base reward keeps the raw score for the within-group comparison, the penalty and the constraint estimate pass through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled training responses, and the advantage keeps the multiplier. On a Qwen3-VL-2B policy with a training-free readout of an open 4B model as the scorer, held-out harm on 1,037 adversarial prompts falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, lower in every seed, where the uncalibrated budget gives 7.6%; over-refusal stays at most 2% on 400 benign queries and MMBench is unchanged. The gain is largest where the intent sits in the image (10.1% -> 5.1%) and grows on the unseen HADES benchmark (28.9% -> 12.8%). Order-preserving distortions of the scores reproduce each predicted controller state in every seed, and the results hold under a map fitted on another judge's labels, an image-reading judge and a human audit.
bullets: Safety budgets fail with ranking-based scorers because mean-score bias miscalibrates Lagrange multipliers, while standard GRPO normalization can cancel their effect.
The method keeps raw rewards for within-group comparisons, maps scorer outputs monotonically for constraint estimation, and preserves the multiplier in the advantage.
On adversarial prompts, harm fell from 8.9% with standard GRPO to 4.8%, versus 7.6% for an uncalibrated budget.
Over-refusal remained at most 2%, MMBench performance was unchanged, and harm reductions extended to image-dependent intents and unseen HADES data.
Results were consistent across seeds and robust to alternative judges and human auditing.

papers.abstract: We present UniSpark-9B, a unified multimodal model that investigates hybrid attention for visual understanding and generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts backbone with approximately 9B parameters in each branch, UniSpark combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation. Autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching jointly support visual question answering, text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and interleaved text-image prediction. In interleaved generation, noisy visual targets are isolated from subsequent predictions, while clean visual representations provide context for later outputs. A blockwise protocol enforces this distinction through attention masks in full-attention layers and recurrent-state retention rules in linear-attention layers. The selected training sources contain 159.7M generation samples, 213.4M understanding samples, and 624.8K interleaved sequences. A four-stage curriculum jointly trains multimodal understanding and visual generation, refining answer accuracy and instruction following while extending image synthesis to 2K. UniSpark scores 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval. Qualitative examples further illustrate its capabilities in interleaved image generation, video synthesis, and video editing. Together, these results demonstrate that hybrid attention provides an effective backbone for unified multimodal understanding and generation.

papers.abstract: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.
bullets: Compiles 50,521 structured Even–Russian entries and 107,543 synthetic examples for translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification.
Uses a three-step Even-specific tokenizer expansion that reduces average tokens per word by 27%, from 4.99 to 3.64.
Fine-tunes Qwen3-VL-4B with LoRA for text tasks and VQA, keeping the vision encoder frozen for visual question answering.
Reports 11.4% exact match and 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for translation, and 65% VQA accuracy.
Releases datasets, benchmarks, and a training pipeline for Even and other low-resource languages.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training approach to improving fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models by amortizing costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. However, vanilla OPD is inherently susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes, thus weakening corrective supervision. To address this, we propose Blink On-Policy Distillation (BlinkOPD), in which the teacher "blinks" at every token: it reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain further strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. By extracting more effective supervision from each on-policy trajectory, BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images (12x less data) than existing OPD methods. Beyond fine-grained perception, BlinkOPD also demonstrates strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination, and multimodal reasoning abilities. Code: https://github.com/Supltz/BlinkOPD
authors: Tangzheng Lian, Hang Zhang, Guanyu Hu, Renjiu Hu, Zhensong Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Jifei Song
bullets: Vanilla OPD can exhibit linguistic momentum, where the teacher follows the student's mistakes instead of correcting them.
BlinkOPD has the teacher read each prefix twice: with visual input (“eyes open”) and without it (“eyes closed”).
A first-glance gain amplifies corrective supervision on rollouts that disagree with the teacher.
It achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using 500 training images, 12× less data than existing OPD methods.
It also improves zero-shot performance across ten held-out benchmarks covering visual perception, hallucination, and multimodal reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of BlinkOPD. The student generates rollouts from the full image I and question q, together denoted by xs. The frozen privileged teacher θ0 reads each student prefix twice: once with its eyes open on the zoomed crop (p+t ), and once with its eyes closed (p∅t , Sec. 3.1). Their log-ratio rt keeps the privileged visual evidence, while the prefix-induced linguistic drift shared by both cancels. A prefix-free first glance of the same teacher flags rollouts whose answer conflicts with it, and the gain is raised by a factor γ on these rollouts (Sec. 3.2). The student is trained toward the resulting distillation target (Sec. 3.3). At test time, the student runs alone in a single pass.

papers.abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

papers.abstract: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. However, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their impressive captioning capabilities, are prone to hallucination, producing descriptions that are inconsistent with the visual input. This problem is significantly amplified in aerial imagery due to its unique challenges such as extreme viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and ambiguous visual entities. Existing hallucination detection approaches either rely on computationally expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or treat the problem as a rigid binary classification task, ignoring the inherent uncertainty in ambiguous cases. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, reference-free framework for hallucination detection and correction in free-form aerial image captioning. Our method leverages state-of-the-art MLLMs, specifically InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal computational overhead. Detected hallucinations are corrected through a dedicated refinement module that improves the factual consistency of the original captions. Extensive experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) demonstrate that our framework significantly reduces hallucination rates while remaining practical for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments. Code is available at: https://github.com/Debolena7/Hal_Detect.
authors: Debolena Basak, Somsubhra De, Maunendra Sankar Desarkar
bullets: Targets aerial-captioning hallucinations worsened by viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and visual ambiguity.
Uses InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL to detect hallucinated content without external references or expensive models.
Applies a dedicated refinement module to correct detected hallucinations in free-form captions.
Experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset show reduced hallucination rates and support real-time use in resource-constrained settings.

papers.abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.
authors: Md Kamrujjaman Mobin, Md Salman Shamil, Md Adnan Arefeen
bullets: Evaluates five EventBench event-camera understanding tasks without using challenge training data.
Renders event bins as red/blue ON/OFF frames, selects and grids bins, then prompts a frozen Qwen3.5 9B model for four tasks; action recognition uses EventGPT-Plus-2B directly.
Achieves 62.28% overall accuracy on 2,084 test questions, ranking 9th of 27.
Performance is strongest on action recognition (80.27%) and causal reasoning (77.22%), and weakest on gesture recognition (54.70%) and event OCR (34.57%).
Post-hoc analysis identifies poorly tightened crops that reduce OCR resolution and a bias toward the first two answer choices in detailed understanding.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in medical large multimodal models (LMMs) have brought promising progress to clinical decision support, yet hallucination, the generation of confident but clinically unverifiable outputs, poses a critical threat to the reliability demanded in high-stakes medical settings. Existing hallucination detection methods, predominantly designed for unimodal settings, fail to capture the visual-linguistic dynamics inherent to medical imaging. We formulate the problem of hallucination detection in LMMs as disproportionate distribution of attention weights across the modalities during answer token generation. We quantify modality-specific attention concentration across layers and heads using the Gini coefficient and demonstrate statistically significant redistribution of attention mass between visual and textual tokens in hallucinated responses. We leverage these features to train a logistic regression-based classifier and evaluate it on two medical LMMs across three medical imaging modalities, demonstrating that our method achieves competitive or superior performance against contemporary hallucination detection baselines.
authors: Sachin Acharya, Niyoj Oli, Shishir Adhikari, Aminu Lawal, Yash Raj Shrestha, Prashnna K Gyawali, Binod Bhattarai
bullets: Targets hallucination detection in high-stakes medical imaging applications.
Uses Gini coefficients to quantify modality-specific attention concentration across layers and heads.
Trains a logistic-regression classifier on attention-based features.
Evaluated on two medical LMMs across three imaging modalities.
Reports competitive or superior performance against existing hallucination-detection baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. MAGIC framework. Given a multimodal input (image-question pair), (a) attention matrices are extracted across L layers and H heads. (b) Each matrix is decomposed into text and visual components, isolating response-token attention to prompt and image tokens. (c) Modality-specific Gini coefficients (Gt, Gv) quantify attention concentration. (d) The coefficients are aggregated into a 2 × L ×H feature tensor. (e) A lightweight logistic regression probe σ predicts hallucination.

Fig. 1. Image, visual attention heatmap, and response attention graph (left to right). (a) Hallucinated: diffuse visual attention (low visual Gini) and concentrated text attention (high text Gini). (b) Non-hallucinated: focused visual attention (high visual Gini) and diffuse text attention (low text Gini).

papers.title: MAGIC: Modality-Aware Gini Inspection for Clinical Hallucination Detection in LMMs
papers.tldr: MAGIC detects clinical hallucinations in medical LMMs by measuring imbalanced attention between visual and textual tokens during answer generation.

papers.abstract: In computer vision, vision-language and self-supervised encoders are two unique paradigms characterized by global language alignment and high-quality vision-only patch representations, respectively. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often use the former because of language alignment, despite the recent rise in vision-centric tasks resembling traditional dense vision tasks that would likely benefit from the high-quality patch representations, raising the question whether self-supervised models could aid MLLMs in vision-centric tasks. To investigate this, we define semantic (in)consistency of patch tokens from language-aligned encoders and identify two sets of tokens, semantically consistent (SCTs) and semantically inconsistent (SITs). Through systematic probing via the removal of SCTs or SITs from the input of modern MLLMs, we show higher reliance on SCTs than SITs, as removal of the former induces larger performance drops. This demonstrates that MLLMs benefit from semantic consistency of vision tokens. With this in mind, we devise a simple yet effective extension of the MLLM training objective that combines traditional language modeling with semantic guidance via minimization of semantic inconsistency. This strategy, named Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), combines the signals of both loss terms to push the vision encoder towards providing semantically consistent tokens, while preserving language alignment. Extensive evaluation shows that SGT outperforms all baselines and MLLMs with specialized vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong scores on text-centric benchmarks, thus setting state of the art on average across all tasks. Our results highlight the importance of combining language alignment and semantic consistency through the lens of MLLMs rather than independently from them and pave the way towards the design of better MLLM vision encoders.
bullets: Problem: Language-aligned vision encoders may provide weaker patch representations for vision-centric, dense-vision tasks.
Method: The study identifies semantically consistent and inconsistent patch tokens and probes their importance by selectively removing them.
Contribution: It introduces Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), which augments language modeling with a semantic-inconsistency minimization objective.
Result: Removing consistent tokens causes larger performance drops, and SGT outperforms the evaluated baselines and specialized vision-encoder MLLMs on vision-centric benchmarks.
Scope: SGT maintains strong performance on text-centric benchmarks and achieves the best average results across the evaluated tasks.

papers.abstract: Automatic evaluation is now central to text-to-image benchmarking, but the verifier that converts generated images into scores is often treated as an implementation detail. We argue that this is unsafe: an automatic benchmark score is a property of the image generator, prompt distribution, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule, not of the generator alone. We study this issue in structural counting, a controlled setting where human-visible counts can be audited. We construct a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects: cell phones, chairs, and traffic lights for object counting, and clover leaflets, dresser drawer fronts, power-strip sockets, and turbine blades for substructure counting. Across 6,240 generated images from Qwen-Image-2512 and FLUX.2-dev, we compare open MLLM verifiers under count-only, reject-aware, zero-shot and few-shot protocols, plus TIFA-like target queries, a detector baseline, and frontier closed-model checks on two hard objects. On a balanced 2,280-image evaluation split, aggregate score matching can coexist with image-level disagreement, and verifier-use protocols and generator distributions change the measured reliability. Every verifier-protocol configuration also shrinks the human score difference between the two generators, by 7.5-25.0 pp, and with a third generator, Z-Image, all four tested protocols reverse the human ordering of Z-Image and FLUX.2-dev on our fixed prompt suite. GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 checks do not remove the failure modes: GPT-5.5 still has only 59.92% clover valid-count fidelity, while Claude Opus 4.7 has lower same-slice agreement ($\kappa=0.432$). We propose reporting automatic benchmark scores with a factorized verifier reliability profile: aggregate score gap, image-level agreement, generator-comparison distortion, valid-image count fidelity, rejection behavior, output compliance, and directional bias.
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
bullets: Automatic scores depend on the generator, prompts, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule—not the generator alone.
A verifier-centric audit covers object and substructure counting across multiple models, protocols, and verifier types.
Aggregate score agreement can hide image-level disagreements, while protocol and generator distributions alter measured reliability.
All tested configurations narrowed human performance gaps, and some reversed the human ranking of generators.
Frontier closed models also showed counting and agreement failures, motivating factorized reliability reporting.

papers.abstract: Radiotherapy contour ranking can support quality assurance, but vision-language model (VLM) gains may reflect supervision, score construction, available inputs, or representation access. We evaluated frozen MedGemma 1.5 in a single-institution study, a 12-patient held-out HaN-Seg test, five-fold cross-fitting on 30 non-test HaN-Seg patients, and transfer without refitting to 120 SegRap2023 patients. On held-out HaN-Seg, a supervised readout of the final prompt state exceeded a supervised readout of the model's yes/no output probabilities by +0.3047 pooled average precision (AP; 95% patient-bootstrap interval [+0.2822, +0.3269]); the advantage persisted against a parameter-count-matched nonlinear control. A readout of projected visual tokens exceeded the final-state readout in cross-fitting and transfer (+0.0706 AP averaged equally across patients on SegRap; 95% interval [+0.0607, +0.0804]), while a structured panel-feature readout remained competitive with visual tokens. The anatomy-conditioned readout did not demonstrate an advantage over the native-feature comparator. These results motivate visual-token and structured-feature controls in medical-imaging VLM evaluations; outcomes were computational or synthetic, not clinical acceptability.
authors: Jaden Moon, Caiwen Jiang, Songlin Zhao, Wei Liu
bullets: Evaluated frozen MedGemma 1.5 for radiotherapy contour ranking across held-out, cross-fitting, and transfer settings.
A supervised readout of the final prompt state outperformed readouts of yes/no output probabilities on held-out HaN-Seg data.
Projected visual-token readouts outperformed final-state readouts in cross-fitting and SegRap2023 transfer; structured panel features remained competitive.
An anatomy-conditioned readout showed no advantage over the native-feature comparator.
Results were computational or synthetic and do not establish clinical acceptability.

papers.title: Supervision-Aware Evaluation of MedGemma for Reference-Assisted Radiotherapy Contour Ranking
papers.tldr: A supervision-aware evaluation finds that MedGemma’s contour-ranking performance depends strongly on the readout representation and available supervision, with projected visual tokens outperforming final-state features in transfer settings.

papers.abstract: Pathologists rarely diagnose from a single image: they scan a section at low power for architecture, zoom into selected fields for cytology, and integrate the evidence across views and scales. Pathology benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, mostly ask about one image or require whole-slide pipelines, and the few that show several fields draw nested regions from cancer slides of one public cohort. We introduce CaseScope, a benchmark of diagnosis from several curated fields of one lesion: CaseScope-Teaching, 436 cases from a residency-training image library, reconstructed, de-identified, harmonised against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist wherever an automated pre-review raised a doubt, and CaseScope-Atlas, 800 cases from 88 published atlases (387 of them figure series of one disease), labelled from the captions by two LLMs that must agree. They cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems and pose 4,679 items in six tasks, from open-ended and ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation to the verification and location of morphological findings. Across twenty-eight open and four proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses are unstable -- the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of the teaching cases -- and wrong answers favour the classic look-alike; open models make little use of the additional fields on teaching cases, where the one-line specimen site matters more, although on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields count about as much as the site; and most open models verify findings barely above chance (median 62.0% vs. 50%, best 81.5%), gaining a median +3.4 points from images; proprietary models reach 83.2-93.2%. Rankings broadly replicate between the sources. The evaluation code is available at https://github.com/Wenchuan-Zhang/CaseScope.
authors: Wenchuan Zhang, Chengyang Zhang, Fengling Li, Ting Yin, Chen Shu, Jie Chen, Shuwan Zhang, Xiaoyan Wu, Zhang Zhang, Yuhao Yi, Jiancheng Lv, Hong Bu
bullets: Introduces two case-level pathology collections: 436 teaching cases and 800 atlas cases spanning 843 entities across 18 organ systems.
Provides 4,679 items across six tasks, including open-ended and ten-way diagnosis, finding verification, and morphological localization.
Across 28 open and 4 proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses were often unstable; the best models were consistently correct across option rotations on 17.9% of teaching cases (open) and 61.7% (proprietary).
Open models used additional fields weakly on teaching cases, while fields became comparably informative to specimen site for atlas cases with at least three fields.
Finding verification by open models was near chance to moderate, with limited image gains; proprietary models performed substantially better.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.
authors: Shunming Liu, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Addresses domain gaps when transferring discrete diffusion generation to autonomous driving.
Optimizes planning representations during supervised fine-tuning to reduce hallucinations.
Uses metric-guided diversity filtering during reinforcement learning to improve exploration.
Introduces Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding, which adapts decoding to scene complexity.
Reports a 29.7% improvement over the unoptimized model and stronger performance than same-architecture autoregressive baselines across closed- and open-loop benchmarks.

Reinforcement Learning: Checkpoints of varying maturity levels are screened based on diversity and accuracy metrics, after which they are fed into the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training process. Inference: dVLM exhibits distinct confidence trends across different driving scenarios. DAD mechanism transforms these trends into specialized inference sequences to optimize output quality.

papers.abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.
authors: Shunming Liu, Jianyi Peng, Cheng Li, Lu Hou, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Targets the gap between front-view-focused MLLMs and the multi-view reasoning required for autonomous driving.

Finds insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning across current MLLMs.
Closed-loop specialist-model evaluations in AlpaSim indicate that stronger multi-view reasoning is associated with better driving performance.

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.
VPR shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing.
The training-free method works directly on the KV cache without attention-map extraction or extra forward passes.
Static VPR improved 97 of 100 model–task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks.
It increased attention to answer-relevant image regions with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies.

papers.abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

bullets: Addresses the gap between narrow medical AI tools and general-purpose models lacking private clinical imaging expertise.
Interprets complex neuroimaging examinations and communicates findings through natural-language conversation.
Diagnoses, localizes, and describes abnormalities; generates comprehensive radiology reports and assesses disease progression across serial exams.
Outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models across internal and international datasets, including resistance to misleading clinical assumptions.
Scope: focused on neuroimaging and trained on routine clinical-care data; the abstract does not specify detailed evaluation metrics or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overview of Neuro-VL training data, workflow, and evaluation. a, We curated the largest neuroimaging dataset to date, containing nearly 1 million studies collected from 450,000 patients, comprising 10 million volumetric scans. The dataset captures the full spectrum of neurological pathology, including neoplastic, vascular, infectious, degenerative, traumatic, and other conditions. b, Neuro-VL was trained to generate robust radiological interpretations of neuroimaging accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace. To reason over image and language input, Neuro-VL integrates a visual encoder with an LLM through a vision-language connector (not shown). The visual encoder incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism inspired by the inherent structure of neuroimaging data and is pretrained using radiology reports, enabling it to extract semantically rich visual features from complex neuroimaging studies. c, We evaluated Neuro-VL across internal health-system cohorts and 24 international public datasets spanning 21 countries. This evaluation covered diverse tasks, including localization, feature description, diagnosis, report generation, and longitudinal disease monitoring, as well as a comprehensive red-teaming evaluation.

Figure 3 | Neuro-VL for longitudinal disease monitoring. a, Schematic of longitudinal neuroimaging interpretation for disease monitoring. Neuro-VL can integrate imaging findings across multiple time points to assess tumor recurrence following treatment. b, Performance of Neuro-VL-Longitudinal, GPT-5.4, and Gemma 4 on change characterization (n=718), disease trajectory assessment (n=710), and intervention characterization (n=132). Results are mean accuracy with 95% CIs. 𝑃 values compare Neuro-VL with the highest-scoring comparator. c, Performance of Neuro-VL-Longitudinal compared with GPT-5.4 and Gemma 4 on longitudinal report generation (n=734). Neuro-VL identifies disease progression characterized by increased tumor burden, new nodular enhancement, extensive surrounding edema, and new mass effect with midline shift.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.
authors: Jingyuan Zhang, Nihao Niu, Xinyang Lv, Beibei Han, Xiaoyun Wang, Yanning Hou, Ke Xu

Dual-View Distillation aligns vocabulary-level probabilities, while differentiable Top-K selection supports discrete pruning.
A shared ranking supports multiple retention budgets with one frozen model.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% versus FastV at 10% retention and preserves 98.74% of baseline MME performance at 30% retention.

papers.abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis models are typically developed for a single machine under a specific set of operating conditions, such that each new machine or condition requires retraining from scratch. This one-machine-one-model paradigm scales poorly. Although transfer learning and domain generalization can reduce the labeling burden, they primarily seek domain-invariant commonality, potentially discarding machine-specific characteristics that are critical for diagnosis. This paper proposes TFC-MMFD, a time-frequency-condition multimodal fusion foundation model for rotating-machinery fault diagnosis under multi-element heterogeneous scenarios. Statistical indicators, time-frequency images, vibration sequences, and textual machine and condition descriptions are tokenized into a unified language-like space, allowing inputs of different physical origin to be represented as a single sequence. A LLaMA backbone, together with cross-modal bidirectional attention and a Q-Former, then distills this sequence into fault-mode queries. Diagnosis is performed by matching these queries against natural-language fault-mode anchors rather than fixed class indices, while regression-adversarial condition disentanglement and condition-conditioned masked pre-training improve robustness to changing conditions. Across four progressive tasks on ten public bearing datasets spanning diverse bearing types, speeds, and loads, TFC-MMFD attains 99.40% accuracy and 99.16% macro-F1, maintains over 80% accuracy on most interpolated unseen conditions without adaptation, and improves from 20.26% to 95.63% accuracy on an unseen machine with only five labeled samples per class. It outperforms the strongest of eight domain-generalization baselines by 10.57 percentage points and compares favorably with a recent bearing foundation model while using less than half of its fine-tuning data.

bullets: Addresses the poor scalability of one-machine-one-model fault diagnosis and the risk of losing machine-specific information through domain-invariant learning.

Uses a LLaMA backbone with cross-modal bidirectional attention and a Q-Former to derive fault-mode queries, matched to natural-language fault anchors.
Condition disentanglement and condition-conditioned masked pre-training improve robustness to changing and unseen operating conditions.
Across ten public bearing datasets, reports 99.40% accuracy and 99.16% macro-F1; it also reaches 95.63% accuracy on an unseen machine using five labeled samples per class.

papers.abstract: The visual world is cluttered: robust vision-language reasoning requires ignoring irrelevant information. Yet vision-language models (VLMs) can suffer substantial accuracy losses when answering questions about a target image with distractors present. Existing mitigations focus on selecting relevant images or limiting information exchange between images. Through a systematic analysis of three open 7-8B VLMs on five perception benchmarks adapted to include distractor images, we show that distractors reduce accuracy even when models correctly identify the relevant image, suggesting that selection alone is not enough. To understand the mechanism behind this interference, we combine attention analysis with targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL and identify middle-layer distractor-to-text connections as a pathway through which irrelevant visual information affects reasoning. We introduce answer consistency regularization, which encourages consistent answer distributions with and without distractors. Without directly constraining attention, this objective reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractor images, consistent with the pathway our analysis implicates. With five distractors, our approach improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline across the five benchmarks while preserving single-image performance.
authors: Marie Amale Huynh, Regev Cohen, Serena Yeung-Levy, Sivan Doveh
bullets: Distractors lower accuracy even when the model correctly selects the relevant image, so image selection alone is insufficient.
Analysis of three open 7–8B VLMs across five distractor-adapted perception benchmarks traces interference to middle-layer distractor-to-text connections.
Targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL support these connections as a pathway for irrelevant visual information to affect reasoning.
Answer consistency regularization reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractors without explicitly constraining attention.

papers.title: Back to the Question: Tracing Visual Distraction Through Text Tokens

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.
authors: Shreya Ajay Kale, Angad Ripudaman Singh Bajwa
bullets: Five open medical VLMs were audited on balanced ChestX-ray14 questions across findings and patient attributes.
HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detected zero of 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, while MedGemma and Lingshu detected 38% and 67%.
The failing models consistently denied pneumothorax with fluent, specific explanations and no abstention, despite chance-level balanced accuracy.
The failure persisted across prompts, resolutions, single-label cases, model scale, and an independent SIIM-ACR dataset.
Hidden-state probes recovered pneumothorax information, suggesting output suppression rather than visual blindness; per-finding recall and specificity are therefore necessary.

Across all 432 pneumothorax-positive cases, Qwen and HuatuoGPT return zero positives.

papers.selection_reason: Audits medical VLMs (MedGemma, Qwen, etc.) to reveal specific failure modes (e.g., zero recall on pneumothorax) masked by aggregate accuracy, analyzing internal representations and output suppression.
papers.title: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Diagnosis-Specific Failure in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Aggregate accuracy can conceal severe, diagnosis-specific failures in medical VLMs, including confident zero-recall detection of pneumothorax despite internally representing the finding.

papers.abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.
authors: Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun, Hanwang Zhang
bullets: Across 10 multimodal configurations and 6 model families, the study contrasts spatial-imagery tasks with symbol-manipulation tasks.
Ablating a vision-language direction in hidden states sharply harms spatial navigation while preserving—and slightly improving—boolean reasoning in Chameleon-7B.
The effect is direction-specific, layer-localized, and extends to mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective-taking.
Vision-shaped thinking is concentrated at 7–8B in the tested models and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in a tested 32B model.
In dual-path models, the causal signal lies in the generation pathway; probe-decodable information in the understanding pathway is not necessarily causally used.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how multimodal training shapes text-only spatial reasoning, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.
authors: Matteo Gabburo, Daniela Baiamonte, Stefano Simonazzi, Silvia Gardini, Sean Cesare Lazzeri, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Introduces MDU, a benchmark with 23,146 examples across 13 document-understanding tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish.
Covers capabilities from text and Markdown extraction to summarization, classification, named-entity recognition, and layout-sensitive extraction.
Evaluates 45 open-weight VLMs ranging from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system, under a shared protocol.
The benchmark is not saturated: the best average score is 69.0, only eight open-weight systems reach 65, and the top two results come from 27B models.
Language and task performance remain uneven as models scale; transcription ability can trade off against semantic extraction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: MDU at a glance. Documents are drawn from license-filtered FinePDFs across five languages and 77 domains; 13 tasks, grouped into seven capability families, are generated over them in both single- and multi-page settings. Each tick on the scale is one of the 45 evaluated systems: the best average is 69.0 and only eight of them reach 65, so the suite is far from saturated.

Figure 2: Single-page versus multi-page performance, averaged over the 45 evaluated models. Bars are means, whiskers one standard deviation across models. Tasks are ordered by the size of the drop. The nine tasks with paired variants are shown; Layout, NE and Passage Extraction and Conditional Summarization exist in single-page form only. The two classification tasks are the only ones where the multi-page variant is easier.

papers.abstract: Prompt-tuning has emerged as a parameter-efficient technique for adapting large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) to downstream tasks while keeping the pre-trained weights frozen. However, prompt-tuned VLMs often suffer from a base-to-novel dual miscalibration problem, where models typically show underconfidence on base classes and overconfidence on novel classes. Current VLM calibration approaches address this dual miscalibration either separately or jointly, but lack a geometric understanding of the hyperspherical embedding space and thus fail to exploit angular discriminative properties to adjust distorted decision boundaries. To address this, we propose M-PFT, a novel angular-margin approach for prompt tuning that introduces two complementary objectives to promote class discriminability and semantic anchoring. This enlarges the angular margin by 1) minimizing the maximum cosine similarity between tunable class embeddings to reduce embedding collapse and 2) minimizing the angular distance between each tunable embedding and its corresponding zero-shot embedding to preserve semantic geometry. Extensive experiments across 9 prompt-tuning methods with various backbones on 15 diverse datasets show that our approach reduces the average calibration error on novel classes, while remaining competitive on base classes and maintaining comparable accuracy. Further analyses reveal that M-PFT effectively adjusts distorted decision boundaries induced by prompt tuning while preserving the pre-trained embedding space, improving calibration with negligible computational overhead.
authors: Udaya Sampath K. Perera Miriya Thanthrige
bullets: Addresses dual miscalibration: underconfidence on base classes and overconfidence on novel classes.
Uses two objectives: separates tunable class embeddings and anchors them to corresponding zero-shot embeddings.
Improves novel-class calibration while remaining competitive on base-class calibration and maintaining comparable accuracy.
Evaluated across 9 prompt-tuning methods, multiple backbones, and 15 diverse datasets.
Adjusts prompt-tuning-induced decision boundaries with negligible computational overhead.

papers.abstract: We propose a multimodal transformer framework for efficiently modeling long1 financial documents that combine structured tabular data with noisy, unstructured2 textual disclosures. The framework represents financial tables as semantically3 enriched token sequences and integrates them with long-form text through a cross-4 attention mechanism that explicitly captures cross-modal dependencies. In par-5 ticular, we augment each numerical variable with a semantic embedding derived6 from its textual definition, enabling the model to encode both numerical magnitude7 and economic meaning. This design yields a more expressive and parameter-8 efficient representation of tabular data compared to value-only embeddings. Using9 a large-scale dataset of financial statements and MD&A disclosures, we show that10 structured numerical features remain the dominant source of predictive signal;11 however, textual information provides consistent incremental gains when incor-12 porated via cross-attention rather than simple concatenation. Our results further13 demonstrate that noisy textual disclosures are most useful when conditioned on a14 stable, semantically structured tabular representation. In particular, using frozen15 variable-level tabular representations as cross-attention queries enables the model16 to weight MD&A chunks differently for each financial variable and observation.17 These findings suggest that cross-attention provides an efficient mechanism for18 table-conditioned aggregation of long-form narrative evidence.
bullets: Financial documents combine structured numerical tables with long, noisy textual disclosures.
Each numerical variable is enriched with an embedding derived from its textual definition, capturing both value and economic meaning.
Cross-attention links table variables to relevant text more effectively than simple concatenation.
Tables provide the dominant predictive signal, while text adds consistent gains when conditioned on structured representations.
Frozen variable-level table representations let the model weight narrative chunks differently for each variable and observation.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors are commonly evaluated on real/fake classification alone, but real-world applications require explanations of the visual evidence behind each prediction. Joint vision-language models struggle with authenticity assessment, producing "real" narratives for manipulated images. To address this, we propose a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline as our submission to the ACM Multimedia 2026 Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge, with methods trained and evaluated on the XPlainVerse benchmark. A vision-foundation-model ensemble first classifies the image, then a Qwen3-VL-8B model generates a decision-conditioned explanation of the visual evidence. For fake images, a second Qwen3-VL-8B compresses that text into a short non-expert summary without using the image. We further apply metric-aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize both explainers against the challenge criteria. Under matched conditions, GRPO raises complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves grounding (entity and evidence F1); our submission ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall.
authors: Luka Dragar, Peter Peer, Vitomir \v{S}truc, Borut Batagelj
bullets: Addresses the gap between real/fake classification and explaining the visual evidence behind predictions.
Uses a vision-foundation-model ensemble for authenticity prediction, followed by a decision-conditioned Qwen3-VL-8B explainer.
Adds a second Qwen3-VL-8B to compress fake-image explanations into short, non-expert summaries without image access.
Metric-aligned GRPO improves complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves entity and evidence grounding F1.
Ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall in the Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge.
