papers.tldr: A decoupled classify-then-explain pipeline, optimized with metric-aligned GRPO, improves the quality and grounding of deepfake explanations.

papers.abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.
bullets: Targets correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget for newly lost correct answers.
Combines a linear probe on first-token logits, image-cluster threshold calibration, and a deterministic “none of the above” veto.
At zero calibration budget on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, it retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points.
At a 0.5% budget, it achieves 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 SFT gains; independent confirmation gives 66.05% with no losses.
Ordinary refusal SFT attains higher abstention but with greater regression cost; results are reported under frozen models and thresholds.

papers.abstract: Personalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as intelligent assistants has recently emerged as an active research topic, where an MLLM is expected to go beyond generic, one-size-fits-all replies, and instead generate responses grounded in user-specific objects, entities, and concepts encountered during interactions. Nevertheless, existing studies mainly focus on personalizing MLLMs on a static, predefined set of personalized concepts and require users to manually and frequently extend this set to accommodate newly emerging concepts, which is infeasible in dynamic-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we recast conventional MLLM personalization as an Open-Set problem, and propose TAME-O, the first long-context open-set personalized MLLM assistant. Specifically, TAME-O introduces a training-free, plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill (CR Skill). It enables the assistant to automatically unlock novel concepts during prolonged human-MLLM interactions while preventing confusion with previously unlocked ones, allowing the MLLM to continually grasp more and more concepts and progressively refine the modeling of known ones. Extensive experiments under the open-set personalization setting underscore the efficacy of our method.
authors: Rongpei Hong, Jian Lang, Ting Zhong, Fan Zhou
bullets: Existing personalization methods rely on a static concept set that users must manually update, limiting use in dynamic environments.
TAME-O is a long-context, open-set personalized MLLM assistant.
Its plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill automatically unlocks novel concepts during extended interactions.
The method helps distinguish new concepts from previously learned ones while progressively refining known concepts.
Experiments in open-set personalization support the effectiveness of the approach.

papers.abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. In this paper, we propose look-ahead state readout (LASER), an anticipation-guided agent for object state readout that uses possible next-step changes to determine which attributes to inspect in the present. Given temporally ordered frames and a target object, LASER converts anticipated changes into targeted visual questions and inspects the current frame to establish attribute values. It then checks state readouts and forecasts against independent observations of subsequent frames, refining a state record used to generate the final description. Reusable textual observation skills guide this process and are refined by tracing discrepancies with reference captions to the responsible instructions. Candidate revisions are selected on separate videos based on improved caption quality without increased contradictions with reference facts. Model parameters remain frozen throughout adaptation and inference, and the revised skills remain fixed during evaluation. Experiment results and further analysis on OSCaR and PLM RCap show consistent improvements of LASER over strong baselines and existing approaches, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.
bullets: Addresses underspecified attributes in multimodal language-model descriptions of changing object states.
Uses anticipated changes to generate targeted visual questions about the current frame.
Validates readouts and forecasts against later frames, then refines a state record for final descriptions.
Adapts reusable textual observation skills by tracing caption discrepancies, without updating model parameters.
Shows consistent improvements over strong baselines on OSCaR and PLM RCap, according to the abstract.

(3) Sequential visual correction checks the readout and hypotheses against the next observation, obtained independently of the hypotheses. Corrected history and local guidance support subsequent inspection; the accumulated state record supports the final description. (4) Feedback-guided skill revision uses source-video traces and reference captions to propose edits, then selects edits on separate selection videos when caption quality improves without increasing reference contradictions. Solid arrows indicate information flow; orange dashed arrows indicate source-trace transfer and skill-library updates for adaptation. The MLLM remains frozen, and the skill library is fixed during evaluation.

Each case shows the input frames and target region, an anticipated change, later visual evidence, the model caption, and the reference. Case 1 links an anticipated forward lean to a visual inspection criterion. Case 2 rejects a standing forecast and preserves the observed transition to sitting. Green contours identify the target.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to locate and interpret subtle evidence within complex scenes. Constructing supervision for this ability is challenging: questions must have correct, unambiguous answers that depend on actual fine-grained visual details rather than coarse cues or language priors. Verifying these properties makes manual annotation labor-intensive and automatic generation difficult for models that themselves struggle with fine-grained perception. Yet the same models can often recognize such details once the region is zoomed in. We exploit this global-to-zoom perception gap and introduce ZoomGain, a data construction pipeline that constructs questions about the full image from visual information gained only by zooming in. It verifies each answer on the zoomed view with multiple models, ensures that each question remains unambiguous in the full image and cannot be answered from language priors, and specifically generates high-quality distractors for multiple-choice questions. With this pipeline and human-only screening (no manual QA editing), we build ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark on which the best of 28 VLMs achieves only 61.08. Failure analysis reveals that models favor a particular type of distractor when answering multiple-choice questions incorrectly. Beyond evaluation, training on just 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the visual perception capabilities of our 4B/9B models, enabling them to outperform several hundred-billion-parameter models across various perception benchmarks. The trained 9B model achieves SoTA performance on several benchmarks, such as 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K. These results establish global-to-zoom perception gaps as a practical basis for scaling fine-grained visual supervision for both evaluation and training. Our code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain.
authors: Haozhan Shen, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Tiancheng Zhao, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of creating unambiguous questions that require genuine fine-grained visual evidence rather than coarse cues or language priors.
Uses a global-to-zoom pipeline to generate full-image questions, verify answers with multiple models, test ambiguity, and create challenging distractors.
Builds ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark; the best of 28 evaluated VLMs scores 61.08.

Training on 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the authors’ 4B/9B models, with the 9B model reaching 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K and outperforming much larger models on reported perception benchmarks.
Human involvement is limited to screening without manual question-answer editing; remaining errors include models’ preference for a particular distractor type.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ZoomGain. (a) Discover anchors and obtain consensus regions through independent grounding. (b) Mine global-to-zoom incremental evidence from paired views to construct questions and reference answers. papers.abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.
authors: Enhao Cui, Junzhi Yang, Yaoshun Lin, Yuhan Feng, Zijian Chen
bullets: The study tests whether left/right judgments come from image content, ViT position codes, or language-model token positions.
Mirroring ViT width positions reproduces flipped-image answers on 84.3–93.2% of CV-Bench left/right questions across several Qwen and InternVL models.
The effect is concentrated in global-attention ViT blocks, especially the final block in Qwen2.5-VL-7B; shifting the position grid also changes many answers.
Mirroring LLM-side token IDs or order produces few left/right changes, whereas reversing object order substantially affects some CV-Bench answers.
What'sUp results qualify the finding: many errors appear tied to relation binding, object localization, or use of the reference object.

papers.title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3

papers.abstract: Text-guided segmentation models receive an image and a short caption about the lesion, and on public benchmarks the caption improves accuracy considerably. On colonoscopy and breast ultrasound, however, the size, count and location words of each caption were computed from the mask that later scores the prediction, and the chest X-ray captions were written by benchmark annotators. We tested what two published models take from them. On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, it is mostly the lesion's extent. Keeping only the size word or the lung-zone phrase recovers 84 to 98 percent of the improvement over an empty caption, and removing it loses 52 to 77 percent. The rest matters little, and a polyp called a rock is segmented just as well. We call this extent leakage. On breast ultrasound, nearly half the captions also name the diagnosis, which carries part of the benefit. Retraining on three datasets shows that models pick up this habit from their training captions, though only partly on breast ultrasound, and that it weakens their segmentation from the image alone. The leak can be measured without training a model, since caption words alone predict lesion area (coefficient of determination 0.54 to 0.77 on six of seven test sets). Without the test mask, the best method we tested, which estimates extent from the image, reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy against the published 77.23. We propose an evaluation protocol that keeps what a caption says about the image apart from what it copies from the label.
authors: Niran Nataraj, Ankita Das, C. Krishna Mohan, Kenji Kawashima
bullets: On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, size or lung-location words recover 84–98% of the gain over empty captions, while removing them loses 52–77%.
Semantic content contributes little in these settings; even replacing a polyp description with “rock” yields similar segmentation.
Breast ultrasound captions partly benefit from diagnosis terms, but extent leakage remains present.
Models learn this shortcut from training captions, which can weaken their image-only segmentation ability.
Caption words alone predict lesion area, and an image-based extent estimate reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy versus 77.23 for the published method.

papers.abstract: Under a fixed frame budget, video understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) depends on whether the sampled frames provide sufficient evidence for the question. Sufficient frame evidence supports direct answering, whereas less informative observations may benefit from reasoning that connects the available cues. We introduce EVAThink, which enhances video understanding through evidence sufficiency-guided training for adaptive thinking. First, Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining constructs evidence-dense and evidence-sparse video views that share the same question and answer under an identical frame budget. It retains pairs where sparse views yield lower direct-answer accuracy than dense views but benefit from explicit reasoning, providing supervision for response-mode selection. Second, Evidence-Guided Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning uses stage-specific rewards to guide training with evidence-based mode preferences and then refine response efficiency, while first-token advantage regularization mitigates mode collapse. Trained on only 6.7K curated samples, EVAThink consistently improves upon the base model across video understanding benchmarks under both 32- and 64-frame budgets, while outperforming strong baselines on average. The code, model, and datasets are available at \href{https://github.com/ChangtiWu/EVAThink}{EVAThink}.
authors: Changti Wu, Ruizhe Fan, Bin Wang, Lei Zhang, Yuxiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses fixed-frame video understanding when sampled views may contain sparse or insufficient evidence.
Mines paired dense and sparse video views with the same question and answer to supervise response-mode selection.
Uses two-stage, evidence-guided reinforcement learning to first encourage appropriate thinking modes and then improve response efficiency.
First-token advantage regularization helps prevent collapse to a single response mode.
Trained on 6.7K curated samples, it consistently improves the base model across benchmarks at 32- and 64-frame budgets and outperforms strong baselines on average.

papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that pretrained image generators can support diverse visual tasks. Yet directly applying them to language-guided unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) segmentation exposes a key limitation: a plausible mask may correspond to the wrong instance among small and repeated objects. We call this mismatch between mask rendering and expression-level target selection the Grounding-Rendering Gap. We present DroneSegEdit, which combines RGB proposal rendering with language-grounded, proposal-constrained verification to select supported foreground while retaining rendered geometry. DroneSegEdit adapts the open-weight LongCat-Image-Edit model using task-specific LoRA and fixed color-to-label decoding. For referring segmentation, a Language-Grounded Spatial Verifier (LGSV) reads hierarchical states from the frozen multimodal large language model backbone to derive expression-conditioned spatial evidence, which is mapped back to the rendered proposal without introducing foreground outside it. On RIS-LAD, DroneSegEdit reaches a new state of the art at 52.78 mIoU, 7.16 points above the previous best. It remains competitive overall on UAVid-RIS and VDD-RIS, with its clearest class-wise gains on compact, application-relevant categories, notably vehicles and humans. A separate verifier-free experiment extends the RGB interface to full-scene parsing: a task-specific adapter jointly renders all classes from one task-level instruction without enumerating class names or palette colors.
authors: Dehua Chen, Long Xin, Jiangtao Wei
bullets: Addresses the Grounding-Rendering Gap: visually plausible masks can target the wrong small or repeated object.
Uses RGB proposal rendering plus proposal-constrained language verification, preserving rendered geometry while filtering unsupported foreground.
Adapts LongCat-Image-Edit with task-specific LoRA and fixed color-to-label decoding.
Achieves 52.78 mIoU on RIS-LAD, 7.16 points above the previous best, and shows notable gains for vehicles and humans.
Also demonstrates verifier-free full-scene parsing from a single task-level instruction.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.
authors: Qinan Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Qihang Jin, Tianyuan Wang, Hongbing Luo, Pengfei Li, Wenjun Lv, Yu Kang, Jian Di
bullets: Aggregate accuracy and consistency can miss whether a VLM judge changes its verdict for the correct reason.
State-Conditional Invariance (SCI) requires presentation stability under semantics-preserving changes and causal sensitivity to outcome-changing interventions.
GridWM-Judge uses deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with full, evidence-removal, counterfactual, presentation, and representation variants.
Five diagnostic tasks expose failures in evidence presentation, encoding, successful-trajectory activation, and paired counterfactual discrimination.
Results support jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) have opened up new possibilities for generating rich interleaved text-image content. However, they generally lack native support for coordinating the two modalities, and translating coarse user requests into coherent multimodal compositions also requires explicit planning. We propose UniWeaver, a structured, model-agnostic harness framework that integrates multimodal planning, generation, and visual feedback to produce coherent interleaved outputs. To train UMMs for this task, we construct UniWeaver-10K, a dataset of 10,000 tasks across 20 task families, paired with execution trajectories guided by UniWeaver. We also introduce UniWeaver-Bench, a task-oriented benchmark systematically assessing text coverage, writing quality, visual coverage, and image-text alignment. Experiments show that UniWeaver achieves state-of-the-art performance and improves interleaved text-image generation across multiple UMM backbones.
authors: Hongxu Chen, Zixuan Zhong, Donghao Zhou, Haodong Li, Xiaomin Yu, Tianhao Li, Shiyao Yu, Zhongwei Wan, Pheng-Ann Heng
bullets: Addresses UMMs’ limited native coordination between text and image modalities and their difficulty translating coarse requests into coherent compositions.
Uses a model-agnostic harness integrating multimodal planning, generation, and visual feedback.
Introduces UniWeaver-10K: 10,000 tasks across 20 task families with guided execution trajectories.
Introduces UniWeaver-Bench to evaluate text coverage, writing quality, visual coverage, and image-text alignment.
Reports improved performance across multiple UMM backbones, with state-of-the-art results claimed by the abstract.

papers.abstract: Event cameras record asynchronous changes in brightness. To use a general visual model as a recording trigger, a system must represent these measurements in a form the model can interpret. We compare direct grayscale accumulation, two temporal encodings, and two intensity reconstructors on paired real event data. On 192 windows from four held-out DSEC recordings, thresholds calibrated only on development data yielded 40 of 52 person detections and 12 of 140 background positives with E2VID. The strongest direct temporal encoding at an admissible fixed cutoff yielded 14 detections and seven background positives. A retrospective comparison at a common 10% background-positive cap yielded 40 detections for E2VID and at most 19 for any direct encoding. FireNet+ had lower preparation cost and produced 21 detections with zero observed background positives at its frozen cutoff. On the same 192 windows, Qwen3-VL-4B yielded 33/52, 2/140 with E2VID and 9/52, 9/140 with the highest-recall direct rendering, the three-bin image (person detections, background positives). A 96-second exploratory replay illustrates the sensitivity of episode capture and recording starts to cutoff selection. The experiments identify a detection benefit from reconstruction under controlled input history and distinguish it from the cost and false starts of continuous triggering.
bullets: Evaluates grayscale accumulation, two temporal encodings, and two intensity reconstructors on paired real event data.
E2VID detected 40/52 person windows with 12/140 background positives, versus at most 19/52 detections for direct encodings at a common 10% background-positive cap.
With Qwen3-VL-4B, E2VID achieved 33/52 person detections and 2/140 background positives; the best direct rendering achieved 9/52 and 9/140.
FireNet+ required less preparation and produced 21 detections with zero observed background positives at its fixed cutoff.
A replay study shows that cutoff selection strongly influences episode capture and recording starts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.
authors: Zhaoyi Liu, Haichuan Zhang, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Bowei Tian, Wanghao Ye, Yufan Zhang, Ang Li
bullets: MRoPE assigns spatial coordinates to both visual and text tokens, potentially affecting text–vision attention.
The work separates intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to study their distinct roles.
It identifies a limitation of shared coordinate layouts that prevents removing cross-modal effects without also losing visual spatial encoding.
Controlled experiments across model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks find that spatial references for text tokens provide little benefit and can impair performance.
Intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained visual grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of attention-specific coordinate assignments for disentangling cross-modal and intra-visual spatial effects. (a) Two coordinate assignments for visual patches. The original coordinates pa = (timg, ha, wa) preserve each patch’s spatial location, while the neutral coordinates p̃a = (timg, h̃, w̃) assign identical height and width coordinates to all patches within an image. Here, h̃ = w̃ = timg for the diagonal text layout. (b) Attention-specific coordinate assignments. Independently selecting original or neutral coordinates for text-vision (T-V) and vision-vision (V-V) attention yields four controlled configurations, while text coordinates and text-text (T-T) attention remain unchanged. (c) Geometric view on the (h,w) plane. In the w/o T-V Spatial configuration, original coordinates preserve spatial relationships among visual patches in V-V attention, while neutral coordinates yield identical relative rotations between any text token and all visual patches in T-V attention. This enables independent evaluation of the two spatial effects.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR
authors: Yanlin Chen, Tang Li, Xi Peng
bullets: Represents visual rationales as concepts paired with pixel-level groundings across multiple abstraction levels.
Uses scalable annotation that combines existing dense supervision with proposal-based grounding and conservative multimodal verification.
Evaluates whether models “look at what they say” by comparing expressed concepts with their grounded visual evidence.
Finds that current MLLMs have limited visual rationale correctness and exhibit different grounding failures across concept levels.
Provides a benchmark and data-construction pipeline for studying visually supported MLLM outputs.

papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly receive UI screenshots as part of bug reports, yet degraded image quality - caused by low resolution, compression artifacts, or small rendered text - can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files. Vision-language models become less reliable as image quality deteriorates, while OCR-assisted approaches may propagate recognition errors from degraded inputs. Both approaches are limited when the visual evidence required for localization is no longer clearly observable in the query screenshot. We propose augmenting coding agents with repository-rendered reference images: crisp screenshots generated from the same codebase that the agent is tasked with modifying. These references provide readable visual evidence of the application's UI while preserving the current, potentially bug-containing implementation state. Because they are generated from the available repository rather than requiring a known bug-free version, they can be produced automatically for reproducible application states without manual image annotation. We evaluate the approach on a controlled benchmark derived from SWE-bench Multimodal by injecting visual UI bugs into a real web application. We vary screenshot degradation and reference-image provision and measure whether the coding agent identifies the correct source file. The results show that reference images improve file localization especially for degraded image quality, increasing the gold file match rate under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. We confirmed with further analysis that the proposed approach recognizes text approximately 12 percentage points better than language biased OCR under the same degradation.
authors: Fumiki Yohena, Toshiaki Sota, Shota Suzuki, Tomoko Okamoto, Michiaki Tatsubori
bullets: Problem: Low-resolution, compressed, or text-heavy UI screenshots can prevent agents from identifying relevant interface elements and code files.
Method: Generate crisp UI reference images directly from the target repository, preserving its current implementation state and avoiding manual annotation or a known bug-free version.
Evaluation: A controlled benchmark based on SWE-bench Multimodal injects visual UI bugs and varies screenshot degradation and reference-image availability.

Results: Reference images improve source-file localization, particularly under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression; text recognition improves by approximately 12 percentage points over language-biased OCR under the same degradation.
Scope: The approach is evaluated on controlled web-application UI bugs and focuses on identifying the correct source file.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.
bullets: Standard VLM benchmarks may reward models for repeating findings named in questions rather than verifying image evidence.
MedScope-4B was trained with lesion-erased views, control edits, and label-derived trajectories to promote evidence-sensitive reporting.
On 507 internal cases, it achieved an evidence sensitivity gap of 0.758 and claimed erased lesions in 9.6% of cases, with no significant loss of real-lesion accuracy.
The effect replicated across another model and unseen inpainting tools, while prompting alone was insufficient.
External testing revealed scope limits: frontier models detected more real lesions, and MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films on a fresh test.

papers.tldr: Training on counterfactual lesion-erased images helps a small medical VLM report findings only when they remain visible, but it does not improve perception and can miss rare critical findings.

papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.
bullets: MAGs combine multimodal node attributes with relational edges and support applications such as e-commerce, social media, and content platforms.
Methods are organized into five integration levels: feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation-model integration.
The survey covers both discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models using a unified message-passing formulation.
It reviews datasets and evaluation protocols, introducing model-independent descriptors including label homophily, degree, clustering, and edge provenance.
It connects multimodal graph learning with AI agents and identifies open questions about when graph structure benefits strong multimodal foundation models.

papers.abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.
authors: Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, Grzegorz J. Nalepa
bullets: Evaluates text-only versus text-plus-graph prompts across 1,500 WebQSP/CWQ questions and six VLMs.
Graph images improve average F1 by 1.85 points, mainly through a +4.65 F1 precision gain on low-complexity questions.
Benefits are largely independent of model scale but highly dependent on visualization layout.
Hierarchical Graphviz layouts and separated paths perform best; image-only prompts and cluttered graphs can hurt performance.
The findings support adaptive prompting that adds diagrams selectively to small, visually sparse subgraphs to limit clutter and token overhead.

papers.abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.
authors: Shanwen Wang, Sirui Wang, Xin Sun, Jungong Han
bullets: Addresses the limited labeled data and weak scene-understanding capabilities of existing landslide detection models.
Uses Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning to support multiple visual tasks with labeled and unlabeled data.
Feeds predicted landslide regions as explicit spatial guidance to a parameter-efficiently adapted vision-language model for reasoning and analysis.
Introduces LandslideVL, a benchmark combining landslide imagery with textual prompts for intelligent landslide analysis.
Experiments on public datasets and LandslideVL report strong quantitative and qualitative performance, including better specialized reasoning than general-purpose VLMs.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Zhongxing Xu, Zhonghua Wang, Zhe Qian, Shiyan Su, Ming Hu, Xiaocheng Zou, Wei Feng, Mingquan Lin, Yuyin Zhou, Yifan Peng, Hamid Rezatofighi, Zongyuan Ge
bullets: MDLM denoising uncertainty generally decreases, but localized entropy spikes are linked to hallucinations.
The method identifies anomalous steps by comparing step entropy with that of a neighboring temporal window.
At spike steps, probability-weighted embeddings preserve multiple semantic hypotheses instead of committing to discrete tokens.
A stability-aware controller performs repeated latent refinement only when needed, then returns to discrete denoising.
Experiments report significant hallucination mitigation across multiple MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes step-aware decoding to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal diffusion language models.
papers.title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
papers.tldr: StepRefine reduces hallucinations in multimodal diffusion language models by detecting entropy-spike denoising steps and temporarily refining token distributions in a continuous embedding space.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.
bullets: Addresses agents overlooking useful tool-returned observations and taking poorly grounded actions that limit later evidence.
Uses Ground-Drop-GRPO to train spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and randomly removed original visual input.
Uses Observation-Gated-MOPD to replace deficient tool actions with canonical actions and continue distillation from the repaired observation.
Evaluated on 14 image and video benchmarks, Reframe outperforms Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD.
Ablations show GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain over outcome-based GRPO.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of GD-GRPO. The policy samples multi-turn tool-use rollouts. After the first successful tool call, the original input o0 is dropped with probability 0.5 while tool-returned observations ot remain visible, so the answer must rely on what the tools have retrieved. Rollouts are grouped by their pre-sampled drop flag di, and advantages are normalized within each subgroup so that dropout does not confound the comparison.

Figure 4. Overview of OG-MOPD. Tool actions of the student policy are checked against annotated evidence using an IoU threshold. Missing, invalid, or poorly grounded actions are replaced with annotation-derived actions to obtain query-relevant observations. Injected action tokens receive NLL supervision, while retained student-generated tokens are trained with MOPD.

Figure 1. Overview of Reframe: visual agents should produce reliable intermediate results and truly look at them. (a) Outcome-based RL without explicit grounding rewards can permit observation neglect. (b) Vanilla MOPD may supervise trajectories conditioned on a poorly grounded observation state. (c) Our GD-GRPO rewards grounded actions and encourages reliance on tool-returned observations. (d) Our OG-MOPD repairs deficient tool actions before continuing distillation.

Figure 2. Construction pipeline of Reframe-100K. We first collect public data sources and preprocess them into a raw data pool. We then drop samples answerable from text alone, and audit the rest with 8 rollouts on the full input (F ) and on the annotated evidence alone (E), discarding samples that are (1) too easy or too hard; (2) insufficiently supported by their evidence. Remaining suspicious samples are diagnosed by Qwen and removed only when a final reviewer confirms an answer or evidence error.

Table 2. Comparison of training paradigms. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best scores. Image-RL, Video-RL, and MixRL use GD-GRPO; MOPD and Reframe distill the same specialists with vanilla MOPD and OG-MOPD. Video-MME-v2, VSI-Bench, and V-STaR report Non-Lin Score, accuracy/MRA, and 100×mAM, respectively; MLVU reports M-Avg.

Table 1. Comparison with representative visual agents. Reframe adopts a predominantly on-policy paradigm to consolidate image and video reasoning within a unified model, while achieving the highest observation dependence and tool gain among the compared models. Observation dependence is measured on V∗. Tool gain is measured across seven image benchmarks.

Table 5. Optimization and reward settings. MOPD denotes the shared configuration of vanilla MOPD and OG-MOPD. The observation gate and injected-action loss are enabled only in OG-MOPD. The tool-reward settings apply only to GD-GRPO.
Table 6. Rollout and batch settings. Counts refer to independently sampled trajectories before turn splitting. Repeated optimization of a rollout does not create additional independent samples.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a post-training framework for visual agentic reasoning with tool-use observation alignment, directly relevant to multimodal LLM post-training and interleaved multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: Reframe improves visual agents’ tool use by aligning both their actions and the observations those actions produce during post-training.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.
bullets: MLLMs can make unreliable predictions when modalities disagree, sometimes favoring the less reliable source.
The work identifies a small set of causally influential attention heads, called arbitration heads, that control visual-versus-textual reliance.
Biasing these heads at inference time enables bidirectional control over modality preference across diverse benchmarks.
Arbitration heads remain stable across calibration-set sizes and generalize across settings.
Code is publicly available at github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of our method. (a) Arbitration head localization: we causally identify attention heads that causally influence modality preference by patching head activations from image-only and text-only inputs into conflicting multimodal inputs and measuring their effects on the answer logit margin. (b) Inference-time intervention: we select the most influential arbitration heads and steer predictions toward a designated modality by adjusting their attention to visual and textual tokens.

Figure 4. Preserving multimodal benefits under sparse modality conflict. The left and right panels evaluate MPS and our method steered towards image and text, respectively. Dotted lines denote unimodal performance. Although unimodal inference avoids modality conflict, it cannot exploit complementary information when the modalities are aligned. Adaptive steering retains this benefit while remaining robust to conflict.
Figure 13. Robustness to visual degradation.

Figure 3. Modality conflict detection for adaptive steering. Top50 union-logit cosine similarities for samples paired with conflicting or aligned context, where lower similarity indicates stronger modality conflict. The dashed line marks the threshold, selected to maximize conflict-detection accuracy on the calibration set.

Figure 5. Effect of steering strength α. Increasing α progressively shifts predictions toward the target modality, with performance saturating at moderate steering strengths. α = 0 denotes the unmodified baseline, and α = ∞ corresponds to hard masking of the competing modality.

Figure 6. Effect of the number of arbitration heads (top-k). Steering an increasing number of top-ranked heads progressively shifts predictions toward the target modality, with the effect saturating at moderate values. The top-k of 0 denotes the unmodified baseline.

Figure 7. Robustness of modality conflict detection using centered logits. Top-50 union-logit cosine similarities after centering each logit vector, for samples paired with conflicting or aligned context. Lower similarity indicates stronger modality conflict. The dashed line marks the conflict-detection threshold calibrated to maximize accuracy on the calibration set.

Figure 8. Robustness of modality conflict detection to calibrationset selection. Top-50 union-logit cosine similarities for samples paired with conflicting or aligned context, using a calibration set generated with random seed 43. The dashed line marks the detection threshold selected to maximize conflict-detection accuracy on the calibration set.

papers.title: Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs
papers.tldr: A lightweight, training-free inference intervention steers MLLMs toward a task-designated modality when visual and textual inputs conflict.

papers.abstract: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.
bullets: Evaluates four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization using two mammography datasets.
Tests robustness with controlled changes to questions, answer-option order, and images.
Models often retain confidence when the mammography image changes.
Shuffling answer options changes the answers of most evaluated VLMs.
Some explanations contradict the models’ final answers, raising trust concerns.

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) encode substantial expert knowledge within their weights, yet their direct application to specialised classification domains such as benthic imagery remains limited. Meanwhile, vision transformers trained on these tasks rely predominantly on low-level visual latents (colours, textures, and shapes) that lack the higher-level reasoning humans employ for identification. We propose Guided Hierarchical Multi-Label (GHiML) learning, a pipeline that extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM conditioned on training data, generates sample-relevant captions grounded in those variables, and fuses the resulting textual embeddings with image embeddings via cross-attention and a per-node gated router. We also introduce the inverted HML score ($d_{\mathrm{inv}}$), a similarity score that evaluates hierarchical multi-label predictions through graph traversal distance and a cardinality penalty, providing an interpretable alternative to existing measures, which are insensitive to realistic degradations in sparse, deep hierarchies. Experiments on BenthicNet, FathomNet and iNaturalist show that the router improves macro $F_1$ over the vision-only baseline by up to 6.7 pp and $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ by up to 21.1 pp on in-domain benthic data, with gains persisting under distribution shift. Ablations locate the contribution of the text itself: on the multi-label biotic hierarchies, removing the per-sample text signal degrades $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ while leaving macro $F_1$ unchanged, consistent with text acting through prediction cardinality rather than node discrimination, whereas iNaturalist, whose annotations are single-label, loses 18.7% of macro $F_1$. Our results support the hypothesis that VLMs contain exploitable specialised knowledge that, when appropriately elicited, can augment classification in domains where direct visual learning is insufficient.
bullets: Extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM and generates captions grounded in each image’s relevant concepts.
Fuses text and image embeddings using cross-attention and a per-node gated router for hierarchical multi-label prediction.
Introduces the interpretable inverted HML score (d_inv), combining graph-traversal distance with a cardinality penalty.
On benthic datasets, improves macro F1 by up to 6.7 percentage points and d_inv by up to 21.1 points over vision-only models, with gains under distribution shift.
Ablations suggest text mainly improves prediction cardinality in multi-label hierarchies, while single-label iNaturalist loses 18.7% macro F1 without it.

papers.abstract: Answer accuracy alone does not distinguish failures in acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application. AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) examines these distinctions through controlled input interventions. Each item contains an audio clip, a multiple-choice question, a task-general rule, and a textual description of the acoustic observations needed to answer. Three conditions progressively supply the rule and observations; a fourth removes the audio while retaining the question and rule. The first correct diagnostic condition assigns an operational response label, without identifying a unique internal cause. The current benchmark contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources, with answer references documented separately from percept extraction. In a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accuracy is 29.3% without supplied information, 31.3% with the rule, and 98.5% with the observations also supplied. No-audio accuracy is 23.9%, with a confidence interval containing the 25.0% chance rate. A family-level knowledge probe associates incomplete rule recall with larger gains from rule provision. These results show the benefit of supplying acoustic observations as text, while incomplete validation, possible recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit stronger failure-attribution claims.
bullets: Targets three stages of audio reasoning: acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application.
Uses four controlled conditions that progressively provide rules, textual acoustic observations, or no audio.
The benchmark has 201 items across 18 families from 9 sources, with answers separated from percept extraction.
In a preliminary Gemini-3.8-flash evaluation, accuracy rose from 29.3% unaided to 98.5% when observations were supplied; no-audio accuracy was near chance at 23.9%.
Incomplete validation, recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit definitive attribution of internal failure causes.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. An AuDiR item illustrated with vehicle speed. The model must recover the percept from the audio and apply the task-general rule to answer the question. The tone trajectory and frequencies are illustrative explanations, not text supplied in the base condition. The gold option is obtained separately by binning the cruise-control speed VS13 records for that pass; it is not estimated from the audio. This separation implements criterion C4 (Section IV-C).

Fig. 2. AuDiR construction and diagnosis. (a) Candidate percept–target pairings are screened and materialized into four inputs. The audio-removed condition ④ probes text-only answerability; current control results are reported in aggregate. Rejection reasons are detailed in Table VI. (b) The first correct response among conditions ①–③ assigns the operational diagnosis; failure under all three is assigned to application. Condition ④ is a separate validity control, not a fourth step in this assignment sequence.

papers.abstract: Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.
bullets: Addresses whether a finite discrete vocabulary can represent the richness of visual content.
Uses a frozen pretrained encoder with lightweight residual modulation and a dual-branch reconstruction-aware objective.
Applies grouped product quantization to expand discrete capacity without increasing spatial sequence length.
Provides unified visual encoding and high-fidelity image decoding across downstream tasks.
Matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 understanding, 4 generation, and 1 image-editing benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 6 Overview of the code-conditioned Refiner. Code embeddings condition a flow decoder through global context tokens and time-conditioned spatial residuals. A multi-step teacher is distilled into an efficient one-step student with adversarial supervision. The timestep t in the diagram corresponds to τ in the equations. Increasing the quantization group count (G64) improves reconstruction fidelity, whereas combining fewer groups (G16) with the one-step Refiner preserves fidelity while enhancing perceptual quality.

Figure 3 Overview of dNaViT. (a) A frozen representation encoder handles arbitrary resolutions, with ResMod injecting multi-level information before group-wise product quantization. The shared discrete codes are decoded by individual ViT decoders into pixel and semantic reconstructions. (b) ResMod fuses intermediate features and predicts a zeroinitialized scale-and-shift residual. (c) Pixel and semantic branches are optimized with image and feature reconstruction losses, respectively.

Figure 4 Tokenization and Unified Codes for Downstream Tasks. (a) At spatial position t, the modulated feature zt is split into G channel groups and quantized with group-specific codebooks E(g), yielding indices (k (1) t , . . . , k (G) t ) and their embeddings. (b) Understanding supplies only code indices to the language model (LM) through newly initialized group-wise embedding tables {W(g)}Gg=1, trained jointly with the LM. (c) Reconstruction concatenates the indexed embeddings from the frozen tokenizer codebooks and feeds them to the pixel decoder Dpix. (d) Generation and editing use a multi-sub-token head atop the LM to predict each position’s multi-level indices, optionally conditioned on a reference image, then decode through the same frozen codebooks and pixel decoder.

papers.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $ρ$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $ρ$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $ρ$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
bullets: ρ measures each attention head’s capacity to couple with rotary positional encodings.
Across four bias-free RoPE models (135M–7B parameters), ρ predicts induction heads with Spearman correlations from −0.55 to −0.74.
Applying YaRN only to the top 50% of positional heads causes less perplexity degradation than applying it uniformly.
The study focuses on bias-free RoPE models and presents targeted YaRN application as a preliminary proof of concept.

papers.abstract: General-purpose vision-language models struggle with crisis imagery due to its inherent noise, ambiguity, and high variability across disaster events - yet timely, accurate scene understanding is critical for humanitarian response. To address this, we introduce DisasterVLG, a large-scale multi-task dataset containing 1.24 million disaster images from 142 countries paired with 33 million structured annotations spanning dense captioning with localization, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded visual question answering (VQA) across diverse hazard types and scene contexts worldwide. Unlike prior disaster benchmarks that focus narrowly on classification, DisasterVLG unifies recognition, grounded reasoning, and uncertainty-aware interpretation. A distinguishing feature is its evidence-grounded annotation design: each VQA instance includes supporting evidence text that links visual observations to answers, alongside positive and negative question pairs, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Visual grounding layer links caption phrases to image regions and relationship statements to subject-object boxes, with explicit labels for visual supports and clues. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct a human-verified test set of 38K images (1.15M annotations) spanning broad geographic regions and disaster types. Experiments with domain-adapted vision-language models demonstrate strong performance across disaster captioning, incident recognition, and grounded VQA, while also exposing the limitations of general-purpose models in crisis-specific reasoning. DisasterVLG establishes a scalable, reproducible benchmark for vision-language models that must reason reliably under real-world uncertainty. We will publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.
bullets: Introduces 1.24M disaster images from 142 countries with 33M structured annotations.
Covers localized dense captioning, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded VQA.
Links answers and descriptions to visual regions, supporting evidence, clues, negative pairs, answer formats, and difficulty labels.
Provides a human-verified test set spanning diverse geographic regions and disaster types.
Experiments show domain-adapted models perform strongly but reveal persistent limitations of general-purpose models in crisis reasoning.

papers.abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.
bullets: Addresses emotion errors when verbal, vocal, and visual cues conflict.
Runs a frozen student model inside a harness that structures observations, transcript, and prosody as citable evidence.
Meta-Harness Evolving uses a stronger Builder to edit and validate the harness offline without seeing evaluation items.
Across 5,507 MME-Emotion items, Recognition improves by 7.6–13.4 points over video-only calls for four students and two Builders.
Most gains come from transcripts and prosody; scaffold and evolved-harness effects are smaller, and evolved gains do not survive Holm correction.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation (MERC) combines lexical, acoustic, visual and conversational cues, but accepting audio and video does not establish their effective or robust use. We audit off-the-shelf Omni models while holding the target transcript and prior textual context fixed and adding, removing or replacing target audio and video. In the primary evaluation of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and the full five-session six-class IEMOCAP set, T+A improves Accuracy in all six model-dataset pairs, with four gains significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Across three source mappings, unrelated A/V (RandA/V) lowers Accuracy relative to Full in all 18 comparisons; all 18 remain significant under dialogue-cluster inference and BH-FDR correction, both on common-valid pairs and when invalid/OOM outcomes are treated as incorrect. Comparisons with modality-omission baselines further distinguish replacement penalties from mismatch-specific harm. A Qwen/MELD case study finds significantly greater gold-vs-best-candidate margin recovery in Late than Early or Middle under decision-query audio knockout, relative to an edge-count-matched Video-Sham control, using Holm-corrected tests. These results distinguish genuine-modality benefit from sensitivity and vulnerability to misleading input.
bullets: Evaluates Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5, and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and IEMOCAP with transcripts and textual context held fixed.
Adding target audio and text improves accuracy across all six model–dataset evaluations, with four gains remaining significant after FDR correction.
Replacing target audio/video with unrelated inputs reduces accuracy in all 18 comparisons, with significance robust to dialogue-cluster and BH-FDR correction.
Omission baselines separate general modality sensitivity from harm caused specifically by mismatched inputs.
A Qwen/MELD case study suggests later-stage audio processing better recovers correct decisions after audio removal than earlier or middle-stage processing.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Reasoning (MER) requires perceiving and integrating emotion cues from multiple modalities. Recent advances increasingly leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to enhance reasoning capacity. However, due to the inherent heterogeneity in conveying emotions across modalities, these models often suffer from modality imbalance and confront flawed emotion understanding. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis on MER models and uncover two key empirical insights. (i) In MER, modality imbalance manifests two distinct failure modes: unimodal over-reliance and insufficient cross-modal utilization, which call for different intervention strategies. (ii) MLLM layers exhibit implicit functional hierarchies in multimodal emotion processing, playing separable roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating cross-modal information. Motivated by these observations, we propose a Layer-Aware Modality Rebalancing (LAMR) framework by explicitly aligning intervention strategies with layer roles. Specifically, we first introduce two quantized metrics for adaptive layer role profiling. In each layer, Modality Entropy (ME) measures the dispersion of modality contributions, and Cross-modal Intensity (CMI) captures the strength of cross-modal interactions. Then, we respectively enhance modality equilibrium in stabilization layers and cross-modal propagation in integration layers. Extensive experiments on two comprehensive MER benchmarks demonstrate that LAMR effectively mitigates modality imbalance and improves emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones, without additional training.
bullets: MER imbalance has two failure modes: over-reliance on one modality and inadequate cross-modal use.
MLLM layers serve distinct roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating modalities.
LAMR profiles layers with Modality Entropy and Cross-modal Intensity.
It balances modality contributions in stabilization layers and strengthens cross-modal propagation in integration layers.
Experiments on two MER benchmarks show improved emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones.

papers.abstract: In modular grounding a frozen detector proposes regions and a vision-language model (VLM) selects one, at lower cost than letting the VLM decode a box, but it is unclear where such systems fail. We hold perception fixed---every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, which contain the referent for at least $99.8\%$ of RefCOCO/+/g queries---and vary the selection interface one factor at a time for two VLMs of one family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B). On RefCOCOg, what the selector reads matters more than how it is built: the VLM's image-conditioned query encodes the referent's location and beats a text-only query by $0.15$--$0.18$ with every head tested (by less for InternVL3-8B, whose vision encoder differs; one head tested). The remaining errors are rankings among a few top candidates; a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding on RefCOCOg, and with Qwen2.5-VL on RefCOCO/+ when also trained on their data. Beyond that distribution it does not: on Ref-L4's Objects365 images, mostly of categories outside training, every trained head falls to $0.19$--$0.28$ while Qwen decoding keeps about $0.8$ (InternVL3's drops too), neither a wider detector prompt nor a class-agnostic proposer closes the gap, and on public reasoning benchmarks Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO full-budget heads trail decoding by $0.19$--$0.37$ although proposals cover most referents. A trained verifier reduces to an existence probe on the VLM's query state and does not beat the VLM's yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.
bullets: Frozen detector proposals contain the referent for at least 99.8% of RefCOCO/+/g queries, isolating proposal selection as the main bottleneck.
Image-conditioned VLM queries encode location and outperform text-only queries by 0.15–0.18 on RefCOCOg across tested selection heads.
Cross-attention selection can match coordinate decoding in-distribution, especially with supervision on the target data.
Out of distribution, selection accuracy drops to 0.19–0.28 on Ref-L4, while coordinate decoding remains about 0.8; broader proposals and prompts do not fix the gap.
Verifier training mainly probes whether a target exists and does not outperform the VLM’s direct yes/no answers on no-target benchmarks.

papers.title: Where Does Proposal Selection Fail? Diagnosing Frozen Vision-Language Queries over Detector Proposals
