papers.abstract: Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.
bullets: Benchmarks can overestimate acoustic understanding because many tasks are answerable from the transcript or question alone.
The study separates lexical tasks from global-attribute tasks (e.g., speaker, emotion) and within-recording structure tasks (e.g., stress, intonation).
Across 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro, open-model deficits are especially large on attribute and structure tasks, with much of the gap tied to recording-specific information.
Linear probes show relevant acoustic information is often readable in early layers but becomes less accessible in later layers.
LoRA adapters trained in these layers, using a content anchor, improve attribute and structure accuracy while keeping lexical accuracy nearly unchanged.

papers.abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.
bullets: SurgKnowBench harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks to evaluate proprietary and open-source multimodal models.
Current models show partial visual knowledge but weak relational, procedural, and workflow understanding.
SurgAgentGym enables agents to use bounded SurgWiki searches and general-purpose visual grounding without additional surgical training.
Tool-mediated inference mainly improves perception-heavy tasks; fine-grained localization and expert assessment remain bottlenecks.
The framework supports future research on agentic approaches to surgical understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses costly, backbone-specific post-training for visual-CoT capabilities.
Disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning components rather than treating it as one capability.
Extracts source-model capability vectors, aligns them to the target activation space, and steers relevant layers at different stages.
Works across heterogeneous LVLMs and benchmarks spanning high-resolution understanding, perception/reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning.
Outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on primary metrics.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-step budget, and online selection baselines. Ablations further validate the importance of semantic coverage, online reward transfer, and stable discovery cadence, establishing DISCOVER as a practical framework for data-efficient multimodal RL post-training.
bullets: Targets wasted rollout and annotation costs from low-signal prompts in verifiable-reward multimodal RL.
Clusters samples semantically, queries diverse representatives, and transfers sparse reward feedback to estimate unannotated-sample utility.
Continuously updates utility using recency-weighted rollouts and selects prompts based on reward variance and difficulty.
Uses utility-based replay after the discovery budget is exhausted.
On ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B, improves mathematical reasoning under a 10% unique-sample budget; ablations support its key design components.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Cluster-balanced online discovery and frozen-pool reweighting. DISCOVER builds a fixed multimodal embedding atlas, clusters the prompt pool, and probes REPR to seed a recencyweighted buffer. During discovery, observed easy/hard prompts (green/red) are admitted across clusters while cosine-KNN transfers sparse feedback to unobserved candidates (yellow). Once the unique-prompt budget is exhausted, the pool is frozen and subsequent GRPO steps reweight replay from the buffer; intensity encodes recency.

Figure 1: DISCOVER pipeline. Offline (green, left): prompts are embedded, clustered via spherical k-means, and seeded with REPR samples. Online (blue, right): GRPO rollouts from πθt feed a recency-weighted buffer; cosine-KNN transfers sparse statistics to unobserved prompts; utility scoring (Eq. 7) ranks all candidates. The budget switch routes scores to cluster-balanced discovery (Eq. 8), which admits new prompts until budget B is exhausted, after which frozen-pool replay (Eq. 9) reweights the existing pool. Both modes return prompts to the policy.

papers.abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.

papers.abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.
bullets: Targets the scalability and resource costs of continuous cooperative perception in multi-agent traffic.
Combines conventional object detection, VLM-based occlusion reasoning, physics-based visibility constraints, and Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Uses real-world connected-vehicle data and evaluates four state-of-the-art VLMs for blind-spot detection and dialogue-based sharing.
Achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind-spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing.
Designed as an interpretable, bandwidth-efficient approach for connected traffic systems.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promise as interactive agents, yet precise, programmatic 3D graphics editing remains difficult to train because existing systems largely rely on closed-source model APIs and lack deterministic, state-verifiable execution environments. We present BlenderFORGE, a trainable data-environment-optimization framework for open-weight MLLM agents that edit explicit Blender scenes through Blender Python (bpy) code generation. BlenderFORGE targets four fundamental state-verifiable editing task families: object placement, shape-key editing, lighting adjustment, and material modification. It integrates three components: (1) a scalable perturbation-based data generation pipeline built from curated assets and large-scale 3D scene repositories; (2) an isolated Blender Sandbox for deterministic code execution, structured state export, and closed-loop reward computation; and (3) a two-stage training pipeline that uses offline teacher trajectories for cold-start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and sandbox-computed rewards for multi-turn tool-agentic Reinforcement Learning (AgentLoop-RL). Experiments across the four task families show that the resulting open-weight Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B BlenderFORGE agents substantially improve over their base models and achieve competitive performance with several zero-shot proprietary MLLM baselines on selected metrics. Additional cross-benchmark evaluations and camera-reframing experiments provide evidence of transfer beyond the original training setting.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training precise 3D-editing agents without closed-source APIs or deterministic execution environments.
Supports object placement, shape-key editing, lighting adjustment, and material modification tasks.
Combines perturbation-based data generation, an isolated Blender Sandbox, offline SFT, and sandbox-rewarded AgentLoop-RL.
Trained Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B agents improve over their base models and are competitive with selected zero-shot proprietary baselines.
Cross-benchmark and camera-reframing evaluations suggest transfer beyond the original training setting.

papers.abstract: Lane-level map updating requires temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state together with the current observation. We introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior to improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary effectiveness of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. A cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models while reserving complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Since its deployment in March 2025, RoadState has supported lane-level map updating across more than 360 cities and reduced overall production costs by 30%. Together with human-in-the-loop auditing, the system maintains robust performance under stress-test conditions. These results demonstrate how domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing, and human quality control can bridge the gap between VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent and physically invalid road semantics caused by occlusions, ambiguous markings, obstacles, and viewpoint changes.
RoadState-VLM predicts the current structured road state from prior observations, symbolic state, and the current image.
Geo-CoT uses a dependency graph as a domain prior to improve consistency across interdependent road-state dimensions.
Reports 94.33% mean accuracy across six dimensions and complementary benefits from Geo-CoT and temporal context.
Deployed across 360+ cities, the cascaded system reduced production costs by 30% while retaining human-in-the-loop quality control.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.
bullets: Introduces FoundationChain, which asks VLMs to infer a crochet pattern from an object image.
Uses hand-crocheting as a tangible, low-cost way to verify whether generated procedures work.
Evaluates 40 patterns from four VLMs through physical execution.
Only four generated patterns are error-free.
Failures reveal weaknesses in visual, geometric, and procedural reasoning that automated checks may miss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made progress in general visual tasks. However, limitations remain in fine-grained visual tasks requiring evidence from minute image regions. Existing methods primarily train models using evidence-related regions while overlooking the influence of extensive background regions, resulting in a limited ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. We propose selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation (SPN-OPSD), which considers both evidence and background regions. Supervision from both views improves the model's ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. Furthermore, selective token-level distillation provides more informative supervision, improving the model's ability to attend to evidence regions in Fine-Grained Visual Tasks. On Qwen3.5-2B, SPN-OPSD improves accuracy on V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite from 76.44%, 45.92%, and 57.43% to 84.82%, 54.56%, and 59.56%, respectively. Similar gains are also observed on Qwen3.5-0.8B.
bullets: Fine-grained visual tasks require extracting evidence from minute image regions, where background content can distract models.
The method uses selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation with both evidence and background views.
Selective token-level distillation provides targeted supervision for attending to relevant regions.
On Qwen3.5-2B, accuracy improves across V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite; similar gains appear on Qwen3.5-0.8B.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted as end-to-end driving planners, yet they suffer from cross-city domain shift. Existing methods treat this shift as a single quantity addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing. We challenge this view on two counts: (i) domain shift in VLM trajectory planners is inherently structured across modality and layer, and (ii) a locate-then-repair recipe matched to this structure outperforms every uniform-objective baseline. We analyse domain shift via activation patching and uncover two regularities. (F1) Modality axis. Image and text tokens exhibit distinct shift patterns in each VLM. (F2) Layer axis. The layer-wise shift partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. These findings recast domain shift as a two-dimensional tensor indexed by modality (image vs. text tokens) and layer, motivating a simple principle: locate where shift occurs, and repair only there. We instantiate this principle in MoLaRx (Modality-Layer Repair), a locate-then-repair framework. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) estimates the domain shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions the layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then applies a matched operator (Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) / low-rank adaptation (LoRA) / freezing) to repair each zone, with the composition adapting automatically to each architecture. We evaluate MoLaRx on three architecturally distinct VLMs (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, and PaliGemma2-3B) across two cross-city benchmarks (nuScenes and Argoverse 2). MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, while using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. In contrast, uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings, highlighting the importance of structure-guided repair.
bullets: Domain shift is structured across image versus text tokens and across model layers, rather than being a single uniform discrepancy.
Activation patching reveals architecture-dependent but dataset-stable layer-wise shift patterns.
MoLaRx estimates a modality-layer shift tensor with the Causal Importance Score and partitions layers into functional zones.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately $10^{-5}$ to $10^6$ Hz, sequence lengths from $10^1$ to $10^6$ samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.
bullets: Introduces MHB, a benchmark with 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains covering highly varied signals and input regimes.
Current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs show limited zero-shot transfer to machine-hearing tasks.
Supervised adaptation alone does not resolve the gap, pointing to a mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs.
MachEar is a lightweight encoder extension designed to adapt pretrained Audio LLMs to these inputs.
MachEar improves machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving existing audio understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual citations show where an answer is supported, but not how the cited content contributes to it. In scientific document question answering, a model may read a value directly, compress several observations, or combine evidence to infer a conclusion. We study typed visual provenance, where a system generates an answer together with source regions and explicit support relations. We introduce ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents, with page, section, and region annotations labeled as Quotation, Compression, or Inference. We further propose VisProve, which augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback. VisProve conditions next-token prediction on localized visual evidence and its estimated support relation through a gated norm-bounded residual. On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve improves Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally. These results suggest that coupling visual grounding with support relation modeling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, while the low absolute Typed-F1 reveals a substantial gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.
bullets: ReViE contains 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents with page, section, and region annotations.
Annotations classify support as Quotation, Compression, or Inference.
VisProve uses Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback to condition generation on localized evidence and support relations.
On document-disjoint ReViE tests, Typed-F1 rises from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24; Page-F1 changes little.
Low absolute Typed-F1 indicates that precise evidence attribution remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can recognize events in images and parse sentences, but it remains unclear when they bind visual Agent-Patient structure to linguistic semantic roles across languages whose role cues depend on morphology, word order or construction. We introduce ROLECUE, a controlled diagnostic that pairs 192 validated two-person action images with German, Turkish, Japanese, English, Korean and Bangla sentences in canonical and patient-first orders. The evaluation separates image-only role recognition, text-only role parsing, direct image-sentence matching, response-compliance behavior and an external modular composition of the model's own component predictions. Across eight recent open-weight VLMs, ROLECUE reveals a structured spectrum: some models fail visual or linguistic component tests, some largely solve the diagnostic, some collapse to constant semantic assent and several show component-joint gaps in which reliable image-only and text-only role predictions do not survive direct joint inference. The largest non-degenerate gaps reach 44.9 percentage points, with final bootstrap intervals confirming that the effect is not a point-estimate artifact. These results reveal multilingual component-joint performance gaps and acceptance biases hidden by aggregate VLM benchmarks and show why component diagnostics are necessary before interpreting joint multimodal errors.
bullets: Evaluates Agent–Patient role binding using 192 two-person action images and sentences in six languages.
Separates visual role recognition, text parsing, image–sentence matching, response compliance, and modular composition.
Across eight open-weight VLMs, identifies visual, linguistic, joint-inference, and constant-assent failure patterns.
Finds non-degenerate component–joint gaps as large as 44.9 percentage points, with bootstrap intervals supporting their robustness.
Shows that aggregate benchmarks can hide multilingual role-binding failures and motivates component-level diagnostics.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.
bullets: Identifies a modality reasoning-access gap: models can read rendered text in images but struggle to reason over the images directly.
Mines synthetic cases where a model succeeds on text but fails on the equivalent rendered image.
Post-trains on these image inputs using GRPO, with SFT and DPO variants also explored.
Training only on synthetic rendered-text images improves performance across diagrams, science, charts, and embodied spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Activation analyses suggest TIGER aligns visual-to-reasoning pathways with text-reasoning states and complements existing visual RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: The task of visual reasoning relative pose identification (VRRPI) has exposed critical weaknesses in the multi-view 3D spatial reasoning capabilities of modern vision-language models (VLMs). We present a systematic analysis of VLMs' behavior in VRRPI, uncovering stable output biases where VLMs disproportionately predict specific motion patterns regardless of visual evidence. To mitigate these inherent biases, we propose self knowledge re-expression with iterative debiasing (SKR-ID), an annotation-free pipeline that adapts VLMs for VRRPI using only randomly extracted unannotated image pairs. SKR-ID transitions VLMs' output mechanism from generic next-token prediction to task-optimized classification heads. The pipeline proceeds in two stages: (1) a cold-start initialization using debiasing object-centric prompts to anchor motion inference in 2D visual evidence; and (2) a recursive logit-ranking mechanism that enforces statistical parity by using the median logit value as a dynamic threshold. Experimental evaluation across frontier VLMs on standard benchmarks demonstrates that SKR-ID significantly mitigates systematic biases. Our method improves open-source VLMs' Macro-F1 scores from 35.0-45.4% to 53.7-58.0%, without using any annotated data. These results show that SKR-ID can effectively improve 3D reasoning performance from a severely collapsed baseline. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/astudentuser/Codes_of_SKR-ID.
bullets: VLMs show stable, evidence-insensitive output biases in multi-view 3D relative-pose reasoning.
SKR-ID adapts VLMs using only randomly selected unannotated image pairs.
It combines object-centric prompts for cold-start visual grounding with recursive median-logit ranking for statistical debiasing.
Across frontier VLMs and standard benchmarks, open-source models’ Macro-F1 improves from 35.0–45.4% to 53.7–58.0%.
The approach targets severely collapsed baselines and does not require annotated data.

papers.abstract: Mental simulation, the ability to reason by constructing and updating internal visual states, is central to flexible human cognition, but remains elusive in current multimodal large language models. Latent multimodal reasoning offers a promising route toward this capability by interleaving text with continuous visual latent blocks, allowing models to maintain internal visual workspaces without decoding them into pixels. In this paper, we ask whether these latent visual states actually matter. Through a direct perturbation analysis across representative latent-reasoning MLLMs, we find that they often do not: dropping, replacing, or shuffling generated visual latents has only minor effects on the model's own final-answer probability, while equivalent perturbations to the linguistic reasoning trace are substantially more damaging. We call this failure mode Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): the model appears to perform interleaved visual reasoning, but routes most answer-relevant computation through text. We further diagnose that MSC follows naturally from existing training objectives: visual alignment can make generated latents resemble helper-image embeddings, but it does not require the decoder to rely on them; subsequent text-only supervision further leaves the semantic role of the latent pathway unidentifiable. To address this, we introduce AnchorSim (Anchored Mental Simulation), a contrastive distillation framework that trains models to make their generated visual latents consequential. Across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks, AnchorSim improves performance, while diagnostic re-evaluation shows that visual perturbations now meaningfully affect predictions. Our results expose a fundamental failure mode of latent multimodal reasoning and demonstrate that mental simulation must be anchored to model behavior in order to matter.
bullets: Identifies Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): perturbing visual latents has little effect, unlike perturbing text reasoning traces.
Attributes MSC to training objectives that align visual latents without requiring downstream reliance on them.
Introduces AnchorSim, a contrastive distillation framework for anchoring generated visual latents to model behavior.
Reports improved performance across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks and stronger sensitivity to visual-latent perturbations.
Shows that effective latent mental simulation requires visual states to be causally relevant to predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AnchorSim. Given an initial image and query, the model produces an interleaved reasoning trajectory consisting of textual thoughts tk and intermediate visual simulations zk. AnchorSim trains the student policy with two complementary signals. First, a visual-blind branch masks the previous generated visual state zk−1 and is stopped from receiving gradients; the student is encouraged to diverge from this blind prediction, preventing “lazy text” reasoning that ignores visual latents. Second, a simulation-anchored teacher, updated as an EMA of the student and conditioned on the ground-truth answer, provides reliable reasoning targets under the full context. The student is optimized to minimize the JSD to the teacher while maximizing the JSD from its visual-blind counterpart, thereby anchoring textual reasoning to the generated visual simulations.

Figure 1: Vision vs. text perturbation impact across four multimodal latent-reasoning models. Each panel reports the mean log-probability (±1 SEM) of the model’s final-answer span. We compare four conditions applied independently to the vision block (blue) and the reasoning text block (purple): Full (unchanged), Drop (removed), Cross (replaced from another sample), and Shuffle (permuted). Step 2 shows them on the vision block; the charts apply them to both blocks in turn. A larger drop from Full indicates that the perturbed block carries more answer-relevant information. In most conditions, perturbing the text block degrades the answer substantially more than perturbing the visual block, indicating that computation is routed primarily through the linguistic stream.

Figure 5: Perturbation analysis. (a) OLS slope S between perturbed and unperturbed answer logprobabilities for Qwen-interleaved and ANCHORSIM, where S ≈ 1 indicates little effect. (b) Closed-loop analysis, where the model regenerates the rest of the trajectory after the perturbation.

CoVT emits a fixed three-encoder visual-block template per trajectory, so all perturbation conditions are evaluated on the full 100-sample set. Vision-side perturbations leave many samples close to the no-impact diagonal, whereas text-side perturbations move a substantial subset below the diagonal. This shows that the model’s final-answer probability is more sensitive to corrupted reasoning text than to corrupted SAM, depth, and DINO pad hidden states.

Points further below the y=x diagonal (dashed) and lower ordinary-least-squares fit slopes (solid lines) indicate a larger performance drop. Across all conditions, the text fit has a lower slope than the vision fit, demonstrating that perturbing the linguistic chain degrades the answer more than perturbing the visual latents.

Figure 12: Qualitative example on SAT-R. The task requires mentally simulating a spatial or viewpoint transformation from a real image. The example illustrates how latent visual states can support intermediate spatial reasoning before the model commits to the final answer.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.
bullets: Targets the combined challenges of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong visual perception capabilities, but existing evaluations largely focus on single-view or multi-view settings with shared camera parameters, leaving the challenge of multi-agent collaborative scenarios underexplored. In such settings, multiple agents observe a shared environment from independent viewpoints, and reliable decisions require reasoning across these independent observations of the same environment. To study this problem, we introduce MaRiO, a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaborative reasoning, and evaluate 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs on it. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) tasks governed by static perception are generally easier than tasks that require transformational event sequences; (2) most models struggle to resolve cross-agent correspondences, with errors increasing with scene complexity; and (3) models show limited ability to leverage geometric cues present in the scene. As an initial step toward addressing these challenges, we explore geometry-guided synthetic view augmentation that generates intermediate transition frames between agent observations, providing auxiliary spatial context that improves performance in certain categories. Overall, our results highlight that multi-agent collaborative reasoning remains an open challenge and an important direction for multimodal embodied systems. The code is available on the project page: https://omarftt.github.io/MaRiO-page/.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) in medical retrieval-augmented generation must be able to say when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray, so understanding whether they can detect such conflicts is important for safe deployment. The sycophancy mask hypothesis holds that these models internally detect conflicts but refuse to report them, concealing a detected contradiction. We introduce a three-part diagnostic that separates concealment from uncertainty: representation probing, activation steering, and two-way forced choice. Across four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays, we confirm behavioral suppression of contradiction and find that a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs, beyond what a simple CLIP model achieves. Steering the learned conflict direction never elicits contradiction, and forcing a binary choice does not recover one; instead, cross-modal attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs. We conclude that these models fail to contradict because the mismatch registers as hedged, gated uncertainty rather than concealed knowledge, calling for re-grounding and uncertainty surfacing. Code is available at https://github.com/mohamed-eldagla/Uncertainty-Not-Concealment/.
bullets: The study examines whether VLMs can detect when retrieved reports conflict with chest X-rays.
A three-part diagnostic combines representation probing, activation steering, and forced-choice testing.
Across four instruction-tuned VLMs, probes distinguish matched from mismatched inputs, but steering and forced choice do not elicit contradiction.
Mismatched pairs reduce cross-modal attention to the image, supporting an uncertainty-based explanation of sycophancy.
The findings motivate re-grounding and explicit uncertainty surfacing for safer deployment.

papers.abstract: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have improved automated radiology report generation, they remain prone to hallucinations, necessitating clinically meaningful risk-control methods. Conformal prediction (CP) provides statistical guarantees, yet existing CP approaches rely on uncalibrated automated extractors and fail to account for the clinical relevance of errors. We introduce clinical admissibility criteria (CLARITY), a framework for evaluating radiology reports that explicitly distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor deviations. To eliminate reliance on automatic judges, we collected radiologist annotations of MLLM-generated reports using CLARITY. By benchmarking CP strategies and automatic evaluation metrics against these expert annotations, we demonstrate that commonly used admissibility proxies systematically fail to detect clinically relevant errors. Our findings reveal that automated admissibility judgments are largely decoupled from true clinical admissibility.
bullets: MLLM-generated radiology reports can hallucinate, creating a need for clinically meaningful risk control.
The framework distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor report deviations.

papers.abstract: Financial candlestick understanding requires locating visual elements, aligning them across trading dates and panels, and combining observations through numerical and financial reasoning. Answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether predictions are supported by chart evidence. We introduce Code-Interactive Financial Candlestick Reasoning and present Fin-Thinker, a model based on Qwen3.5-9B that generates and executes code to acquire evidence and perform computations. The model uses the returned observations to guide subsequent reasoning. To train these capabilities, we construct FinKLine-32K with 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories collected through teacher-guided student exploration. These include successful solutions with and without error recovery. Our three-stage training framework combines foundational visual-code fine-tuning, financial process supervision of successful reasoning and corrective continuations, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. For evaluation, we introduce FinKLineBench with 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types to assess answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately. On FinKLineBench, Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the best-performing direct-answer baseline among those evaluated and its base model with sandbox access, respectively. Training-stage ablations further show that financial process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning yield successive improvements in both answer accuracy and GPT-5.6-judged grounded accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the need to locate and align chart elements across dates and panels while combining visual, numerical, and financial reasoning.

Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the evaluated direct-answer baseline and its sandbox-enabled base model; ablations support the value of process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.
authors: Lingyun Song, Ziyao Chen, Kang Pan, Xiaolin Han, Yifei Zhang, Xiaoqi Wang, Yudai Pan, Xuequn Shang
bullets: Targets locality erosion and catastrophic forgetting during sequential factual updates.
Restricts updates toward the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces.
Uses a dynamically computed risk mask to protect stability-critical factual parameter regions.
Integrates edited knowledge at inference with prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion.
Experiments on two multimodal benchmarks show competitive performance across five metrics and stability over 1,000 sequential updates.

papers.abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .
authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Jingyu Xiao, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 124 real-world webpages across 7 domains and 33 animation types, paired with reference videos and original static assets.
Provides a two-dimensional evaluation protocol measuring static appearance fidelity and animation fidelity across aligned frames.
Finds that webpage animation reconstruction is harder than reproducing static visual appearance.
Shows that explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve coding-agent reconstruction quality.
Reports that rapid, continuous motion is more difficult to reproduce than discrete state transitions.

papers.abstract: Shallow-water UAV imagery provides centimeter-scale observations of benthic environments, but water-induced distortions complicate interpretation. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic zero-shot benchmark of unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for both assessing water-induced distortions and restoring shallow-water imagery within the same model framework. We evaluate five open-weight unified MLLMs with frozen pretrained weights and without access to paired reference images or descriptions of the true seabed. The benchmark contains 1,000 image pairs: 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes created by applying synthetic water distortions to real shallow-water imagery and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes. Three independent human annotations cover five distortion types. We evaluate four assessment prompts (P0-P3), from direct instruction to structured task decomposition, on all 1,000 images and four diagnosis-guided restoration prompts (R0-R3) on a common 100-image subset. Assessment varies substantially by model and prompt, with systematic prediction biases and a best pooled balanced accuracy of 0.654 for distortion presence. The best pooled PSNR gain is +0.255 dB, no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS, and some outputs alter scene structure or hallucinate content. Two restoration-only baselines also show limited transfer: InstructIR achieves a pooled PSNR gain of +0.040 dB, while PromptFix degrades all four pooled metrics under every prompt. These results show that recognizing shallow-water degradation does not imply reliable physical restoration and provide a reproducible baseline for future work.
authors: Dario Scilla, Omar A. Lopez, Mattia Rosso, Kasper Johansen, Matthew F. McCabe
bullets: Evaluates five frozen, open-weight unified MLLMs on distortion assessment and restoration without paired references or true-seabed descriptions.
Uses 1,000 image pairs spanning semi-synthetic UAV scenes and fully synthetic through-water scenes, with human annotations covering five distortion types.
Assessment performance varies by model and prompt; the best pooled balanced accuracy for detecting distortion presence is 0.654.
Restoration gains are minimal: the best pooled PSNR improvement is +0.255 dB, while no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS.
Some restorations alter scene structure or hallucinate content, showing that degradation recognition does not ensure physically reliable restoration.

papers.abstract: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.
authors: Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, St\'ephane Lathuili\`ere
bullets: Problem: A single prompt must balance base-class specialization with preservation of CLIP’s zero-shot behavior, causing conflicting objectives and limited generalization.

Method: Train separate specialization and generalization prompts from a base-trained prompt, connect them through a low-loss text-feature interpolation corridor, and merge their features using a fixed coefficient.
Regularization: Use a Visual Anchor KL term to preserve CLIP’s image-level class-similarity distribution, while enforcing class-permutation invariance.
Theory: Fano’s inequality links violations of class-permutation invariance to reduced novel-class accuracy through prompt–base-label mutual information.

Results: Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, with interpolation curves extending beyond the single-prompt trade-off point.

Each grid point is re-normalized per class before the joint base+novel CE loss is evaluated; construction details in Appendix G. Before DMC (left): the single-prompt baseline traces the linear path; the inset shows the base–novel trade-off, with base and novel accuracies crossing over as α varies. During DMC (middle): the two prompts start collapsed at fŵ2 (epoch 0) and separate during training. After DMC (right): the converged DMC corridor lies inside the low-loss valley, with the operating point at α = 0.20 marked by the star; the inset confirms base and novel accuracies are both high and stable along the corridor.

papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.
authors: Xiangqun Zhang, Likai Wang, Zekun Qian, Rui Zhou, Ruize Han, Wei Feng
bullets: Formulates cross-view dense video object captioning (CVDVOC), combining synchronized multi-camera evidence instead of processing views independently.

Introduces CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate cross-view tracking and caption quality.
The reference framework uses VECA for cross-camera association and CEG to integrate reliable, non-conflicting caption evidence.
It reports CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 in-domain and 33.48 cross-domain on scene-disjoint tests.

papers.abstract: Large language models have expanded beyond text to vision, audio, and other modalities, but understanding raw electromagnetic (EM) signals remains challenging. Wideband recordings can contain millions of samples, whereas existing waveform-based EM models are primarily evaluated on short in-phase and quadrature (IQ) segments, leaving long-recording understanding and detailed description insufficiently explored. We introduce LEMMO, a large EM model for instruction-driven recognition and description of long raw IQ recordings. LEMMO combines a linear-attention EM encoder with anti-aliased temporal resampling to process up to eight million complex samples. Its EM-text interaction module conditions learnable queries on instructions before retrieving signal evidence. Compact queries support recognition, while structured queries with auxiliary factual supervision organize scene-level properties, signal attributes, and cross-signal relationships for detailed description. We also construct and release a unified 1.38-TB corpus of real-world and synthetic EM signals, including LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc. Compared with MERLIN-LoRA, LEMMO improves mean EM-Bench perception accuracy by 15.77 %, mean strategy-generation ROUGE-L F1 by 4.38 points, and mean LEMMO-ShortQA accuracy by 14.31 %. It also improves categorical and numerical fact F1 on both LEMMO-LongDesc tasks while preserving its language backbone's MMLU performance. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/N1rv4n4/LEMMO and https://huggingface.co/datasets/DaftJun/RFLAS, respectively.

papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.
authors: Jiakai Yang, Haoye Zheng, Yixiao Yue, Qinqin Yang, Zhong Chen, Shuhui Cai, Congbo Cai

Experiments show automated design and optimization across varied objectives and constraints, with improved parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models and diffusion generators have driven rapid progress in brain-to-image generation, while EEG-based reconstruction is still constrained by low signal-to-noise ratio and cross-subject semantic shifts. Zero-shot cross-subject reconstruction poses even greater challenges: EEG semantic embeddings learned from source subjects deviate from the manifold of image embeddings of the unseen target subject, particularly when neither target labels nor target image embeddings are available. To address this issue, we introduce the Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration (SPSC) framework, which first uses Object Mask Contrastive Regularization (OMCR) with object identity for backend training, and then constructs Subspace Candidate Gate (SCG) to achieve label-free semantic correction for target subjects during inference. Specifically, OMCR regularizes the conditioning space with object-level positive samples to preserve object-level feature neighborhoods within the reconstruction prior and low-level branch, while SCG exploits training image prototypes and batch statistics of unlabeled target EEG to select candidates for each task within subspaces of image prototypes. Under the leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) setting across ten subjects on the THINGS-EEG dataset, SPSC improves the cross-subject reconstruction from 0.552 to 0.713 on CLIP and from 0.612 to 0.745 on Alex.5. These significant gains indicate that the semantically calibrated conditions can better support generation for the target subjects under label-free inference.

papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.

papers.tldr: DR-BOLT enables VLMs to adaptively answer quickly or reason deeply by correcting mismatches between fast/slow reference behavior and sampled responses during offline training.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
bullets: Recasts long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem under a fixed budget.
Plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to refine candidate evidence segments into compact memory.
Combines sparse low-resolution global frames with dense high-resolution local frames from refined memory.
Outperforms budget-matched uniform sampling and frame-selection/agentic methods on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench.

figures.caption: Figure 2: AdaAlloc pipeline. AdaAlloc splits a fixed visual-token budget B between low-res global context (blue) and high-res local evidence (orange). (1) From a sparse overview O, an MLLM planner picks a policy π and generates queries Q. (2) A temporal grounder (UniversalVTG) localizes Q; the MLLM refines the candidates into M∗, discarding an off-topic clip and the first return to the stove. (3) The MLLM answers from a global stream Eg and a local stream El drawn from M∗.

Figure 3: Qualitative example on LVBench. The overview supplies global context, while the question’s request to read a handwritten number motivates a LOCAL-HEAVY policy for detailed inspection. AdaAlloc retrieves multiple temporal candidates and refines them into a compact memory that preserves the decisive interval. AdaAlloc correctly answers 25, while Uniform predicts 5.

Figure 1: Visual token allocation for long-video reasoning. Uniform sampling preserves global coverage but loses fine details, while retrieval-based selection focuses on a few clips but can lose context. AdaAlloc allocates a fixed token budget between low-resolution global coverage and highresolution local evidence for both context and fine-grained verification.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning under token budgets, with a novel token allocation framework.
papers.title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: AdaAlloc is a training-free framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between global context and localized detail for long-video QA, improving accuracy over uniform sampling by up to 10.5 points.

papers.abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
authors: Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Introduces a reality-monitoring paradigm that independently varies image content and injected concepts.
Models report what they see, whether a thought was injected, and the thought’s identity, enabling separate content and source evaluation.
Among six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably detected injected concepts, with few false alarms.
Source attribution remained fragile: strong or visual-pathway injections were often reported as seen, while visible objects suppressed correct thought reports.
The same issue affects ordinary captioning, where injected objects appeared in captions of real photographs.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Can a VLM tell what it sees from an injected thought? (a) We add a concept direction to language-model activations at image tokens (sight, pink) or answer positions (thought, yellow). We then ask what the model sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. (b) Verbatim answers from Gemma-3-27B. Thought injections use layer 37 and α=0.2, except for the stronger thought (α=0.4) and the laptop example (layer 33). The sight injection uses a visual concept direction at image tokens in layer 21. The model can name an injected thought while correctly naming a visible object (green). A stronger thought is instead reported as visible, and a sight injection makes the model describe pizzas in a zebra photograph (orange). Photographs: COCO [13].

Figure 5. Injected concepts enter captions more often than yes/no answers. On 108 COCO photographs whose annotations do not include X , a visual concept direction at image tokens causes 87% of captions to mention X . Changes in yes/no answers about X are much smaller. When asked about the object actually present, the model answers yes on 96% of photographs.

Figure 7. Instructed imagery. The model writes a fixed sentence about the image (“This is a photo of a Y .”) under “imagine a X”, “do not think about a X”, or no instruction. (a) Change in cosine between the residual stream and the concept direction of X , averaged over the sentence tokens (95% CI over 150 concepts), with an unrelated concept Z as control. (b) Fraction of concepts for which “imagine” exceeds “do not think”.

It restores clean introspection under the INJECTED-first prompt (p1), with false alarms shown by the dotted line. Under the adapted introduction of Lindsey [14] (p4), it increases detection reports without restoring identification. (b) Real-image token states are replaced with gray-image states from layer k onward. Replacement by layer 15 restores clean introspection. Later replacement leaves it suppressed, while the injected concept is frequently reported as visible.

Figure 2. Identification depends on depth and strength. (a) Clean introspection in Gemma-3-27B across layers and relative strengths α, on 50 selection concepts. A cross marks configurations with fewer than half of responses well formed. (b) Best clean rate per layer against relative depth for all six VLMs, restricted to well-formed configurations.

Figure 3. Prompt framing changes reports of the same injected content. Results use our introduction, layer 37, α=0.2, and 150 concepts per prompt. Separation sentence: the prompt states that an injected thought is separate from the image; SEEN/ INJECTED first: which field is requested first. Each prompt produces 0 false alarms in 62 no-injection trials.

Figure 6. Injections in the visual stream. (a) Fraction of concepts whose visual vector (image-token mean, or the token after the image) has the same concept’s text vector as its nearest neighbor (chance 0.7%). (b) At layer 21, visual concept vectors injected into image tokens are reported as seen but almost never as injected; random directions are detected as injected but carry no content.

Figure 8. Where a visual concept can be injected (Gemma-327B, gray image, 150 concepts). A visual concept direction added at image tokens is reported as seen from layer 5 to layer 21 but not at the projector output or at layers 29 and 37, and is almost never reported as injected. The shaded band marks the layers at which text positions read the image (Sec. 6).

papers.selection_reason: Investigates source attribution and introspection in VLMs, relevant to multimodal foundation model understanding.
papers.title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
papers.tldr: A new test shows that vision-language models rarely distinguish injected thoughts from visual content, and even when they detect them, they often misattribute their source.

papers.abstract: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.
bullets: The study separates visual reading from algorithmic counting using paired questions on the same drawings with different complexity classes.
Transcription probes and text-only controls distinguish perception errors from computational failures.
In chain-of-thought, Gemini models usually read small diagrams correctly but struggle as answer size grows more than as complexity class changes.
With exact transcriptions and code, the primary model counts correctly even on 10×10 grids, shifting the bottleneck to visual reading.
A rotated second view with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, versus 57/96 when repeating the upright view.
