papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone

The benefit of insulation depends on supervision and evaluation setting rather than being universally protective of VLM capabilities.

papers.abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.
authors: WonJun Moon, Seongchan Kim, Dahun Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the underuse of MLLM compositional understanding when queries are trained only with direct contrastive supervision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.
authors: Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel, Morgan Wack
bullets: The study examines how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement validity in MLLM-based video analysis.

papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.
authors: Zijun Huang, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Targets compositional image-caption verification involving objects, attributes, counts, and relations.
Uses a shared multimodal backbone as Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer in a closed-loop training process.
Derives rewards from detecting informative mismatches and producing visually grounded repairs.
Improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families.
Enhances visual-detail robustness, while broader multimodal-task gains are limited and benchmark-dependent.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PROVE. A single Qwen backbone is reused under three role prompts: Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer. Given a clean image-caption pair, the Mutator produces a localized caption perturbation, e.g., changing an attribute from “red” to “blue”, to create a hard image-text mismatch. The Verifier first judges the perturbed caption and returns a decision-feedback pair (y1, r1) that diagnoses the mismatch. Conditioned on this feedback, the Repairer generates a revised caption, which is then checked by the same Verifier to obtain (y2, r2). Rewards from the two verification rounds train the shared model with DrGRPO, so perturbation, verification, and repair co-evolve within one multimodal backbone.

papers.abstract: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.
authors: Junzhe Chen, Tian Qin, Eugenie Shi, Tianshu Zhang, Qiang Ju, Lijie Wen

Prioritizes masked positions whose predictions gain more from the image.
Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO report consistent hallucination reduction and improved multimodal reasoning across benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.
authors: Junfeng Wang, Jiawei Liu, Yongchao Xu, Tao Jiang, Jiangbo Ai, Jin Zhang, Chong Wang, Qixing Zhang

papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: https://github.com/parkquasar/Image-Retrieval-Heads.
authors: Junsung Park, Sangwon Yu, Donghun Kang, Yeongtak Oh, Jaewon Jeong, Gyeongtae Yoo, Han Cheol Moon, Jungbeom Lee, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Introduces ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for analyzing image retrieval at the attention-head level.
Identifies sparse pointer heads via attention over image-token spans; a single head performs competitively with external vision-language retrievers on naturalistic multi-image retrieval.
Introduces writer heads whose value-weighted outputs retain enough information to identify the target image.
Pointer and writer heads are largely distinct, with only 35–47 overlapping among the top 100 selected by each criterion.
Set-partition ablations find the most consistent causal effects in the pointer–writer intersection, while one-criterion heads are less reliably useful than random controls.

papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic head-level analysis of image retrieval in large vision-language models, with implications for multimodal foundation-model understanding.
papers.title: Heads That Write, Not Just Point: Image Retrieval Heads in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LVLMs contain specialized attention heads that both locate and transmit information about the image relevant to a question, with their overlap most important for multi-image reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.
authors: ZhengXian Wu, Qianhao Nie, Zhuohong Chen, Junjie Gao, Yuyao Zhang, Yunyao Yu, Hangrui Xu, Cheng Cheng, Guiyu Ma, Jin Zhang, Xingzhong Xu, Kai Yang, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Introduces 204 human-written tasks spanning 7 domains and 25 subdomains.
Covers set-wise, sequential, hybrid wide-deep, competitive disambiguation, and visual-structure-guided search.
Each task includes a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules for overall success and intermediate results.
Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solved 26.47% of tasks.
Findings highlight challenges in linking visual evidence with retrieved information to produce complete answers.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates multimodal agents on visual search involving spatial relations, fitting multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: VisSearch-Bench evaluates how well multimodal agents manage and connect visual evidence across long-horizon web search tasks, revealing substantial difficulty even with search tools.

papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is among the oldest and most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence. This survey reviews its development, focusing on the Foundation Model Era. We define OCR through faithful transcription: within a specified visual scope, OCR should completely reconstruct the text, notation, and document structure observable in the source image, and every textual, notational, or structural element in the output must be verifiable from visual evidence in that image. We trace the development from specialist OCR models toward unified models, examining joint text detection and recognition, structured sequence generation, and the use of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). We organize contemporary OCR systems into five coexisting families: modular toolkits and task-specific models, specialized document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial products and managed services. We compare their architectures, data, and training, examining hallucination and omission, insufficient spatial grounding, and inference cost in generative OCR. We review evaluation from character and scene text recognition to parsing individual structural elements and full-page transcription, highlighting gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure. Finally, we summarize the challenges facing OCR and discuss directions for future research. We continuously track related work at https://github.com/zhihengli-casia/Awesome-OCR-in-the-Foundation-Model-Era.
authors: Zhiheng Li, Zongyang Ma, Jiaxian Chen, Cheng Cui, Yi Liu, Ziqi Zhang, Chunfeng Yuan, Bing Li, Xiang Bai, Weiming Hu
bullets: Defines OCR as complete reconstruction of all visually observable text, notation, and document structure without unsupported output.
Organizes current systems into five families: modular/task-specific models, document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial services.
Reviews joint detection-recognition, structured generation, and pretrained vision-language model approaches.
Highlights generative OCR challenges including hallucinations, omissions, weak spatial grounding, and inference cost.
Identifies evaluation gaps involving output definitions, component attribution, real-world capture conditions, and visible structural content.

These evaluation directions expand and coexist; VLM diagnostic suites may combine transcription and understanding tasks. Within a specified visual scope, OCR aims to completely recover visible text, notation, and document structure, with every output element verifiable against the source image. Main coverage spans printed, handwritten, and scene text; formulas as notation; and tables, layout, and reading order as structure. Key information extraction, question answering, translation, and retrieval are downstream tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Survey of OCR systems organized around foundation-model-era vision-language models, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: OCR in the Foundation Model Era: From Specialist Models to Unified Models
papers.tldr: This survey examines OCR’s shift from specialist systems to unified and foundation-model-based approaches, emphasizing faithful, visually verifiable transcription of text and document structure.

papers.abstract: Nighttime images are inherently susceptible to complex, compound degradations, making accurate quality assessment exceptionally challenging. Score-based IQA methods condense quality into a single number, lacking the multi-dimensional, language-grounded reasoning required for nighttime evaluation. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a more comprehensive alternative, yet remain constrained by a critical data gap: existing real-world IQA datasets are overwhelmingly daytime-centric and often built from outdated captures, while synthetic alternatives lack nighttime-specific degradation modeling, yielding artifacts far removed from authentic nighttime conditions. To bridge this gap, we present NightIQA, a dataset and benchmark suite purpose-built for MLLM-based nighttime IQA. It comprises three core components: NightIQA-Real, a real-world dataset of 1,769 high-resolution images that we captured ourselves with modern equipment, encompassing six canonical distortion types and structured multi-dimensional annotations; NightIQA-Bench, a benchmark of 1,078 visually grounded multiple-choice questions tailored to MLLM-based nighttime IQA, organized around a four-level evaluation hierarchy spanning Perception, Technical Assessment, Localization, and Reasoning; and NightIQA-Syn, an inherently scalable, scene-aware synthesis pipeline that jointly models global-level and instance-level degradations, with an initial release of 80k high-fidelity images alongside the full generation code. Fine-tuned on NightIQA with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Qwen3-VL-8B outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models, highlighting the value of domain-specific data and structured supervision.
authors: Yiding Tian, Jiaojiao Yi, Jiayuan Lu, Pufan Xu, Jinlin Wu, Changyuan Wen, Hongyuan Yu
bullets: Addresses the lack of realistic, nighttime-specific IQA data and the limitations of single-score assessment.
NightIQA-Real contains 1,769 high-resolution real-world images covering six distortion types with multidimensional annotations.
NightIQA-Bench provides 1,078 visually grounded multiple-choice questions across perception, technical assessment, localization, and reasoning.
NightIQA-Syn offers a scene-aware pipeline modeling global and instance-level degradations, with an initial release of 80k images and generation code.
Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuned with SFT and GRPO outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models.

papers.selection_reason: Uses MLLMs for nighttime image quality assessment, fits multimodal LLM topic.
papers.title: NightIQA: A Comprehensive Dataset and Benchmark for MLLM-Based Nighttime Image Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: NightIQA introduces a real, synthetic, and benchmark dataset suite to enable multidimensional, language-grounded nighttime image quality assessment with MLLMs.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
authors: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
bullets: LVLM inference is costly because it processes hundreds or thousands of visual tokens.
The method observes that tokens evolve from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives during encoding.
It identifies this role-transition point, selects global representatives from later stages, and recursively retrieves complementary local tokens from earlier stages.
Across multiple LVLMs, it retains strong performance under substantial token reduction.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 91.6% of dense-model performance with 32/576 tokens; on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, it provides up to 5.95× CUDA-latency speedup.

papers.selection_reason: Role-aware visual token pruning for LVLMs; directly addresses token pruning and eviction in efficient multimodal inference.
papers.title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: BtsPruner is a training-free, role-aware method that aggressively reduces visual tokens while preserving both global context and local details in LVLMs.

papers.abstract: Time-series interpretation often requires both numerical observations and textual context. Integrating these inputs into a pretrained language model raises a representation question: how should a signal enter the model's token sequence? We present TEMPO, which extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization. A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics, and text are then processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers. Adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters. With a Qwen3-4B backbone and task-specific fine-tuning, TEMPO achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis. Time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples further illustrate how this interface combines signal representations with textual context. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of discrete vocabulary extension for time-series understanding.
bullets: Addresses how numerical signals can be integrated into pretrained language-model token sequences.
Uses a context-aware Transformer tokenizer with finite scalar quantization to encode four-step patches into 625 discrete codes.
Combines signal tokens, scale statistics, and text through the LLM’s existing self-attention layers.
Adapts the model by training new token embeddings and DoRA adapters while keeping the tokenizer frozen.
Reports macro-F1 scores of 89.0% for activity recognition, 85.0% for sleep staging, and 86.0% for bearing-fault diagnosis; also demonstrates time-series question answering.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) routinely name objects that are absent from the image. Latent steering can reduce this failure in one model forward pass, but a fixed gate treats early and late decoding steps by the same criterion. We observe that predictive entropy varies sharply within free-running generation, while states that commit to short answers occupy a narrow, confident band. We exploit this temporal mismatch by using uncertainty as a causally available, token-local control signal for an existing steering gate. We propose Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification (EGDR), which lowers the intervention threshold when entropy derived from the preceding step's already available logits is high and retains the calibrated operating point when it is low. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, the underlying static gate lowers CHAIR CS/CI from 53.00/15.30 to 32.00/14.30; replacing only its constant threshold with EGDR further lowers them to 29.00/13.60. At a matched 58% intervention rate, the corresponding static control obtains 30.50/14.00. The gain over the static gate holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and grows with the generation budget, while POPE scores and general multimodal capability remain effectively unchanged. EGDR requires no additional model forward pass and adds roughly 2% measured latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/alvi-uiu/EGDR.
authors: Riasad Alvi, Md. Asaduzzaman Shuvo, Md. Ahashan Habib, Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi
bullets: Targets object hallucination caused by LVLMs naming objects absent from images.
Adjusts an existing steering gate using entropy from the preceding step’s available logits: higher uncertainty triggers stronger intervention.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces CHAIR CS/CI from 32.00/14.30 with a static gate to 29.00/13.60 with EGDR.
The improvement also holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and increases with the generation budget.
Maintains POPE and general multimodal performance, adding roughly 2% measured latency.

This requires no additional forward pass or trained parameter. (c) The adaptive threshold admits states missed by the static gate; at the first token, ê = 0 and τeff = τ .

Figure 1. Overview of EGDR. Both gates share v, ℓ∗ and α; only the threshold differs. (a) A static gate applies one threshold τ at every step. (b) EGDR lowers it to τeff(t) using the entropy of the preceding step’s logits, rescaled to the calibrated band, and so corrects states the static gate misses; at t=1, ê=0 and τeff=τ . papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
bullets: Addresses the lack of guarantees for language-model arithmetic and the externalization of tool-based computation.
Uses Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter; each pass reads three cells and emits a digit, carry/borrow, and next operation, while fixed runtime controls the sheet.
A Lean proof reduces correctness for all input lengths to checking the finite set of views presented by the runtime; this does not hold when steps access earlier outputs.
All 2,446 deployment views passed, and the model handled signed arithmetic, multiplication, division, square roots, and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length.
The system solved all reported browser test problems and supports symbolic polynomial operations, while a multiplicative adapter gate preserves the base model when arithmetic is unused.

papers.abstract: Promptable perception, from GroundingDINO to Rex-Omni, puts one model behind one prompt interface and returns coordinates for any localisation task. Every model in that line was built for photographs; none has been given a sketch. We present Sketch-Omni, to our knowledge the first perception MLLM built to work on sketches and from them. On a sketch, the sketch is the image, and text prompts detect, point, resolve object and spatial referring expressions, and ground affordances in it. From a sketch, the sketch is the prompt, and a drawing of one object localises that object in a photograph, even among several of the same category, a query that neither a category name nor a photo exemplar can pose. Two obstacles stand in the way. A photo-trained model's attention is tuned to colour and texture, which a sketch does not have, and no dataset pairs a drawing with the one instance it depicts among others of its kind. We build the training data instead of collecting it. An edge detector turns every labelled photograph into a sketch-like drawing that keeps the photograph's labels, and two constructions produce sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing data. On top of this, photo-guided relation alignment passes each photograph and its edge sketch through the same model and trains the sketch pass to reproduce how the photograph pass relates phrases to patches and patches to each other. Not one training label is drawn by hand. Sketch-Omni reaches 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation against 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with a lead that doubles when the photograph holds several instances of the queried category, and it is best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks. Code, model, and a hand-annotated benchmark of 2754 sketch-to-photo links will be released.
authors: Dongyu Wang, Dar-Yen Chen, Zhiming Hong, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of sketch-capable perception models and the difficulty of identifying one instance among multiple same-category objects.
Builds training data automatically by converting labelled photos into edge sketches and constructing sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing datasets.
Uses photo-guided relation alignment to transfer phrase–patch and patch–patch relationships from photographs to sketches.
Achieves 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation versus 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with larger gains in multi-instance scenes.
Performs best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks; a hand-annotated benchmark of 2,754 sketch-to-photo links is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) aims to segment objects from unseen domains using only a few annotated references. Recent Segment Anything Model (SAM)-based methods have advanced CD-FSS, yet their reference-target visual matching is highly sensitive to target appearance variations. SAM3 introduces text-conditioned segmentation, enabling natural-language descriptions to guide segmentation across target images, but directly using the category name as the condition still yields unstable performance under severe domain shifts. We propose Reference Inversion for SAM3 (RI-SAM3) that leverages SAM3's large-scale vision-language pre-training to learn suitable textual tokens for each target category. RI-SAM3 comprises three core designs: (i) Bi-level Reference Inversion that learns complementary tokens before and after the frozen text encoder: the former remain anchored in SAM3's text space while the latter represent the category more flexibly; (ii) Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning combines these tokens differently as object queries evolve across decoder layers; and (iii) Presence-aware Confidence Supervision that jointly supervises query confidence and target presence for reliable predictions. With SAM3 frozen, RI-SAM3 optimizes around 12K parameters only per category and it efficiently segments each target in a single forward pass with reusable textual conditioning without per-sample reference-target visual matching. Extensive experiments over multiple widely adopted benchmarks show that RI-SAM3 achieves superior performance consistently in CD-FSS tasks, together with strong robustness, efficiency, and generalization.
authors: Jiahao Nie, Yun Xing, Wenbin An, Qixin Zhang, Yap-Peng Tan, Alex C. Kot, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses unstable SAM-based segmentation under severe domain shifts and target appearance variation.
Learns complementary category tokens before and after SAM3’s frozen text encoder through bi-level reference inversion.
Uses layer-adaptive textual conditioning and presence-aware confidence supervision for more reliable predictions.
Optimizes only about 12K parameters per category and segments targets in one forward pass without per-sample visual matching.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistently superior performance, robustness, efficiency, and generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed RI-SAM3 framework. Bi-level Reference Inversion (BRI) learns reference word tokens z∗w and reference concept tokens z∗c from annotated references, collectively termed inverted reference tokens. Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning (LTC) combines them with layer-specific fusion coefficients α∗ to produce the bi-level reference tokens T ∗ c for conditioning frozen SAM3. Presence-aware Confidence Supervision (PCS) jointly supervises query-level classification and global presence scores. Once learned, T ∗ c is reused for target segmentation without references or visual matching.

Figure 1: Motivation for Reference Inversion for SAM3 (RI-SAM3). Right: RI-SAM3 achieves higher mIoU (↑) and a lower standard deviation of per-image IoU (↓) than GF-SAM and the category-name prompt baseline, demonstrating improved accuracy and stability.

papers.abstract: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
authors: Farid Hasanov, Riccardo Renzulli, Bahram Zonooz, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Decebal Constantin Mocanu
bullets: Addresses overconfident answers unsupported by available visual or textual evidence.
Mines sparse autoencoder features linked to abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set during prefill.
Evaluated with LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B and Qwen3.5-2B across multimodal and language abstention benchmarks.
Produces a better balance between correct answers and appropriate abstention than uncertainty-based post-hoc rejection baselines.
Works best for image–question or question–answer incompatibility and mathematical reasoning, but is weaker for absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
authors: Louis Bradshaw, Irmak Bukey, Daniel Chenyu Lin, John Thickstun, Chris Donahue
bullets: Introduces PianoBench, a benchmark for musical perception and reasoning across matched acoustic and symbolic inputs.
Built from a multimodal dataset containing over 20,000 hours of piano instruction transcripts and musical commentary.
Open-weight audio-language models reach at most 52.8% accuracy, only modestly above a no-audio control.
Frontier models achieve up to 93.2% with chain-of-thought when musical content is provided as text, revealing an audio-perception gap.
Instruction tuning on interleaved musical instruction improves Qwen 3.5 9B Base’s transcript-based zero-shot accuracy from 42.8% to 56.0%.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Schematic construction of PianoBench (clockwise from top left). Speech and piano activity form a source timeline. An LLM with access to the source timeline proposes questions, answers, audio intervals, and distractors. A model ranks distractors without hearing the music. A human checks the passages and answer choices, retaining Q1 and rejecting Q2.

Figure 1: We release PianoBench, a benchmark for evaluating music perception and reasoning in LLMs. PianoBench is derived from PianoTalk, a training-scale (20k hours) dataset of interleaved commentary and music transcripts, which is derived from instructional piano videos. Figure 2: PianoTalk data recipe. Starting from seed videos, we crawl related videos and YouTube channels. An LLM evaluates video metadata to select videos likely to contain both speech and piano. papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks multimodal language models on musical perception and reasoning across audio and symbolic inputs.
papers.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models

papers.abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.
bullets: Addresses early optimization instability when adding non-text modalities to frozen language models.
Uses zero-initialized, learnable gated cross-attention inserted across six decoder layers.
At initialization, the bridge preserves pretrained behavior exactly, with reported output discrepancy of 0.00e+00.
On Falcon-40B held-out evaluation, gate-on performance improves loss from 4.3469 to 2.2201 versus the gate-off baseline.
The approach is evaluated with frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b backbones; results reported primarily for Falcon-40B.

papers.title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
papers.tldr: IGCA stabilizes multimodal conditioning of frozen language models by starting as an exact no-op and gradually enabling cross-attention.

papers.abstract: Inference-time steering in vision-language models often entangles query-relevant reasoning dynamics with low-level perceptual noise, causing collateral degradation on correct predictions. We propose Question-Contrastive Visual Steering (QCVS) to isolate task-specific intervention directions via double-differential activation probing. By contrasting spatial layout perturbations under the target query against a generic description reference, QCVS cancels task-agnostic visual artifacts without ground-truth supervision. A dual-threshold gating mechanism then evaluates relative interaction strength and signal amplitude, selectively applying a single bounded hidden-state update only when necessary. Empirical evaluations across multiple scales of Qwen3.5 (2B to 9B) and DeepSeek-VL2 on DynaMath and We-Math demonstrate that QCVS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy gains under sparse coverage (approximately 22%-30%). Crucially, QCVS yields repair rates up to 13.98% while suppressing collateral damage down to 0.41%, proving high intervention precision and computational efficiency.
bullets: Targets task-relevant reasoning signals while filtering out low-level visual perturbation noise.
Uses double-differential activation probing with spatial-layout contrasts and a generic-description reference, requiring no ground-truth supervision.
Applies a single bounded hidden-state update through dual-threshold gating only when intervention is warranted.
Evaluated on Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-VL2 across DynaMath and We-Math, with sparse coverage of approximately 22%–30%.
Reports repair rates up to 13.98% and collateral damage as low as 0.41%, alongside state-of-the-art accuracy gains.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Motivation and computation of QCVS. (a) Describing a scene and counting water-filled glasses require different evidence. The BLINK [19] example has dataset label 3; the crops are human-selected illustrations, not model outputs. (b) One visual encoding feeds a frozen Qwen3.5 model: two questions and three visual conditions give six prefix readouts. (c) Paired clean–control differences at each final assistant-prefix token ta yield the interaction µ. Its direction defines a bounded edit; R and A determine selection. A selected input receives one update at (ℓ∗, ta) in a fresh clean-prefix replay; otherwise, decoding uses the retained clean hybrid state.
Fig. 2. Fixed-action coverage sweep on Qwen3.5-4B/DynaMath. Curves show repairs, harm and net change as percentages of all inputs; net change equals accuracy gain (pp).

Table 2. Cross-backbone generalization performance on the DynaMath benchmark. Experiments are conducted on DeepSeek-VL2Tiny (1.0B active parameters) and DeepSeek-VL2-Small (2.8B active parameters) with model-specific calibration. Metrics follow Table 1. Bold marks the highest accuracy per model.
Table 3. Ablation of QCVS components on Qwen3.5-4B (DynaMath). ∆Acc. is accuracy gain over Base (pp); Rep. and Dmg. are in %. All settings use 25.01% coverage except Ungated (100%).

papers.selection_reason: Inference-time steering of vision-language model reasoning via activation probing; directly relevant to multimodal LLM methods.
papers.title: QCVS: Question-Contrastive Visual Steering for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: QCVS improves multimodal reasoning at inference time by selectively steering hidden states to correct errors while minimizing harm to correct predictions.

papers.abstract: Earth observation (EO) workflows require selecting among known outcomes, estimating confidence, and processing large volumes of imagery. Generative vision-language models can address these tasks, but autoregressive decoding is computationally costly and their confidence estimates are unreliable. Decision models offer an alternative, returning probabilities over candidate answers in a single forward pass. However, their accuracy, calibration, and transfer across EO tasks remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these properties through a diagnostic study of d3-flash (8.4B parameters) across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks. We find that compositional reasoning transfers well and calibration improves over its Qwen3.5-9B backbone on 24 settings, while counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain challenging. To address these limitations, we adapt d3-flash through low-rank fine-tuning on public EO training splits, producing EO-Jev. EO-Jev improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28. It also achieves an average gain of 8.0 points across 12 held-out settings and lower expected calibration error than specialists on 21 of 28 settings. These improvements come at a modest cost of 1.8 points in general decision performance. Our results demonstrate the potential of adapting general decision models into competitive EO generalists while highlighting persistent challenges in quantitative perception, option-order consistency, and calibration under distribution shift.
bullets: Decision models provide single-pass probabilities over candidate answers, avoiding the costly decoding and unreliable confidence of generative vision-language models.
A diagnostic study evaluates d3-flash across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks.
Compositional reasoning transfers well, but counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain difficult.
Low-rank fine-tuning yields EO-Jev, which improves over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28.
EO-Jev gains 8.0 average points on 12 held-out settings and improves calibration, with a modest 1.8-point decline in general decision performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 EO-Jev Architecture and Training. EO images (single images, pre/post pairs or time series) are paired with typed questions with predefined answers. General decision data is replayed in 20% of each batch. The vision encoder and text tower Φθ process the images and questions, respectively. A frozen readout Wr converts the final hidden state h into option probabilities p. Training: LoRA adapters in the vision encoder and text tower are optimized using KL divergence against target distributions q, with an additional ranked probability score (RPS) on ordinal questions. Inference: merged adapters (W + BA) enable single-pass predictions at d3-flash cost. Answers are accepted when confidence exceeds a per-question threshold τq and otherwise deferred to an analyst. Examples and probabilities are illustrative.

papers.title: EO-Jev: Decision Model for Earth Observation
papers.tldr: EO-Jev adapts a general decision model for Earth observation, improving accuracy and calibration across diverse EO tasks while retaining some challenges in quantitative perception and distribution shift.

papers.abstract: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.
bullets: Addresses interoperator variability caused by manual caliper placement in ultrasound biometry.
Uses clinical measurement questions and language-model decision representations to query shared dense ultrasound features.
Generates endpoint probability maps rather than directly predicting coordinates, capturing localization uncertainty.
Trains jointly with landmark-localization and clinical-measurement losses.
On the FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, reports 22.50-pixel MRE and 15.38 measurement MAE, outperforming compared baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of Kev-Bio. Qwen3.5 and USFM provide visual tokens to the language model, while DINOv2 contributes additional localization features. Clinical questions are encoded into decision states at ⟨decide⟩ tokens, which generate queries for each landmark endpoint. A convolutional-based Pixel Neck combines features from the three visual encoders into a shared dense feature map. Endpoint queries are matched against this map to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived.

Fig. 2 Qualitative comparison across nine ultrasound views. Landmark predictions from Kev-Bio (red) and US-Foundation (blue), with ground truth shown in green. Values indicate mean landmark error in pixels.

Fig. 4 Question-conditioned landmark localization. Different clinical measurement questions produce distinct landmark probability maps on the same ultrasound image. Green circles denote ground truth, and yellow regions indicate predicted spatial distributions.

Fig. 3 Spatial probability maps and error detection. (a) Landmark probability maps showing confident and ambiguous predictions. (b) Landmarks are ranked by decreasing map entropy, and curves show the fraction of localization errors captured in each clinical domain. Errors are defined using ground truth as deviations exceeding 5% of the image diagonal. The black marker indicates the overall result, and the dashed line represents random selection.

papers.tldr: Kev-Bio is a vision-language model that predicts ultrasound caliper landmarks as spatial probability maps, improving automated biometry across nine anatomical views.

papers.abstract: Geospatial text spotting involves locating and transcribing geographic labels, such as road names, district names, and landmarks, in raster maps. These labels are often small, densely arranged, and arbitrarily oriented. Although Arabic text recognition has been studied extensively in documents and natural scenes, Arabic geospatial text spotting remains underexplored. We introduce ARABGEOTEXT, an Arabic-centric benchmark covering 970 geographic locations in Riyadh and Jeddah, with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type. For each location, we pair an OpenStreetMap (OSM) rendering with a composite created by overlaying that rendering on the corresponding remote sensing (RS) imagery. The paired views preserve label content and pixel geometry, allowing evaluation across different backgrounds. Geographic partitions support in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting. Experiments with direct Qwen3.5-4B spotting show difficulties in recovering all labels within a tile. We therefore propose a tool-augmented vision-language framework that combines YOLO26 localization and crop rectification with Qwen3.5-4B recognition adapted through low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting across both image views and test cities. With localization held fixed, reader adaptation further improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ArabGeoText.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored task of locating and transcribing small, dense, arbitrarily oriented Arabic geographic labels.
Provides 970 locations in Riyadh and Jeddah with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type, pairing OpenStreetMap renderings with remote-sensing composites.
Supports in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting across different visual backgrounds.
Combines YOLO26 localization, crop rectification, and LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B recognition.
The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting, while reader adaptation improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader.

papers.abstract: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.
bullets: Extends InpaintCOCO to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families.
Introduces 953 minimal-pair examples for multilingual fine-grained visual understanding.
Evaluates CLIP-like vision-language encoders and large language models on multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval.
Lower-resource language performance is driven more by available language data than by typological similarity to English.
Models often prefer incorrect English captions over correct non-English captions; English bias varies by architecture, with Gemma 3 strongest and Qwen 3 weakest among tested models.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) typically process large numbers of multimodal tokens from audio-visual inputs, incurring substantial computational costs and a large memory footprint for the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive token pruning can alleviate this problem while maintaining competitive performance on multiple-choice tasks, which require only a single option as output. However, we observe substantial quality degradation when generating long-form, open-ended responses. We attribute this gap to query-guided selection, which can retain sufficient evidence for answer selection while discarding details needed for comprehensive generation. This motivates reducing overlapping information across tokens, termed structural redundancy, while preserving diverse content. However, the retained representations may still contain precision redundancy due to unnecessarily high numerical precision in their cached values. To address these two levels of redundancy in token representations, we introduce a training-free framework named R$^2$-Omni. First, Structure-Aware Token Consolidation (STC) consolidates redundant representations using spatiotemporal similarity in video and local continuity in audio. Then, Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation (SSPA) allocates value precision to the retained representations according to the estimated reduction in attention-output error under quantized keys, with query attention and audio-visual alignment providing a semantic prior. Extensive experiments on long-form generation benchmarks demonstrate an average 5.0$\times$ reduction in the memory footprint while preserving 97.98% of baseline generation quality and achieving a 1.48$\times$ end-to-end speedup, highlighting the benefits of jointly reducing structural and precision redundancy.
bullets: Targets quality degradation from aggressive token pruning in long-form, open-ended generation.
Uses Structure-Aware Token Consolidation to merge structurally redundant video and audio representations.
Uses Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation to assign lower or higher value precision based on estimated attention-output sensitivity.
Achieves a 5.0× average memory-footprint reduction, 97.98% of baseline generation quality, and a 1.48× end-to-end speedup.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on long-form generation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: An image that is hard to classify on its own may have a helpful neighbor in the same unlabeled batch. Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) score images independently and leave this evidence unused. We study small unlabeled query batches with no labeled examples. Visual similarity can reflect pose or background, so it may connect images from different classes. Each image's scores over the class vocabulary offer another way to choose neighbors. We introduce Behavioral Affinity Transduction (BAT), which builds a sparse graph from these class-response profiles. The graph supplies neighbor evidence during prediction. For EM-Dirichlet, it also screens candidate classes and initializes assignments. BAT plugs into direct and iterative readouts of a frozen VLM. Across diverse datasets, BAT improves the mean accuracy of every tested readout. In the main RN50 comparison, soft and hard EM-Dirichlet gain $4.22$ and $2.72$ percentage points.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that frozen VLMs classify images independently and ignore batch-level evidence.
Builds a sparse graph from each image’s class-response profile rather than relying only on visual similarity.
Uses graph-based neighbor information with direct and iterative readouts of a frozen VLM.
For EM-Dirichlet, BAT screens candidate classes and initializes assignments.
Improves mean accuracy across all tested readouts; in the main RN50 comparison, gains are 4.22 and 2.72 percentage points for soft and hard EM-Dirichlet.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.
bullets: Addresses unstable uniform distillation caused by varying surgical sample difficulty, ambiguity, and clinical context.
Uses predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency to create a continuous easy-to-hard curriculum.
Aligns teacher and student at feature, logit, and probability levels while shifting from teacher imitation to task supervision.
Evaluated on Surg-396K across five dialogue paradigms, where it consistently outperforms strong distillation baselines.
Produces memory-efficient models with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed complexity-aware curriculum framework for progressive distillation. Teacher confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency are fused into a permissive complexity score, which guides continuous curriculum pacing from easy-first sampling to balanced training. This pacing is coupled with progressive objective interpolation and hierarchical representation alignment, jointly establishing a more structured optimization process that enables stable and efficient compression of surgical vision-language models.

Figure 1: Overview of the proposed SurgPace framework. Given surgical multimodal data, a teacher model first estimates sample complexity offline using complementary confidence and geometric consistency signals, which are permissively fused so that lower scores indicate easier samples. The resulting complexity estimates are then used to guide online curriculum training, where easier samples are emphasized earlier and harder samples are gradually incorporated as training progresses. During this process, the student model learns from the teacher through hierarchical representation alignment at the probability, logit, and feature levels, while a progressive objective schedule adjusts the balance of supervision over time. Together, these components enable stable and efficient compression of surgical MLLMs into a lightweight student model with reduced computational demands.

papers.abstract: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. We introduce DR Pixel, the first open-source end-to-end multimodal DR agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit, operating over a corpus of 1.06M pages. To evaluate this setting, we construct DRPixelBench, a benchmark on scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. Surprisingly, page-native DR already works well without training, outperforming OCR-based baselines across state-of-the-art models like GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Qwen3.6-27B, while requiring fewer tool calls. We next turn to DR training. A key challenge is that teacher trajectories for agentic supervised finetuning are noisy, mixing critical reasoning and action steps with redundant or failed attempts. To address this, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting, a fine-grained credit assignment method that weights individual reasoning and action steps by their counterfactual contribution to the final answer. Our training improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points on DRPixelBench, and likewise outperforms the untrained baseline on four existing benchmarks. On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, DR Pixel comes within 1.8 points of an oracle that is given the gold pages directly. Our results suggest that the conventional OCR-then-retrieve pipeline is not only unnecessary but suboptimal: directly retrieving and reasoning over visual document pages makes complex DR both more effective and more efficient.
bullets: Targets the loss of information from OCR-only processing of figures, tables, equations, and layout.
Introduces an open-source multimodal agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit over 1.06M pages.
Introduces DRPixelBench, a scientific-paper benchmark requiring multimodal document reasoning.
Counterfactual credit reweighting improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points.
On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, the system comes within 1.8 points of an oracle with gold pages; scope is centered on complex scientific documents.

papers.abstract: While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced multimodal reasoning, existing frameworks suffer from a critical "perception-reasoning gap." Due to an over-reliance on seemingly relevant visual tokens, even minor perceptual perturbations can propagate through the reasoning process, leading to compounding hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose MIRA, a training framework that improves robustness to erroneous visual contexts while enhancing logical reasoning ability. By injecting filtered, deceptive visual contexts during training, we construct challenging "hard traps" that stress-test the model's robustness to misleading information. Furthermore, we introduce a group-wise reflection-triggering mechanism that enables the model to autonomously detect and rectify inconsistencies between visual cues and logical constraints, which is ultimately internalized as an intrinsic policy behavior. Importantly, MIRA does not rely on human annotations. Experimental results across multiple reasoning and perception benchmarks show that MIRA yields an average 7% improvement on in-domain benchmarks, with consistent improvements on vision-centric benchmarks. These findings highlight that active error recovery is essential for robust multimodal reasoning. Comprehensive ablation studies and analyses further provide insights into why MIRA is effective.
bullets: Addresses the perception–reasoning gap, where small visual errors can trigger compounding hallucinations.
Injects filtered deceptive visual contexts to create challenging “hard traps” during training.
Uses group-wise reflection triggers to help models identify and correct conflicts between visual evidence and logical constraints.
Reports an average 7% improvement across in-domain benchmarks, with consistent gains on vision-centric benchmarks.
Ablations and analyses support the importance of active error recovery for robust multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Cloth-changing person re-identification (CC-ReID) is still very challenging, and no method clearly dominates: methods that lead on one benchmark collapse on the others, because they rest on different identity cues. We show that a general-purpose vision-language model (VLM), used zero-shot as a judge for reranking a short candidate list, beats the expert retrieval models it reranks by a wide and consistent margin. On the four scenarios of CHIRLA, a long-term CC-ReID benchmark that no publicly released Re-ID model is trained on, reranking the candidates of two frozen experts raises rank-1 on every scenario, by 12.9 points on average over the best expert and 9.4 over the best naive ensemble of the two, with no component fine-tuned on the target data. Merging both experts' shortlists matches or beats reranking the stronger expert's shortlist alone, at lower cost. Introducing a VLM does, however, come at a cost: almost all of the pipeline's FLOPs are spent on it. We therefore borrow a criterion from ensembling and invoke the VLM judge only where the two experts disagree at rank 1. This threshold-free gate removes 40% of the calls, and a comparable share of total compute, with no significant drop in rank-1, trading 1.8 to 3.8 points of mAP. Judging remains the dominant cost, but on a benchmark where dedicated experts stall, we find a frozen general-purpose model to be the strongest judge of identity. The code is available at https://github.com/bdager/JudgeReID.
bullets: CC-ReID remains difficult because existing methods rely on different identity cues and do not generalize consistently across benchmarks.
The method uses a VLM as a zero-shot judge to rerank short candidate lists from two frozen expert retrieval models.
On all four CHIRLA scenarios, reranking improves rank-1 by an average of 12.9 points over the best expert and 9.4 over their naive ensemble, without target-data fine-tuning.
Merging both experts’ shortlists matches or exceeds reranking the stronger expert alone at lower cost.
Calling the VLM only when experts disagree at rank 1 removes 40% of calls with no significant rank-1 loss, though mAP drops by 1.8–3.8 points; VLM judging remains the main computational cost.

papers.abstract: Misleading charts can lead vision-language models to conclusions that conflict with underlying data. Existing work focuses on inference-time strategies, while training-time supervision remains less explored. We present VizDAGuide, a DAG-structured supervision method for misleading-chart question answering. The method represents intermediate reasoning states and their dependencies as a directed acyclic graph, assigns supervision weights according to their roles, and serializes the graph into a unified training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference. Experiments on two benchmarks across Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models show improvements over a content- and weight-matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline on both answer formats. Process-level evaluation shows gains in grounding and operation execution, while ablations indicate that dependency structure and weighted supervision are most effective when combined. These results support DAG-structured weighted supervision for misleading-chart question answering.
bullets: Targets chart questions where visual presentation can conflict with the underlying data.
Represents intermediate reasoning states and dependencies as a directed acyclic graph.
Serializes weighted graph supervision into one training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference.
Improves answer performance over a matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline across two benchmarks and Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models.
Process-level gains occur in grounding and operation execution; dependency structure and weighting work best together.
