papers.abstract: With the popularization of livestreaming applications, automatic camera tuning has become indispensable for ordinary users to enjoy high Quality of Experience (QoE). However, the existing Image Quality Assessment (IQA) methods face two challenges in camera tuning. First, they struggle to identify subtle quality difference between images, which is common in camera tuning. Second, the ability to explain fine-grained differences and to provide suggestions for camera tuning are even more lacking. To address these challenges, we first construct FGLive-Comments, an instruction tuning dataset with rich annotations of both preferences for fine-grained image pairs and quality reasoning from global and local visual evidence, which supports selective adjustment recommendations of camera parameters. Based on FGLive-Comments, we develop Q-CamTuning, a multimodal large language model for livestreaming camera tuning. Its progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework learns quality-aware visual representations, enhances fine-grained reasoning with global-local evidence, and maps quality issues to camera-parameter adjustment directions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Q-CamTuning outperforms existing IQA models in both quality scoring and fine-grained image pair ranking. User study also validates its ability to recommend camera tuning suggestions.
bullets: Addresses IQA limitations in distinguishing fine-grained quality differences and generating actionable tuning guidance.
Introduces FGLive-Comments, an instruction-tuning dataset with pairwise preferences, global-local quality reasoning, and adjustment recommendations.
Uses a progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework to connect visual quality issues with camera-parameter directions.
Outperforms existing IQA models in quality scoring and fine-grained image-pair ranking.
A user study supports its ability to provide useful camera-tuning suggestions.

papers.abstract: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.
bullets: Evaluates assistance quality across event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output.
Combines controlled videos of hazards and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol.
Includes 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance and 110 requiring silence, covering 555 intervention events.

papers.abstract: Interleaved multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves the visual reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models by dynamically incorporating visual evidence during reasoning. However, existing methods primarily select evidence from historical context. When the reasoning focus shifts, history-guided evidence may remain focused on prior regions and fail to cover the visual information required by the next step. We refer to this lag between visual evidence and subsequent reasoning demands as Temporal Evidence Myopia. To address this issue, we propose Lookahead Prediction-guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing (LPAVR), a training-free test-time framework. LPAVR transforms Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) from a decoding acceleration mechanism into a lookahead signal for anticipating upcoming reasoning intent. During MTP decoding, the draft head generates multiple future tokens, while the target model verifies them in parallel and retains the longest prefix consistent with its decoding trajectory. This target-verified prefix contains near-future semantics, which LPAVR uses to construct lookahead-guided visual evidence and assess whether history-guided evidence covers the indicated regions. If the coverage is sufficient, the history-guided evidence is retained; otherwise, LPAVR switches to the lookahead-guided evidence. This better aligns the visual context with upcoming reasoning and improves consistency between draft predictions and target-model decoding. Experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that LPAVR improves both reasoning accuracy and the acceptance rates of MTP speculative tokens, jointly enhancing visual reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.
bullets: Addresses Temporal Evidence Myopia, where history-based visual evidence lags behind shifts in reasoning focus.
Uses Multi-Token Prediction as a lookahead signal rather than only for decoding acceleration.
Retains historical visual evidence when coverage is sufficient and switches to lookahead-guided evidence otherwise.
A training-free, test-time framework evaluated across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Reports improved reasoning accuracy and higher acceptance rates of speculative tokens.‌

papers.title: Lookahead Prediction-Guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing for Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: LPAVR uses verified future-token predictions to refocus visual evidence toward upcoming reasoning needs, improving multimodal reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects and their spatial relationships evolve in 3D space over time remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), particularly under changing viewpoints. Recent approaches incorporate geometric information into reasoning, but explicit supervision for temporally ordered 4D state evolution and its use as intermediate evidence remains limited. We introduce \textbf{Trace4D}, which trains VLMs to predict 4D state sequences and reason over their inter-timestep changes alongside temporal visual observations. Its 4D-grounded chain-of-thought (CoT) explicitly represents 4D states, analyzes temporal visual context, and connects both as evidence for the answer. We construct Trace4D-Train from in-the-wild videos with 600K 4D perception examples and approximately 70K grounded QA examples, and train with joint supervised fine-tuning followed by geometry-aware GRPO. At inference, Trace4D predicts 4D states and reasoning directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model. Experiments on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D show improved QA accuracy over the base VLMs and benefits from reasoning over 4D state changes and temporal visual observations.
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty in tracking object states and spatial relationships over time under changing viewpoints.
Predicts temporally ordered 4D states, analyzes their changes, and combines them with temporal visual observations in grounded chain-of-thought reasoning.
Trains on in-the-wild videos with 4D perception and grounded QA supervision, followed by geometry-aware GRPO.
Performs inference directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model.
Shows improved QA accuracy on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D over the base VLMs.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.

papers.abstract: Clinical evidence is inherently relational: medical images are interpreted with prior studies, cross-modal examinations, reports, and localized findings, and retrieving relevant evidence is therefore central to clinical interpretation. Recent foundation models increasingly encode these heterogeneous sources into shared embedding spaces, yet existing embedding evaluation often focuses on isolated matches, leaving unclear whether current models retrieve relevant evidence across changes in modality, appearance, and granularity. We introduce MedHEB, a unified benchmark with 107 retrieval tasks from 54 datasets, including both in-distribution and held-out-source evaluation, across three axes: evidence form (2D images, 3D volumes, text), pairing type (image--image, image--text, text--text, and modality-bridging visual matching), and relevance granularity (global, question-conditioned, region-level). Under a single ranking protocol, MedHEB varies clinically relevant evidence definitions to test whether embedding proximity remains meaningful across heterogeneous evidence, including modality-bridging visual retrieval and region-level text-to-region retrieval. Across representative models, performance is uneven across retrieval families: models strong on conventional image--text or text--text retrieval are less reliable on modality-bridging and region-level tasks. Current embedding spaces capture some clinical relationships well but do not yet provide balanced retrieval across heterogeneous evidence. We further provide MedEmb, an MLLM-based reference embedding model trained on the MedHEB ID split, as a reproducible baseline for unified 2D--3D--text medical retrieval. We release MedHEB with preprocessing scripts, evaluation code, access manifests, and MedEmb to support research on clinically meaningful medical embeddings.
bullets: Introduces 107 retrieval tasks spanning 54 datasets, with in-distribution and held-out-source evaluation.
Covers 2D images, 3D volumes, and text; image–image, image–text, text–text, and modality-bridging retrieval.
Tests global, question-conditioned, and region-level relevance under a unified ranking protocol.
Finds uneven performance: models effective on conventional retrieval are less reliable for modality-bridging and region-level tasks.
Releases MedEmb, a reference embedding model, plus benchmark resources and evaluation tools.

papers.abstract: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold. On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one. These results support task-specific correction while highlighting the remaining tradeoff between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.
bullets: MAGAR-Bench contains 4,000 multimodal samples across 26 assembly families and evaluates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework separately.
Minimal Rework measures the distinct parts moved within a validated recovery candidate set, rather than counting actions.
MAGAR uses a frozen supervised-fine-tuned policy, task-specific candidate structures, and a learned selector with intervention thresholds.
On held-out assembly families, Overall task-balanced performance rises from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks.
Among 209 interventions, 70 fix errors and 22 introduce errors, showing a remaining tradeoff between correction and prediction preservation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.
bullets: Standard RLVR gives identical outcome-based credit to all generated tokens, ignoring their visual relevance.
NAS-PO models visual allocation with a visual-mass policy and spatial routing with a conditional visual policy.
NAS-AS redistributes signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts, while AAC aligns attention patterns with successful trajectories.
It substantially outperforms leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain benchmarks at both 8B and 32B scales.
VRS analysis suggests optimized attention focuses on visually load-bearing regions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of NAS-PO. Given an image–query pair (I,Q), the standard GRPO pipeline produces G clean rollouts and verifier-derived group-relative advantages Ai. Using the same clean rollouts, NAS-PO reads native attention ai,t(j) and losslessly decomposes its visual component into a visual-mass policy qi,t, which captures whether and how much a response token relies on the image, and a conditional visual policy ρi,t, which captures where attention is routed over visual tokens. The visual-mass policy also provides visually active indicators ci,t shared by NAS-AS and the conditional branch of AAC. At the trajectory level, NAS-AS summarizes visual reliance into a bounded factor αi and forms Ãi = αiAi. At the token level, AAC aligns q on all valid response tokens and ρ on visually active ones under the unshaped positive-advantage gate [Ai]+. The shaped policy-gradient objective and the adaptively weighted AAC loss jointly update the policy.

papers.abstract: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
bullets: Reframes floodwater-level detection as an explicit visual reasoning task to address weak interpretability and poor cross-scene generalization.
Uses Qwen2.5-VL with Group Relative Policy Optimization and a HydroKG-based path reward to supervise reasoning without requiring extensive reasoning annotations.
Introduces HydroLevel, a 3,000-image floodwater benchmark for training and evaluation.
Outperforms conventional vision baselines by 4.0 percentage points in-domain and 13.6 percentage points out-of-domain; out-of-domain performance drops 4.4 points.
4-bit quantization reduces GPU memory usage by 57% and latency by 43%, while confidence-based routing improves safety and reduces cloud computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed collaborative edge-cloud traffic monitoring network. The system leverages 5G technology to aggregate multi-source floodwater imagery from Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), vehicles (dashcams), and Roadside Units (RSUs). These diverse data streams, captured from heterogeneous viewpoints, are transmitted to the cloud server or processed locally, where the proposed HydroReasoner framework performs efficient and interpretable floodwater level reasoning.

Fig. 2. The overall framework of HydroReasoner. The pipeline comprises three stages: (I) Reasoning Path Generation: the policy model performs explicit reasoning on the input floodwater image and outputs a structured reasoning path. (II) HydroKG Path Verification: the reasoning path is parsed into candidate triples and verified against HydroKG for structural completeness and consistency with domain grading rules. (III) Reward Shaping and GRPO Update: the verification result, together with format and accuracy signals, forms a composite reward that drives the policy update.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about surgical video -- which phase is underway, which instruments act, and when events occur -- underpins operative documentation, workflow analysis, and skill assessment. Yet surgical visual question answering is still largely built on single frames and closed labels that cannot express a duration, an ordering, or a count, and the video models that lift the frame limit typically compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding the temporal evidence the answer needs. Worse, the answers are structurally heterogeneous, spanning five incompatible structures -- binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal -- that no single training signal scores uniformly well. We propose SurgQ-VLM, a two-stage model for surgical video question answering. Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B: cross-attention conditions both streams on the question, and each clip's visual tokens shrink 49x from the raw ViT patches (11x vs. post-merge backbone tokens). Stage 2 post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer structure (micro-F1 for label sets, normalised error for counts, a content-timing blend for temporal windows). On a sealed 21,840-question test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 pp K-Acc (2.0 pp attributable to the answer-type-aware reward), concentrated in the structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L). Code is available at https://github.com/DhruvMakwana/SurgQ-VLM.
bullets: Targets limitations of frame-based and uniformly compressed video QA, especially for duration, ordering, and counting questions.
Uses a two-stage architecture: question-conditioned slow/fast visual compression followed by GRPO post-training.
Applies answer-type-specific rewards for binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal answers.
On a sealed 21,840-question test split from Cholec80 and CholecT50, achieves 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10× BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot.
GRPO improves keyword accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, with gains concentrated in structurally difficult answer types.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance in translating WebUI screenshots into HTML/CSS. However, when they faced multiple frameworks (React/Vue/Angular), they often suffer from negative transfer that leads to compilation failures. These failures commonly stem from mixing framework specific syntax and violating framework constraints. This paper studies supervised fine-tuning for multi-framework WebUI code generation and proposes a phase-wise MLLM tuning method driven by compatibility and heterogeneity signals across frameworks. We first apply a normalization mapping that preserves each framework's native syntax while suppressing noise from variable naming and literal content. We then estimate cross framework heterogeneity and compatibility offline, and automatically derive training groups and their ordering by maximizing a phased objective. Finally, we perform phase-wise adapter tuning to reduce cross framework interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our proposed method improves both generation quality and compilation success rate compared with baselines.
bullets: Addresses negative transfer when generating React, Vue, and Angular code from screenshots.
Normalizes examples while preserving native framework syntax and reducing naming/content noise.
Uses offline compatibility and heterogeneity estimates to derive training groups and their order.
Applies phase-wise adapter tuning to mitigate framework-specific syntax mixing and constraint violations.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report improved generation quality and compilation success over baselines.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive means for neurological and mental health assessment, yet existing EEG models are typically developed for individual tasks and are difficult to unify across heterogeneous signal configurations and assessment objectives. Large language models (LLMs) offer a common interface for multiple tasks, but adapting heterogeneous EEG signals to a shared LLM raises a key challenge: how to preserve task-specific signal characteristics while enabling effective language-side parameter sharing. To address this problem, we propose EEG-HealthLLM, a unified and parameter-efficient framework for heterogeneous EEG health assessment. We introduce an Asymmetric Hierarchical Adaptation Strategy: task-specific EEG adapters preserve heterogeneous spatio-temporal dynamics, while a unified shared LoRA is injected into the LLM backbone (e.g., Phi-3) to capture shared high-level assessment semantics across tasks. We further establish EEG-HealthBench by reorganizing five existing EEG resources into paradigms covering epileptic seizure detection, major depressive disorder assessment, anxiety risk assessment, depressive symptom risk assessment, and emotional state assessment under a unified subject-independent protocol. Extensive experiments show that EEG-HealthLLM achieves an average balanced accuracy (BAC) of 69.58%, ranking first among the evaluated methods in both average BAC and macro-F1. Compared with independent single-task LoRA adaptation, it improves average BAC from 67.70% to 69.58% while reducing the aggregate language-side adapter footprint by 80.0%. Further analyses reveal task-dependent cross-task interactions and trade-offs, supporting the proposed hierarchical adaptation strategy. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Marui-88/EEG-HealthLLM.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining heterogeneous EEG configurations and multiple neurological and mental-health assessment objectives.
Uses asymmetric hierarchical adaptation: task-specific EEG adapters retain spatio-temporal characteristics, while shared LoRA captures common assessment semantics in an LLM backbone.
Introduces EEG-HealthBench, a unified subject-independent benchmark spanning five EEG assessment paradigms.
Achieves 69.58% average balanced accuracy and ranks first among evaluated methods in average BAC and macro-F1.
Compared with independent single-task LoRA, improves average BAC from 67.70% to 69.58% while reducing aggregate language-side adapter footprint by 80.0%.

papers.abstract: Purpose: To compare two multimodal System 1 decision models (Clef 27B, d1 3B) with three generative vision-language models read out zero-shot from a single answer token (Qwen3.8-27B, which is Clef's backbone; Gemma 4 31B; MedGemma 1.5 4B) on seven radiology tasks. Methods: All models ran locally on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The System 1 models returned a probability for each option in one pass; for the generative models, probabilities were read from the log-probabilities of the option letters. Tasks covered chest CT and radiograph reports (CT-RATE, PadChest), device MR safety records (GUDID), tubes and lines on chest radiographs (RANZCR CLiP), chest CT volumes (CT-RATE), brain MRI motion (MR-ART) and MRI sequence (BraTS 2021), 4,435 cases in total. The primary endpoint was AUROC with bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: All five models retrieved report findings well (AUROC 0.93-0.99). Clef ranked higher than its backbone on CT volumes (0.749 vs 0.668) and tube and line radiographs (0.812 vs 0.766) and lower on motion (0.625 vs 0.709), but it changed decisions more than ranking: it identified 90 of 100 FLAIR volumes, a class its backbone never chose, and cut calibration error on CT volumes from 0.436 to 0.072. d1 was within 0.04 of Clef on reports while using 3 to 9 times less energy per request, but was weak on images. Gemma 4 31B ranked device MR safety best (0.854) and MedGemma 1.5 4B ranked motion best (0.821), yet MedGemma was at chance on MRI sequences and answered "severe" for 93% of motion scans. Conclusion: A single-token readout turns open generative models from several families into usable decision models without retraining, but no model was best on every task and each had task-specific answer biases, so models and decision thresholds should be chosen on local cases.
bullets: Compared two multimodal System 1 models with three generative vision-language models across seven radiology tasks and 4,435 cases.
All models performed strongly on report-finding retrieval, with AUROCs of 0.93–0.99.
Clef improved over its backbone on CT volumes and tube/line radiographs, while showing weaker motion performance and improved CT-volume calibration.
The smaller d1 model approached Clef on reports with substantially lower energy use but performed poorly on images.
No model was consistently best; task-specific biases support selecting models and thresholds using local cases.

papers.abstract: We present See, Think, Use, a protocol that traces each answer of a vision-language model to perception, reasoning or the use of perception. The diagnosis shows a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.
bullets: The protocol separates failures into seeing, thinking, and using visual evidence.
It uses localization and text-replacement probes, plus counterfactual image pairs, without model-weight access or answer labels for the use measure.
Across two model families and six datasets, the most effective intervention depends on the task family.
Models often follow their perception except when images conflict with common priors; localization-first prompting can repair this when localization is correct.
Stage-based compute allocation approaches the best uniform policy at lower cost and outperforms random allocation when a targeted intervention helps.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception and reasoning failures in vision-language models and allocates test-time compute, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: See, Think, Use: Diagnosing Perception and Reasoning Failures in VLMs
papers.tldr: See, Think, Use diagnoses whether VLM errors arise from perception, reasoning, or failure to use perception, enabling targeted test-time computation.

papers.abstract: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.
bullets: Introduces the Benchmark Card, which separates safety signals arising from the scene, request, or benchmark files, and applies it to six benchmarks.
Finds severe leakage in MSSBench chat: image size alone achieves 82.3% accuracy, while other benchmarks contain design-based shortcuts.
Proposes Spot-Stop, decomposing the gap between ranking and binary labelling into threshold, score-overlap, and pair-specific ordering effects.
Most of 14 open MLLMs rank safe versus unsafe scenes better than they label them; shared-threshold calibration and label-free recentering reduce this gap.
Recentring on unlabeled scenes from the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

papers.selection_reason: Audits and analyzes the behavior of Multimodal LLMs on situational-safety benchmarks, providing a framework for understanding label reliability.
papers.title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Situational-safety benchmark scores can reflect dataset artifacts and calibration—not just an MLLM’s understanding of scene safety—so the paper proposes tools to audit and improve their interpretation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $τ$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between roughly 1 Hz scene-semantic updates and 20–50 Hz reactive control.
Caches VLM context and combines it with high-frequency visual features from a compact robot-video-pretrained encoder.
Conditions the flow-matching action expert on cache age and trains it with realistic cache-age histories and staleness-mimicking pixel corruption.
On LIBERO, achieves 95.2% success at a 1 s semantic refresh and 94.5% at 2 s, versus 96.3% for a frequency-matched anchor.
Adds zero-latency chunk-boundary correction and a verdict gate that freezes execution under instruction–scene mismatch.],

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Leap-VLA overview. Slow system: the VLM runs at fslow over a token sequence that appends, after the prompt and the observation, the chain-ofthought region; it produces the cached context C and the chain-of-thought-supervised anchor features, and its reasoning region is emitted as the structured output shown. Because attention is causal, the prompt-region features the expert consumes are unchanged by the appended block (Sec. III-B). Fast system: the flow-matching expert runs at ffast, consuming C and fresh fast-stream features through one pluggable token-block interface: image tokens from the frozen motion-aware encoder (dual-frame, robot-pretrained with reconstruction, optical flow, and depth). The measured cache age τ conditions the expert via AdaRMS, proprioception enters as a dedicated input token, and the control rate f is passed to the action head; training samples τ from the physical episode history.

papers.title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
papers.tldr: Leap-VLA enables high-rate robot control by reusing low-rate VLM semantics while adapting to cache staleness with fresh visual input and age-aware action prediction.

papers.abstract: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.
bullets: Targets reliable perception of UI components and synthesis of structured, executable interfaces.
Uses an 80-category, two-level taxonomy with supervision for category prediction, OCR, color recognition, and grounding.
Generates UIs progressively as DSL outputs from requirement–screenshot–JSON training tuples.
Applies online GRPO with server-side rendering and LLM-based and contrastive preference evaluation.
Reports strongest referring/dense-grounding results on its benchmark and the best composite generation score among compared compact models; finer perception also improves generation.

papers.title: UI-UG 2: Advancing Mobile UI Understanding and Generation with Fine-Grained Supervision and Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison learned by prior within-instance self-supervised methods.
Pairs two visual instances, mixes their local elements, and trains the model to separate them by origin while restoring spatial, temporal, or geometric order.
Uses diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum to create richer automatically verifiable rewards from unlabeled data.
Applied to cross-image jigsaws, 3D depth, and video temporal ordering, with reported gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding across benchmarks.
Evaluations across model scales and families indicate broad generality, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

papers.title: Learning to Group and Order: Cross-Instance Self-Supervised RL for Vision-Centric MLLMs

papers.abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.
bullets: On a selected 400-question screen capped at 256 tokens, GRPO raises answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%.
Most wrong-to-correct changes involve previously unextractable responses: 33 of 39 transitions; all 87 base unextractable responses hit the token cap.
Checkpoint-verified reconstruction yields only a +0.75-point accuracy gain at 512 tokens, compared with +8.25 points at 256 tokens.
On the full 2,511-question development set, recovery-enabled tuning cuts mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain.
Results are limited by selected-screen and provenance constraints and apply to Ornith alone; they do not establish cross-model transfer.

papers.abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.
bullets: Matched-harness accuracy increased from 73.78% to 75.43% (+1.65 percentage points; bootstrap interval [+0.84, +2.41]).

A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison found no detected average improvement, with uncertainty insufficient to establish equivalence.
Findings are limited to the recorded tuning configuration and do not claim superiority over matched supervised tuning or identify specific grounding mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.
bullets: Targets hallucinated or image-ungrounded findings that limit clinical trust in VLM-generated radiology reports.
Decomposes reports into predicates, grounds them using DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM evidence, verifies them with program-of-thought code, and rewrites reports.
On a 4,145-image held-out split, it significantly improved precision for 8/14 CheXpert classes and F1 for 5, without significant metric decreases.
For MedGemma-4B, micro-precision rose from 19.2% to 46.8% and micro-F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%.
Also improved results for LLaVA-Med and MAIRA-2, suggesting applicability across multiple VLM report generators.

papers.abstract: Local image--text matching can find strong evidence for individual concepts yet favor captions with incorrect attribute--entity bindings. We introduce ConstraintMatch, a training-free inference method that turns entity-level regional consistency into an explicit matching cost. On the same frozen condition--region similarity matrix, it compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity. Their gap quantifies the score advantage obtained by relaxing the shared-region constraint. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap by keeping category evidence fixed while jointly shifting an entity's attribute maps. Per-entity clipping prevents cancellation across residuals, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. ConstraintMatch uses pooled embeddings, and spatial calibration requires no additional encoder calls. With parameters fixed per backbone across tasks, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 percentage points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen~2B and CORE~2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the respective gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points. Controlled analyses distinguish the effects of shared-region matching and candidate score calibration. The results establish entity-level evidence selection as a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.
bullets: Addresses incorrect attribute–entity bindings that can survive conventional local image–text matching.
Uses a training-free inference cost comparing independent versus shared regional evidence for each entity.
Calibrates the cost with spatial references, clips per-entity residuals, and subtracts the scaled mean from global similarity.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for clinical image understanding, but their computational and memory requirements hinder deployment on resource-constrained clinical hardware. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical compression strategy without retraining, yet its effectiveness depends strongly on the calibration data. We propose CoreCalib, a training-free and quantizer-agnostic framework for constructing compact calibration sets that preserve the target medical VQA distribution. CoreCalib stratifies data by clinical question class, identifies representative visual modes using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, and expands selected images into class-balanced question-answer pairs. On Kvasir-VQA-x1, we evaluate CoreCalib with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using a fixed 128-pair budget. CoreCalib achieves the best METEOR with all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L with MASQuant and GPTQ. With W4A8 MASQuant, it improves METEOR from 0.5672 with COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering approximately 41% of the degradation relative to BF16. These results support CoreCalib as a data-centric component for resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. Project page: https://magnusdtd.github.io/CoreCalib/ .
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying medical VLMs on hardware with limited compute and memory.
Constructs calibration sets by balancing clinical question classes and selecting representative visual modes with frozen DINOv2 features, UMAP, and HDBSCAN.
Is training-free and quantizer-agnostic, evaluated with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using 128 question-answer pairs on Kvasir-VQA-x1.
Achieves the best METEOR for all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L for MASQuant and GPTQ.
With W4A8 MASQuant, raises METEOR from 0.5672 using COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering about 41% of the degradation relative to BF16.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of CoreCalib and its role in resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. (A) A medical VLM provides strong clinical VQA capability but requires substantial computational resources; PTQ converts it into a low-bit model intended to reduce the resource burden across a spectrum of computing environments. (B) CoreCalib constructs a compact calibration workload by (1) stratifying the medical VQA data by clinical question class, (2) selecting densityaware representative images using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, (3) expanding representative images into multiple QA pairs and balancing them across question classes, and (4) forming a small calibration set, such as 128 QA pairs from 23 images. (C) The calibration set can be used with different PTQ methods, including MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG, to produce a quantized medical VLM with improved capability retention.

papers.abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.
bullets: Addresses text-only extraction, fragmented context, and numerical hallucinations in electrochemical literature curation.
Combines hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration to process text, tables, and figures.
Extracts electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and measured physicochemical properties.
Achieves an F1 score of 0.97 on a manually annotated battery-electrolyte benchmark of 232 papers.
Produces ElectroChemDB from 15,000 research articles and supports electrolyte property prediction models.

Extracted records are standardised using external chemistry tools and databases, verified by domain experts, and consolidated into ElectroChemDB, enabling downstream machine-learning tasks including property prediction and materials discovery.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? Existing methods typically keep image-conditioned failures in their original image-text form, implicitly assuming that pixels are the right route for unlearning whenever pixels appear in the input. We challenge this assumption by constructing modality-decomposed versions of VLM benchmarks, enabling controlled comparisons among image-only, text-only, and multimodal representations of the same examples. Our modality-mixing experiments show that unsafe instruction-following behavior is more effectively suppressed through textual representations than through images alone, while purely text-only unlearning can still weaken visual grounding when the target behavior depends on visual evidence. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce ModRoute, a gradient-guided per-sample modality routing strategy that selectively converts high visual-pressure examples to text-only form while keeping the remaining examples multimodal. Notably, on VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ModRoute has the strongest composite unlearning-utility score of 0.847 at $γ=0.5$, a 2.5% improvement over the best random-switching score and $\geq$46% better than pure multimodal or text unlearning. Overall, our results show that effective VLM unlearning depends not only on the objective, but also on the composition and per-sample modality routing of the unlearning data.
bullets: The work reframes VLM unlearning as both an objective-design and data-representation problem.
Modality-decomposed benchmarks enable controlled comparison of image-only, text-only, and multimodal unlearning inputs.
Textual representations better suppress unsafe instruction-following, but text-only unlearning can harm visual grounding.
ModRoute uses gradient-guided, per-sample routing to convert high visual-pressure examples to text-only form and retain multimodal inputs for others.
On VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, it achieves a composite score of 0.847, outperforming random switching by 2.5% and pure routing baselines by at least 46%.

papers.abstract: Answering a complex question about a long video is a grounding problem: the answer turns on a few seconds of evidence, and vision-language models remain well below human accuracy at finding them. The standard way to spend extra test-time compute on this kind of video reasoning is best-of-N selection: sample several chain-of-thought answers from a fixed model, then let a second model re-watch the video and pick one. Such pipelines are reported by a single headline number, their margin over a majority vote. That number conflates two effects with opposite deployment consequences: the benefit the second model adds by selecting among candidates, and the benefit it would have supplied by solving the question itself. We separate them, measuring the Selection Increment (SI) -- selection accuracy minus the same verifier's accuracy with the candidates withheld -- alongside the margin over self-consistency, across five long-video benchmarks. The Selection Increment is largest for the weakest verifiers: a verifier that solves poorly on its own leaves the candidates the most room to help. Beating the majority vote follows the opposite profile: where the vote already sits near its ceiling no verifier we test improves on it; below that ceiling only the strongest do. On Video-Holmes, the two come apart on a single pool of candidates -- a weak verifier gains +19.3 points from the candidates yet lands 7.1 points below the vote, while the frontier verifier gains the least and beats the vote. The weakest verifier also shows a failure mode: on EgoSchema it picks by where an option sits in the list rather than by what the video shows. Read as a merit score, SI puts a verifier that fails to beat a majority vote at the top of its ranking; read as an audit, it says which of the two effects a headline number delivers. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/best-n-selection-video-reasoning.
bullets: Introduces Selection Increment (SI): verifier accuracy with candidates minus its accuracy when candidates are withheld.
Across five long-video benchmarks, weaker verifiers gain more from candidate answers, while stronger verifiers are more likely to beat majority vote.
On Video-Holmes, a weak verifier gained 19.3 points from candidates but remained 7.1 points below the vote; the frontier verifier gained less but surpassed it.
The weakest verifier showed positional-choice bias on EgoSchema, selecting based on option order rather than video evidence.
SI is useful as an audit of where gains come from, but is misleading as a standalone merit ranking.

figures.caption: Figure 1: What a best-of-N verifier pipeline measures. A base generator (Qwen3.5-27B) samples N=8 chain-of-thought rollouts per question, each ending in a candidate letter. Three rules score that same pool: majority voting; the verifier selecting among the candidates after re-watching K frames; and the same verifier with the candidates withheld. Their differences define our two axes, ∆maj and SI.

Figure 2: Selection Increment vs. gain over selfconsistency. Each point is a (benchmark, verifier) pair; lines link the two verifiers on one benchmark. SI>0 and beating self-consistency are dissociable. Solver policy; VRBench: first 1,000 questions (118 of 960 videos).

Figure 3: Selection Increment by benchmark and verifier. SI (selection accuracy minus the same verifier answering directly, both under the Solver policy) for the Muse holistic-48 verifier (blue) and GPT-5.6 Sol (red). GPT-5.6 Sol yields positive SI on all three benchmarks while Muse splits (negative on TempCompass)—not because GPT is the stronger selector but because its standalone accuracy typically sits below Muse’s, leaving the candidates more room, consistent with SI tracking standalone accuracy inversely (Section 4). VRBench cells use the first 1,000 questions of its split (118 of 960 videos).

Table 4: Base × verifier on Video-Holmes (full 2 × 2). Selection Increment (Panel A) and gain over self-consistency (Panel B, selection vs. majority@8), in points, for a weak and a strong verifier (Qwen-27B, standalone 27.7; Muse, 59.4) over a Qwen- and a Muse-generated candidate pool (each split n=1,837; the Muse-verifier cells use matched n=1,808/1,807). SI is a column effect; beating self-consistency is set by the verifier. Cell-level tests and provenance: Appendix E.

Table 5: Position bias by response mode, weak verifier (Phi-3.5-Vision). Modes are disjoint and separated by output length. All tests are exact two-sided binomial McNemar on non-empty picks; Alift is 100(bA−cA)/n. Marker-mode A-lift magnitudes are withheld pending independent verification: no marker-mode cell reaches significance in any of the ten arms as scored here, each on its own full row set, and every marker-mode |A-lift| is below 4 points, though at these per-arm n that is a failure to distinguish the marker mode from zero rather than a demonstration that it is unbiased—the closest cell sits just above α, at p=0.0501. Accuracies are under the Solver policy.

Table 7: Answer-position bias on EgoSchema is a weak-verifier property. Per-verifier A-lift (pick-“A” rate minus gold-“A” rate, in points, under the Solver scoring policy; gold-“A” = 20.2%, gold mode E, n=500), ordered weak to strong. Only the weak cross-family verifier Phi-3.5-Vision lifts “A” above gold, at both of its compute budgets; every capable verifier stays within 1.4 points of gold.

Table 6: Base × verifier on TempCompass (full 2 × 2). Selection Increment and gain over selfconsistency (∆maj), in points, for a weak (Qwen-27B) and a strong (Muse) verifier over each of two candidate pools. SI is a column effect (large for the weak verifier, near zero for the strong one on both bases); beating self-consistency is a row effect (attainable on the harder Qwen-base pool, out of reach on the near-saturated Muse-base pool). The two axes are governed by different factors. The three small ∆maj cells (+0.9, −0.3, −0.4) are effectively at parity; the row effect is clearest in the Muse column (+7.9→−0.4). Provenance. SI is reported with both of its legs—selection and standalone—at the original 1,024-token generation cap, since re-measuring one leg alone would mix compute budgets within a single difference. Each SI cell is differenced on its verifier’s matched non-empty support. The two Qwen-27B ∆maj cells are re-measured at 8,192 tokens with a corrected answer extractor; the Muse cells never bound the cap but retain the original extractor (Appendix B). In both base-varying 2 × 2s the base axis moves the generator’s frame budget together with its identity—the Qwen-base pools read 64 frames, the Muse-base pools 32—so a row effect is a property of each pool as produced rather than of model identity alone.

Table 3: The two axes come apart on full splits. Solver-policy (prior-work convention) accuracies for the Muse holistic-48 and GPT-5.6 Sol verifiers; majority is the shared 27B majority@8 baseline. The headroom h is a per-benchmark property of the candidate pool and predicts neither delta. VRBench cells use the first 1,000 questions of its split (118 of 960 videos); deltas are McNemar-significant at α=0.05 unless marked n.s.

Table 1: Base and verifier roles. All headline best-of-N results fix Qwen3.5-27B as the base generator and vary the verifier; two base-varying 2× 2s (Video-Holmes, TempCompass; Section 4) also vary the base. The standalone solver is the same verifier answering directly from its own K frames.

Table 8: Answer-position bias is a pathology of under-capable verifiers. Per-verifier A-lift (pick-“A” rate minus gold-“A” rate, in points; under the Solver scoring policy) across benchmarks. Where a benchmark induces the bias, the weak verifier (Phi-3.5) lifts “A” above gold, whereas the capable same-family self-verifier sits below gold on both cells we re-measured without a truncating generation cap (MLVU-Test −2.2, Video-Holmes −2.8); no capable cross-family verifier lifts “A” above gold by more than 1.4 points (on Video-Holmes the frontier GPT-5.6 Sol is likewise robust, −1.2). TempCompass induces no default for any verifier. Compute budget caveat. The Qwen3.5-27B (self) column was first measured at a 1,024-token cap that truncated the verifier’s own response. Four cells were re-measured at 8,192 tokens with a corrected answer extractor. Both Qwen3.5-27B cells change sign—by −8.0 points on MLVU-Test and −5.0 on Video-Holmes—and raising the cap alone accounts for −6.4 and −4.4 of that, flipping both signs by itself; the extractor only deepens them. The other two are Phi-3.5 positive controls: its cap and extractor effects are exactly zero (its longest MLVU-Test response is five tokens, so the cap never bound), and re-measuring moved its Video-Holmes A-lift by only 0.22 points—from the +4.2 printed here to +4.0—through run-to-run sampling alone. That residual, against flips of 8.0 and 5.0 points, is what attributes the reversals to the cap rather than to the act of re-measuring. Phi-3.5 entries are the original run; the significance tests of Section 5 use the re-measured one, which changes no survivor. Every remaining entry, including the other two Qwen3.5-27B cells (−0.8, +0.6), is uncorrected: original extractor, 1,024-token cap. Phi-3.5 on EgoSchema is shown at 48 frames; dashes mark cells not run.

papers.selection_reason: Separates selection versus solving effects in best-of-N video reasoning, directly relevant to video-language understanding and VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Selecting or Solving? What Best-of-N Verification Delivers in Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: Best-of-N video reasoning gains must be split into candidate-selection benefit and the verifier’s own solving ability, because these can point to opposite conclusions.

papers.abstract: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, $μ$m, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.
bullets: Representation changes alone shifted accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within a model, especially for photon-energy tables and plots.
Changing the query from wavelength to photon energy helped some model–view pairs by 16–50 points but hurt others by up to 25.
When relevant extrema were removed, unadapted models rarely responded “undetermined.”
LoRA fine-tuning improved trained formats but could exploit truncation as a shortcut; training on answerable truncations largely prevented this.
The released tasks, per-response results, and code support evaluation of representation invariance and missing-evidence handling.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One MOCLIP scope instance in wavelength and energy coordinates. Shading marks the queried interval and is added for illustration only; model inputs state the interval in the question.
Figure 3: MOCLIP compare accuracy (core variants) after adaptation; markers identify seeds and dashed curves show the unadapted model.

papers.abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.
bullets: Motivation: Standard next-token captioning lacks an explicit variable linking words to visual regions, weakening referential grounding.
Method: Solve an entropic optimal-transport assignment between content words and regions, with a NOTHING option for non-referential words and capacity limits enforcing mutual exclusivity.
Results: On SAYCam, alignment improves word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38.

Controlled studies show the constrained formulation outperforms a row-wise softmax under realistic non-reference rates and matches adult cross-situational learning patterns across ambiguity conditions.
Scope: The method improves captioning-based grounding but does not outperform a contrastive model on that model’s benchmark.

papers.abstract: A deep understanding of scientific literature often relies on interpreting figures that contain key information beyond the main text. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract insights from these figures can significantly accelerate knowledge discovery. Existing works on Scientific Visual Question Answering rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible and require large computational resources. Instead of designing complex architectures, we propose RE- SciVQA, which focuses on improving the quality of retrieved context and fine-tuning small LLMs with parameter-efficient LoRA training. Using a simple query expansion step, relevant section headers are appended to the original question to improve the retrieval coverage. In addition, a simple adjustment of similarity scores is applied using figure references and caption alignment. On the SciVQA benchmark, RE-SciVQA achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 score of 73.9%, outperforming chart-focused models such as UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%), and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Our relevance-enhanced RAG setup also improves the exact match by 11.9% and the fuzzy match by 29.5% compared with a standard RAG baseline, resulting in an overall gain of 14.3%. We also examine closed-ended infinite visual questions, a category in which chart-understanding models often struggle. Our experiments show that using plot digitization instead of synthetic captions leads to an 18.5% improvement for this question type.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost and limited accessibility of existing Scientific VQA pipelines.
Expands questions with relevant section headers and adjusts retrieval scores using figure references and caption alignment.
Uses LoRA to fine-tune smaller LLMs rather than relying on complex architectures or resource-intensive training.
On SciVQA, reports a 73.9% ROUGE-1 F1 score and improves exact and fuzzy matching over standard RAG.
For closed-ended infinite visual questions, plot digitization improves performance over synthetic captions by 18.5%.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.
bullets: Covers six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers.
Provides parallel audio and video inputs to assess cross-modal consistency and complementary information use.
Evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs show substantial performance bottlenecks, with tcpWER frequently exceeding 100%.
Highlights fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key open challenges.
