papers.abstract: Multi-step visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers complex questions by repeatedly retrieving visual evidence, updating an intermediate state, and deciding whether to continue searching or answer. Yet retrieving relevant evidence does not ensure its effective use throughout the reasoning trajectory. As multi-step reasoning progresses, redundant sources occupy context capacity needed for missing evidence, observations tied to resolved requirements or unproductive searches linger in context, and visual sources are revisited with insufficient detail for fine-grained reading. We term this loss of usable evidence over a reasoning trajectory trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation. To address it, we propose Trajectory-Aware Evidence Coordination (TAEC), a training-free framework that coordinates evidence use around unresolved answer requirements. TAEC tracks these requirements in a shared trajectory state to guide which evidence enters the context, how accumulated memory is retained, and at what level of detail visual evidence is examined. Under a unified evaluation protocol on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc, TAEC achieves the best overall performance against leading training-free visual RAG baselines, with the highest average accuracy across multiple proprietary vision-language models. These results demonstrate that aligning evidence with evolving reasoning needs improves evidence use throughout multi-step visual RAG.
bullets: Addresses trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation, where redundant, outdated, or insufficiently detailed evidence hinders ongoing reasoning.
Uses a shared trajectory state to track unresolved answer requirements.
Guides context inclusion, memory retention, and the visual-detail level used for evidence examination.
A training-free framework evaluated on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc.
Reports the best overall performance among leading training-free visual RAG baselines across multiple proprietary vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.
authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Yoonwoo Jeong, Hyunseok Lee, Minsu Cho, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between discrete language reasoning and continuous image generation.

Achieves a 7-percentage-point GenEval gain over BAGEL and outperforms token-based reasoning under parallel and sequential test-time scaling.

papers.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.
authors: Lidong Lu, Lidong Zou, Xinyi Mao, Jiaxin Lv, Zhenquan Li, Liangrui Dong, Tong Lu, Guo Chen
bullets: Introduces PanoVideoBench, a manually annotated benchmark with 1,000 questions across five categories and 15 types.
Evaluation of 11 models finds cross-view tracking and integrating evidence across space and time to be the main weaknesses.
Constructs PanoVideoCoT with 13,465 reasoning QA pairs from verified panoramic observations and agentic explorations.
Trains PanoVideoReasoner using Panoramic CoT SFT and evidence-privileged on-policy self-distillation.
Achieves 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving its backbone by 12.5 points and prior state of the art by 2.6 points.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.
authors: Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu, Huiguang He
bullets: Targets the unclear correspondence between MLLM internal criteria and the latent structure of human cognition.
Uses a 66-dimensional semantic space derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out judgments.
Trains models to predict both triplet choices and linguistic rationales grounded in the inferred salient dimension.
Improves consistency with human similarity judgments while retaining competitive multimodal benchmark performance.
Searchlight RSA on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset shows increased model–human representational alignment.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Cortical projection of representational alignment improvements across subjects. The heatmaps visualize the voxel-wise difference in ∆̃RSA(c) scores between the aligned and baseline Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct model. Darker colors indicate better representational alignment between models and human brain. Consistent positive shifts are observed, demonstrating that our alignment framework robustly shifts the MLLMs internal representational geometry to be more human-like.

Figure 1: Overview of triplet-level semantic dimension attribution. (a) Human similarity judgements are collected via crowdsourcing. Then learning a representational embedding space via SPoSE yields the multidimensional mental representations of natural objects. (b) For one triplet, we compute the original softmax probability based on the entire representational embedding for all pairs. We then iteratively prune each dimension from the representational embedding space and compute the changes in softmax probabilities relative to those obtained with the full embedding as the relevance score for that dimension. By sorting these relevance scores in descending order, we establish a hierarchical ranking of dimensional importance. The top-1 dimension yielding the maximum probability change is regarded as the most salient semantic dimension driving the human decision-making.

Figure 3: (a) Overview of hybrid dataset. The total dataset includes three subsets: Single-image (126K samples), Multi-image (102K samples), and Cognitive-Alignment (80K samples). (b) Examples. The examples include Spot the Difference, Image Edit Instruction, Visual Storytelling, LLaVAR, COCO Caption, and Odd-One-Out tasks.

Figure 2: Pipeline for dimension-grounded reasoning enhancement. This pipeline illustrates the process of reasoning enhancement via LLM. For one triplet with their textual descriptions and the most salient semantic dimension d∗ driving human decision-making, we integrate them into the structured prompt Prompt(T , cap(T ), d∗). LLM is then utilized exclusively to enhance reasoning. By injecting the dimension d∗, we guide the LLM to perform targeted reasoning enhancement. This effectively converts discrete cognitive criteria for decision-making into explicit CoT rationale r(d∗).

Figure 5: Stability of alignment shifts across different extraction depths. The cortical projections display the alignment improvements ∆̃RSA(c) of subject 1 computed using features from the last layer, the second-to-last layer, and the concatenation of the last four layers. Darker regions reflect better alignment improvement. The spatial distribution of these positive shifts remains consistent regardless of the extraction depth, confirming that the achieved representational alignment with human cognition is robust and not a selective layer choice.
Figure 6: Comparison of choicebased RSMs between Qwen2.5-VL7B and human.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/kreshuklab/Open-Weight-MLLMs-Cannot-Compare-What-They-Cannot-Name
bullets: The study tests MLLM comparison of ant body-part sizes in synthetic images, motivated by scalable biological image analysis.
Models succeed on some parts but fail on others despite equivalent visual comparison difficulty.
In-context learning strategies and a related object-recognition task are evaluated.
Results suggest recognition-driven grounding failure: unrecognized structures are mapped to familiar concepts, impairing comparison.
Vision-encoder analysis supports the possibility that fine-grained structure is poorly preserved without semantic support.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.
authors: Yuquan Li, Xinyang Jiang, Yuhao Xue, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Addresses ill-defined MICL tasks whose solutions depend on uncovering rules from examples.
Uses multimodal large language models to construct rule-centric data and provide explicit rule-induction supervision.
Trains models in two stages with mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Experiments across diverse MICL settings show consistent gains and more stable performance.
The approach focuses on settings where latent rules can be inferred from demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.
authors: Mo Shahdloo, Faegheh Sardari, Mathew Salvaris
bullets: Addresses the loss of spatial and fine-grained visual information caused by text-only communication between modular VLMs and SLMs.
Uses a lightweight codec with a domain encoder mapping VLM states into the SLM embedding space and a LoRA-based attention decoder for visual prefixes.
Trains only about 1.6M parameters, or 0.2% of the combined model size, while keeping both models frozen.
Reports higher performance than matched text-communication baselines on CLEVR, GQA, and Flickr8k.
Demonstrates compatibility across models with different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Noori Bae, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Identifies Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR), where models answer correctly despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate reasoning.
Shows that CVMR tokens have distinct attention patterns from well-grounded tokens.
Introduces GRIT, which uses gradient masking to incorporate visual grounding into RLVR training.
Introduces GRIT-Bench for evaluating text-rich reasoning across text length and reasoning depth.
Experiments report improved reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Jaesung Jun, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Problem: Always-on CoT can cause overthinking, misaligning visual grounding with the query.
Method: Estimate input difficulty from attention-map entropy; high entropy triggers CoT, while low entropy skips it.
Robustness: Bidirectional Rethinking reverses the initial reasoning choice when the output fails.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks and improves inference efficiency.
Scope: Training-free adaptive inference for multimodal reasoning segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the proposed DA-CoT framework during inference. The aggregated attention entropy Hagg, computed over the pre-identified layers L, is used to adaptively decide whether to trigger CoT reasoning. If Hagg ≥ τ , the model follows the Difficulty-Aware Prompting Path with CoT for structured reasoning; otherwise, it takes the direct path without CoT for efficient inference. When the initial reasoning path fails to produce a valid output, a discrete flipping signal activates the Bidirectional Rethinking Path, enabling re-evaluation and recovery from overthinking or underthinking. The final bounding boxes or point prompts are then passed to the segmentation head to produce the reasoningaware segmentation result.

Figure 2. Qualitative examples illustrating the contrasting effects of CoT prompting in reasoning segmentation. Left: CoT-detrimental cases, where CoT leads to misgrounding by overthinking spatial reasoning; without CoT, the model correctly identifies the target with concentrated attention and low entropy. Right: CoT-beneficial cases, where CoT enhances performance in ambiguous scenarios by guiding reasoning towards the correct region, as reflected in high-entropy attention maps. The visualized attention entropy (bottom right of each map) provides an intrinsic signal that distinguishes when CoT is helpful or harmful.

papers.abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Shuo Hong, Jiaxin Ma, Xidi Cai, Qianli Ma
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between blocking malicious instructions and retaining useful information from attacked media.
Uses on-policy self-distillation: a student processes attacked inputs while learning token-level behavior from a frozen base model viewing the erased version.
Evaluated across image, audio, and video with two model sizes, achieving near-zero observed attack success while maintaining near-clean-input task utility.
On 3B audio, ERASE achieves 60.1% attacked-input accuracy versus ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level.
Reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio, with out-of-domain accuracy near the base model level.

papers.abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.
bullets: Introduces BSTRB, a benchmark of 8,398 noisy text images from 1,699 real-world video sequences with high-fidelity annotations.
Fine-tunes Hawkeye on BSTRB to read illegible text under motion blur and low resolution.
Hawkeye matches much larger VLMs overall and outperforms them on text at or below 20 pixels.
Characterizes the resolution threshold where current VLMs begin to fail.
Scope: focuses on degraded scene text, especially conditions relevant to smart glasses and other egocentric settings.

papers.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.
bullets: The study introduces a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score by measuring text–audio distance in valence–arousal–dominance space.
The score is validated against human judgments and tested across acted, conversational, and spontaneous speech using three audio-capable models.
Audio-related incongruence increases prediction errors across all three corpora, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance.
Supervised classifiers show the opposite pattern, implicating how audio-language models combine evidence rather than the underlying signal.
Text-only effects are inconsistent across models; a lexicon-free version of the score preserves the central finding and outperforms simpler label-free alternatives in consistency.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview. Text and audio are mapped into a shared VAD space; their Euclidean distance is converted to a continuous incongruence probability pincon via a two-component GMM fitted on training distances. LLM predictions are evaluated stratified by pincon, and compared against VAD-feature baselines.

Fig. 4. Within-emotion incongruence effect (OR of error) by corpus. Values >1 (red) mean incongruence harms recognition of that emotion; <1 (blue) mean it helps. Sadness and anger, the classes with the most characteristic prosody, are helped wherever their effect is significant; the classes that are harmed differ by corpus. (MELD has no “happiness” class; its positive label is “joy”.)

Fig. 5. Adjusted association between pincon and error from the cluster-robust logistic model, with controls for emotion, prototype distance, length and duration (95% CIs). Circles are GPT-audio on all three corpora; triangles are Qwen2.5-Omni and diamonds GLM-4-Voice on the matched MELD and MOSEI samples. Filled markers have intervals that exclude 1. For GPT-audio the text+audio association is positive in every corpus, while the text-only association changes sign across corpora. Qwen2.5-Omni agrees in direction on MELD (1.14) without reaching significance, and GLM-4-Voice shows no significant association, in line with its much weaker accuracy.

Fig. 3. Paradigm dissociation on eNTERFACE (test split, T2 text+audio for the LLMs). Audio LLMs lose accuracy on incongruent utterances, whereas discriminative classifiers trained on the same six VAD features gain accuracy, because a larger cross-modal gap makes classes more separable. This is consistent with the harm arising during raw multimodal integration rather than from the VAD features (the baselines are supervised, however, so this is not by itself proof of mechanism).

Fig. 6. Convergent validity: the text+audio incongruence effect under the lexicon-based pincon (NRC lexicon + audeering audio-VAD; blue) versus a fully neural, lexicon-free pincon (EmoBank-trained text-VAD regressor + WavLM audio-VAD; orange), under the identical cluster-robust specification. Filled markers exclude OR=1. On eNTERFACE and MOSEI the neural score reproduces the text+audio association found with the lexicon-based one; on MELD it does not, so the convergence is partial.

papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $\tau$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

bullets: Supports speech, text, and image inputs while generating natural-language responses and tool calls.
Uses a two-stage speech adaptation process combining supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and distillation-based losses.
Trains on automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues with efficiency optimizations for online teacher–student distillation.
Reports strong performance across Big Bench Audio, Speech-BFCL, τ-Voice, English EVA, and experience pass@1, with 1.91-second mean latency in thinking mode.
Deployed on a custom serving platform for interactive voice conversations.

papers.abstract: Detailed image captioning is usually framed as an amount problem: a model should mention more visual facts while avoiding hallucination. However, autoregressive VLMs generate captions as ordered sequences, and later generations may be produced under weaker or noisier visual grounding. We therefore argue that long-form captioning should be studied not only by what facts are mentioned, but also by where they appear. We introduce a position-aware rubric representation that decomposes dense human references into atomic visual claims, verifies generated captions against those claims, and induces a quartile-wise composition of supported, hallucinated, and generic content. This lens reveals two qualitatively different failures in long captions: models tend to produce unsupported specificity in the middle, while the final portion often escapes into vague, non-evidential language rather than simply accumulating more hallucination. A same-reference human control does not exhibit these patterns; additional human audits examine the visual validity of the induced labels. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose PAGER (Position-Aware Grounded Evidence Reinforcement), a GRPO training objective with separate signals for supported fine-grained middle evidence, evidence-bearing tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length control. The result is a closed loop: the same ordered claim representation identifies where long captions fail and supplies the position-specific reward needed to repair those failures. Experiments on detailed-caption benchmarks show that PAGER improves position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while preserving competitive global caption quality.
bullets: Long captions often become unsupportedly specific in the middle and vague or non-evidential near the end.
A position-aware rubric decomposes references into atomic visual claims and evaluates supported, hallucinated, and generic content by caption quartile.
PAGER applies position-specific GRPO rewards for grounded middle evidence, evidential tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length.
Experiments show improved position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while maintaining competitive overall caption quality.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems often suffer from over-concentrated results when optimized for accuracy, limiting recommendation diversity. While diversity has become an important objective, existing methods still face fundamental limitations from both semantic and structural perspectives. On the one hand, multimodal recommender systems provide rich semantic signals, yet are often treated as auxiliary to ID embeddings, leading to ineffective semantic utilization for diversity. On the other hand, the accuracy--diversity trade-off persists during training, where accuracy gains often come at the cost of diversity. We show that this phenomenon is fundamentally governed by both the structural properties of learned representations and the dynamics of optimization. To address these challenges, we propose MOSS, a unified framework for multimodal decoupling through semantic and structural shaping. Specifically, we first introduce an MLLM-based Decoupled Feature Extraction module to disentangle multimodal content into informative representations. To enhance semantic utilization, we design a Category-aware Embedding Selection module that extracts compact, category-aware semantic features. To address structural limitations, we propose two complementary modules: Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation, which alleviates representation collapse by integrating collaborative and multimodal propagation, and Entropy-based Diversity Regularization, which mitigates optimization bias by promoting balanced category exposure. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MOSS consistently achieves a superior accuracy--diversity trade-off over strong baselines.
bullets: Targets over-concentrated recommendations and the persistent accuracy–diversity trade-off.
Uses MLLM-based decoupled feature extraction and category-aware semantic selection to better exploit multimodal content.
Combines alternating dual-graph propagation with entropy-based regularization to reduce representation collapse and balance category exposure.
Experiments on real-world datasets show a consistently better accuracy–diversity trade-off than strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language model (VLM) post-training is commonly evaluated through answer accuracy. We examine how changes in accuracy and training objectives relate to image-conditioned decisions in a controlled Qwen2.5-VL-3B study on PMC-VQA. We compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) restricted to the language model, expanded multimodal adaptation scopes, standard answer-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a counterfactual evidence objective. On 2,000 clean-test questions, language model LoRA SFT changes correct-image accuracy by +1.10 percentage points (95% paired bootstrap CI:-0.85 to +3.05), while visual-benefit events decrease by 2.40 points and image sensitivity decreases by 5.60 points. Paired records reveal 155 acquired and 203 lost visual-benefit events. Broader adaptation yields lower correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT. Standard GRPO produces mixed-reward groups and parameter updates, with an uncertain clean test accuracy change. A generation audit reveals that canonical option scores can follow a different token path from generated answers. With scores taken along the greedy generation path, the evidence target improves on the training set; its gains over standard GRPO remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses. Sample-level analyses trace how evidence scores, decision margins, and generated answers change during post-training. This empirical and measurement audit identifies gaps between optimization activity, target acquisition, and useful held-out visual behavior.
bullets: Evaluates SFT, LoRA, broader multimodal adaptation, standard GRPO, and a counterfactual evidence objective in Qwen2.5-VL-3B on PMC-VQA.
Language-model LoRA SFT slightly increases correct-image accuracy, but decreases visual-benefit events and image sensitivity on clean-test questions.
Broader adaptation performs worse on correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT; standard GRPO yields mixed rewards and uncertain test changes.
Evidence-target gains appear on training data but remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses.
Generation audits show that canonical option scores may not reflect the token path used for generated answers, complicating measurement.

papers.abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.
authors: Lidong Lu, Jiaxin Lv, Liangrui Dong, Xinyi Mao, Lidong Zou, Zhenquan Li, Tong Lu, Guo Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 546 real-world images and 4,595 questions across 651 target-specific groups.
Tests appearance counting, physical-entity counting, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance–entity correspondence.
Evaluates 40 MLLMs; the strongest model answers all questions correctly in only 13.36% of groups.
Performance worsens when one entity creates multiple appearances or appearances span different observation modes.
Higher resolution offers limited gains in complete-group accuracy, while jointly answering related questions helps substantially.

papers.title: PhysCount: Do MLLMs Count Visual Appearances or Physical Entities?
papers.tldr: PhysCount shows that MLLMs can count visible appearances more easily than they can infer the underlying physical entities they represent.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features provides broad coverage by constraining all directions equally, but lacks semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. To address these issues, we propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. Specifically, TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.
authors: Yubo Cui, Xianchao Guan, Zheng Zhang
bullets: VLMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, while robustness fine-tuning can damage pretrained image–text alignment and zero-shot performance.
Feature matching covers visual directions broadly but lacks semantic focus; prediction matching is semantic but limited by candidate texts and probabilities.
TRAG builds anchor-level constraints from the text encoder’s response directions and magnitudes to local embedding variations.
These constraints are aggregated using image–anchor relevance, producing image-adaptive guidance.
Experiments across architectures and tasks report state-of-the-art clean and robust performance, with better preservation of pretrained image–text relationships.

papers.abstract: We revisit advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and observe that any token-level advantage admits a two-stage factorization: a \emph{sample-level baselining} step that converts scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal, and a \emph{token-level credit assignment} step that distributes that signal over the trajectory. Existing estimators typically address only one of these stages: affine baselines preserve the shape of each task's reward law, so heavy tails and binary cliffs propagate into the gradient, while token-level credit rules tie the size of each token's update to raw confidence scales and need not conserve the total credit issued by the verifier. We propose \textbf{TACE} (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a two-stage estimator that addresses both stages. At stage~(S1), we replace linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, which gives a common population reward law across tasks and caps finite-sample outliers deterministically. At stage~(S2), we rank-calibrate a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalize the clipped token weights to have mean one, so credit is redistributed across tokens while its total mass and sign are conserved. We prove population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE obtains the strongest results on a majority of the benchmarks but does not dominate every setting.
authors: Lang Chen, Zongxin Xu, Borui Wang, Anran Liu, Shitong Chen
bullets: Existing GRPO advantage estimators can propagate heavy-tailed or binary reward scales across tasks.
TACE uses optimal transport to map scalar rewards to a standard normal, aligning reward distributions and deterministically capping finite-sample outliers.
It rank-calibrates within-trajectory evidence contrasts and normalizes clipped token weights to conserve total credit.
The method provides inter-task moment equity, tail bounds, mass conservation, boundedness, and sign anchoring.
On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE performs best on most benchmarks but not in every setting.

Stage (S2), ours (starting from the evidence ratio of Yang et al., 2026): runs πθ under non-privileged (PS) and privileged (PT ) contexts, rank-calibrates the per-token log-evidence within the trajectory, and applies a sign-anchored, mean-one (mass-preserving) magnitude weight wi,t. The composed token advantage Âi,t = Ai · wi,t plugs into the standard GRPO clipped surrogate.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are now used as zero-shot judges of image quality, but their color judgments are rarely tested with colorimetric ground truth. We present a five-task benchmark based on the CIE colorimetric framework: AWB pair judgment, skin-tone bias direction, CCT estimation, CIE Delta E 2000 pair ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants. We test eight MLLM endpoints, including four Qwen3-VL variants, GLM-4.5V, GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.7, and Gemini-3.1-Pro. The models often solve coarse binary AWB judgments, but they remain weak on numeric CCT estimation and on some fine color-difference judgments. On ColorChecker-24 stimuli, the three closed-weight frontier models reach CCT MAE of 715-1056 K, compared with 1358-2133 K for the five open-weight models. A non-ColorChecker control shows that this advantage is partly template-dependent. The results suggest that current MLLMs have useful color words and coarse visual priors, but their color judgments are not reliably calibrated to CIE-computable color differences.
authors: Shuwei Yue, Kaida Xiao, Zhihua Wang, Qiao Chen
bullets: Introduces five tasks covering white-balance judgment, skin-tone bias, CCT estimation, Delta E 2000 ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants.
Evaluates eight MLLM endpoints, including Qwen3-VL variants and several closed-weight models.
Models often succeed on coarse binary AWB judgments but struggle with CCT estimation and fine color-difference comparisons.
Closed-weight frontier models show lower CCT errors than open-weight models on ColorChecker-24, though the advantage is partly template-dependent.
Overall, useful color vocabulary and visual priors do not ensure reliable calibration to CIE-computable color differences.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now process hour-long videos, making extended multi-turn dialogue over a single video a natural mode of use. Sustaining such a dialogue requires more than answering each question in isolation: the model must retrieve and reuse information established earlier in the conversation, both what it has seen and what it has said, an ability we term in-context video memory. Existing video QA benchmarks leave this ability unmeasured: their questions are mutually independent, never reference one another, and each is answerable from the video alone, so nothing ever requires carrying information across turns. We introduce VideoMemBench, in which each sample pairs a single video with a long multi-turn dialogue, whose turns are connected by typed cross-turn dependencies: an Episodic Dependency refers back to a visual episode described in an earlier turn, probing memory of what the model has seen, while an Answer Dependency builds on the model's own earlier answer, probing memory of what the model has said. Every dependency is verified considering two properties: 1) necessity, meaning the question cannot be answered without its earlier turns, and 2) non-leakage, meaning the question does not restate the information from its earlier turns. To enforce these properties, we design a construction pipeline with three LLM roles: a planner, a generator, and a judger, with each dialogue reviewed by human experts. VideoMemBench comprises 326 videos with 2,476 turns, of which 1,387 depend on earlier turns, including multi-parent dependencies and long-range call-back. Among over 20 evaluated open- and closed-source MLLMs, Claude Opus 5 performs the best with an overall score of only 45.7\%, highlighting the challenge of in-context video memory. Our dataset and evaluation are released.
authors: Zhengdong Hu, Chao Wang, Kaituo Feng, Huanjin Yao, Mingfei Lu, Hehe Fan, Yi Yang
bullets: Evaluates in-context video memory rather than independent video question answering.
Tests two dependency types: recall of earlier visual episodes and reuse of the model’s own prior answers.
Ensures dependencies are necessary and non-leaking, using planner, generator, and judger roles plus human review.
Contains 326 videos and 2,476 dialogue turns, with 1,387 turns dependent on earlier turns.
Across 20+ open- and closed-source MLLMs, the best reported overall score is only 45.7%, underscoring the difficulty.

figures.caption: Figure 2 The VideoMemBench construction pipeline. Starting from a curated video pool, a planner specifies turn intents and a typed dependency graph. A generator constructs the dialogue turn by turn, while a judger checks necessity, non-leakage, and visual grounding, returning failed turns for regeneration. Completed dialogues are checked against the plan and reviewed by human experts.

Figure 1 Example of VideoMemBench with cross-turn dependencies: Independent turns (e.g., T1, T8) establish visually grounded facts; dependent turns refer back to earlier turns through expressions such as “the scene from T1” or “the target from T1”, without restating earlier content. An Episodic Dependency (e.g., T2) requires recalling what the model has seen: the model must recover which scene T1 described before answering the question. An Answer Dependency (e.g., T3, T4) requires recalling what the model has said : each builds on the answer produced at an earlier turn.

Figure 4 Analysis of factors affecting in-context video memory. (a) Accuracy on dependent turns by dependency distance, measured from the current turn to its earliest parent; the dashed line shows the mean across all evaluated models. (b) Accuracy on dependent turns by the number of parents. (c) Independent- and dependent-turn accuracy by dialogue position for two models: the light segment shows dependent-turn accuracy, the full bar height shows independent-turn accuracy, and the dark segment represents their difference. (d) Accuracy on answer-dependent turns under self-rollout and oracle histories. Oracle histories replace previous model responses with ground-truth answers.

For each dialogue, the expert replays the video in the top panel, where the evidence window of the current turn is marked on the timeline, and reads the dialogue turn by turn, where the parent turns and the type of each dependency are highlighted. The expert answers the current question before the reference answer is revealed, then marks the turn as correct, answer wrong, dependency not required, wording leaks a parent, or duplicate, and edits the question, the options, or the answer in place. A dialogue is retained only after every turn has been marked correct or revised, and the interface records each decision together with the time spent on the turn. papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($\kappa$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).
bullets: The study compares two probing benchmarks, SVO and SugarCrepe, with retrieval over full datasets for six vision–language models and 100 image/caption queries.
On SVO, handcrafted-negative accuracy is higher than accuracy against retrieved negatives (85% vs. 77%); ten retrieved negatives are as challenging as 200–430 random negatives.
On SugarCrepe, handcrafted negatives are harder than retrieved negatives, showing that probe difficulty depends on negative construction.
Incomplete SVO relevance labels substantially depress retrieval scores: human labels identify the top result as correct for 54–90% of queries, versus 6–21% under benchmark labels.
Passing a probe does not predict retrieving the correct item first; the LLM assessor shows moderate agreement with human annotators.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models can both generate and understand images within a single set of weights, offering an opportunity to use image synthesis as training supervision for visual comprehension. However, existing visual chain-of-thought methods rely on human-annotated helper images during training and require slow image generation at test time. We present SelfThinker, the first self-evolving framework that turns a unified model's self-generated visual thoughts into stronger understanding without human image annotations. Given a visual problem, SelfThinker samples candidate helper images from its generation pathway and uses its frozen understanding pathway to score each candidate via conditional pointwise mutual information. High-utility visual thoughts then refine the generator via flow matching and serve as privileged teacher context for on-policy self-distillation. At inference, SelfThinker reasons directly from the original image in text without generating intermediate images. Although trained only on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, SelfThinker transfers broadly to natural-image and spatial benchmarks, raising the seven-benchmark average of ThinkMorph-7B from 52.7 to 64.0 (+11.3 points). Controlled image-perturbation probes further show that SelfThinker surpasses ThinkMorph-7B by up to 40.4 points and its pretrained BAGEL-7B backbone by up to 23.2 points across fine-grained and spatial perception tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhangquanchen/SelfThinker.
bullets: Addresses reliance on human-annotated helper images and costly image generation at test time.
Samples candidate visual thoughts and scores them with the frozen understanding pathway using conditional pointwise mutual information.
Uses high-utility thoughts for flow-matching generator refinement and on-policy self-distillation.
Trained on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, it transfers to natural-image and spatial benchmarks.
Raises ThinkMorph-7B’s seven-benchmark average from 52.7 to 64.0, while inference avoids intermediate image generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of SelfThinker . The upper-left Self-Evolution panel summarizes the closed loop of imagining candidate visual thoughts, verifying reliable ones, and evolving into a stronger model. Imagine: a shared UMM with Generation and Understanding pathways produces candidate visual thoughts and decoded answers. Verify: the frozen Understanding pathway scores each candidate by its log-likelihood utility, calibrates the acceptance threshold against thoughts from other problems, and selects the top verified thought under the ground-truth answer or majority vote. Evolve: the verified thought is distilled into the Student Understanding pathway via on-policy token-level JSD distillation from the EMA Teacher (SelfThinker), supported by flow-matching generator refinement (SelfThinker -Gen). No human image annotation is used

papers.abstract: Tumor delineation is required for radiotherapy planning, yet automatic segmentation is limited by errors, predominantly false positives, that distort dose and increase editing time. The radiology report accompanies the scan and localizes disease at the suborgan level, but existing text-promptable models condition on short referring phrases, and most operate in 2D. We present RepConTUR, a single native-3D early-fusion multimodal model that conditions volumetric abdominal tumor segmentation on the narrative report. We extend AbdomenAtlas 3.0 to a suborgan-level promptable segmentation dataset and generate report-based VQA pairs, yielding four report-derived tasks on the same annotations: referring segmentation (RES), report-grounded segmentation (GSEG), report generation (RRG), and visual question answering (VQA). We train RepConTUR, comprising a 3D CT encoder, an early-fusion language model, and a native-3D segmentation module, jointly on the four tasks. Across liver, kidney and pancreas, RepConTUR attains the highest Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), instance-wise precision, and detection F1 among the text-promptable baselines, and adding the report raises mean precision while leaving recall comparable. Against two vision-only specialists, nnU-Net and the report-supervised R-Super, RepConTUR attains the highest value on every in-domain metric for liver and pancreas and the highest mean DSC, recall, precision, and detection F1 over the four out-of-distribution public cohorts. Ablations indicate that conditioning on the narrative report raises detection F1 from 0.499 to 0.528 within the same model, that joint GSEG training raises RES F1 from 0.450 to 0.482, and that the native-3D segmentation module raises GSEG F1 from 0.139 to 0.528 over its 2D counterpart. Code is available at https://github.com/Oncosoft-Research/RepConTUR.
authors: Seunghwan Lee, Sangjoon Park, Jongmin Lee, Yoon Jo Kim, Wonyoung Cho, Jin Sung Kim, Han Joo Chae
bullets: Addresses false-positive tumor delineation errors that increase radiotherapy-planning dose distortion and editing time.
Combines a 3D CT encoder, early-fusion language model, and native-3D segmentation module, jointly trained on segmentation, report generation, and VQA-related tasks.
Extends AbdomenAtlas 3.0 with suborgan-level report-promptable annotations and four report-derived tasks: RES, GSEG, RRG, and VQA.
Outperforms text-promptable baselines on DSC, instance precision, and detection F1 across liver, kidney, and pancreas; report conditioning improves mean precision with comparable recall.
Ablations show gains from report conditioning, joint GSEG training, and native-3D segmentation; evaluation focuses on abdominal tumors and specified public cohorts.

papers.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.
authors: Subhashini Venugopalan, Jenny Tan, Taylor Roper, Jimmy Tobin, Anton Kast, Alicia Martin, Sam Sepah, Amy Pavel
bullets: Targets inline audio descriptions that must fit naturally into existing video silences, including diverse user-generated content.
MTG-AD contains 36 hours of professionally annotated video and more than 8,000 descriptions created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals.
MTG-AD-Eval provides fine-grained, actionable metrics, including rendered-audio assessment of speech overlap and timing.
Frontier MLLMs describe visual events well and reduce overlaps, but still show weaknesses in narrative pacing and flow.
Automated metrics correlate significantly with human ratings; users narrowly prefer human descriptions but find MLLM outputs highly beneficial for comprehension.

papers.abstract: Medical diagnostic reasoning requires verifiable links between visual evidence and clinical knowledge, yet current medical vision language models are aligned with objectives that reward the wrong behavior. Uniform supervised fine tuning lets easy cases dominate updates while clinically critical boundary cases saturate prematurely. Sparse rewards based only on final-answer correctness cannot assess anatomical grounding or clinical logic, inviting reward hacking through answer shortcuts. We propose MedCBR, a two-stage alignment framework coupling boundary-aware preference optimization with rubric-grounded reinforcement learning. First, we construct counterfactual boundary preferences at the model's capability frontier using empirical pass rates and preference pairs that share reasoning prefixes but diverge at decisive diagnostic branches. Difficulty Weighted Boundary Preference Optimization (DBPO) concentrates learning on this calibrated boundary region. Second, we distill reusable clinical rubrics from boundary trajectories and activate them according to prediction entropy. Entropy Gated Grounded Policy Optimization (EGPO) rewards answer correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity while suppressing rubric noise on reliable samples. A reference policy anchored to the boundary-aligned model couples population-level boundary priors with instance-level uncertainty, making diagnostic reasoning more accurate and clinically grounded. Experiments on six medical benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong general, specialized, and reinforcement learning baselines, reaching 61.2% average accuracy with the largest gains on challenging differential diagnosis tasks. Ablations show super-additive gains: combining the two stages exceeds the sum of their individual improvements.
authors: Hongyu Bai, Jiaqi Zeng, Chunzheng Zhu
bullets: Targets two alignment issues: easy cases dominate supervised updates, while answer-only rewards miss anatomical grounding and clinical reasoning.
Uses DBPO to learn from counterfactual preference pairs at the model’s empirical capability frontier, emphasizing decisive diagnostic branches.
Uses EGPO to activate distilled clinical rubrics based on prediction entropy and reward correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity.
Across six medical benchmarks, MedCBR reaches 61.2% average accuracy and shows its largest gains on challenging differential-diagnosis tasks.
Ablations indicate the two stages provide super-additive benefits when combined.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding is crucial for robots to understand language instructions with visual observations. This paper addresses the problem of visual grounding uncertainties, where a robot uses a black-box vision-language model (VLM) to ground free-form natural-language instructions to target objects. Prevailing methods derive uncertainty from the VLM itself. Yet, outputs of the VLM, e.g., generated uncertainties, are from the same parameters and structures producing the predictions, and inherit the bias. We give a formal Bayesian definition of the problem that treats the VLM prediction as an observation. An external surrogate Bayesian model then quantifies per-query uncertainty over a local neighborhood of a held-out calibration set, decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components. A hierarchical retrieval across input modalities realizes a compact joint-space neighborhood, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. The estimator further integrates with conformal prediction or model-based planning for active visual grounding, where robots are allowed to take verbal or physical actions to ground targets. Across grounding benchmarks and state-of-the-art VLMs, it consistently improves both calibration and task performance. On a real Fetch robot under open-world instructions, it enables principled trade-offs between confident action and information gathering, substantially improving robustness.
authors: Hanbo Zhang, Tianrun Hu, Cedar Site Bai, Anxing Xiao, David Hsu
bullets: Targets biased uncertainty estimates produced internally by black-box vision-language models (VLMs).
Treats each VLM prediction as an observation and decomposes local uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components.
Uses hierarchical cross-modal retrieval to construct compact joint-space neighborhoods from held-out calibration data.
Integrates with conformal prediction and model-based planning for active visual grounding through verbal or physical actions.
Improves calibration and grounding performance across benchmarks and VLMs, including more robust behavior on a real Fetch robot.

papers.abstract: Thinking vision-language models reason for thousands of tokens, yet still miss small details in high-resolution images. Zooming methods pay for extra inference passes, and outcome rewards never tell the model where to look at. In Qwen3.5-4B, we find that the bottleneck is selection, not seeing: a few attention heads, which we call localization heads, pick the evidence out of thousands of visual tokens; ablating four of them costs 13.2 points more than ablating four random heads, and their focus fades as the reasoning grows. We therefore propose Localization-Head Alignment (LHA), which makes attention a training signal: whenever the reasoning states a visual fact, these heads learn to look at the focal region rather than the background, as an auxiliary loss in both SFT and RL training. On benchmarks of V*, HR-Bench 4K and TreeBench, LHA lifts Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy, the best single-pass 4B result we evaluate, ahead of multi-pass zooming and released 7B models. Alignment alone adds 1.8 points over otherwise identical training while shortening reasoning by 20%, and the gains carry over to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
authors: Yuan Wang, Wei Wu, Hongning Wang
bullets: The main bottleneck is selecting visual evidence, not processing high-resolution images.
A small set of localization heads identifies relevant regions; disrupting four causes a 13.2-point larger accuracy loss than disrupting random heads.
LHA uses an auxiliary attention-alignment loss whenever reasoning states a visual fact, and supports both supervised and reinforcement learning.
On V*, HR-Bench 4K, and TreeBench, LHA improves Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy and reduces reasoning by 20%.
The approach also transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B, but its scope is evaluated on the reported benchmarks and models.

papers.abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently fail to recognize culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions. Effectively injecting this long-tail knowledge into existing models remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate knowledge editing as a targeted alternative by introducing CulturalBind, a benchmark comprising 3.2K images of 1K concepts from 6 domains, designed to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge as well as concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation reveals that textual and visual knowledge is decoupled: models often demonstrate text-based knowledge of cultural concepts but fail to identify them from images. We then evaluate editing methods in single and sequential scenarios. Although current methods successfully correct individual visual recognition errors, they exhibit low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the model's broader parametric knowledge. Furthermore, performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing, highlighting the need for comprehensive adaptation approaches that better consolidate multimodal knowledge over time.
authors: Malvina Nikandrou, Georgios Pantazopoulos, Ioannis Konstas, Alessandro Suglia
bullets: Cultural knowledge from underrepresented regions is often poorly recognized in images despite being known textually.
CulturalBind benchmarks 3.2K images covering 1K concepts across 6 domains for cross-modal knowledge and editing evaluation.
Current editing methods can fix individual visual recognition errors but have limited cross-modal portability.
Sequential editing causes rapid performance degradation, revealing weak knowledge consolidation.
The findings motivate more comprehensive methods for sustained multimodal adaptation.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

Uses initial token pruning, then progressively prefills omitted tokens during decode or scheduling gaps.
Supports full-attention and hybrid recurrent models through attention visibility control and affine state mapping.
Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads.
With 30% initial token retention, recovers 77.7% and 60.4% of hard-pruning quality loss on MultiVerse and ConvBench; TTFT falls by up to 24.1% on MultiVerse with under 0.5% TPOT increase.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jins7/LatentWeave.
authors: Fanci Meng, Kun Wang, Guibin Zhang, Xinlei Yu, Jiaming Zhang, Ming Li, Yang Wang
bullets: Targets error accumulation and limited control in autoregressive latent reasoning.

Ablation and efficiency studies separately examine latent optimization, anchor training, and added test-time computation.

papers.abstract: View- and target-specific echocardiography AI models capture useful but complementary information and may not achieve sufficient predictive performance in isolation. A learned ensemble is a natural way to combine these outputs, but heterogeneous models typically require each output to be converted into a binary decision, probability, confidence score, or fixed-length feature vector. We developed a supervised large language model (LLM)-based late-fusion module that directly aggregates view-specific predicted finding statements and predicted measurements in language space and learns a case-level fusion function. In patient-level three-fold cross-validation of 859 examinations from 646 patients, the proposed method integrated heterogeneous outputs within a single framework, performed comparably to the best-performing reference strategy evaluated, and outperformed a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training. These results suggest that a supervised LLM can combine multiple upstream models without model-specific output conversion or feature engineering that requires medical knowledge.

papers.abstract: We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.
authors: Yunhang Shen, Zhangquan Chen, Xiaotian Li, Zhongpeng Cai, Qing Zhou, Zekai Zhang, Kun Zhang, Zezhong Wu, Jian Hu, Haihan Gao, Heting Gao, Xin Li, Yinsong Liu, Deqian Jiang, Di Yin, Haoyu Cao, Xing Sun, Bing Liu, Yanqiu Qu, Yunfei Wu, Kun Yin, Zhixiang Wei, Yongxiang Hua, Qianyu Li, Xiaoxing Hu, Peiyuan Zhang, Lijiang Li, Dong Xu, Zhenchuan Yang, Yiliang Jiang

OSAD uses self-generated rollouts and refreshed reference models for self-evolving post-training.
A single 5B-parameter checkpoint reports leading results on OmniDocBench v1.6 and among open-weight models on OmniParsingBench, especially for audio and video.
It also performs strongly on chart parsing, chemical fingerprints, and typeset sheet-music transcription; code and weights are public.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of omni-modal parsing architectures. We compare how visual and audio inputs are encoded before reaching the language model in the conventional design and in Youtu-Parsing-Omni. (a) Existing omni-modal parsers encode pixels and audio with two separately pre-trained towers, whose streams first meet inside the language model. (b) Youtu-Parsing-Omni replaces both towers with a single encoder, Youtu-Omni-Encoder.
