papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/DawnLIU35/EVAN.git.
authors: Chenxi Liu, Tianyi Xiong, Yanshuo Chen, Heng Huang
bullets: RLVR outcome rewards can miss whether reasoning is grounded in images, allowing language-prior shortcuts.
EVAN identifies visually dependent examples and masks discriminative image patches to generate plausible, ungrounded negative responses.
These negatives are used as bounded auxiliary penalties during policy optimization to suppress shortcut learning while preserving stability.
Experiments on challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks show improved modality balance and performance over strong RLVR baselines.
Scope: the approach targets multimodal reasoning settings where visual evidence is necessary.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to significant progress in visual reasoning capabilities. However, existing benchmarks curate image-question pairs pertaining to object categories with few instances, enabling trivial object referencing and limited visual ambiguity. In this work, we introduce MIMO-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs in a Multi-Instance per Multi-Object categories (MIMO) setting. Each image-question pair in our benchmark pertains to instances belonging to object categories with multiple instances. The presence of such similar feature distractors causes hindrance in basic visual reasoning tasks, necessitating the referring expression to be composed of multiple visual subtasks to uniquely and unambiguously identify the target object. MIMO-Bench comprises 3,802 image-question pairs across attribute binding and numerical counting tasks. Despite impressive performances on existing benchmarks, both SOTA open-source (InternVL, QwenVL) and proprietary (Gemini, GPT-5) models exhibit substantially lower performance on MIMO-Bench, highlighting their limitations in the MIMO setting. The benchmark will be made publicly available.
authors: Saumya Mundra, Ajoy Mondal, Vineeth N Balasubramanian, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Existing visual-reasoning benchmarks often contain few object instances, allowing relatively easy object reference.
MIMO-Bench introduces 3,802 image-question pairs involving multiple instances across multiple object categories.
Tasks cover attribute binding and numerical counting, requiring multi-step referring expressions to disambiguate targets.
Both open-source models such as InternVL and QwenVL and proprietary models such as Gemini and GPT-5 perform substantially worse in this setting.
The benchmark is intended to be publicly available.

papers.abstract: Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task. We find that state-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference, even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses further reveal that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or they overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances. These findings underscore the significant challenges remaining in context-aware multimodal understanding.
authors: Chenyang Yu, Zhaomin Xiao, Yan Huang, Eduardo Blanco
bullets: Introduces duration commonsense reasoning as a task for interpreting human mobility and social context.
Builds a geotagged-tweet corpus co-annotated by humans and LLMs.
Evaluates vision-language models, including with multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Models often miss important context, hashtags, and semantic nuances while overemphasizing salient visual details.
Results highlight persistent challenges in context-aware multimodal understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual rule reasoning asks whether multimodal models can recover an abstract concept from a few examples. Existing studies either infer rules from visual examples but evaluate only classification or verbalization, or supervise executable generation with rules provided as input. Consequently, the relationship between visual rule understanding and reliable rule instantiation remains insufficiently explored. We present Bongard-Forge100k, a controlled benchmark, together with RuleForge, a backbone-agnostic framework that jointly learns visual rule understanding and rule-conditioned executable generation. The benchmark contains 108,797 problems: 86,000 for training, 19,297 for testing familiar rules, and 3,500 for testing held-out rule compositions. The framework progresses through rule-understanding training, joint understanding and scene-program supervision, and refinement via execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay. Executing generated programs under multiple random seeds provides verifiable feedback on executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness. With UniLIP as the primary backbone, RuleForge improves multiple-choice accuracy over the base model by 20.93 percentage points on familiar rules and 28.42 percentage points on held-out rule compositions, while increasing scene-level rule satisfaction on familiar rules from 2.91% to 70.99%. Additional experiments on InternVL3.5, Qwen3-VL, and Show-o2 demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training data and framework across diverse multimodal architectures.
authors: Weifeng Xu, Yaxiong Wang, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Introduces Bongard-Forge100k, a 108,797-problem benchmark covering familiar rules and held-out rule compositions.
Uses staged training: rule understanding, joint understanding with scene-program supervision, and execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay.
Evaluates generated programs through execution across random seeds for executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness.
With UniLIP, improves multiple-choice accuracy by 20.93 points on familiar rules and 28.42 points on held-out compositions.
Raises familiar-rule scene satisfaction from 2.91% to 70.99%; results extend across several multimodal backbones.

papers.abstract: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 537 camera-captured handwriting pages containing about 18.7k words and 163k strokes.

Uses pseudo-label trajectories filtered by OCR agreement and human verification, with IAM-OnDB providing recorded-trajectory evaluation.
Evaluates trajectory fidelity, rendered-stroke readability, and style similarity across four open-source and three closed-source VLMs.
Closed-source models—especially Gemini-3.1-Pro—generate legible trajectories close to references, with the ranking replicated on IAM-OnDB.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.
authors: Lu Wang, Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Existing systems often assume complete information, risking endless waiting or hallucinated answers when video or user intent is unclear.

It includes 438 videos and 2,714 manually annotated frame-level windows labeled wait, ask, or answer.
Models remain substantially challenged: the strongest reported model reaches 52.18% on the Ask-F1 metric.
The benchmark covers both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, emphasizing proactive information seeking.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.
authors: Wenqi Li, Xiangjue Dong, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: On pain-neutral Harvard sentences, where pain is conveyed only through voice, all seven LALMs perform at chance; references and few-shot examples help by at most six balanced-accuracy points.
On spoken pain ratings, models achieve 87.5–99.7% balanced accuracy, suggesting performance depends strongly on task and available linguistic information.
HEAR traces pain information from audio to prediction: pain is decodable in early representations but declines in deeper layers, along with most associated acoustic cues.
Stronger models can perceive large acoustic changes yet still fail to infer pain; reinjecting recovered cues as structured text improves pairwise prediction by up to 32 points.

Table 11: Construction and validation of the audio perturbations. We select ten representative acoustic attributes spanning the four parameter groups across 88 features. Each manipulation aims to shift its target eGeMAPSv02 parameter(s) while leaving parameters of other feature families unchanged (parameters within one family are inherently correlated). Shifts are measured on 24 recordings, each from a different training speaker, as the perturbed recording minus its matching null resynthesis (same tool at zero strength), divided by that parameter’s mean within-speaker SD over the training speakers. Target shift is the median of this shift over the 24 recordings, oriented so that a leading − on a target parameter means it is expected to decrease, and averaged over the target parameters when a cue has several. Range: for each cue and direction, the candidate strength whose Target shift is closest to ±1 SD. Largest off-target feature: the parameter with the largest median absolute shift after excluding the target’s own family (e.g., all F0 parameters for the pitch cues). Its ratio to |Target shift| is flagged when above 0.5 but is only reported, not used for filtering. RMS level is matched to the original recording for every manipulation except Loudness. Filtering. A setting passes calibration if |Target shift| ∈ [0.5, 1.5] and none of the 24 recordings fails processing; passing settings are shown in bold, and non-bold settings are excluded. WORLD could not lower jitter, shimmer or breathiness (Target shift ≈ 0), so these cues were tested in the increase direction only, contrasting a 2× against the 1× strength. Pairs: test recordings (760 in total, from 10 held-out speakers) for which both perturbed versions of a cue were processed successfully; the effect of each bidirectional cue is estimated from the + versus − version of the same recording. Cues marked † were excluded from the analysis because more than 5% of their 1×/2× pairs showed no achieved change in the target parameter (jitter 10.0%, shimmer 8.9%, breathiness 9.3%). In total we generated 18,240 test-set versions for the 17 passing settings and 7 null resyntheses (4 failed, all Pauses), 2,280 2× WORLD versions, and 4,560 round-trip null resyntheses for the PSOLA and speech-rate cues. a Each sample is multiplied by (e/ẽ)k−1, where e is the smoothed Hilbert envelope, ẽ its median and k the exponent; k > 1 exaggerates and k < 1 flattens loudness fluctuations. b Non-speech stretches detected by WebRTC VAD are resampled to the given multiple of their length; speech is left unchanged. c One of the 24 calibration recordings also failed processing. d 760 minus 4 recordings whose perturbation failed and 1 recording whose + and − versions had identical target values.

papers.selection_reason: Studies audio large language models as multimodal systems and traces acoustic information through their reasoning.
papers.title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: Current audio LLMs encode pain-related vocal cues early, but largely fail to use them for pain reasoning and prediction.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
authors: Yu Liu, Youxing Li, Yuedong Tan, Zhiwei Yang, Zihan Su, Hanqi Feng, Shaojie Zhang, Libin Liao, Zihao Wan, Chenxu Wu, Cong Cao, Fangfang Yuan, Yanbing Liu, Ziheng Chen, Pei Fu, Radu Timofte, Zongwei Wu, Nicu Sebe, Barnabas Poczos, Jian Luan
bullets: Addresses when to introduce fresh experience, complementing methods that focus on what experience to generate.
Uses reward variation and training accuracy to detect declining learning signals without validation or test scores.
Generates multimodal questions from a static library of model-authored programs with independently checkable answers.
Automatically verifies task properties and refresh rules, while separately auditing generated answers.
Raises average performance from 57.77 to 61.05 using 800 fresh tasks.

papers.abstract: The large-scale digitisation of medieval manuscripts creates a growing need for automated iconographic indexing. We evaluate two complementary paradigms for this task on 9,735 full-folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts: generative Vision-Language Models (VLM) and supervised discriminative classifiers (SDC). The VLM experiments evaluate fine-tuning, structured JSON decoding, taxonomybased candidates generation, and deterministic reranking. The discriminative experiments evaluate flat, hierarchy-aware, and patch-attention heads over a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Our results highlight key functional differences: ML-Decoder (SDC) achieves the strongest overall retrieval performance (precision@1 of 0.696, MRR of 0.806), with loss calibration (Asymmetric Loss) serving as the primary performance lever. While SDCs provide superior precision and reliability within a closed vocabulary, VLMs offer strong semantic generalization and broad taxonomic coverage, particularly through structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking (hierarchical F1 of 0.559). Furthermore, model behavior strongly depends on concept abstraction: SDCs excel at perceptually grounded descriptive concepts, whereas VLMs provide useful hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes. Finally, we find that enforcing explicit hierarchy within model architectures limits coverage compared to spatial feature aggregation. Overall, rather than competing approaches, SDCs and VLMs emerge as complementary components for future hybrid indexing systems combining structured retrieval with exploratory annotation assistance. As a methodological contribution, we define the soft F1 metric to provide a taxonomy-aware evaluation that credits semantically close predictions based on lowest common ancestors.
authors: Vincent Jolivet (ENC, CJM), Lucas Terriel (ENC), Chahan Vidal-Gor{\`e}ne (CJM, ENC)
bullets: Evaluates generative VLMs and supervised discriminative classifiers on 9,735 folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts.
ML-Decoder achieves the strongest retrieval performance, with precision@1 of 0.696 and MRR of 0.806; Asymmetric Loss is the main performance lever.
VLMs show broader taxonomic coverage and semantic generalization, especially with structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking.
Classifiers perform best on perceptually grounded concepts, whereas VLMs better support hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes.
The approaches are complementary: the study proposes hybrid systems and introduces taxonomy-aware soft F1 evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: VLM pipeline for TIMEL classification. All strategies share one backbone(Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, full SFT; a QLoRA Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline reported separately)and diverge only at three stages. Four output-encoding families differ in target representation and decoding constraint: (A) flat French labels, optionally trie-constrained (V5); (B) opaque tm-xxxx identifiers (V4, abandoned); (C) explicit root-to-leaf pathswith trie, minimum-label and beam constraints (V6/V6.1 and the staged HCoT variant V7); (D)the retained categorised-JSON target (V9), a bare TRL SFTTrainer decoded greedily. Predic-tions are parsed to a flat leaf set, optionally refined by post-processing (consistency, semantic/self-embedding remap, multimodal LLM-judge), then scored. The TIMEL taxonomy supplies trie pre-fixes (A-V5, C), JSON category keys and the consistency filter (D), and the ancestor sets used bythe hierarchical metrics.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs), which can process and generate diverse modalities within a single framework, have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, when these models undergo continual learning on multiple tasks across different modalities, their learning and forgetting dynamics remain poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Specifically, we report three findings. First, the severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. Second, a within-model asymmetry: the generation side of a UMM is markedly more fragile than its understanding side. Third, what post-training adds is the first to be forgotten: purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84\% to 90\%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable. Together, these results clarify how parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape UMMs' learning and forgetting dynamics, offering a starting point for developing continually evolving UMMs.
authors: Xinrui Wang, Zhihao Chen, Jia Tang, Alexandra Gomez-Villa, Bartlomiej Twardowski, Joost van de Weijer, Songcan Chen
bullets: Greater modality-specific parameter isolation reduces cross-modal interference.
The generation side is substantially more fragile than the understanding side.
Post-training capabilities, such as personalized generation, are forgotten first, while pretrained capabilities remain stable.
The findings provide design guidance for building continually adapting multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's $\rho \leq 0.42$ ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's $\rho > 0.9$ ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.

bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized tasks, training data, and fine-grained evaluation for generating interleaved text and images.

The suite shows low redundancy between metrics, 83.3% agreement with human judgments, and strong consistency across expert evaluators.
Benchmarking four UMM families reveals distinct capability profiles; post-training with IntReal-100K improves interleaved generation.
Results suggest modality-specific optimization can benefit interleaved generation without joint text-image training at every stage.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show strong performance in radiology report generation (RRG) and medical visual question answering (Med-VQA), producing free-form clinical descriptions and answers from medical images. However, they may generate clinically meaningful statements that lack visual evidence or contradict image content. We refer to these errors as visually irrelevant hallucinations and investigate them at the phrase level. We propose CLEAR (Counterfactual Localized Evaluation of Alignment and Response), a model-agnostic post-hoc framework for phrase-level hallucination risk estimation. CLEAR decomposes generated responses into visually assessable clinical phrases. For each phrase, phrase-conditioned grounding identifies a candidate visual region, which is selectively perturbed by a localized counterfactual intervention. CLEAR characterizes the intervention using two complementary auditing cues: response cues, capturing semantic and clinically meaningful changes in the generated response, and alignment cues, measuring changes in image-phrase compatibility. These cues are normalized and jointly modeled to estimate phrase-level hallucination risk. Across four datasets spanning RRG and Med-VQA, CLEAR outperforms state-of-the-art hallucination detection baselines across multiple medical and general-purpose VLMs. On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR improves AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23%. Its effectiveness is further validated on a GT-derived controlled VIH benchmark. These results establish visually irrelevant hallucination as an important fine-grained reliability failure mode in medical VLMs and demonstrate the value of model-agnostic visual-support auditing for more trustworthy multimodal clinical generation.
authors: Ke Zou, Nan Zhou, Tao Yang, Meng Liu, Linchao He, Zehui Liao, Ling Huang, Guangren Huang, Yidi Chen, Yi Zhang, Hu Chen, Huazhu Fu
bullets: Medical VLMs can produce clinically meaningful statements that are visually unsupported or contradict the image.
CLEAR is a model-agnostic, post-hoc framework that decomposes outputs into visually assessable phrases.
It grounds each phrase to a candidate region, perturbs that region, and combines response-change and image–phrase alignment cues to estimate hallucination risk.
Across four radiology report generation and Med-VQA datasets, CLEAR outperforms existing detection baselines across multiple VLMs.
On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR raises AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23% and is additionally validated on a controlled benchmark.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

Uses Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization to reward response format, intermediate reasoning fields, and final syndrome predictions.
Fu-TCM-27B achieved a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% across six benchmarks, leading all evaluated benchmarks.
Case analyses found that more accurate intermediate reasoning fields were generally associated with better final syndrome selection.

papers.abstract: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.
bullets: Targets prompts to like, follow, join private groups, or click external links that may lead to fraud.
Combines OCR with a multimodal LLM for joint discrimination and temporal grounding of textual and visual cues.
Evaluates OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a zero-shot MLLM across detection, latency, token use, and deployment complexity.
Uses a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling after finding reward hacking and detection–localization trade-offs.
On 2,419 annotated videos, OCR+MLLM raises mIoU to 26.52 versus 14.49 for keyframe OCR+LLM and detects non-textual inducements missed by text-only methods.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

bullets: Super has 120B total and 12B active parameters with multimodal capabilities; Lightning has 30B total and 3B active parameters for text.
Training combines distillation, long-context training, speculative decoding, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning; Super also uses Indic and software-engineering mid-training.
Super supports reasoning across text, images, video, and interactive tools, with parallel-agent execution and self-verification for test-time scaling.
Reported results include up to 9.82-point gains on Indian-language benchmarks, 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, and up to 21.8% longer speculative-decoding acceptance.
Deployment techniques include MTP boosting and NVFP4 quantization, with up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.selection_reason: Open MoE hybrid Mamba-Transformer LLMs with long-context training, multimodal capabilities, and efficient deployment.
papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
papers.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning are open hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE models optimized for efficient reasoning, long-context, multimodal, and agentic AI workloads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ground language in visual evidence, yet their semantic reasoning can be exploited through transferable black-box adversarial attacks. Existing attacks typically allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions. We introduce VISTA (Vulnerability-Informed Semantic Transfer Attacks), a black-box framework that identifies semantically vulnerable visual regions from an MLLM's responses without access to gradients, logits, parameters, or internal representations. VISTA supports two attack settings: (i) VISTA-Proxy, a pure-transfer setting that probes an open-source MLLM and transfers the resulting adversarial examples to unseen commercial MLLMs without querying them; and (ii) VISTA-Victim, a query-assisted setting that probes the target MLLM to capture model-specific semantic vulnerabilities. VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts, then uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97 % attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 30 dB. Notably, VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93 % ASR without querying the final victim, demonstrating that response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between surrogate-model saliency and how unseen MLLMs actually interpret visual regions.
Builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts.
Uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing with a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions.
Supports pure-transfer VISTA-Proxy and query-assisted VISTA-Victim attack settings.
Reports up to 97% ASR with PSNR above 30 dB; VISTA-Proxy reaches up to 93% ASR without querying the final victim across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.

papers.abstract: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ
bullets: Quantization error is not a reliable predictor of semantic fidelity; larger-error discrete representations can perform better.
Effective bit budget, rather than quantization error alone, is a key driver of downstream understanding.
Existing quantizers saturate as added codebooks provide diminishing semantic information.
Factorized Vector Quantization uses complementary fixed-dimensional feature views with symmetric parallel codebooks to reduce this saturation.
The resulting model matches continuous-representation performance, including fine-grained OCR, and reports strong gains over prior discrete-representation models.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of FVQ. During quantizer training, multiple dense projections produce complementary views of the same visual feature, which are quantized in parallel by independent codebooks. The selected codewords are combined through tight-frame synthesis for feature reconstruction. In the subsequent VLM training stage, the quantizer is frozen, and only the resulting discrete indices are mapped to newly initialized token embeddings for multimodal understanding. The nine-metric average is computed over MMMU, MathVista, MMStar, OCRBench/10, ChartQA, CharXiv-DQ, CharXiv-RQ, DocVQA, and InfoVQA.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Tongkun Guan, Zhibo Yang, Mingkun Yang, Haocheng Wang, Wei Shen, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Targets perception degradation during MLLM post-training, where subjective dense captions make reliable rewards difficult.
Perception RL converts verified caption errors into fixed-label QA pairs with rule-based rewards, using chain and multiple-choice formats.
Perception Agentic RL handles unresolved dense cases through multi-turn tool use, with Coordinate Injection and grounding-aware process rewards to reduce spatial errors.
Uses shared cold-start SFT followed by single-turn and multi-turn perception RL.
Achieves 71.6% average accuracy across seven benchmarks, exceeding the same-tool base model by 15.7 points and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 5.2 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Perception RL: from perceptual errors to rewardable QA. (01) Perception tree construction: A hierarchical capability map and model probing reveal perceptual weaknesses, guiding specialized and general data-construction routes. Appendix ?? expands the displayed tree with additional skills and associated failure modes. (02) Rewardable QA construction: A multi-agent pipeline mines and verifies errors in the base model’s captions, then composes them into questions with unambiguous answers. MCQs combine unrelated errors, while chain QA connects correlated errors. (03) Rule-based reward for RL: The resulting QA pairs provide exact-match rewards for training the model’s visual perception. The error distribution and example errors are illustrative.

Fig. 1: PERCEPTRL: making real-world perception rewardable, and training it at two levels. Center: How it becomes rewardable. Open-ended captions contain useful perceptual information but are difficult to score with direct rule-based rewards. We extract and verify perceptual facts from these captions, then formulate QA pairs with fixed answer labels for rule-based training (top). The pipeline organizes tasks from multiple perception families (e.g., color, spatial position, counting, functional state, orientation), using a perception tree to guide data construction (Section 3.2). The difficulty axis is what divides the two levels. Level 1: Perception RL. A single look suffices here, so we train single-turn visual QA under a rule-based outcome reward. The left panel shows what this must fix: an error entering at the perception level is inherited by an otherwise correct reasoning chain, so the answer is wrong for a purely perceptual reason. Level 2: Perception Agentic RL. This tail, where objects are small, scenes are cluttered, or details require magnification, resists a single look, so the model inspects the image over multiple grounded turns with a code interpreter. The right panel illustrates how a grounding error, where a predicted crop or annotation misses its target, can affect subsequent observations. Its propagation and accumulation across successive tool interactions constitute coordinate drift. Coordinate Injection corrects these grounding errors during data construction, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity (Section 3.3).

Fig. 3: Perception Agentic RL: correcting and supervising spatial grounding during multi-turn visual inspection. (01) Coordinate drift. A misplaced annotation changes the visual evidence available to later turns. Subsequent spatial operations can inherit this error, leading to repeated or missed counts. (02) Coordinate Injection (CI). During trajectory construction, CI identifies the intended target of each spatial operation, corrects its coordinates using a VLM judge or the LocateAnything detector, and re-executes the code before the next turn. The corrected trajectories provide cold-start SFT data. (03) Grounding-aware process reward. During RL, a fidelity judge evaluates the predicted boxes and points against their intended targets in the original image. The resulting per-turn rewards complement the final-answer reward and supervise intermediate spatial accuracy (Equation 17).

TABLE 3: Perception training QA across domains. Singleturn QA is the full pool used for Perception RL (Level 1). Agentic QA is a strict subset selected from this pool after Level-1 training: the trained model generates eight rollouts per query, and queries with empirical accuracy < 5/8 are retained for Perception Agentic RL (Level 2).

papers.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
papers.tldr: PerceptRL improves fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs by turning verified caption errors into rewardable QA tasks and training multi-turn visual inspection with grounding-aware feedback.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) to solve complex visual problems, but also exposes them to CoT hijacking: an adversary implants a backdoor through poisoned fine-tuning so that a visual trigger induces a hijacking turn, redirecting an otherwise faithful reasoning chain to an attacker-chosen answer. However, since the hijack acts within the reasoning chain, existing multimodal backdoor defenses designed for MLLMs that answer directly struggle to detect it. Moreover, inspecting the chain itself does not reliably expose the hijack, since the hijacking turn can resemble honest self-correction in form. In this paper, we find that honest reasoning tends to revise its answer at high-entropy "aha moments", whereas a hijack can overturn a confident answer through a near-deterministic turn. To quantify this contrast, we formalize this phenomenon as belief inertia, the cumulative next-token entropy of a reasoning span minus the answer-belief revision it induces, with markedly lower values for hijacked spans than for honest reasoning spans. Since hijacking tokens are also image-dependent, we further improve detection by restricting the measure to image-dependent spans, yielding visual belief inertia (VBI). Building on this, we propose InertiaGuard, a training-free, test-time detector that flags a trace when its VBI falls below a threshold calibrated on a small set of clean traces. Across various attacks and benchmarks, InertiaGuard achieves higher detection performance than existing baselines, while generalizing to different model architectures and trigger types.
bullets: CoT hijacking redirects a model’s reasoning and answer after an attacker implants a backdoor triggered by an image.
Existing defenses struggle because hijacks occur inside reasoning chains and can resemble honest self-correction.
The paper defines belief inertia as reasoning-span token entropy minus the resulting answer-belief revision.
Visual belief inertia (VBI) focuses this measure on image-dependent spans, improving sensitivity to visual hijacks.
InertiaGuard is a training-free, test-time detector calibrated on a small set of clean traces and performs better than existing baselines across attacks, benchmarks, architectures, and trigger types.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT hijacking combines low belief inertia with strong image dependence. Each dot is a reasoning step (gray: clean; red: hijacking) sampled from a validation set. (a, b) Hijacking steps induce large belief revisions B at low entropy cost H , resulting in lower belief inertia than clean reasoning. (c, d) Because hijacking steps also exhibit strong image dependence, adding this criterion filters out most low-inertia clean steps while retaining hijacking steps.

Figure 2: Illustration of INERTIAGUARD. Although the model initially recognizes the stop sign, a trigger-induced hijacking turn redirects its answer from (b) to (a). To detect this redirection, INERTIAGUARD first identifies image-dependent steps, then compares the belief revision across spans containing these steps with their cumulative entropy. Because the hijacking span induces a large revision at little entropy cost, its belief inertia falls below the calibrated threshold, causing the trace to be flagged.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes InertiaGuard, a test-time detector for backdoored multimodal reasoning models, utilizing 'visual belief inertia' (VBI) to identify hijacking turns based on entropy differences in reasoning chains.
papers.title: Detecting Chain-of-Thought Hijacking in Backdoored Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: InertiaGuard detects visual trigger-induced chain-of-thought hijacking by identifying unusually deterministic answer revisions in multimodal reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are deployed as zero-shot judges of image aesthetics, and panels of several models are recommended, on thin evidence, as the way to make such judges reliable. On two human-rated datasets, EVA and PARA, we find that a panel of holistic judges never significantly beats its best member, whether the verdicts are averaged or fused by a learned combiner. What a panel is worth depends on what it is fed. We therefore have each model score each image on the five dimensions of a frozen, human-written rubric and fuse those scores, alongside each model's verdict, across model families with an out-of-fold combiner. The dimension scores measure what their labels claim: with the overall human score partialled out, a dimension prompt carries more attribute-specific information than the holistic prompt in 28 of 30 model-attribute cells. Fused, they beat the best single VLM in all ten three-family panels on EVA (against that best single model, +0.07 Spearman rho for the strongest trio and +0.10 for the pre-declared one, and +0.06 and +0.07 when averaged over twenty fold partitions; against the panel mean, the primary test gives +0.118 on its EVA design set), and on PARA they reach parity under Spearman rho and a small, non-significant loss under Kendall tau-b, where one model already captures 85% of the human noise ceiling. It is not a feature-count artefact: giving the same combiner an equal number of pure holistic columns, split from the same repetitions, does not reproduce it. The gain costs a few hundred labels, which do not transfer between datasets, and 4.8x the API calls on EVA; we report it with paired bootstraps and Kendall tau-b, alongside a failed pre-registration and the configurations that lost.
bullets: Holistic judge panels never significantly outperform their best member on EVA or PARA.
Models score five frozen, human-written rubric dimensions, and an out-of-fold combiner fuses these scores with holistic verdicts across model families.
Dimension prompts provide more attribute-specific information than holistic prompts in 28 of 30 model–attribute comparisons.
Dimension-aware fusion beats the best single VLM across all ten EVA three-family panels, while reaching parity or a small non-significant loss on PARA.
The approach requires a few hundred dataset-specific labels and 4.8× more EVA API calls; labels do not transfer between datasets.

papers.title: Feed the Panel Dimensions, Not Verdicts: Rubric-Decomposed Fusion of Vision-Language Aesthetic Judges

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
authors: Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang, Shilei Wen
bullets: Addresses the weakness of language-only reasoning traces, which can lose access to relevant video evidence.
Constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments instead of relying only on coordinates or pasted crops and frames.
Uses visual token prediction over an input-video-derived vocabulary to unify visual reconstruction and text generation.
Supports interleaved text and visual latent states, with a reinforcement-learning extension that jointly optimizes visual and text token actions.
Improves performance across multiple video benchmarks, particularly on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

papers.abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.
authors: Ananth K Suresh, Aveen Dayal, Gouthaman KV, Aditya Pola, Vineeth N Balasubramanian
bullets: Refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with effects that vary across individual samples and models.

Supervised and preference-based post-training increase refusal more strongly, but may produce responses that refuse while still attempting an answer.
Intervening on a refusal-related activation direction yields smaller but transferable changes across prompts without indiscriminate refusal on tested answerable images.
The study evaluates three MLLMs on MoHoBench and emphasizes separating evidence recognition from general refusal tendencies.

papers.abstract: When a multimodal model computes 17+35 from text or 91-39 from a rendered image, it produces the same answer, 52. Does it use one internal concept of number for both, or separate machinery for each path? Similarity metrics such as RSA or CKA cannot settle this question. They give the same score to identical and to rotated directions, and two representations can look alike only because both prepare the same output digits. We therefore use causal interventions. For four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction), we learn a small subspace of Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream in which swapping coordinates swaps the model's answer. The subspaces answer three questions. First, do the conditions write numbers along the same directions? They do not. Reusing a subspace from text in an image on the same operation recovers only 53.2% of its causal effect. A single rotation and rescaling maps one subspace onto the other and raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinates. Second, does this shared geometry only reflect the digit the model is about to print? To test this, we split each subspace into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions that it cannot see. The 13 hidden directions still carry the number, yet changing them barely alters the digit being written. Third, what are these hidden directions for? A model must emit a multi-digit answer one digit at a time, so it can compute the full result early and keep it in reserve. When two numbers share their first digit, swapping the number in the hidden directions leaves the digit being written intact and redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases. The model thus forms an abstract numerical concept upstream and unfolds it across time: multimodal representations share meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames.
authors: Oriol Juan Sabater, Alex Ferrando de las Morenas, Pau Rodr\'iguez, Xavier Suau
bullets: Text and image arithmetic use distinct subspaces, but a learned rotation and rescaling aligns them, recovering 91.4% of the causal effect.
Similarity measures alone cannot distinguish shared numerical concepts from representations that merely support the same output digits.
Numerical information exists in hidden directions not directly read by the output layer, beyond the directions controlling the next digit.
Swapping hidden numerical states redirects later digits in 77.6% of cases while preserving the current digit, indicating early computation of the full answer.
The evidence is limited to four conditions: text/image inputs paired with addition/subtraction in Gemma4-12B-it.

papers.abstract: This report presents the implementation and validation of two end-to-end multimodal adaptation pipelines for 3D-aware visual question answering on a custom spatial dataset. The first pipeline fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B, which augments RGB observations with metric-scale 3D point maps; the second adapts Qwen3-VL through memory-efficient QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The completed engineering stack covers dataset conversion, image-annotation alignment, monocular geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpoint management, batch inference, and automated evaluation. On the target spatial benchmark, HiSpatial adaptation increases overall accuracy from 1.73% before fine-tuning to 79.89% at 3,600 steps. On a separately collected styled split, accuracy improves from 14.9% to 55.1%, indicating transfer beyond the original training set. The Qwen3-VL pipeline is likewise implemented end-to-end for both 8B- and 32B-scale models using mixed-domain QLoRA adaptation. The resulting accuracy improves from 20.74% to 45.27% for Qwen3-VL-8B and from 30.79% to 47.60% for Qwen3-VL-32B. Together, these results establish two complementary and reproducible adaptation pipelines for geometry-aware and general-purpose multimodal spatial reasoning. These results establish a reproducible engineering foundation for subsequent work on metric 3D reasoning, spatial grounding, and domain-adapted multimodal systems, while also identifying training-data composition as a central factor in preserving general multimodal capability during specialization.
authors: Yu Zhang, Xiaogang Wang, Yuhang Cheng, Jingrui Li, Wenbo Chen

The engineering stack includes data conversion and alignment, geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpointing, inference, and automated evaluation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). Despite its empirical effectiveness, we show that outcome-level optimization can introduce an undesirable shortcut amplification effect, whereby models increasingly favor text-prior answers even when they are not supported by the visual evidence. To characterize this behavior, we investigate the training dynamics of video RLVR through the lens of perceptual uncertainty, analyzing how predictive uncertainty evolves under video-conditioned and text-only contexts. Our analysis identifies a perceptual uncertainty collapse phenomenon, in which RL training continuously sharpens the model's answer distribution while the uncertainty reduction attributable to visual evidence progressively diminishes. A further gradient-direction analysis reveals that such confidence enhancement becomes increasingly less aligned with visually grounded uncertainty reduction and is instead dominated by text-prior compression. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bifocal Self-distillation Policy Optimization (BSPO), a self-distillation framework that regulates policy updates with two complementary distributional signals. Specifically, BSPO derives empirical reasoning principles from intra-group correct and incorrect rollouts to identify reasoning-sensitive tokens, and introduces shortcut-aware visual perturbation to penalize predictions that remain invariant when task-relevant visual evidence is weakened. By adaptively reweighting the original RL advantage, BSPO preserves the task-solving benefits of RLVR while promoting updates that are both reasoning-sensitive and visually grounded. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of BSPO in improving video reasoning performance and strengthening visual faithfulness.
authors: Jiafeng Liang, Xianhao Ou, Tao Ren, Rongchuan Mu, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Bing Qin
bullets: RLVR may make models increasingly confident in text-prior answers unsupported by video evidence.
Perceptual uncertainty collapse occurs as visual evidence contributes less to uncertainty reduction during training.
Gradient analysis links this confidence growth more to text-prior compression than to visual grounding.
BSPO combines self-distillation from correct/incorrect rollouts with shortcut-aware visual perturbations to guide policy updates.
Experiments show improved video reasoning performance and stronger visual faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu

papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning. Driven by carefully designed local quality assessment reward functions, our model exhibits exceptional image quality understanding on VGSR-2K, a new dataset we propose specifically for local quality evaluation, significantly outperforming existing open-source MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Furthermore, the local quality evaluation task can effectively enhance the model's performance on the degradation perception task.
authors: Weichang Wang, Liyu Chen, Shuyue Guan, Jie Hu, Fei Gao, Wei Li, Nannan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing MLLM-based IQA methods that mainly provide holistic, image-level evaluations.
Uses a two-stage training strategy: cold-start training followed by reinforcement learning with local quality assessment rewards.
Introduces VGSR-2K, a dataset designed for local image-quality evaluation.
Reports strong local quality understanding and outperformance of the compared open-source MLLMs on VGSR-2K.
Finds that local quality assessment also improves degradation perception.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the proposed VGIQA framework. The framework follows a two-stage training paradigm. Stage 1 (Cold Start): The Qwen-based foundation model is initialized via SFT using CoT reasoning data distilled from Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] to establish structural formatting and inject IQA priors. Stage 2 (Multi-Task GRPO): Reinforcement learning jointly optimizes Local Quality Assessment, Degradation Perception, and Score Regression. Alongside a shared format reward, task-specific rewards are dynamically routed: a dedicated local reward exclusively supervises the local task (computing zero for non-local tasks), evaluating spatial bounding boxes via Hungarian Matching, negative DIoU, and F1 Score. Meanwhile, global tasks are optimized via verifiable score and classification/intensity rewards, unifying local-and-global quality evaluation.

Fig. 4: Overview of the VGSR-2K dataset construction pipeline. The dataset is curated via a rigorous human-in-the-loop pipeline. (1) Candidate Generation: Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] and Seed1.6-VL independently process LR-SR image pairs, yielding six candidate spatial bounding boxes. (2) Double-Blind Selection: Two annotator groups select the most consistent candidate; consensus establishes the baseline, while divergence prompts expert resolution. (3) Double-Blind Correction & Merging: Annotators refine baselines by adding or removing boxes. Corrections are merged via the Hungarian algorithm with a negative DIoU cost metric, extracting the MBR for matched pairs. (4) Final Review & Balancing: After expert review, pristine LR-HR image pairs are introduced as negative samples (with empty annotations) to calibrate spatial predictions and prevent trivial over-generation.

Fig. 2: Example applications of the proposed VGIQA framework. Built upon a Qwen-based foundation model, VGIQA achieves comprehensive quality understanding via multi-task reinforcement learning. While existing models (e.g., Q-Insight) are limited to holistic Score Regression and Degradation Perception, VGIQA explicitly bridges the gap in fine-grained Local Quality Assessment. Driven by novel visual grounding rewards, it adopts a rigorous "look and then judge" paradigm—precisely localizing spatial artifacts before formulating final judgments.

Fig. 1: Qualitative visualization of the local quality assessment results. Given a reference image, a distorted image to be evaluated, and a user query, VGIQA produces more reliable and accurate responses compared with the state-of-the-art RL-based IQA method Q-insight and the general large vision-language model Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct [1].

papers.abstract: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
authors: Saifullah Saifullah, David Dembinsky, Stefan Agne, Andreas Dengel, Sheraz Ahmed
bullets: Addresses the limited XAI research for models combining document text, layout, and images, especially in high-stakes applications.
Adapts existing XAI methods and metrics to multimodal documents and develops efficient multi-target variants for tasks such as semantic entity recognition.
Systematically evaluates 13 XAI methods across 3 tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 metrics.
Finds that only a few methods perform consistently across evaluation criteria; Occlusion performs best overall.
Diagnostic analyses reveal modality contributions, spatial attribution patterns, and potential dataset biases; code is publicly released.

papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming in is a common training-free remedy. However, most existing zooming pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally and never revisit a wrong answer. To address these issues, we propose AdaGround, a training-free framework with three components: (1) Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming, which sets the magnification, field of view and zoom depth of each sample from the model's own estimate of the target size; (2) Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement, which uses one marked-click Yes/No verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding and, with an existence query, decide when to abstain; and (3) Compositional Structure Grounding, which composes spreadsheet cells from their headers. On Qwen3-VL models, AdaGround surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, and its gains carry over to held-out UI-Vision. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/AdaGround
authors: Bingchao Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Chengyu Wang, Jun Huang, Jie Yang, Wei Liu, Dacheng Tao

On Qwen3-VL, improves over the backbone by 7.4–20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, with gains transferring to held-out UI-Vision.
