papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to ground generated text in the correct image regions, and existing explainability methods, such as attention maps and Logit Lens, often produce poor spatial explanations due to weak text-to-vision attention and sink tokens. We propose \textbf{Angular Relevance} ($R_L$), a simple visualization measure based on cosine similarity between visual token embeddings and unembedding-matrix rows. Because $R_L$ is invariant to token norm, it produces substantially sharper and more faithful heatmaps than attention maps or Logit Lens on out-of-the-box models. Without any training, $R_L$ yields competitive referring-expression segmentation (RES), outperforming prior diagnostic maps and CLIP-based training-free methods. To preserve localized object information during cross-modal mixing, we introduce \textbf{Angular Object-Aware Loss (AOL)}, an auxiliary loss that directly supervises visual token embeddings to align angularly with the vocabulary directions of their corresponding object concepts. Finetuning with AOL alongside the standard next-token prediction objective significantly sharpens object localization in heatmaps, showing that the VLM's own visual tokens can be used directly for grounding and improving RES, without training any segmentation heads and without degrading general VQA performance. We further demonstrate that the learned grounding also transfers to category-level segmentation of object categories not seen during training.
bullets: Addresses weak text-to-image grounding and poor spatial explanations from attention maps and Logit Lens.
Introduces Angular Relevance, a cosine-similarity measure between visual token embeddings and vocabulary unembedding directions.
Uses Angular Object-Aware Loss to supervise visual tokens toward the vocabulary directions of corresponding object concepts.
Achieves competitive referring-expression segmentation without training and improves localization after finetuning with AOL.
Grounding transfers to unseen object categories for category-level segmentation; scope is demonstrated in autoregressive VLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual grounding in autoregressive VLMs via angular supervision and auxiliary loss; directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Angular Supervision for Visual Object Grounding in Autoregressive Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Angular Relevance enables sharper, training-free visual grounding, while Angular Object-Aware Loss improves object localization and segmentation in autoregressive VLMs without adding segmentation heads or harming VQA.

papers.abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Junxin Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Xiangchen Song, Weiqiao Shan, Runsong Zhao, Xinyu Liu, Shunjie Xing, Yifu Huo, Dingyang Lin, Qiuyu Gu, Yongyu Mu, Chenglong Wang, Changliang Li, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the underweighting of high-entropy, low-visual-dependency tokens in prior advantage-reshaping methods.
Uses visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain selectively at high-entropy positions.
Maps the combined signal to positive token-level weights for reshaping sequence-level advantages.
Evaluated on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, PEAR achieves the highest average performance among tested baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Also reports leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves perception and exploration in large vision-language models via adaptive advantage reshaping.
papers.title: PEAR: Adaptive Advantage Reshaping for Perception and Exploration in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: PEAR improves multimodal reasoning by adaptively boosting high-entropy tokens that have low visual dependency, encouraging both better perception and broader exploration.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.
authors: Xiutian Zhao, Luqi Sun, Bj\"orn Schuller, Berrak Sisman
bullets: The study identifies cognitive-impairment contrast neurons (CICNs) in decoder MLPs across eight open LALMs using two speech corpora.
Ablating small CICN sets produces large, class-directed prediction shifts in 3 of 5 eligible models, including transcript-only decisions.
Interventions localize influence before the final answer position, especially after speech or transcript evidence, mainly by shifting decision direction.
Frozen CICN activations support strong within-Pitt linear readouts (0.92–0.97 AUC), but matched random and all-neuron readouts perform similarly.
Findings separate concentrated causal control of outputs from broadly distributed information useful for CI detection; CICN unit-budget advantages remain exploratory.
papers.selection_reason: Causal interpretability of large audio-language models fits multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Concentrated Causal Influence, Distributed Diagnostic Information: Cognitive Impairment Decisions in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: In LALMs, a small set of neurons can causally steer cognitive-impairment decisions, while diagnostic information is broadly distributed across representations.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces Sense-Aligned Grounding Evaluation (SAGE), a unified 10-candidate image-selection benchmark that reformulates VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse into a shared term-centric protocol covering noun-, verb-, and entity-centered grounding. SAGE includes confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to probe target-term grounding beyond direct caption--image compatibility. We further propose Gloss-Augmented Reasoning (GAR), a training-free framework combining definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification. Experiments show that strong VWSD performance does not transfer uniformly across grounding settings. With Gemma3-12B, definition augmentation improves all three subsets, while constraint-guided reasoning improves VWSD and yields particularly strong gains on VerSe, but is less effective on WikiDiverse. Combining the two signals achieves the best macro-average performance, improving Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22. These results show that SAGE supports both unified evaluation and fine-grained analysis of explicit semantic reasoning across grounding settings.
authors: Sunjae Kwon, Suhaas Kiran DG, Zonghai Yao, Talha Chafekar, Deepali Singh, Hong Yu
bullets: Recasts VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse as a shared 10-candidate, term-centric benchmark covering nouns, verbs, and entities.
Adds confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to test grounding beyond direct caption–image matching.
Introduces GAR, a training-free approach that combines gloss/definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification.
Definition augmentation helps across all subsets; constraint-guided reasoning helps VWSD and especially VerSe but is less effective on WikiDiverse.
Combining both signals raises Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22 with Gemma3-12B and provides the best macro-average performance.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a unified multimodal grounding benchmark and training-free gloss-augmented reasoning framework for multimodal large language models.
papers.title: SAGE: Sense-Aligned Multimodal Grounding Evaluation with Gloss-Augmented Reasoning
papers.tldr: SAGE unifies multimodal grounding evaluation across senses and shows that combining definition grounding with constraint-guided reasoning improves performance, though gains vary by grounding setting.

papers.abstract: A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director's choices and the casters' commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.
authors: Zixian Gao, Lixin Xiu, Penghao Luo, Xiangcheng Cao, Ziqi Cai, Zhen Li, Erwin Wu, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses live broadcast production from raw player-camera feeds, without access to future events or a pre-directed broadcast.
Scans all cameras at low resolution each second, uses a hold-or-switch policy, then views the selected camera at high resolution before speaking.
Maintains only aired visuals, commentary, and recent context while allowing other views to expire, keeping processing cost bounded over arbitrarily long streams.
Introduces a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with per-hero cameras, director choices, and caster commentary.
Outperforms rule-based and zero-shot directors, including GPT-5; its commentary wins 29.2% of Proact-VL comparisons against GPT-4o.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video-language model for live esports directing and commentary; fits video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: DirCast: Live Esports Directing and Commentary with a Single Streaming Video-Language Model
papers.tldr: DirCast is a streaming video-language model that jointly selects live esports camera views and generates commentary using only past observations.

papers.abstract: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
authors: Junhao Wang, Yidou Chen, Li Lu, Hongwei Yao, Xiaodan Li, Mengjie Wu, Yuefeng Chen, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren
bullets: Evaluates omni-modal guardrails across safety, utility, and reliability.
Covers over 183k samples from 35+ sources across text, image, audio, video, and cross-modal inputs.
Benchmarks 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails under a unified safety-risk taxonomy.
Finds that OLLMs can moderate content effectively without guardrail-specific tuning, but guardrails struggle with concealed harmful intent and sophisticated jailbreaks.
Reveals limited cross-modal safety understanding, including safety hallucination and over-reliance on textual patterns.
papers.selection_reason: Comprehensive safety benchmark for omni-modal LLMs and guardrails, relevant to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability
papers.tldr: Omni-UBench is a comprehensive benchmark showing that omni-modal guardrails remain vulnerable to cross-modal jailbreaks, safety hallucinations, and text-driven over-sensitivity.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
bullets: Frozen perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical signals and post cited evidence to a shared board.
An integration agent combines observations with retrieved examples, while a critic may request one revision.
Deterministic verification checks citation validity and whether final emotion claims are entailed by the evidence.
Failures are attributed to components and failure types, then converted into validated targeted prompt patches.
On MER2025, targeted adaptation improves F-score by 0.6–2.2 points across four MLLMs, including 52.3→54.5 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
papers.selection_reason: Applies an agentic framework with prompt-space adaptation to multimodal emotion reasoning using frozen MLLMs, fitting both Multimodal Foundation Models and Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: An Agentic Approach with Evidence-Grounded Verification for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning in Conversation
papers.tldr: An evidence-grounded agentic pipeline diagnoses multimodal emotion-reasoning errors and adapts prompts without updating model weights.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
bullets: Addresses gaps in prior multimodal bias benchmarks, which cover limited categories or fail to make target group attributes visually clear.
Extends the language-only BBQ benchmark into seven bias categories using controlled visual scenario generation.
Validates generated images through automated VQA screening and human inspection.
Evaluates 23 open-source MLLMs in text-only, image-only, and image-with-context settings to isolate modality effects.
Vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average; models recognize depicted attributes with 90–95% accuracy but often still produce stereotypical answers.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for social biases in multimodal LLMs across text and vision, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: Melange: A Synthetic Visual Bias Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Melange is a synthetic benchmark showing that visual inputs can substantially worsen social bias in multimodal large language models despite strong visual attribute recognition.

papers.abstract: Financial forecasting from earnings conference calls requires models to reason over complex corporate disclosures, market expectations, and subtle communication signals. However, existing financial benchmarks are often limited to unimodal inputs or single-task settings, making it difficult to evaluate whether multimodal large language models (LLMs) can support real-world financial analysis. In this paper, we introduce MM-FinEval, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal LLMs across multiple financial tasks. MM-FinEval spans a diverse timeline from 2019 to 2022. The entire proposed dataset contains 2,045 S\&P 500 conference earning calls as inputs and 12 financial task labels as outputs. Each input contains three modalities: a word-to-word text transcript of the earning call, the corresponding presentation slides used during the call, and the entire audio recording. To establish a rigorous evaluation framework, we analyze 19 baseline models across three distinct model categories: Image-Text, Audio-Text, and Any-to-Any configurations. We observe that small-size Any-to-Any models processing all three modalities achieve strong performance, even when compared against larger proprietary models restricted to two-modality inputs. This indicates that our tri-modal dataset design introduces useful, non-redundant information. These results validate that text, audio, and visual data serve as important, complementary signals that mimic the decision-making process of expert human analysts.
bullets: Covers 2,045 S&P 500 earnings calls from 2019–2022 with 12 financial task labels.
Each example combines transcript text, presentation slides, and full audio recordings.
Evaluates 19 baseline models across Image-Text, Audio-Text, and Any-to-Any configurations.
Small Any-to-Any models using all three modalities perform strongly relative to larger proprietary models using only two.
Results suggest that text, audio, and visual signals provide complementary information for financial analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating multimodal LLMs across text, audio, and visual inputs fits the multimodal foundation models scope.
papers.title: MM-FinEval: A Multi-Task Multimodal Benchmark for Real-World Financial Forecasting
papers.tldr: MM-FinEval is a tri-modal, multi-task benchmark for testing multimodal LLMs on realistic financial forecasting from earnings calls.

papers.abstract: Audio large language models (AudioLLMs) operate reactively, responding only when queried. We introduce proactive audio assistance, where an AudioLLM monitors an audio stream and autonomously decides when to alert the user from a single natural-language intent, motivated by wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users. We propose Interrupt and Silent Modeling (ISM), a model-agnostic paradigm that embeds proactive decisions into LLM decoding via two special tokens: \texttt{<interrupt>} and \texttt{<silent>}, capturing four states: onset detection, sustained-relevance triggering, irrelevance suppression, and de-duplication. Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, ISM achieves 99.6\% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50. On noisy Epic-Sounds kitchen audio, ISM achieves the highest interrupt F1 without domain-specific training, the only method maintaining strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression. Streaming evaluation confirms real-time viability with 3.5-second average latency.
bullets: Addresses the reactive nature of AudioLLMs, with potential wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users.
Uses two special decoding tokens—<interrupt> and <silent>—to model onset detection, sustained relevance, suppression, and de-duplication.
Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, it achieves 99.6% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50.
On noisy kitchen audio, it maintains strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression and requires no domain-specific training.
Streaming evaluation indicates real-time feasibility with 3.5-second average latency.
papers.selection_reason: Extends an audio LLM with proactive interrupt/silent decoding, fitting multimodal large language model research.
papers.title: I'll Keep an Ear Out: Teaching AudioLLMs Proactive Audio Assistance
papers.tldr: ISM enables AudioLLMs to proactively monitor audio and alert users at the right moments without explicit queries.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
bullets: Exact-counting ability is model-specific, with the reported R80 range spanning 3–150 dots across 9 models.
Marking items improves counting for only 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs; it can hurt imprecise pointers and rarely outperforms simpler routines.
Tag-level audits classify errors as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, exposing whether answers are grounded in the visual trace.
Precise pointers tend to derive answers from their tags, while dense scenes primarily cause omissions and models seldom revise after tagging.
Traversal order following, order-invariant counting, and regular-versus-scattered advantages dissociate, indicating multiple underlying counting capacities.
papers.selection_reason: VLM counting evaluation based on spatial marking and ordering is directly relevant to spatial reasoning diagnostics in multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A developmental counting-inspired tagging procedure reveals that VLMs’ counting failures are mainly serial, omission-prone, and poorly self-corrected, while producing useful auditable traces rather than reliably improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: System One models produce probabilistic judgments that software can consume directly, making reliable confidence as important as answer accuracy. Yet joint training across text, images, and video remains underexplored, and the contributions of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD) are difficult to separate. We introduce UniJev, a trimodal framework that scores candidate answers with a shared head under joint supervised training across text, images, and video. Supervised decision models improve accuracy over their backbone readouts across all three modalities, while the existing RLCD algorithms change accuracy little and have inconsistent effects on visual calibration across recipes. These findings motivate a separate supervised objective for confidence calibration. We introduce Cora (Confidence--Outcome Reliability Alignment), which groups current predictions by confidence and optimizes each prediction's confidence toward the empirical accuracy of its bin. At both 2B and 9B, Cora lowers image and video expected calibration error (ECE) while preserving accuracy, without a reinforcement stage. We release our code at https://github.com/wjnwjnwj/UniJev.
bullets: Joint supervised training improves answer accuracy across text, images, and video compared with backbone readouts.
Existing reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions has little effect on accuracy and inconsistent effects on visual calibration.
Cora calibrates confidence by aligning binned predictions with their empirical accuracy.
At both 2B and 9B, Cora lowers image and video ECE while preserving accuracy, without reinforcement training.
The study focuses on text-image-video System One decision models and releases its code publicly.
papers.selection_reason: Trimodal decision models with joint text, image, and video supervision, plus confidence calibration, directly fit multimodal foundation model research.
papers.title: UniJev: Separating Accuracy from Calibration in Trimodal System One Decision Models
papers.tldr: UniJev shows that trimodal accuracy and confidence calibration can be improved separately, with Cora reducing visual calibration error without sacrificing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) perform well on complex question answering but often show a reasoning gap, where explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reduces accuracy compared to direct answers. We hypothesize that long reasoning sequences shift attention away from the audio input. To address this, we propose SPARE (Semantic Prediction for Audio REasoning), which introduces a register token aligned with the final conclusion using a cosine similarity loss with a Sentence-BERT embedding. This conditions the model's latent space with the target semantic goal before reasoning begins. Experiments on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN show improved zero-shot reasoning and stronger early attention to audio without additional inference cost.
bullets: Addresses the reasoning gap in Large Audio Language Models, where explicit Chain-of-Thought can hurt accuracy.
Uses a register token trained to match the final conclusion’s Sentence-BERT embedding via cosine similarity.
Conditions the model’s latent space on the target semantic goal before reasoning.
Improves zero-shot reasoning and early attention to audio on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN.
Adds no inference-time cost, though the abstract does not specify quantitative gains or broader limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Improves large audio language model reasoning via semantic summary prediction, fitting multimodal LLMs with additional modalities.
papers.title: Enhancing Audio Reasoning via Semantic Summary Prediction
papers.tldr: SPARE improves audio reasoning by conditioning the model on the intended conclusion before it begins reasoning.

papers.abstract: Existing vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable for fine-grained visual perception. In this report, we present WeVisOne-VL (WeChat Vision All-in-One), a powerful VLM that unifies object-level and pixel-level perception through structured next-token prediction. It supports multiple visual tasks including object detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting, enabling localization at any user-specific granularity, from points and boxes to masks and alpha mattes. Architecturally, we integrate a lightweight pixel decoder into the VLM via a special token to generate instance-level pixel outputs. We train the model with a three-stage curriculum SFT followed by mixed-task RL. Across over 30 benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates leading performance on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, while maintaining robust rejection for object-absent queries. By releasing WeVisOne-VL to the open-source community, we hope to advance VLMs from broad visual understanding toward truly reliable perception systems for real-world deployment.
authors: Tianming Liang, Junyi Pan, Yuxi Li, Canmiao Fu, Zhipeng Huang, Chong Sun, Chen Li, Jing Lyu
bullets: Targets the unreliability of existing VLMs in fine-grained visual perception.
Uses structured next-token prediction with a lightweight pixel decoder connected through a special token.
Supports user-specified localization granularity, including points, boxes, masks, and alpha mattes.
Trained with a three-stage supervised fine-tuning curriculum followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning.
Reports leading performance across more than 30 benchmarks and robust rejection of object-absent queries; released open source.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language model for object-level and pixel-level perception, fitting multimodal foundation model research.
papers.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
papers.tldr: WeVisOne-VL unifies object- and pixel-level visual perception in one VLM, supporting tasks from detection and OCR to segmentation and matting.

papers.abstract: Training-free personalization adapts a frozen vision-language model (VLM) to recognize user-defined concepts from only a few exemplars by retrieving concept entries at inference time. While recent retriever-based methods enrich each concept with descriptive evidence, they largely treat concepts in isolation, so the retrieved information can be plausible yet non-discriminative, especially when the personalized concept set contains highly confusable, fine-grained categories. We argue that personalization is inherently relational: correct recognition depends on the specific distinctions between a concept and its nearest alternatives. To this end, we propose ReCoG, a Relational Concept Graph for retrieval-augmented personalization. ReCoG represents concepts as nodes and augments them with directed edges that explicitly capture discriminative cues between concept pairs, elicited by a frozen VLM during database construction. At inference, ReCoG retrieves a shortlist and resolves ambiguity via explicit pairwise comparisons conditioned on the corresponding relational edges, selecting the concept that consistently wins against competing candidates. We also introduce FINGER benchmark to test personalized recognition on confusable concept sets. Across FINGER, ReCoG substantially outperforms prior methods, with the largest gains in the most confusable regimes. ReCoG also achieves consistently best performance on established personalization benchmarks including captioning and VQA, confirming that relational evidence is broadly beneficial beyond fine-grained settings. Project Page: https://csy-98.github.io/ReCoG/
bullets: Addresses the weakness of treating personalized concepts independently, which can produce plausible but non-discriminative retrievals.
Builds a relational concept graph with concepts as nodes and directed edges encoding pairwise distinguishing cues elicited by a frozen VLM.
Resolves inference-time ambiguity through explicit comparisons between shortlisted candidates using their relational edges.
Introduces the FINGER benchmark for personalized recognition on confusable concept sets.
Reports strong gains on FINGER, especially in highly confusable settings, and best performance on established captioning and VQA personalization benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Relational concept graph for training-free retrieval-augmented personalization of vision-language models.
papers.title: ReCoG: Relational Concept Graph for Training-Free Personalization
papers.tldr: ReCoG improves training-free VLM personalization by modeling discriminative relationships between user-defined concepts, enabling better recognition of highly confusable categories.

papers.abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.
authors: Tianyu Lu, Kaicheng Yang, Jiangtao Feng, Keyue Qiu, Yawen Ouyang, Yixin Wu, Xinbo Zhang, Lihao Wang, Wei-Ying Ma, Hao Zhou
bullets: Uses one discrete token space for protein sequences, structures, and natural language.
Employs bidirectional or semi-bidirectional diffusion interactions to support global residue communication and long-range contact modeling.
Unifies folding, inverse folding, sequence and structure understanding, and sequence and structure design.
Reports competitive benchmark performance, including a single-sample folding TM-score above 0.8 under strict homology control.
Achieves 62.37% on sequence understanding, comparable to the cited top-tier LLM baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal diffusion language model for language, protein sequence, and structure, directly relevant to multimodal and language foundation models.
papers.title: Trion-1: Unifying Language, Protein Sequence, and Structure with Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Trion-1 is a unified protein diffusion language model that jointly handles sequence, structure, and natural language for understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.
authors: Ronald Fecso, Jos\'e Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber, Virginia Mares, Andreas Pollreisz, Hrvoje Bogunovi\'c
bullets: Introduces RetinaGroundBench, the first retinal OCT benchmark for biomarker visual grounding.
Contains 815 ophthalmologist-annotated B-scans, 4,537 bounding boxes, 13 biomarkers, and 8 diseases.
Proposes AggIoU to evaluate fragmented predictions by measuring coverage of the union of overlapping boxes.
Across 27 open-source MLLMs, grounding remains weak despite stronger biomarker-presence classification.
RetGrounder raises grounding F1 from 23.7% for the best general-purpose model to 33.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and fine-tuned MLLM for visual grounding of retinal OCT biomarkers.
papers.title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: RetinaGroundBench shows that MLLMs can recognize retinal OCT biomarkers far better than they can localize them, while OCT-specific fine-tuning substantially improves grounding.

papers.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.
authors: Chi-En Dai, Chih-Pin Tan, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting subjective, context-dependent musical valence alongside arousal.
Uses auxiliary-dataset demonstrations to refine predictions from a task-specific base model rather than predicting emotion scores directly.
Evaluates text-based ICL with lyrics and generated audio captions, and multimodal ICL with raw audio.
On the held-out MER60 test set, text ICL raises valence R² from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 shots; multimodal ICL reaches 0.346 with 10 shots.
Results support training-free, inference-time ICL as a strategy for continuous music-emotion prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLM in-context learning with text and raw audio inputs for music emotion prediction; fits multimodal LLM applications.
papers.title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Training-free in-context learning substantially improves continuous music valence and arousal prediction, especially valence, by refining a small base model’s outputs with textual or audio demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.
bullets: Museum catalogue metadata is heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across regions.
A two-phase study combines analysis of natural metadata variation with controlled probes that fix object identity while varying fields and image access.
Metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behavior; field type strongly shapes grounding, omission, and inference.
Images can improve visual grounding but may also increase unsupported interpretation.
Evaluation should measure field- and claim-level support, not only input coverage or reference similarity.
papers.selection_reason: Probes field-level grounding in LLM-generated descriptions with varying metadata and image access, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
papers.tldr: More metadata does not reliably improve museum descriptions: field type and image access determine whether LLMs ground, omit, or invent details.

papers.abstract: Text-to-music alignment is commonly evaluated by the global similarity between text and audio embeddings, which collapses all described attributes into a single score and obscures which ones are missing. We instead introduce MQAScore, which verifies each atomic musical concept along five clip-level dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage) by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers affirmatively to a binary question. To assess evaluator reliability, we construct verification labels from presence/absence annotations and LLM-guided concept substitutions, and propose the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator responds to meaning-changing substitutions. Experiments show that concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, and MQAScore can be a more reliable and interpretable fine-grained complement to global similarity for evaluating text-to-music alignment.
authors: Wei-Jaw Lee, Chun-Ping Wang, Xuanjun Chen, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of global text-audio similarity scores, which hide which attributes are missing.
Evaluates atomic concepts across genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage dimensions.
Uses a large audio language model to answer binary presence questions for each concept.
Introduces verification labels and a Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio to assess evaluator reliability.
Experiments indicate improved evaluation for both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, complementing global similarity with more interpretable scores.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a large audio language model for fine-grained text-music alignment evaluation, relevant to multimodal LLMs beyond vision-language.
papers.title: MQAScore: Fine-Grained Text-Music Alignment Evaluation via Large Audio Language Model
papers.tldr: MQAScore provides fine-grained text-to-music alignment evaluation by checking whether each described musical concept is present in the audio.

papers.abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA
authors: Qiuyu Kong, Zanxi Ruan, Marco Cristani, Yiming Wang
bullets: Problem: Existing methods underuse informative non-salient text and context, causing retrieval degradation when salient content is reduced.
Method: Decomposes image–text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views using visual saliency estimation and LLM-based text decomposition.
Method: Uses auxiliary objectives to align salient and contextual views across modalities.
Contribution: Provides a modality-independent, plug-and-play saliency-aware finetuning framework.
Result: Improves long-text retrieval and robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks, with consistent gains for existing tuning methods.
papers.selection_reason: Saliency-aware finetuning for long-text image-text alignment is directly relevant to multimodal LLM alignment and robustness.
papers.title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
papers.tldr: RoSA mitigates saliency collapse in long-text image–text alignment by jointly learning salient and non-salient contextual semantics.

papers.abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.
authors: Ignacy Kolton, Wenxuan Li, Zongwei Zhou, Jaros{\l}aw B. \'Cwik{\l}a, Arkadiusz Sitek, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Szymon P{\l}otka
bullets: Addresses objective misalignment in token-level maximum likelihood training, which can miss key diagnoses or add incorrect ones.
Introduces an architecture-agnostic differentiable loss operating on decoder token probabilities.
Uses asymmetric pooling to reward sufficient probability for supported diagnoses while suppressing spurious probability for unsupported alternatives.
Evaluated across several 3D MedVLMs on abdominal CT report-generation benchmarks, including in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.
Improves diagnostic faithfulness while retaining competitive conventional language-generation performance and adds no inference-time computation.
papers.selection_reason: Asymmetric diagnostic supervision for MedVLMs is a transferable objective for improving multimodal LLM faithfulness.
papers.title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
papers.tldr: Diagnostic Loss improves radiology report generation by emphasizing supported diagnoses and suppressing unsupported ones without changing model architecture or inference.

papers.abstract: Auxiliary patient data can improve chest X-ray report generation, but directly concatenating heterogeneous clinical information with visual tokens produces long, variable-length decoder prompts and may expose the model to redundant or image-irrelevant context. We propose ICGF-CXRMate, an image-conditioned clinical context compression and gated fusion framework. Learnable queries are first conditioned on the current chest X-ray representations and then attend to the patient-data sequence, compressing it into a fixed number of clinical context tokens. Gated cross-attention selectively integrates these tokens into the visual stream, while the compressed tokens are retained in the decoder prompt as a direct clinical pathway. Experiments on linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations show that ICGF-CXRMate improves report quality while reducing the average prompt length. In Stage~2, it improves RadGraph-F1 from 24.00 to 28.86, CXR-BERT similarity from 56.86 to 62.80, and BLEU-4 from 5.14 to 7.96 compared with CXRMate-ED, while reducing the average prompt length from 373.89 to 288.37 tokens, corresponding to a 22.9\% reduction. After self-critical sequence training, ICGF-CXRMate outperforms CXRMate-ED on six of eight report-quality metrics in Stage~3. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of image-conditioned compression, gated fusion, and direct retention of the compressed clinical tokens.
authors: Vu Minh Tran, Thuc Huynh, Son Thanh Luu, Doanh C. Bui
bullets: Addresses redundant, image-irrelevant, and variable-length auxiliary clinical data in chest X-ray report generation.
Uses image-conditioned learnable queries to compress patient data into a fixed number of clinical context tokens.
Applies gated cross-attention to integrate compressed context into visual features while retaining a direct clinical pathway in the decoder prompt.
On linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations, Stage 2 improves RadGraph-F1, CXR-BERT similarity, and BLEU-4 over CXRMate-ED while reducing average prompt length by 22.9%.
Ablations support complementary benefits from compression, gated fusion, and direct token retention; after self-critical training, it leads on six of eight report-quality metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Image-conditioned context compression and gated fusion for multimodal report generation is transferable to MLLM context efficiency.
papers.title: ICGF-CXRMate: Image-Conditioned Clinical Context Compression and Gated Fusion for Chest X-ray Report Generation
papers.tldr: ICGF-CXRMate compresses image-relevant clinical context and selectively fuses it with chest X-ray features, improving report quality while shortening decoder prompts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with in context learning compared to their textual counterparts. Our preliminary study shows that VLMs rely on textual shortcuts and underutilize the visual demonstrations. We therefore hypothesize that VLMs are insufficiently trained to perform visual in-context learning (vICL). To this end, we construct MIME, a task-agnostic vICL training set without textual shortcuts. We ensure the instruction does not state the rule linking the demonstration images to their answers, so the model must infer it from the visual demonstrations. Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy by 8.1 to 18.0 points across three VLMs, preserves single-image performance, and improves multi-image and text only in-context learning. In contrast, stating the rule in the training data sharply reduces this gain. We further propose DTAD (Demonstration Text Attention Dropout), which randomly withholds demonstration labels during training so that the VLM must infer the rule from the demonstration images. While achieving comparable vICL accuracy to fine-tuning on MIME, DTAD yields more consistent attention to the demonstration images. On TrueMICL, Qwen3-VL-8B trained on MIME matches frontier models such as Claude Opus 5, and surpasses them with DTAD. Finally, adding MIME to the instruction-tuning mix of LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles its vICL accuracy without hurting single-image abilities, whereas a same-size multi-image set improves it only slightly. These results suggest that vICL data should be a standard component of VLM training.
authors: Nimrod Shabtay, Asaf Yehudai, Avihu Dekel, Eli Schwartz, Raja Giryes
bullets: VLMs often underuse visual demonstrations because training enables textual shortcuts.
MIME is a task-agnostic training set whose instructions omit the rule connecting images and answers.
Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy across three VLMs while also benefiting multi-image and text-only in-context learning.
DTAD randomly hides demonstration labels, producing comparable vICL gains and more consistent attention to images.
Adding MIME to LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles vICL accuracy; results support including vICL data in standard VLM training.
papers.selection_reason: Training VLMs for visual in-context learning directly targets multimodal large language model capabilities.
papers.title: Watch and Learn: Teaching Visual In-Context Learning by Removing Textual Shortcuts
papers.tldr: Training VLMs to infer rules from visual demonstrations—rather than textual shortcuts—substantially improves visual in-context learning without harming single-image abilities.

papers.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Yidi Wang, Yile Li, Siqi Zeng, Yingjie He, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao hu
bullets: Introduces 327 hand-written text–image–audio queries across 86 scene groups and 18 ambiguity categories.
Each item has a unique answer only when all three modalities are available; removing one leaves multiple plausible answers.
Evaluations of 14 omni-modal systems show strong item-level results but substantially weaker scene-level disambiguation than humans.
Models rely insufficiently on audio, especially when text and images are present; removing answer options worsens performance sharply.
Provides an ambiguity taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocols for evaluating cross-modal disambiguation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an omni-modal ambiguity-resolution benchmark and diagnostic protocol for multimodal LLMs across text, image, and audio.
papers.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: TRIAD benchmarks whether multimodal large language models can resolve ambiguity that requires jointly using text, images, and audio.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantage estimation, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction to propagate final rewards through visually important reasoning steps, without extra rewards, additional rollouts, or inference-time changes. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-OV-7B, RECAP consistently improves over GRPO and VPPO, yielding $+6.1$--$+6.5$ HallusionBench gains over the SFT base while preserving reasoning and text-only performance. Results on larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human evaluation further demonstrate robust improvements in image-grounded reasoning.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Chenxin Li, Yingjie He, Zhenyu Yu, Fengyu Zhou, Jiachen Qian, Lei Wei, Shuang Chen, Jiachen Li, Eric Hanchen Jiang, Rongchao Zhang, Zhengtao Yao, Hoi Leong Lee, Guansu Wang, Kaiyue Zhou
bullets: Long chain-of-thought can cause VLMs to drift from visual evidence because training often rewards only the final answer.
Visual revisit peaks predict correctness and are causally important: masking them hurts accuracy, while adding them can recover some failed answers.
RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantages, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction within GRPO, without extra rewards, rollouts, or inference-time changes.
Across three VLM backbones, RECAP improves over GRPO and VPPO, including +6.1–+6.5 HallusionBench points over the SFT base.
Additional evaluations support robustness across larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human judgments.
papers.selection_reason: Improves image-grounded reasoning in VLMs by leveraging visual revisit signals during long chain-of-thought, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: RECAP: Looking Once Is Not Enough for Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: RECAP improves vision-language reasoning by using moments when models revisit image evidence to better assign credit during reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Visual perception should be iterative and task-directed, with representations refined in response to the question and the need for further processing. While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly support extended reasoning, their visual tokens are still typically acquired in a single, task-agnostic encoder pass. This creates an evidence-acquisition bottleneck: models may reason longer without refining the visual evidence needed to answer the question. We propose LoopLook, a lightweight encoder-side recurrent perception framework that equips pretrained VLMs with adaptive visual depth. LoopLook recurrently revisits a middle-to-late window of the vision encoder, injecting question representations at each loop to guide visual refinement. A learned stopping mechanism adaptively determines the recurrent depth, while a token-wise Mixture-of-Looks (MoL) combines representations from different loops, allowing each visual token to selectively integrate information acquired across recurrent steps. Across four backbones and eight benchmarks, LoopLook consistently improves performance over the baseline, yielding gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench. Our analysis shows that LoopLook progressively refines visual attention and adaptively allocates depth according to task difficulty. It also better preserves task-relevant visual information under reduced input resolution, while increasing time to first token (TTFT) by only 5.1-6.5%. By bringing recurrence from reasoning back into perception, LoopLook transforms visual perception from a one-shot glimpse into an adaptive process of recurrent refinement.
authors: Wencheng Ye, Anning Hu, Hongye Fang, Tianyi Wang, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses the evidence-acquisition bottleneck caused by one-pass, task-agnostic visual encoding.
Recurrently revisits a middle-to-late vision-encoder window, injecting question representations to guide refinement.
Uses learned adaptive stopping and token-wise Mixture-of-Looks to select and combine information across loops.
Improves results across four backbones and eight benchmarks, with gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench.
Allocates more depth to difficult tasks, preserves relevant information at lower resolution, and increases TTFT by 5.1–6.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Adds recurrent question-guided visual refinement to pretrained VLMs, improving multimodal reasoning and perception.
papers.title: Loop to Look Better: Learning Adaptive Depth for Question-Guided Perception in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopLook enables VLMs to adaptively revisit and refine visual representations based on the question, improving performance with modest inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. Mutating either input can change the expected answer, so an output change is not by itself a failure. Some failures appear only when both inputs are mutated; attributing them to the combination requires testing each mutation alone. We present VLTest, a black-box VLM testing approach. It generates image variants by editing VQGAN latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, filters variants likely to change the expected answer, and tests each variant alone before testing combinations, so every joint failure has four matched cells. A VLM judge confirms a failure only after checking that the input keeps the expected answer. On three tasks with eight VLMs, including two commercial API models, the oracle confirms 81.7% of the candidates, with 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates. Under the same budget, VLTest's generators find 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as SINVAD and TextFooler, and its joint tests find 91 to 197 attributed joint failures per 1,000 joint calls, 1.3 times as many as the same pairing applied to the baselines' variants.
authors: Bin Duan, Jintao Lin, Guowei Yang
bullets: Generates image variants via VQGAN latent-code editing and text variants through rewrite, expansion, and pruning.
Filters variants likely to preserve the expected answer, then tests image-only, text-only, and combined mutations in four matched cells.
Uses a VLM judge to confirm failures while checking answer preservation; it confirms 81.7% of candidates with 88.8–94.6% precision against human labels.
Across three tasks and eight VLMs, VLTest finds 1.8–2.5× more confirmed failures than SINVAD and TextFooler under the same budget.
Four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates and enables attribution of failures specifically to image-text interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Black-box testing of vision-language models for joint image-text failures; relevant to VLM reliability and robustness.
papers.title: VLTest: Finding Joint Image-Text Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: VLTest black-box tests vision-language models for reliable image-text and joint-input failures using matched single- and combined-mutation checks.

papers.abstract: Mixing requires not only applying processing but also assessing the resulting mix. Audio-language models can provide conversa- tional mixing advice, but existing evaluations do not separately test whether they can judge specific mixing issues. Since professional supervision for such judgments is scarce, we construct a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at multiple severity levels and use it to train MixJudge, a language-queryable audio critic. MixJudge shows its ability to retrieve mixing issues, distinguish opposite issues, and order the severity of an issue. Moreover, its judgments transfer to menu selection: given a set of processing candidates, MixJudge often favors versions acoustically closer to a held-out professional version, demonstrating how explicit mixing judgment can support comparison and downstream mixing decisions.
authors: Kuan-Hsun Ho, Yuan-Chiao Cheng, Yen-Tung Yeh, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the lack of separate evaluation and professional supervision for specific vocal-mixing judgments.
Uses a curriculum covering 11 vocal-mix issues across multiple severity levels.
Can retrieve requested issues, distinguish opposing issues, and order issue severity.
Its judgments transfer to processing-menu selection, often favoring candidates acoustically closer to a held-out professional mix.
Scope: focuses on vocal-mix issues and comparative downstream selection; the abstract does not quantify performance.
papers.selection_reason: A language-queryable audio critic is a multimodal language model with transferable relevance to multimodal foundation-model evaluation and instruction following.
papers.title: MixJudge: Learning a Language-Queryable Critic for Vocal Mixing
papers.tldr: MixJudge is a language-queryable audio critic trained to identify, distinguish, and rank the severity of vocal-mixing issues, with judgments that help select better processing options.

papers.abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.
authors: Minhyuk Seo, Minjae Lee, Chaeeun Lee, Wei Lin, Muhammad Jehanzeb Mirza, Tinne Tuytelaars, Jonghyun Choi
bullets: Problem: MLLMs often rely on textual cues instead of task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, causing hallucinations, poor cross-benchmark generalization, and forgetting.
Method: ProCoRe uses contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data, rewarding captions aligned with matching images and penalizing mismatches.
Results: It improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over Qwen-VL-3-8B.
Scope: The method is evaluated across benchmarks and compared with ICL-data-dependent approaches.
Contribution: The authors introduce PICL, a personalized captioning benchmark designed to test genuine understanding of visual demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Improves multimodal in-context learning by enhancing visual grounding in MLLMs via contrastive reinforcement learning, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Visual Grounding First, Multimodal In-context Learning Follows
papers.tldr: ProCoRe improves multimodal in-context learning by strengthening visual grounding without training on ICL-formatted examples.

papers.abstract: LLM correctors of ASR output are judged by aggregate WER, which hides what they fix and what they break. We decompose every WER change exactly into repaired tokens, damaged tokens and insertions, and use this to ask what the source audio adds to a corrector. We compare correction with and without the audio, for the model's own draft and for the output of an independent recogniser, on three corpora. With Gemini 2.5 Flash, text-only correction of its own draft breaks 13-32% of already-correct transcripts; with the audio, 1-3%. Damage falls in both settings. Repair falls against the own draft and rises against the recogniser. On medical dictation, kept insertions cancel the gain in net WER. The open-weight Voxtral, which rarely edits, does not show this pattern. Prompts differ between the two arms, so the contrasts bound the effect of the audio and do not isolate it.
authors: Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, Kirill Borodin, Nikita Vasiliev, Mikhail Gorodnichev, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Aggregate WER is decomposed into repaired tokens, damaged tokens, and insertions to expose correction trade-offs.
Gemini 2.5 Flash text-only correction damages 13–32% of already-correct outputs from its own draft; adding audio reduces this to 1–3%.
Audio reduces damage in both settings, but repairs decrease on the model’s own draft and increase on an independent recognizer’s output.
On medical dictation, retained insertions offset the net WER improvement.
Voxtral rarely edits and does not exhibit the same damage pattern; differing prompts mean the audio effect is bounded rather than isolated.
papers.selection_reason: Audio-grounded LLM correction of ASR output is a multimodal LLM application, and the repair-damage decomposition is a transferable evaluation method for multimodal language models.
papers.title: Text-Only LLM Correctors Break Correct Transcripts: A Repair-Damage Analysis of Audio Grounding in ASR Error Correction
papers.tldr: Audio grounding substantially reduces the tendency of Gemini 2.5 Flash to damage already-correct ASR transcripts, but its net benefit depends on the recognizer, domain, and retained insertions.

papers.abstract: Visual mathematical reasoning can fail before reasoning begins: when a vision-language model (VLM) misreads a diagram, subsequent reasoning proceeds from false premises. This perceptual bottleneck is especially pronounced in smaller models, while accurate textual descriptions can substantially narrow the gap to larger models. Because obtaining such descriptions at inference requires additional annotation or model calls, we propose minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation. Using reference figure descriptions and verified reference solutions as training-only information, a teacher scores incorrect student rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, and only teacher-disfavored tokens contribute to the corrective loss. Correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. This preserves on-policy supervision while avoiding full-response imitation. Across model scales, the method requires no descriptions at test time and meets or exceeds the corresponding base model supplied with a reference figure description at inference. It also improves perception-oriented performance, particularly low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external mathematics and perception benchmarks. Because the minimal-edit teacher evaluates corrections rather than generating its own solution, the method remains effective with a frozen same-size teacher, although its gains are smaller than with a larger teacher on most metrics.
authors: Wen Ye, Ailin Deng, Zirui Wang, Shixing Yu, Han Zhang, Tian Yun, Nikhil Mehta, Tarun Kalluri, Xuefei Cao, Xuezhe Ma, Hengduo Li
bullets: Targets perceptual errors in visual mathematical reasoning, especially for smaller VLMs.
A teacher scores incorrect student rollouts using reference descriptions and solutions available only during training.
Only teacher-disfavored tokens receive corrective loss; correct rollouts use task-reward reinforcement learning.
Improves perception and transfers to external math and perception benchmarks across model scales.
Works with a frozen same-size teacher, though larger teachers generally provide greater gains.
papers.selection_reason: Improves vision-language model reasoning via on-policy corrective distillation, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Edit, Don't Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: Minimal-edit on-policy distillation teaches VLMs to correct visual misreadings without requiring figure descriptions or extra model calls at test time.

papers.abstract: LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments.
