authors: Haowei Wang, Hao Lin, Qi Zhu, Jiayi Ji, Deyi Ji, Liujuan Cao, Rongrong Ji
bullets: OPD can produce accurate answers even when relevant image regions are masked or replaced with noise, revealing weak visual grounding.
CV-OPD contrasts teacher outputs from answer-relevant positive crops and unrelated negative crops under the same student prefix.
Its Contrastive Divergence Loss encourages students to distinguish useful from irrelevant visual features.
A Discrepancy Aware Gate selects visually relevant tokens using token- and sample-level discrepancies.
Experiments on broad fine-grained visual benchmarks show reduced shortcut behavior and improved visual reasoning in existing VLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Contrastive on-policy distillation improves VLM visual reasoning and reduces shortcut reliance.
papers.title: CV-OPD: Contrastive Vision On-policy Distillation
papers.tldr: CV-OPD improves vision-language model distillation by forcing students to rely on relevant visual evidence rather than answer-based shortcuts.

papers.abstract: Learning new tasks in multimodal continual instruction tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge. Although multi-expert LoRA distributes learning across experts, updates to a dense low-rank expert can still affect many output features. We introduce Monarch-MoE, which replaces the dense factors in LoRA experts with block-diagonal factors connected by a fixed permutation. This structure provides blockwise gradient isolation: individual block-pair updates affect only one output block, while connections between all input and output blocks are maintained. To make these compact experts practical on memory-limited hardware, we combine batched computation, fused forward operators, and an optimized backward pass. Across three continual-learning methods evaluated on MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, Monarch-MoE improves first-task retention while reducing adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively. In the main comparison, first-task forgetting is as low as 0.52 percentage points on MLLM-DCL and 0.10 on UCIT, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance. Our implementation supports fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with lower measured memory use and competitive runtime in the evaluated settings. Together, these algorithmic and systems improvements make structured experts a practical option for continual adaptation on memory-limited hardware.
authors: Xi Zhang, Boyu Diao, Zesen Chen, Ruiqi Liu, Hangda Liu, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Targets catastrophic forgetting when learning new multimodal tasks.
Replaces dense LoRA factors with block-diagonal factors linked by a fixed permutation, isolating updates by output block while preserving global connectivity.
Uses batched computation, fused forward operations, and an optimized backward pass for memory-limited hardware.
Across MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively, while improving first-task retention.
Runs fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Monarch-MoE, a structured expert architecture for multimodal continual instruction tuning to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. A strong technical contribution to Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Monarch-MoE: Structured Experts for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.tldr: Monarch-MoE uses block-structured LoRA experts and optimized computation to reduce forgetting and adapter memory in multimodal continual instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.
authors: Sida Li, Yuanxin Liu, Linli Yao, Shicheng Li, Xu Sun, Haoli Bai, Xiaohui Li
bullets: Introduces FG-Sudoku, a benchmark organized by grid size and required deductive steps.
Finds that frontier MLLMs struggle with complex long-range dependencies, especially 9×9 puzzles.
AdaC-GRPO dynamically selects training batches using online rollout accuracy to track the model’s learning frontier.
Enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach Gemini-2.5-Flash and close 62.2% of the accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro.
Generalization is validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.
papers.selection_reason: RL curriculum for long-horizon visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
papers.tldr: AdaC-GRPO uses adaptive curriculum learning to overcome sparse rewards and improve long-horizon visual Sudoku reasoning in multimodal language models.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.
bullets: LALMs may hallucinate absent sounds; Audio-Aware Decoding’s blank-audio comparison can be confounded by removing the entire clip.
The study localizes evidence with CLAP similarity, removes it via spectral gating, and compares it with random-window removal across multiple models and conditions.
After matching removal duration, localized ablation outperforms random removal, but raw detection behavior varies by model.
Combining blank and language-prior contrasts improves Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, outperforming AAD alone.
Grounding profiles do not transfer consistently between models; the study reports limitations and releases code.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes audio grounding and hallucination in large audio-language models, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
papers.tldr: A black-box causal audit shows that audio-grounding evidence and hallucination mitigation are model-dependent, while duration-controlled localization and combined contrastive decoding improve reliability in tested settings.

papers.abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.
authors: Yixuan Li, Minghao Lv, Xuenan Xu, Zihao Zheng, Mengyue Wu
bullets: Addresses coarse difficulty estimation in adaptive reasoning for large audio-language models.
Derives five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments.
Learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning across stages.
On MMAU-test-mini and MMAR, it improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens.
Shortens reasoning for easy instances while preserving performance on difficult ones.
papers.selection_reason: Difficulty-aware adaptive reasoning for audio-language models, relevant to multimodal LLMs and inference efficiency.
papers.title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
papers.tldr: SWEAR improves audio-language reasoning efficiency by allocating effort according to fine-grained, stage-specific difficulty.

papers.abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.
authors: Chandravardhan Singh Raghaw, Shahid Shafi Dar, Arnav Nishith Sharma, Shrey Modi, Nagendra Kumar
bullets: Targets lengthy, unstructured reports that may miss diagnostic cues and multi-view information.
Stage 1 uses disease-aware visual-textual alignment and prior-guided attention to model current and prior scans.
Stage 2 applies GraphRAG-guided clinical retrieval and an LLM to produce QA pairs with diagnostic summaries.
On two public chest X-ray benchmarks, it outperforms prior methods on lexical and clinical metrics.
The approach is evaluated specifically for chest X-ray reporting and depends on clinical-knowledge retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal radiology report generation using visual-textual alignment and LLM.
papers.title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
papers.tldr: CliQ-RRG generates concise, interpretable QA-style radiology reports by aligning image and text representations with disease knowledge and retrieving graph-grounded clinical evidence.

papers.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
authors: Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Addresses high inference cost from repeated cross-view observations and processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer.
GeoSemZip builds compact 3D voxel-token representations using semantic saliency and spatial coverage, while retaining discarded information in contextual anchors.
GroupRoute uses late entry, early exit, and recoverable group-wise skipping to adapt visual computation to token relevance.
Using a 67K-sample compression-aware post-training set, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of dense-model performance on two 7B 3D VLMs.
It accelerates LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×, demonstrating applicability to models with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses 3D visual tokens and skips LLM layers for efficient 3D VLMs, directly relevant to token pruning and multimodal efficiency.
papers.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
papers.tldr: GeoGR makes multi-view 3D vision-language models substantially faster by compressing redundant scene tokens and selectively routing visual tokens through LLM layers while preserving most performance.

papers.abstract: Visual interventions provide a training-free way to reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models. However, an intervention may have little leverage at some layers and may damage a correct answer even when it changes the output. We investigate where visual interventions retain leverage and when they improve predictions. First, we apply the same visual-residual edit at successive decoder layers, matching its RMS strength across depth. Across six checkpoints from three model families, we observe a persistent drop in intervention effect and define its operational onset for this edit as the \textbf{Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB)}. With boundaries fixed on calibration queries, held-out effects on disjoint evaluation queries before EAB are $13.78\times$--$26.10\times$ larger than those after it. Comparison with intermediate readouts shows that the edit can lose leverage before answer preferences stabilize. Second, we compare counterfactual subtraction across presence, attribute, and relation questions. Subtraction can correct a misleading preference, leave a decision unchanged, or remove a preference supporting the correct answer. Based on these observations, we develop calibrated selective routing, which preserves the original prediction unless calibration supports an intervention for the question type. It improves full-set attribute accuracy by $1.56$--$1.81$ percentage points across three checkpoints, while universal subtraction is neutral or harmful.
authors: Qiji Zhou, Junyi Hu, Peiyu Wang, Yue Zhang
bullets: Visual-residual edits lose predictive leverage at later decoder layers, defining an operational Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB).
Across six checkpoints from three model families, pre-EAB held-out effects are 13.78×–26.10× larger than post-EAB effects.
Interventions can correct misleading preferences, have no effect, or disrupt preferences supporting the correct answer.
Calibrated selective routing improves full-set attribute accuracy by 1.56–1.81 percentage points across three checkpoints.
Universal counterfactual subtraction is neutral or harmful, highlighting the need for selective application.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes layer-wise visual interventions in multimodal LLMs to reduce hallucinations and proposes selective routing, directly relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: The Evidence Anchoring Boundary: Where Visual Interventions Matter and When They Help in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Visual interventions help multimodal LLMs mainly before an Evidence Anchoring Boundary, so calibrated, question-aware routing is safer than applying them universally.

papers.abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.
authors: Yingjie Zhu, Han Cheng, Xuefeng Bai, Youcheng Pan, Yang Xiang, Kehai Chen
bullets: Introduces 8,000 benchmark instances covering 8 graph-theoretic tasks across partial and temporal multi-graph views.
Ensures each problem cannot be solved from any single view alone, isolating evidence-composition ability.
Decomposes performance into Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning using 29 diagnostic tasks and 64,000 instances.
Evaluates 15 LVLMs and identifies cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as key bottlenecks.
Temporal constraints and more numerous views further expose capability limits.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and diagnostics for LVLM multi-graph reasoning; directly relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: MVGraph: Benchmarking LVLMs on Evidence Composition across Multi-View Visual Graph
papers.tldr: MVGraph benchmarks whether LVLMs can combine evidence across multiple visual graph views, revealing major weaknesses in cross-view alignment and relation composition.

papers.abstract: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.
authors: Yueying Li, Jingxuan Fan, Kiant\'e Brantley, Sham M. Kakade, Hanlin Zhang
bullets: Uses a linear head over a frozen Qwen3-VL intermediate layer, training original web captions to outrank perturbed versions.
Selecting the intermediate layer is critical, improving performance by 5.8 points over using the last layer.
A single recipe matches or exceeds GPT-4o across three benchmarks at 32B and leads VL-RewardBench by 6.6 points.
With equal pair budgets, perturbation-based training outperforms curated RLAIF-V pairs by 3–5 points.

Benchmark scores do not fully identify reward behavior: perturbation choice affects hallucination judgments, while verifier-driven bootstrapping improves CHAIR and image-generation pass rate despite lower benchmark scores.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised vision-language reward modeling on frozen VLM, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
papers.tldr: An unsupervised intermediate-layer reward head trained on caption perturbations can provide low-cost, task-specific multimodal rewards without human preference labels.

papers.abstract: Modern video-language models are increasingly treated as general-purpose video reasoners, yet it remains unclear whether they robustly capture temporal dynamics in safety-critical settings such as driving. We study this question through controlled ego-motion tasks that require identifying actions from driving videos. Across video-language models, we find that standard prompting, visual prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought prompting remain unreliable and highly task- and model-dependent, with persistent class biases, although newer models show substantial task-specific few-shot gains. In contrast, lightweight LoRA finetuning and simple probes trained on intermediate visual features recover strong motion-discriminative performance, indicating that motion-relevant cues are often present inside the models but are not reliably used by the final video-to-language pathway. These results suggest that, in driving, current video-language models remain unreliable temporal reasoners and often behave more like frame-level, bias-driven recognizers than dependable temporal world models.
authors: Shiva Sreeram, Erfan Aasi, Tsun-Hsuan Wang, Alaa Maalouf, Daniela Rus
bullets: The study evaluates temporal understanding through controlled ego-motion action-identification tasks in driving videos.
Standard, visual, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting are unreliable and strongly dependent on the task and model.
Models exhibit persistent class biases, though newer systems can gain substantially from task-specific few-shot examples.
Lightweight LoRA finetuning and probes on intermediate visual features achieve strong motion discrimination.
Findings suggest final video-to-language pathways underuse temporal cues, causing models to act more like frame-level recognizers than temporal world models.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluation of temporal reasoning in video-language models for driving.
papers.title: Mind the Temporal Gap: Evaluating Video Models for Temporal Understanding in Driving
papers.tldr: Current video-language models often fail to reliably understand temporal dynamics in driving videos, despite containing motion-relevant information that lightweight adaptation can unlock.

papers.abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .
bullets: Combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet and sliding-window attention, shared projections, block-wise attention-residual aggregation, sparse MoE layers, and a multi-scale byte codec.
Uses uniform-noise denoising across a shared byte space intended for text, images, audio, video, lidar, and control streams.
Convergence checks overfit one 440-byte sentence at 1–15M parameters; both tested attention variants reach minimum loss near 10⁻³ at 3,000 steps.
Codec choices produce different early optimization behavior, while the apparent shared-projection benefit is attributed to convergence speed rather than capacity.
Results do not establish generalization, multimodal training, model superiority, or the proposed throughput; larger pretraining is planned.
papers.selection_reason: Byte-level multimodal foundation model with linear attention and MoE; fits multimodal LLM and efficient attention interests.
papers.title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
papers.tldr: Kairos proposes a byte-level multimodal foundation-model design and finds that its components can optimize on a tiny text-only memorization task, without yet demonstrating generalization or multimodal usefulness.

papers.abstract: Spatial coding agents significantly improve spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by using external tools to generate verified execution traces. However, this paradigm inherently suffers from prohibitive inference-time overhead and external dependencies. In this paper, we explore whether an MLLM can internalize this agentic capability to operate entirely tool-free. We begin with a simple observation: prompting an MLLM with summarized execution traces of a spatial coding agent naturally unlocks the model's internal spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Motivated by this, we introduce SpatialOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework that internalizes spatial reasoning into a standalone MLLM by formulating verified agent traces as privileged information. To mitigate privileged-information leakage during distillation, we introduce Repetition-Aware Distillation, which combines repetition masking with unlikelihood regularization. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that self-distilling SpatialOPSD achieves higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO on both spatial and OOD datasets, exhibiting superior performance and generalization.
bullets: Targets the inference overhead and external dependencies of tool-using spatial coding agents.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to treat verified agent traces as privileged reasoning information.
Introduces Repetition-Aware Distillation with repetition masking and unlikelihood regularization to reduce privileged-information leakage.
Experiments report higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO across spatial and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
Scope: focuses on internalizing spatial reasoning in standalone MLLMs without external tools.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets spatial reasoning in MLLMs via self-distillation from coding agent traces, fitting spatial intelligence and multimodal LLM subtopics.
papers.title: SpatialOPSD: Self-Distilling Spatial Intelligence from Verified Coding Agent Traces
papers.tldr: SpatialOPSD distills verified spatial coding-agent traces into an MLLM, enabling tool-free spatial reasoning with improved benchmark performance and generalization.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models answer questions about speech, sound, and music, yet their accuracy drops sharply on tasks that need fine-grained acoustic analysis. Judging which of two speakers has the higher pitch demands iterative signal-level reasoning that a content question does not. Current models spend the same computational depth on both. We introduce AdaLoop, a lightweight recurrent module that learns how many latent refinement steps a given audio--question pair requires. A shared transformer block iterates over the audio representation, guided by the question, while a learned halting mechanism exits the loop once the representation is ready. AdaLoop adds fewer than 3\% of the base model's parameters and plugs into any audio encoder--language model pair without modifying either component. Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR, AdaLoop raises the average accuracy by 2.9 to 3.8 points, with the largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks where the model learns to apply deeper reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed reasoning depth and the varying acoustic-analysis demands of audio questions.
Uses a shared transformer block for question-guided recurrent refinement of audio representations.
A learned halting mechanism determines when further refinement is unnecessary.
Plugs into existing audio encoder–language model pairs without modifying either component.
Improves average accuracy by 2.9–3.8 points across three models and three benchmarks, with largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks.
papers.selection_reason: Extends audio language models with adaptive latent reasoning, fitting multimodal large language models with an additional audio modality.
papers.title: AdaLoop: Adaptive-Depth Latent Reasoning for Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: AdaLoop adaptively allocates iterative latent reasoning to audio questions, improving accuracy especially on fine-grained acoustic tasks with under 3% additional parameters.

papers.abstract: Continuous emotion control in text-to-image generation requires a model to improve affective alignment without changing the objects, layout, or scene described by the prompt. Existing supervised emotion-injection methods often optimize feature-space proxies and may therefore exhibit emotion-semantic drift, in which stronger emotional conditioning is accompanied by unintended content changes. We address this problem with a flow-matching image-generation framework that combines continuous valence-arousal (VA) conditioning, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a neutral semantic anchor. The deterministic probability-flow ODE is converted into a marginal-preserving SDE, yielding non-degenerate transition densities for trajectory sampling and policy-ratio estimation. A frozen CLIP-based VA regressor supplies a terminal reward measuring the distance between the predicted and target VA coordinates, while an image generated from the same prompt under zero VA conditioning provides a feature-space reference for semantic preservation. A reduced denoising schedule is used for online RL sampling, whereas the original schedule is retained at inference. Experiments on 3,300 prompt-emotion combinations show substantially lower valence and arousal errors than the VA-conditioned baseline and an improved CLIPScore relative to EmotiCrafter, with a measurable trade-off in reference-free image quality. The results support anchor-regularized Flow-GRPO as a practical approach to balancing emotional alignment and semantic consistency in continuous-affect image synthesis.
bullets: Targets emotion-semantic drift, where stronger affect changes unintended image content.
Combines continuous valence-arousal conditioning, GRPO reinforcement learning, and a neutral semantic anchor.
Uses a frozen CLIP-based valence-arousal reward plus feature-space comparison with zero-emotion images.
Evaluated on 3,300 prompt-emotion combinations, achieving lower valence/arousal errors than a VA-conditioned baseline and improved CLIPScore versus EmotiCrafter.
Reports a measurable trade-off in reference-free image quality.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses continuous emotion control in text-to-image generation using flow-matching and reinforcement learning, fitting multimodal generation.
papers.title: Balancing Emotional Alignment and Semantic Consistency in Image Generation via Reinforcement Learning with Valence-Arousal Anchoring
papers.tldr: Anchor-regularized Flow-GRPO improves continuous emotional control in text-to-image generation while preserving prompt semantics, though with a trade-off in reference-free image quality.

papers.abstract: Audio-based Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can generate detailed natural-language descriptions of complex acoustic scenes, yet it remains unclear which parts of the input audio support each generated token. This is particularly challenging because acoustic evidence is distributed across time and frequency, and concurrent sound events may overlap temporally while occupying different spectral regions. We introduce STAG, to our knowledge the first post-hoc framework for token-level spectro-temporal grounding of captions generated by audio-based MLLMs. STAG estimates the temporal support for each generated token using target-token-specific vocabulary projections of the encoded audio representations, measures frequency-band relevance through controlled spectral occlusion, and combines the two signals into a spectro-temporal relevance map. We evaluate STAG against ten post-hoc explanation methods across four grounding benchmarks, where it achieves the best event-localization performance on every dataset, and apply it to eight audio-language backbones without parameter updates. Counterfactual deletion further shows that removing the identified evidence selectively reduces confidence in the corresponding event and frequently removes it from the regenerated caption. These results provide behavioral support for the faithfulness and selectivity of the explanations.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of grounding token-level explanations when overlapping sounds occupy different spectral regions.
Combines target-token-specific temporal evidence from audio representations with frequency relevance from controlled spectral occlusion.
Evaluated against ten post-hoc methods across four grounding benchmarks, achieving the best event-localization performance on each dataset.
Applied to eight audio-language backbones without parameter updates.
Counterfactual deletion supports explanation faithfulness: removing identified evidence lowers confidence in the related event and often removes it from the caption.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc token-level spectro-temporal grounding for audio MLLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM interpretability.
papers.title: What Did the MLLM Hear? Token-Level Spectro-Temporal Grounding for Audio MLLM Explainability
papers.tldr: STAG explains audio-MLLM captions by locating the time–frequency regions that support each generated token.

papers.abstract: Ambiguity is often treated as a bug for AI systems to resolve---but in human communication and culture, ambiguity can also be a generative resource. From humour to politics to art, people express themselves in words and images that are open enough to invite different interpretations, yet constrained enough to be interpretable. We operationalise this notion of calibrated ambiguity with a task drawn from the parlour game Dixit. We compare differences in clues generated by human vs multimodal language models, based on a novel coding rubric for calibrated ambiguity, and find that models consistently exhibit ambiguity collapse (i.e., their outputs are over-specified, leaving no room for multiple legitimate interpretations). Unlike human clues, AI-generated clues also exhibit cultural flattening; they almost never make reference to culturally-situated knowledge, even when prompted to use allusion and figurative language.
bullets: The study examines ambiguity as a useful feature of communication rather than merely an error to eliminate.
It compares human and model-generated image clues using a novel coding rubric for calibrated ambiguity.
Models consistently show “ambiguity collapse,” reducing room for multiple legitimate interpretations.
Unlike humans, models rarely invoke culturally situated knowledge, even when prompted to use allusion and figurative language.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of ambiguity and cultural reference behavior in multimodal language models.
papers.title: Calibrated Ambiguity in Multimodal Language Models: Humans reach for cultural references, while models describe the picture
papers.tldr: In a Dixit-inspired task, multimodal language models produce overly specific, culturally flattened clues, unlike humans who use calibrated ambiguity and cultural references.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often struggle to identify and use geometric relations in diagrams. Recent methods address this challenge by converting geometric entities, relations, and constraints into explicit textual representations for the model to reason over. However, effective formalization is highly non-trivial: on Geometry3K, structure injection fixes 28 errors but introduces 13 new ones among 200 examples. Redundant relations can distract the model, while ambiguous references to diagram elements can lead it to apply constraints incorrectly. This suggests that the key challenge is not merely extracting more geometric facts, but organizing them into representations that support downstream reasoning. To fully exploit the power of formalization, we further propose GeoReform, a reflective formalization evolution framework that treats formalization as an optimizable policy rather than a fixed parser output. GeoReform executes the full reasoning pipeline, collects failed rollouts, diagnoses defects in the current representation, and mutates the policy to better select, ground, group, and present geometric entities, relations, constraints, and targets. On Geometry3K, GeoReform improves Qwen3VL-2B accuracy from 42.0\% to 56.0\%. Extensive experiments and analyses across geometry reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that effective formalization is crucial for improving multimodal geometry reasoning.
authors: Jialu Wang, Ruichen Zhang, Xiaoou Liu, Hua Wei, Tianlong Chen
bullets: MLLMs often struggle to identify and correctly use geometric relations in diagrams.
Fixed formalization can add distracting or ambiguous relations, sometimes creating new errors.
GeoReform treats formalization as an optimizable policy rather than a fixed parser output.
It diagnoses failed reasoning rollouts and mutates how entities, relations, constraints, and targets are selected, grounded, grouped, and presented.
Experiments across geometry benchmarks show that effective formalization is important for multimodal geometry reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Reflective formalization policy for multimodal geometry reasoning directly targets spatial and geometric reasoning in MLLMs.
papers.title: GeoReform: Reflective Formalization Evolution for Multimodal Geometry Problem Solving
papers.tldr: GeoReform improves multimodal geometry solving by iteratively refining how diagrams are formalized for reasoning, raising Qwen3VL-2B accuracy on Geometry3K from 42.0% to 56.0%.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models learn mostly from paired image-text data or annotated video, and raw web video is rarely used to further train an existing language model. We study whether raw video, with no captions and no text loss, can serve as mid-training data for a pretrained language model. Frames are encoded into continuous visual tokens, and the language model learns to predict the next visual token. We mid-train Qwen3-1.7B on raw clips from YT-Temporal-1B and then apply the same image-text instruction tuning to it and to the model without mid-training, so that the two differ only in mid-training. The mid-trained model scores 2.9 points higher on average across four video benchmarks and 5.1 points higher across ten image benchmarks, spanning perception, document, and chart tasks. Text performance is preserved even though mid-training includes no text, with an average of 48.9 across 14 text benchmarks compared with 48.0 for the model without mid-training. Analyses across training show that the image and video gains emerge within 30% of training and plateau thereafter, varying by less than 0.5 points. Predicting captions fails to outperform next-visual-token prediction, demonstrating that video mid-training can remain purely self-supervised without the computational overhead or labeling noise of automated captioning.
authors: Jaedong Hwang, Xiaoqian Shen, Ernie Chang, Changsheng Zhao, Chong Zhou, Saksham Suri, Qi Qian, Zechun Liu, Lemeng Wu, Qinsi Wang, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Wei Wen
bullets: Raw, uncaptained web video can be used to mid-train a pretrained language model.
The method encodes frames as continuous visual tokens and trains the model to predict the next visual token.
After identical image-text instruction tuning, mid-training yields +2.9 average points on four video benchmarks and +5.1 on ten image benchmarks.
Text performance is preserved: 48.9 average across 14 text benchmarks versus 48.0 without mid-training.
Gains appear early and plateau; caption prediction does not outperform next-visual-token prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised raw-video mid-training of MLLMs via next visual token prediction improves video and image understanding.
papers.title: Mid-Training Language Models on Raw Video
papers.tldr: Mid-training a language model on raw video by predicting visual tokens improves downstream video and image understanding while preserving text performance, without captions or text supervision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly evolving toward continuous audio--visual reasoning, creating an urgent need for evaluations that expose their capability limits. Audio--visual captioning is an ideal diagnostic task, yet current benchmarks face a coupled trade-off: whole-caption scores provide coverage without localization, local probes provide localization without coverage, and unconstrained LLM judges introduce instability. We introduce OmniCapBench (Omni-Video Caption Benchmark), a benchmark that reframes audio--visual caption evaluation as a deep-structured diagnostic framework. OmniCapBench shifts the prediction target from free-form text to sets of atomic, verifiable evaluation units across three tracks: entity references, visual shots, and audio events, enabling reliable scoring with deterministic constraint checks and localized LLM-based semantic comparisons. With 786 densely annotated videos, OmniCapBench effectively distinguishes MLLM perception errors, including temporal grounding failures, identity drift, cross-modal misalignment, and hallucinated descriptions. Evaluating frontier MLLMs reveals strong local perception but weak long-horizon audio--visual reasoning, particularly in identity drift and cross-modal misalignment, providing a fine-grained roadmap for omnimodal development.
authors: Zhongyu Yang, Jiale Tao, Ruitao Chen, Zuhao Yang, Yingfang Yuan, Xueliang Zhao, Auden, Kai Wang, Shuai Shao, Biao Wang, Steve Yves, Qinglin Lu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between broad whole-caption coverage, localized evaluation, and unstable unconstrained LLM judging.
Decomposes captions into three tracks: entity references, visual shots, and audio events.
Combines deterministic constraint checks with localized LLM-based semantic comparisons for reliable scoring.
Uses 786 densely annotated videos to identify temporal grounding failures, identity drift, cross-modal misalignment, and hallucinations.
Finds that frontier MLLMs show strong local perception but weaker long-horizon audio-visual reasoning, especially for identity drift and cross-modal alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Fine-grained audio-visual captioning benchmark for MLLMs; fits video understanding and multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: OmniCapBench: A Deep-Structured Evaluation Framework for Fine-Grained Audio-Visual Captioning
papers.tldr: OmniCapBench evaluates audio-visual captioning through atomic, verifiable units to diagnose fine-grained MLLM perception and reasoning failures.

papers.abstract: Streaming Video Large Language Models (VLMs) enable continuous video understanding, yet existing benchmarks focus on low-dynamic scenarios. Under bounded context budgets, models must balance temporal history, spatial resolution, and temporal granularity; sparse sampling at 1--2 FPS misses fast events. We introduce FastBench to evaluate high-dynamic perception in real-world video streams. Its trajectory-grounded pipeline combines QA generation from high-FPS clips, filtering of questions answerable at 2 FPS, answer verification using SAM3 and CoTracker3 trajectories, and three rounds of human inspection. FastBench contains 306 QA pairs across eight domains, six capabilities, and forward, instant, and backward temporal scopes, with human-annotated evidence intervals. We also present ProactiveFrame, a training-free baseline that adjusts incoming frame rates through text tokens. A dual-tier sliding window retains recent high-FPS observations while downsampling older ones into sparse history. Experiments reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model, Gemini-3.5-Flash, scores only 50.7%. Denser sampling improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 32.9% at 2 FPS to 44.6% at 24 FPS, but gains saturate as history is compressed. ProactiveFrame outperforms sparse uniform sampling by 5.4 and 1.5 percentage points, yet remains well below oracle-guided focusing, showing that current VLMs struggle to determine from the stream alone when finer temporal perception is needed. FastBench provides a testbed for high-dynamic streaming video understanding. Code and data: https://github.com/Ashone3/FastBench.
authors: Yuxuan Hu, Weikang Shi, Yang Bo, Xudong Lu, Xintong Guo, Shuhan Li, Yuyang He, Huankang Guan, Peiwen Sun, Yunqiao Yang, Wenbo Li, Rui Liu, Hongsheng Li
bullets: Introduces a benchmark for high-dynamic real-world video understanding across eight domains, six capabilities, and multiple temporal scopes.
Builds 306 QA pairs from high-FPS clips with trajectory-based verification, human inspection, and annotated evidence intervals.
ProactiveFrame adaptively adjusts frame rates using text tokens and a dual-tier sliding window.
The strongest evaluated model reaches only 50.7%; Qwen3-VL-8B improves from 32.9% at 2 FPS to 44.6% at 24 FPS.
Adaptive sampling beats sparse uniform sampling but remains far below oracle-guided focusing, revealing difficulty in knowing when finer temporal perception is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for high-dynamic streaming video understanding with VLMs; fits video understanding and multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: FastBench: Can Streaming VLMs Perceive High-Dynamic Real-World Streams?
papers.tldr: FastBench shows that current streaming VLMs struggle to perceive fast events, even with denser frame sampling or adaptive streaming strategies.

papers.abstract: Single-image, multi-image, and video deep research require different visual operations but share a workflow of visual grounding, external retrieval, and fact composition. A key challenge is to preserve the dependencies linking localized visual anchors, entity relations, source-supported facts, and answer-producing operations. We introduce OneSearch-VL, a unified agent centered on the Visually Grounded Evidence Graph (VGEG), which encodes these dependencies as a shared task-level reference for data construction, process supervision, and operation-level evaluation. Our VGEG-based data engine constructs and verifies multi-image and video questions and filters expert trajectories. Using these data, we assemble OneSearch-VL-SFT-110K and OneSearch-VL-RL-10K for SFT and RL, respectively. We further derive the Evidence-aware Visual-Grounded Rubric reward (EVGR) from VGEG annotations to supervise evidence traceability and visual grounding during RL. For fine-grained evaluation, we construct OneSearch-MI-Bench and OneSearch-Video-Bench, organizing questions by the research operations encoded in their VGEGs. Experiments show that OneSearch-VL-8B improves over Qwen3-VL-8B with tool access by 20.2 and 17.6 percentage points on the two new benchmarks, respectively, while also achieving substantial gains across 7 image benchmarks and VideoDR. Project repository: https://github.com/appletea233/OneSearch-VL
authors: Hongyu Li, Manyuan Zhang, Kaituo Feng, Shu Chen, Dian Zheng, Hao Li, Hao Yu, Zhangquan Chen, Zoey Guo, Ray Zhang, Shaofei Huang, Tianrui Hui, Linjiang Huang, Si Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving links among visual regions, entities, retrieved evidence, and answer-generating operations.
Introduces the Visually Grounded Evidence Graph (VGEG) as a shared representation for data construction, process supervision, and operation-level evaluation.
Provides SFT/RL training resources and the evidence-aware EVGR reward for improving visual grounding and evidence traceability.
Builds fine-grained multi-image and video benchmarks organized by research operations.
The 8B model outperforms Qwen3-VL-8B with tool access by 20.2 and 17.6 percentage points on the two new benchmarks, with additional gains on seven image benchmarks and VideoDR.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal research agent with visual grounding and video/image deep research; fits VLM-based reasoning and video understanding.
papers.title: OneSearch-VL: Unified Multimodal Deep Research Agent for Image and Video
papers.tldr: OneSearch-VL unifies image and video deep research through a visually grounded evidence graph that guides data, training, rewards, and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with spatial, embodied, physical, and temporal reasoning. We hypothesize that these failures reflect a shared deficit in visual transition reasoning, and test whether this capability can serve as a shared training primitive, one that different models can learn from different supervision sources and reuse across different tasks, with a systematic training recipe. Existing benchmarks document these deficits separately but do not support controlled comparisons across scenes, actions, and reasoning operations. We therefore introduce WOVEN, a training source and benchmark for visual transition reasoning that organizes transition supervision by scene, action, and reasoning type, using diverse, realistic rollouts from video-pretrained generative models: 36,076 examples across 20 scene types, 5 action types, and 8 reasoning types. We first evaluate 38 frontier MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B) and find a substantial and systematic deficit: even the strongest models fall far below humans, and the failures recur across model families and persist with scale. We then train MLLMs at multiple scales on WOVEN and find that they learn a shared capability that transfers broadly: training subsets of only about 2,000 items each collectively improve 22 of 26 external benchmarks by up to 27.3 percentage points, and WOVEN data can replace 30-50% of a task's own training data with comparable accuracy. Controlled comparisons further yield a training recipe for visual world modeling, validated prospectively on held-out benchmarks: select supervision by the reasoning operation it teaches rather than by the actions, scenes, or domains it shows, and prefer larger changes to the visual state for robustness. Our work establishes visual transition reasoning as a reusable foundation for systematic visual world-model training in MLLMs.
authors: Zheyu Fan, Yue Zhang, Mingkai Deng, Kangrui Wang, Qineng Wang, Canyu Chen, Jie Hao, Xing Fan, Chenlei Guo, Eric P. Xing, Mohit Bansal, Manling Li
bullets: Introduces a training source and benchmark with 36,076 visual-transition examples spanning 20 scene types, 5 actions, and 8 reasoning types.
Evaluates 38 frontier MLLMs and finds systematic gaps versus humans that persist across model families and model scale.
Training on small WOVEN subsets improves 22 of 26 external benchmarks by up to 27.3 percentage points.
WOVEN data can replace 30–50% of task-specific training data while maintaining comparable accuracy.
Finds that selecting supervision by reasoning operation—and favoring larger visual-state changes—supports robust transfer across tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Training source and benchmark for visual transition reasoning in MLLMs; relevant to video world models and multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs

papers.abstract: Skill-augmented agents improve sample efficiency by distilling successful trajectories into reusable strategies. Yet most existing approaches remain text-centric, linearizing spatial layouts and action-state correspondences into language that loses critical geometric structure. Recent efforts have begun incorporating visual evidence, but construct and update skills separately from policy optimization, leaving their mutual improvement underexplored. We propose ViSkill, a visual-native skill learning framework that encodes successful interactions as composite visual skill cards directly accessible to VLM agents. Retrieved skills guide both inference and reward shaping, while successful trajectories are distilled back into the library, forming a closed feedback loop in which skill accumulation and policy improvement reinforce each other. An optional cold-start mechanism further accelerates early-stage learning. Evaluated on Sokoban, FrozenLake, and PrimitiveSkill, ViSkill achieves an overall success rate of 0.89, rising to 0.91 with cold-start initialization, outperforming all evaluated proprietary and open-source baselines while converging faster than standard PPO. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/ViSkill.
authors: Hongxing Li, Dingming Li, Yixin Li, Yong Du, Wenqi Zhang, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yueting Zhuang, Yongliang Shen

The abstract reports faster convergence than standard PPO and better performance than evaluated proprietary and open-source baselines.

papers.title: ViSkill: Reinforcing VLM Agents with Evolving Visual-Native Skills
papers.tldr: ViSkill improves VLM agents by learning and reusing visual-native skill cards in a feedback loop that jointly strengthens skills and policies.

papers.abstract: Large Multi-modality Models (LMMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding and generation, but still face challenges in visual editing, particularly in following complex instructions, preserving appearance consistency, and supporting flexible input formats. To study this gap, we introduce RISEBench, the first benchmark for evaluating Reasoning-Informed viSual Editing (RISE), and extend it to RISEBench++, a more comprehensive and fine-grained benchmark for this emerging task. RISEBench++ extends the taxonomy into a hierarchical scheme spanning six reasoning dimensions: Temporal, Causal, Spatial, Logical, and Counterfactual Reasoning, together with Hybrid Reasoning integrating multiple reasoning types across multi-turn edits. These dimensions are further decomposed into 12 subcategories and 65 fine-grained task types. We expand input formats to include multi-image conditioning and scale the benchmark to 1000 human-annotated test cases, released in English and Chinese. We also improve our evaluation framework, assessing Instruction Reasoning, Appearance Consistency, and Visual Plausibility with human judges and an LMM-as-a-judge approach for more reliable and calibrated judgements. Beyond benchmarking, we introduce RISE-Agent, a training-free agentic framework integrating reasoning-driven planning, tool-augmented execution, and verifier-guided refinement, outperforming most strong existing approaches across diverse RISE tasks. We evaluate 58 visual editing approaches, including 34 open-source models, 19 closed-source models, and 5 agentic methods. The results reveal substantial challenges in reasoning-based visual editing, with even the strongest evaluated approach, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, achieving only 56.6% accuracy. RISEBench++ highlights the limitations of contemporary editing models, provides insights, and indicates future directions for reasoning-aware visual editing.
authors: Xue Yang, Peiyuan Zhang, Yilun Zhu, Qihao Yang, Mingxin Liu, Xiangyu Zhao, Ziqian Fan, Zhaokai Wang, Yan Li, Yifan Yang, Xu Yang, Xiaosong Jia, Yue Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Junchi Yan

papers.title: Reasoning-Informed Visual Editing
papers.tldr: RISEBench++ evaluates reasoning-intensive visual editing across diverse tasks, while RISE-Agent uses planning, tools, and verification to improve performance, revealing substantial limitations in current models.

papers.abstract: A single multimodal large language model (MLLM) struggles to excel simultaneously at detection, localization, description, and reasoning in multimodal industrial anomaly understanding (MM-IAU). We show that in-domain training does not close this gap. On MMAD, a widely adopted MM-IAU benchmark, trained specialists reach at most 75.5% accuracy in defect localization, against 92.3% for human experts, and even detect anomalies less accurately than their untrained base model. Meanwhile, different MLLMs offer complementary strengths but share this weakness in fine-grained perception, so combining them alone cannot remove it. We therefore propose SiGMA, a spatially grounded multi-agent framework that divides labor between heterogeneous MLLM agents and a dedicated visual defect expert. A multimodal searcher supplies industrial knowledge and normal references, the defect expert turns query-reference comparison into calibrated anomaly evidence, and a label-free reliability controller weighs each source by task-wise competence and query-level evidence quality. SiGMA reaches 85.2% average accuracy on MMAD, 4.0% above the strongest trained specialist and Gemini-2.5-Pro and within 1.5% of human experts. Even with three agents of at most 9B parameters, it reaches 84.4%, and new MLLMs join without retraining.
authors: Xingwu Zhang, Duanyang Du, Huiling Zhu, Jiayue Dai, Yixiao Liu, Guozhi Liu, Zhihan Zhang, Zijun Long
bullets: Trained specialists still lag human experts in defect localization and can underperform their untrained base models.
Different MLLMs have complementary strengths but share weaknesses in fine-grained visual perception, so simple combination is inadequate.

On MMAD, SiGMA achieves 85.2% average accuracy, within 1.5 percentage points of human experts; a three-agent variant reaches 84.4%.

papers.title: Is In-Domain Training Enough for Fine-Grained Industrial Anomaly Understanding?
papers.tldr: In-domain training alone is insufficient for fine-grained industrial anomaly understanding, while SiGMA’s spatially grounded multi-agent design substantially improves performance by combining complementary MLLM and visual-expert capabilities.

papers.abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can describe increasingly complex visual scenes, token-level grounding becomes crucial. Yet, when an MLLM generates "the yellow banana on the left", established grounding approaches focus on what is in the image ("banana"), overlooking tokens that help describe which instance is meant ("yellow", "left"). In this work, we ask whether frozen MLLM representations contain decodable grounding information about the referred instance across generated tokens, extending to modifiers such as attributes, spatial expressions, and relational/action terms. To address this question, we introduce OTTER, a lightweight supervised probe over frozen MLLM representations that uses Optimal Transport (OT) to align generated tokens with visual regions and produce compact grounding maps. Our results show that (i) instance-discriminative visual information can be decoded from modifier tokens, with the clearest evidence for spatial terms, but (ii) is not confined to them, as contextualized object nouns also carry referential information; (iii) the recovered grounding remains informative under context perturbations, while selected regions remain relevant to generation; and (iv) the learned OT-based grounding extends beyond the controlled setting to free generation and cross-dataset transfer.
authors: Barbara Toniella Corradini (AI for Good), Caterina Gallegati (University of Siena, Italy), Ludovica Genovese (AI for Good), Vittorio Murino (AI for Good)
bullets: Problem: Existing grounding methods emphasize object nouns and overlook modifier tokens that disambiguate the intended instance.
Method: OTTER uses a lightweight supervised probe with Optimal Transport to align generated-token representations with visual regions and create grounding maps.
Finding: Spatial modifiers provide the clearest instance-discriminative signals, while attributes, relations/actions, and contextualized nouns also carry referential information.
Robustness: Grounding remains informative under context perturbations, and selected regions remain relevant to generation.
Scope: The learned grounding generalizes from controlled experiments to free generation and cross-dataset transfer.

papers.title: From What to Which: Decoding Modifier Grounding in Frozen MLLMs
papers.tldr: OTTER shows that frozen MLLMs encode which visual instance is referred to not only in object nouns, but also in modifiers such as spatial and attribute terms.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made remarkable progress in bridging vision and language, facilitating various perception tasks essential for human-machine interaction, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, existing MLLM-based perception methods predominantly rely on text-based coordinate representation, which suffers from excessive token overhead, or fixed-range quantization, which suffers from range and precision constraints, especially for 3D domains with unbounded spatial range and high localization accuracy requirements. To address these challenges, we propose a dynamic vector decoding method named DVD, which unifies the representation of 2D and 3D perception tasks. Specifically, we first transform diverse perceptual representation (i.e., 2D bounding boxes, 2D masks, and 3D bounding boxes) into 1D vector sequences, which are then mapped to compact discrete tokens in the high-dimensional space. Then, a lightweight de-tokenizer enables seamless integration with MLLMs by decoding output tokens back to original 2D and 3D perceptual representations. Extensive experiments on 2D and 3D perception benchmarks including RefCOCO series, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, nuScenes demonstrate that DVD achieves superior performance in 2D and 3D tasks and reduces significantly the token overhead and inference latency. DVD provides an efficient and general framework for integrating perception capabilities into MLLMs, overcoming the inherent limitations of existing methods.
authors: Jinghua Hou, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of text-based coordinates and the range/precision limits of fixed quantization, particularly for unbounded 3D scenes.
Converts 2D boxes, 2D masks, and 3D boxes into 1D vector sequences mapped to compact discrete tokens.
Uses a lightweight de-tokenizer to reconstruct the original 2D or 3D representations from MLLM outputs.
Evaluated on RefCOCO, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, and nuScenes, with reported strong performance across 2D and 3D perception tasks.
The abstract reports reduced token overhead and inference latency, while the method unifies representation across perception tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in MLLMs for perception tasks using dynamic vector decoding to reduce token overhead, relevant to both Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: DVD: Dynamic Vector Decoding for Efficient MLLM-based Perception
papers.tldr: DVD efficiently represents 2D and 3D perceptual outputs as compact dynamic vector tokens, reducing token overhead and inference latency in MLLM-based perception.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal embeddings naturally involve both shared representations and modality-specific features across heterogeneous inputs. However, existing omnimodal embedding methods often rely on a single shared parameter space over mixed-modality data, limiting structural separation between universal and modality-specific representations. To address this, we propose Syn-Omni, a unified framework for structured omnimodal adaptation with modality specialization and controlled cross-modal collaboration. Specifically, we introduce Orthogonal Modality-Expert LoRA (OME-LoRA), which decomposes adaptation into a shared LoRA path for universal semantics and modality-expert LoRA paths for modality-aware specialization. Furthermore, Progressive Synergy Routing (PSR) enables experts to first establish modality-specific priors, then gradually interact with other modality-experts for cross-modal synergy. Evaluated across 81 diverse tasks spanning image, video, audio, and audiovisual modalities, Syn-Omni consistently outperforms omnimodal baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured specialization and cross-modal progressive collaboration.
authors: Youngtaek Oh, Qiyu Wu, Hiromi Wakaki, Junmo Kim, Yuki Mitsufuji
bullets: Addresses the limitation of single shared parameter spaces, which can blur universal and modality-specific representations.
Uses Orthogonal Modality-Expert LoRA to combine a shared adaptation path with modality-specific expert paths.
Introduces Progressive Synergy Routing, allowing experts to establish modality-specific priors before interacting across modalities.
Evaluated on 81 tasks covering image, video, audio, and audiovisual inputs.
Consistently outperforms omnimodal baselines across the evaluated tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for omnimodal embeddings with structured specialization and cross-modal collaboration, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Syn-Omni: Structured Specialization and Progressive Collaboration for Omnimodal Embeddings
papers.tldr: Syn-Omni improves omnimodal embeddings by separating shared semantics from modality-specific knowledge and progressively enabling cross-modal collaboration.

papers.abstract: Text prompting is an indirect interface for poster generation, requiring users to encode inherently two-dimensional composition intent into a one-dimensional sequence of words. We introduce a Spatial Canvas Interface that enables users to directly compose generation intent in space through four complementary binding types: semantic, identity, text, and pixel, together with Text Specifications for individual elements and global appearance. Based on this interface, we develop Compo, a poster generation model adapted from a pretrained image editing model to understand Spatial Canvas inputs and Text Specifications. Compo supports both direct inference, where users explicitly construct the canvas, and agentic mode, where a high-level request is automatically translated into a planned Spatial Canvas. To train Compo, we develop a scalable pipeline that automatically constructs supervision data for different binding types and their combinations, enabling efficient adaptation without training a specialized poster generator from scratch. We further introduce a benchmark that evaluates adherence to individual binding types and their joint composition. Experiments show that Compo achieves stronger compositional controllability than both general-purpose image generation models and dedicated poster generation systems while maintaining high visual quality. By decoupling intent specification from visual generation, our work shifts poster generation from prompting toward composing.
authors: Yitong Wang, Fangyun Wei, Jinjing Zhao, Sirui Zhang, Hongyang Zhang, Dong Chen, Bo Dai, Yan Lu
bullets: Users express poster intent spatially through semantic, identity, text, and pixel bindings, plus element-level and global text specifications.
Compo adapts a pretrained image-editing model to interpret Spatial Canvas inputs in direct and agentic generation modes.
An automated supervision pipeline supports training across binding types and their combinations without building a specialized poster generator from scratch.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a spatial canvas interface for poster generation, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: From Prompting to Composing: A Spatial Canvas Interface for Poster Generation
papers.tldr: Compo replaces one-dimensional text prompting with a spatial canvas for more controllable, high-quality poster generation.

papers.abstract: In text-guided image editing, describing the desired change is often straightforward, but identifying the intended object or region can be cumbersome, especially when several objects look alike. We introduce a new image editing interface that lets users place spatial marks and optional short notes directly on the image. Together, these annotations form a canvas instruction that specifies where to edit and what to change. Our editor, VibeEdit, follows these instructions to perform object addition, removal, replacement, attribute modification, and movement without a separate text prompt. We construct 1.55 million source-target edit pairs with object masks and structured edit descriptions, from which we render canvas instructions during training. We adapt Qwen-Image-Edit with layer-decoupled conditioning that separately encodes source images and canvas instructions for image editing. We train the model with region-weighted supervised fine-tuning, followed by rubric-guided reinforcement learning to improve edit completion, local edit quality, and preservation of unedited regions. We evaluate VibeEdit on an independently constructed, human-curated benchmark of 419 cases emphasizing target selection among similar objects. VibeEdit achieves a VLM rubric score of 79.9 and an outside-region PSNR of 32.8 dB, compared with 67.4 and 24.0 dB for FireRed, the highest-scoring text-instructed baseline in our evaluation.
authors: Jinjing Zhao, Fangyun Wei, Yitong Wang, Xiuyu Wu, Yunuo Chen, Yang Yue, Sirui Zhang, Wenbo Wang, Hongyang Zhang, Dong Chen, Yan Lu, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses ambiguous target selection when multiple similar objects appear in an image.
Supports adding, removing, replacing, modifying, and moving objects through canvas instructions.
Trains a Qwen-Image-Edit-based model with separate source-image and canvas-instruction conditioning, region-weighted fine-tuning, and rubric-guided reinforcement learning.
On a 419-case human-curated benchmark, VibeEdit scores 79.9 on a VLM rubric and 32.8 dB outside-region PSNR, outperforming the reported text-instructed baseline.

papers.title: VibeEdit: Image Editing with Canvas Instructions
papers.tldr: VibeEdit enables precise text-free image editing by combining spatial marks with optional brief notes on the canvas.

papers.abstract: Electromagnetic spectrum monitoring increasingly requires flexible analysis beyond task-specific recognition and detection. Multimodal large language models offer a unified interface, but extending vision-language models (VLMs) to raw I/Q signals requires tokenization that balances fidelity against a strict budget. For signals, dense encoding causes token costs to grow with observation length, whereas fixed-resolution compression may discard short-duration or localized signal evidence. Thus, we propose \textbf{BATok}, a budget-adaptive signal tokenizer that adjusts token capacity to the input length while allocating that capacity according to the signal content. BATok constructs candidate representations from signal-derived features using lightweight multi-resolution branches, then combines a local energy prior with learnable queries to resample these representations into compact signal tokens. The number of tokens adapts to the input length while remaining strictly bounded. The resulting tokens are projected into the language embedding space of VLMs. We further introduce \textbf{EMSpec-Instruct}, a multimodal instruction dataset aligning raw I/Q signals, waterfall images, and language supervision for modulation recognition, structured detection, and language-conditioned signal grounding. Experiments show that BATok learns effective signal representations and achieves competitive performance across all tasks.
authors: Lei Zhai, Zhihao Chang, Shuyuan Yang, Zhixi Feng
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between dense signal encoding costs and fixed-resolution compression that can lose localized evidence.
Uses lightweight multi-resolution signal features, a local energy prior, and learnable queries to resample inputs into compact tokens.
Projects the resulting signal tokens into the VLM language-embedding space for multimodal instruction following.
Introduces EMSpec-Instruct, an instruction dataset pairing raw I/Q signals, waterfall images, and language supervision.
Reports competitive performance in modulation recognition, structured detection, and language-conditioned signal grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Extends VLMs to raw signal modality with budget-adaptive tokenization and instruction data, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Instruction-Conditioned Electromagnetic Spectrum Understanding via Budget-Adaptive Signal Tokenization
papers.tldr: BATok enables VLMs to understand raw I/Q signals by adaptively allocating a bounded number of content-aware tokens based on signal length and structure.

papers.abstract: Processing long visual token sequences from high-resolution images makes multi-step reasoning computationally expensive for multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Existing one-shot pruning and aggregation methods compress visual tokens into a fixed context before decoding. However, visual evidence needs can shift as reasoning unfolds, making it difficult for a fixed compressed context to retain all the details needed across stages. To address this challenge, we propose ViMoD, a lightweight framework that maintains a compact visual context while preserving access to original fine-grained evidence as reasoning needs evolve. Deformable Aggregation of Region-wise Tokens (DART) learns content-adaptive groups and aggregation capacities, constructing compact Coarse representations linked to recoverable original Fine tokens. Temporal Routing for Adaptive Contextual Evidence (TRACE) integrates decoding history to anticipate upcoming evidence needs and select, retain, or replace active Fine-token groups. Selected Fine tokens augment the persistent Coarse context in the frozen backbone, enabling stage-specific evidence access without continuously attending to all visual tokens. On Qwen3-VL-4B, ViMoD outperforms all evaluated baselines on all eight reasoning benchmarks at a 20% target visual token budget, improving the mean normalized score by 39.0% over the strongest evaluated one-shot baseline. These gains are achieved with only 0.0546% additional trainable parameters relative to the frozen backbone.
authors: Yicheng Xue, Han Wu, Jufeng Yang, Minjing Dong, Xinghao Chen, Hanting Chen, Jianyuan Guo
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed one-shot visual-token compression for multi-step reasoning.
